title: IMF Expands Aid Package for Argentina -- Update
text:
By Jeffrey T. Lewis and Ryan Dube 

The International Monetary Fund agreed to boost its bailout package signed with Argentina in June, providing additional financial support and accelerating the disbursement of funds as the administration of embattled President Mauricio Macri confronts market turbulence and social unrest.

Argentina Finance Minister Nicolas Dujovne and IMF Managing Director Christine Lagarde said Wednesday that the new agreement will increase the bailout size by almost 15% to $57.1 billion, providing an extra $19 billion in financing through the end of 2019, when Mr. Macri's term ends. It commits Argentina to maintaining a floating exchange-rate regime without intervention.

"The Fund remains fully committed to helping Argentina tackle the problems that it faces," Ms. Lagarde said during a joint news conference with Mr. Dujovne in New York.

The deal seeks to address concerns about the country's ability to service its rising debt load and secure funds to cover government spending.

"This will permit our country to leave behind the path of turbulence we've been exposed to recently and return the Argentine economy to the structural conditions we need for stable growth," Mr. Dujovne said.

The deal still needs to be approved by the IMF's board to take effect.

The expanded program will aim to reduce the country's double-digit inflation by replacing inflation targets with monetary base goals to contain the money supply, the IMF said. It also will require the central bank to maintain its high interest rate, which was increased to 60% in August.

The IMF added that the central bank will be able to conduct limited intervention in the foreign-exchange market only if there is "extreme overshooting of the exchange rate."

The central bank won't intervene in the exchange market when the exchange rate is between 34 pesos and 44 pesos to the U.S. dollar, Argentina's new central bank president Guido Sandleris said later on Wednesday. The peso closed weaker Wednesday at 38.52 to the dollar.

Mr. Macri was forced to ask the IMF for help earlier this year, after rising interest rates in the U.S. pummeled the peso and investors sold assets in emerging markets. But the aid package failed to contain the peso's steady weakening, forcing the government in August to ask for more IMF funds and faster disbursements. The Argentine currency has lost half of its value against the dollar so far this year.

"I don't imagine Argentina will be able to tap external markets again very soon, after all they're going to have a very deep recession, high inflation, uncertainty about the election next year, so there are still a lot of fundamental questions about how stable the macro situation is going to be," said Gustavo Rangel, Latin America's chief economist for ING. "It will take some time for them to really be able to access the market again."

Mr. Dujovne then announced austerity measures in early September, including deep cuts to subsidies and public works as part of an effort to balance a wide budget shortfall and meet IMF conditions.

The IMF deal comes a day after Argentina's central bank president, Luis Caputo, unexpectedly resigned less than four months into the job amid reports of disputes with the fund over the bank's exchange rate policy. Under Mr. Caputo, the central bank intervened in the foreign-exchange market, burning billions of dollars in reserves to contain the peso selloff. The IMF objected to that, backing a free-floating currency.

He was replaced by Mr. Sandleris, a top Finance Ministry official who was educated at Columbia University. On Tuesday, Mr. Sandleris said the central bank's main objective is to reduce inflation, currently at 34%.

Mr. Sandleris said at a press conference that the central institution will ensure zero nominal growth in the monetary base -- bills and coins in circulation and banks' deposits at the central bank -- between now and next June in its effort to bring inflation down, which he added implies a significant monetary contraction.

Argentina's economy contracted 2.7% in July from the year-earlier month as the country's financial crisis hit consumer demand. In the second quarter, the economy fell 4.2% from a year earlier.

The economic crisis has rattled Mr. Macri's administration as it faces growing anger among Argentines upset with the sharp contraction and high inflation. On Tuesday, Argentina's powerful unions held a national strike, warning that it would increase protests if the government doesn't reverse austerity measures.

"If there isn't a plan B, there won't be a truce with Argentina's union movement," said union leader Juan Carlos Schmid.

After taking office in late 2015, Mr. Macri had hoped to avoid social upheaval by gradually unraveling his predecessor's free-spending policies rather than implementing the kind of economic shock therapies that sparked unrest and led to the downfall of previous presidents. His government relied heavily on foreign credit to plug the deficit, raising concerns among economists as the cost of servicing the debt now increases due to the weaker peso.

Argentina's debt ratio will reach 84% of gross domestic product by the end of the year, compared with 57% a year earlier, consultancy Oxford Economics said this week. "Argentina's debt-to-GDP ratio is rising at an unsustainable pace," the firm said.

Write to Jeffrey T. Lewis at jeffrey.lewis@wsj.com and Ryan Dube at ryan.dube@dowjones.com

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

title: Argentina  Central Bank  to Sell Up to $150M If Peso Breaches 'Non- Intervention  Zone' -- Market Talk
text:
2255 GMT [Dow Jones}--Argentina's central bank says it will stop intervening in the foreign-exchange market when the exchange rate is between 34 pesos to 44 pesos to the US dollar. But if it breaches the upper limit of the so-called "non-intervention zone," central bank president Guido Sandleris says the monetary authority will sell up to $150M to shore up the peso, which has depreciated sharply this year. The change in policy comes as the IMF agreed to increase its bailout program for Argentina, after objecting to the central bank's FX interventions while calling for a free-floating currency. title: Argentina  Central Bank  Sees Inflation Declining on New Policies -- Market Talk
text:
2230 GMT [Dow Jones] -- Argentina's central bank president, Guido Sandleris, says it could take a few months for inflation to start declining after the monetary authority scrapped inflation targets in favor of monetary base goals to contain the supply of money. "We are attacking the root cause of inflation," Sandleris says. "The objective is that it will decline as fast as possible." The change in policy comes as the IMF boosted its bailout package for Argentina to $57.1B from $50B. The central bank also committed to not intervene in the exchange market when the exchange rate is between 34 pesos to 44 pesos to the USD, Sandleris says. Argentina's interventions were a cause of conflict with the IMF, which supports a free-floating currency. (ryan.dube@wsj.com; @duberyan)

title: New president of Central Argentina is aligned with IMF policy
text:
Advocates of a new agreement, Argentine President Mauricio Macri and IMF Managing Director Christine Lagarde dined in New York on Monday night. Only it was enough that twelve hours of the meeting happened so that the resignation was made public Luis Caputo to the headquarters of the Central Bank of Argentina (BCRA), that during its short management incessantly intervened the market to avoid that the dollar rose, without success nor endorsement of the Background. In his place comes Guido Sandleris, closer to the vision of the multilateral organization and defender of the exchange rate float.

Although it is a country accustomed to changes in the head of the Central - only one president has finished his term in 83 years of history and the previous one, Federico Sturzenegger, resigned just three months ago - the news did not fall well in the market. Today, the dollar reached around $ 40 Argentine pesos and although it moderated its fall during the day, closing at $ 38.2 was the most depreciated currency in the world.

The "personal reasons" with which BCRA justified the departure of Caputo did not convince. According to Marcos Buscaglia, founding partner of Alberdi Partners and former chief economist of Bank of America, "Caputo wanted more firepower to intervene in the exchange market, there was even talk of implementing a system of exchange bands, as Chile had in the nineties, But the IMF is looking for something else, a floating exchange rate. "

Also in conversation with La Tercera , Martin Alfie, chief economist of Radar Consultora, argues that "the IMF with its conditions already took two presidents of the Central Bank (...) It is a total loss of sovereignty of the management of exchange policy."

Indeed, until today the main advisor of the Ministry of Finance, Guido Sandleris is a declared defender of the model that currently operates in our country. "Having a floating exchange rate has its cost, which is to lower inflation slower, but adjust to external shocks and cushion the impacts on the economy," he told Infobae in May.

Today, the new monetary authority, said in a brief statement that "the main objective of the Central Bank is to reduce inflation." But although he wants to turn the page, without a new agreement with the IMF on the table, the debate continues. "A floating exchange rate can work in developed economies or emerging markets with a long history of stability, but not in Argentina. I think the idea of ??having bands is better, "said Matías Carugati, chief economist at Argentine consultancy Management & Fit.

The entry New president of Central Argentina is aligned with IMF policy was first published in La Tercera.

title: UPDATE 5- Argentina  peso firms as  central bank intervenes , IMF voices support
text:
(Adds S&P negative credit outlook, paragraphs 4, 15-16)

By Scott Squires and Jorge Otaola

BUENOS AIRES, Aug 31 (Reuters) - Argentina's beleaguered peso bounced back slightly on Friday after the central bank auctioned $250 million in dollar reserves and the International Monetary Fund issued a strong statement of support for President Mauricio Macri's government.

But with frustration rising over inflation of more than 30 percent and austerity measures required under a $50 billion IMF standby deal, Agriculture Ministry employees protested budget cutbacks and members of the opposition Citizens' Unity party called for countrywide marches against Macri Friday evening.

The party's leader, former President Cristina Fernandez, a proponent of government intervention in the economy, may run against Macri for president next year, raising further questions about the country's economic prospects. She has, however, been tarred by a graft scandal marked by the jailing of several former officials.

Macri is caught between voters tired of fiscal belt-tightening measures already implemented and investor pressure to unveil further spending cuts. Ratings agency S&P said it revised its outlook on Argentina to negative from stable due to risks that the government may not be able to implement its economic plan.

"We lost our jobs because of the government's orthodox, fundamentalist policies," said Jorge Harvez, 63, an office worker with the agriculture ministry who was fired on Thursday.

One of about 250 protesters blocking traffic in front of the ministry's main office in Buenos Aires, Harvez blamed layoffs on the austerity push.

"We will continue blocking the streets until we force the ministers to negotiate with us," he said.

A spokesman said the Agriculture Ministry had laid off 548 people, most in a division that assists small-scale farmers, "to make more efficient use of state resources."

UNPOPULAR IMF

Many Argentines blame the IMF for budget cuts that plunged millions into poverty during the 2001-02 economic crisis.

The peso strengthened 6.08 percent on Friday to close at 37 to the dollar after the central bank said it would auction $675 million in foreign reserves. On balance the currency lost 25.89 percent against the greenback in August and 49.59 percent so far this year.

It lost 20 percent on Wednesday and Thursday alone after Macri said he would ask the IMF to advance disbursements under a $50 billion financing deal. The announcement raised alarms among investors that Argentina might be hard pressed to fund its 2019 deficit.

"Argentina has the full support of the Fund and we are confident that the strong commitment and determination of the Argentine authorities will help the country overcome the current difficulties," IMF spokesman Gerry Rice said in a statement.

The statement helped the peso stabilize, at least temporarily, said Ignacio Labaqui, an analyst for New York consultancy Medley Global Advisors.

"IMF support is definitely helpful at this stage," he said.

In its statement, S&P said it maintained its credit rating for Argentina at B+ - several notches below investment grade - because Macri's commitment to austerity measures should help sustain investor confidence. But it said the recent depreciation in the peso threatened to keep inflation high.

SPENDING CUTS

The government is expected to announce a policy package containing further spending cuts. But more belt tightening will meet strong opposition, as discontent with Macri grows over high inflation, a weak economy and subsidy cuts that have jacked up household heating and water bills.

With more austerity on the way, and utility prices set to rise again in the fourth quarter, low and middle income Argentines are hard-pressed to pay household costs. Yet the IMF and investors want more fiscal tightening.

"If the government fails to deliver a convincing austerity package, the peso will probably slide further and another large interest rate hike would be likely," consultancy Capital Economics said in a research note.

The central bank has already hiked its monetary policy rate to 60 percent.

IMF Managing Director Christine Lagarde and Finance Minister Nicolas Dujovne were scheduled to meet on Tuesday "to advance the dialogue," Rice said.

Speaking to reporters on Thursday night, Dujovne said the government would announce new economic measures on Monday, and would target a 2019 primary fiscal deficit below the 1.3 percent of gross domestic product agreed with the IMF. (Additional reporting by Hugh Bronstein, Luc Cohen, Gabriel Burin and Rodrigo Campos in New York Editing by Leslie Adler, Steve Orlofsky and David Gregorio)

title: UPDATE 10-IMF studying Argentina request for early help as peso crashes
text:
* Peso suffers biggest one-day slide in almost three years

* Markets fret about Argentina's ability to pay its debt next year

* Central bank intervenes but fails to stop peso's fall

* Unions denounce fiscal belt-tightening but more cuts planned (Recasts with IMF response)

By Hugh Bronstein and Jorge Otaola

BUENOS AIRES, Aug 29 (Reuters) - The International Monetary Fund said it was studying a request from Argentina to speed up disbursement of a $50 billion loan program after a collapse in investor confidence in President Mauricio Macri's government sent the peso tumbling more than 7 percent on Wednesday.

It was the biggest one-day decline in the peso since the currency was allowed to float in December 2015. It closed at a record low of 34.10 per U.S. dollar and is down more than 45.3 percent against the greenback this year, prompting massive central bank interventions.

Nerves are frayed in Latin America's No. 3 economy as it struggles to break free from its notorious cycle of once-a-decade financial crises. The last one, which was punctuated by a 2002 debt default, tossed millions of middle-class Argentines into poverty.

The run on the peso prompted Argentina to turn to the IMF for the $50 billion credit line earlier this year. As part of the deal, Argentina's government pledged to speed up plans to reduce the fiscal deficit.

But given the peso's continued depreciation, which makes the country's dollar-denominated debts more expensive to pay, investors are increasingly concerned that the IMF help may not be enough.

"We have agreed with the International Monetary Fund to advance all the necessary funds to guarantee compliance with the financial program next year," Macri said in a televised address on Wednesday. "This decision aims to eliminate any uncertainty."

"Over the last week we have seen new expressions of lack of confidence in the markets, specifically over our financing capacity in 2019," Macri said.

IMF Managing Director Christine Lagarde responded by saying in a statement that the multi-lateral lender's staff would "reexamine the phasing of the financial program." She said that the "more adverse international market conditions" had not been "fully anticipated" when the IMF and Argentina reached the deal in June.

"Authorities will be working to revise the government's economic plan with a focus on better insulating Argentina from the recent shifts in global financial markets, including through stronger monetary and fiscal policies," Lagarde said.

Argentina has $24.9 billion in peso- and foreign currency-denominated debt payments due next year, according to official data.

Speaking to reporters after the IMF statement was issued, Treasury Minister Nicolas Dujovne said the government would reduce the size of its financing program, but did not provide specifics

UNION TO PROTEST BELT-TIGHTENING

If Macri was trying to calm investors, it did not work.

"The market is saying: 'Just the fact that you are engaging in this conversation makes me very, very nervous,'" Daniel Osorio, president of New York-based consultancy Andean Capital Advisors, said in a telephone interview.

The peso's decline has contributed to a jump in inflation, which hit a 12-month rate of 31.2 percent in July. In response, the central bank has hiked interest rates to 45 percent and sold more than $13 billion in reserves, including $300 million in an auction on Wednesday.

All that, combined with the budget cuts promised to the IMF that will slow down public works projects, is contributing to a recession that will result in an economic contraction of 1 percent this year, according to the government. That could hurt Macri's re-election prospects in next year's presidential race.

The June signing of the IMF deal reduced the need for costly bond market funding and briefly steadied the peso. The government has since announced more than $2 billion in budget savings, a process Macri promised to continue.

"We will accompany the IMF support with all necessary fiscal efforts," said Macri, who was elected in 2015 on a free market platform after eight years of deep government intervention in the economy under previous President Cristina Fernandez.

Argentina's biggest labor group, the CGT, said on Wednesday it will call a 24-hour general strike on Sept. 25 to protest Macri's belt-tightening measures. Two smaller union groupings said they will go on a 36-hour strike on Sept. 24 to protest the IMF, which many blame for the 2002 crisis.

"I know that these tumultuous situations generate anxiety among many of you," Macri said. "I understand this, and I want you to know I am making all decisions necessary to protect you." (Reporting by Hugh Bronstein and Jorge Otaola Additional reporting by Luc Cohen and Scott Squires; Editing by Alistair Bell and Leslie Adler)

title: Emerging Markets Fight Back Against  Currency  Slides -- Market Talk
text:
1019 ET - Emerging-market central banks are tapping a roughly $6 trillion stash of foreign reserves as they struggle to contain deepening currency declines. Emerging-market central banks used roughly $57 billion in foreign reserves in June, according to preliminary forecasts from research firm Exante Data, which would rank as the largest monthly intervention since late 2016. Central banks in Brazil, India and Argentina have been actively intervening in currency markets in recent months, but their efforts have had mixed results. The Brazilian real is down 14% against the dollar this year, while the rupee is down 7% and the Argentine peso is down 34%. (chelsey.dulaney@wsj.com; @chelseydulaney)

0953 ET - The resignation of the U.K. minister responsible for overseeing the U.K.'s plan to quit the EU has increased the chances of Britain crashing out of the bloc or delaying the country's exit, says Daiwa Capital Markets. "The UK government looks to be in chaos," says Daiwa's Chris Scicluna . "Even if May continues to hold her position as PM, the noises from David Davis and key Brexiter backbenchers strongly suggest she would now fail to force through Parliament any final withdrawal agreement - which, even if it were based on Friday's Cabinet agreement, would still likely require further concessions to be made to Brussels. So the likelihood of a no-deal Brexit or Article 50 extension, and/or a new UK general election, all look to have increased." (philip.waller@wsj.com)

0950 ET - The U.K. is going to ask the European Union for the chance to stay in the single market for goods and agriculture, and to apply different tariffs to the EU . Where tariff rates differ, the U.K. would collect fees on the EU 's behalf. ING says "the EU will almost certainly say no" to these proposals. There could be practical issues of the U.K. collecting potentially higher EU tariffs. There are also concerns that different tariffs "could encourage smuggling." And the thought of a third country collecting EU tariffs is "reportedly unpopular in Brussels." Moreover, if the U.K. stays in the single market could be seen as cherrypicking and the EU "is worried that other countries could seek similar concessions." (olga.cotaga@wsj.com; @OlgaCotaga)

0943 ET - US government bonds fall as the market prepares for the Treasury's scheduled auctions of three-, 10- and 30-year debt this week. The auctions follow Friday's Labor Department report which showed that the economy continues to add jobs at a steady clip, yet without producing the kind of pressure for higher wages that many economists have been expecting given the tight labor market. The yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury note rose to 2.858% from 2.831% Friday. (daniel.kruger@wsj.com)

0939 ET - An acceleration in U.S. core inflation may feed through into eurozone government bonds, causing their yields to rise, even if there is no sign of eurozone core inflation picking up through the summer, Julien-Pierre Nouen, chief economist at Lazard Frères Gestion, tells Dow Jones Newswires in an interview. "We could have a second-round effect from what happens in the U.S.," Mr. Nouen says, referring to U.S. core inflation having reached the Federal Reserve 's 2% target. If core inflation increases again, it may make the Fed more inclined to raise interest rates further, lifting yields. This may in turn have a contagion effect on European government bond yields, he says. U.S. core price inflation, which the Fed follows closely, rose 2% on the year in May, Commerce Department data released end-June showed.(emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha)

0938 ET - Improving purchasing managers' surveys on eurozone economic activity suggest long-term government bond yields in the region have potential to rise, Julien-Pierre Nouen, chief economist at Lazard Frères Gestion, tells Dow Jones Newswires in an interview. "We think PMI data play a large part in the moves of long-term bond yields," Mr. Nouen says. "If there is a sign of economic rebound, with better PMI indices in the summer, it could lead to bond yields going higher," Mr. Nouen says. In 2018, the German 10-year Bund yield peaked in early February at around 0.77%, when the release of PMI data for January showed a peak for January, he says. (emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha)

0938 ET - Economic models show that trade tariffs announced by the U.S. so far may not have much impact on growth but the effect on financial market sentiment will be important, Julien-Pierre Nouen, chief economist at Lazard Frères Gestion, tells Dow Jones Newswires in an interview. Some surveys have shown that companies are starting to worry, which "may lead to some delay in capital expenditures," Mr. Nouen says. Trade tensions have come at a time when global growth is good, so the impact could be like putting sand into the machine: not enough to stop it but possibly causing a little slowdown in growth. "But if things escalate, we could have a bigger impact," Mr. Nouen says. (emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha)

0937 ET - In light of the Italian government's fiscal expansion plans, investors will be keeping a close eye on Italy's upcoming rating reviews, given the possibility of potential downgrades for the country, Julien-Pierre Nouen, chief economist at Lazard Frères Gestion, tells Dow Jones Newswires in an interview. "The question is obviously how the budget will go down with the European Commission and how it will go down with the rating agencies," Mr. Nouen says. DBRS is scheduled to review Italy on July 13, followed by Fitch Ratings on Aug. 31 and Moody's Investors Service on Sept. 7 and S&P Global Ratings on Oct. 26. (emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha)

0937 ET - Market fears over Italy's populist government have calmed for now, but investors remain wary over its plans for sizeable fiscal spending and these concerns could return to haunt markets in the autumn, says Julien-Pierre Nouen, chief economist at Lazard Frères Gestion. "I wouldn't say the market isn't worried," he tells Dow Jones Newswires in an interview. The 10-year Italian-German bond spread is still around 240 basis points, "still significant" and well above its pre-election levels, Mr. Nouen says. The 10-year Italian-German spread stood at 139 basis points on the last trading day before the March 4 election. While the Italian government clarified that it doesn't want to exit the euro, the budget is a concern given that "Italy has very little fiscal space," with a debt-to-GDP ratio around 130% and a "very low" trend growth level, Mr. Nouen says. (emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha)

0936 ET - The European Central Bank 's forward guidance that it will keep interest rates at present levels at least through summer 2019 and its commitment to reinvest maturing bonds may further encourage eurozone countries to issues ultra-long government bonds, Julien-Pierre Nouen, chief economist at Lazard Frères Gestion, tells Dow Jones Newswires in an interview. Ultra-long bonds have a maturity of 15 years or longer. "We think the ECB will buy a significant part of its portfolio in long-term bonds," Mr. Nouen says. "These reinvestments will keep yields at a low level, it will make issuance at long maturities still interesting." Ultra-long government bond issuance in the eurozone has mushroomed in recent years as the European Central Bank 's asset purchase program led to cheap funding.(emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha)

0936 ET - The seasonal slowdown of government bond issuance in the eurozone in the summer is typically supportive of bond valuations. However, the seasonal pick-up of supply in the autumn is unlikely to weigh on bond prices significantly, Julien-Pierre Nouen, chief economist at Lazard Frères Gestion, tells Dow Jones Newswires in an interview. Valuations shouldn't be impacted "because supply will be in line with what has been forecast at the beginning of the year," Mr. Nouen says. There is a little growth shortfall in the eurozone but that won't necessarily lead to a bigger deficit than currently forecast, Mr. Nouen says. The European Central Bank 's EUR45 billion asset purchase in 4Q and the prospect of EUR180 billion reinvestment in 2019 are "quite significant," Mr. Nouen says. (emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha)

0922 ET - A fall towards the June 14 low of 1.1563 in EUR/USD, the day of the last European Central Bank meeting, could happen, says Societe Generale , but it will depend "on whether the return to calm waters for the remnibi and Chinese equity markets can endure." Also, it will depend on "how emerging market currencies respond to whether the U.S. moves ahead with the second tranche of trade tariffs." The remnibi has been falling massively on the past days, dragging down other emerging market currencies and pushing the dollar up. But most of the EM currencies are up against the dollar on Monday. For now, EUR/USD "almost entirely" recovered the losses of June 14, last trading up 0.3% at 1.1778 on Monday. (olga.cotaga@wsj.com; @OlgaCotaga)

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

title: The dollar exceeded $ 29 and bonds and shares were also hit
text:
The value of the marked a new record yesterday in the local place when surpassing the $ 29 for the sale to the public (it closed to $ 29.57 in average) after brushing the $ 30 in a day in which the market seemed to want to remind the Government that the run It did not end and that the distrust towards the future of the economy is growing.

Two tests: one, the new fall of 3% that the Buenosairean Stock Exchange scored (going against the rest of the stock exchanges) to raise to 14% its losses in the week despite its recent requalification. The other, the 2.3% slippage in the bonds of the Argentine debt most operated abroad, which increased its yield to 9.5% and boosted the country risk to 613 points, its highest level in three years.

The nominal maximum for the exchange rate, which led the devaluation to 3.1% on the day and increased it to 15.8% in the month, to 42% in the two-month period and to 52.5% in the same period 2018, confirms that the peso is today the most depreciated currency in the world. Its collapse yesterday was recorded in a day that showed the dollar stable against other emerging currencies, but weakened against similar ones: it fell 0.9% according to the Dollar Index, a parameter that measures it against the euro, the yen, the pound , the Canadian dollar, the Swedish krona and the Swiss franc.

And it was also verified at the end of a round where the Central Bank (BCRA) again intervened the square after several days of not doing so to try to defend its value, reinforcing the usual supply of foreign currency that the Treasury has made since it received IMF funds to obtain pesos to cover its deficit and, at the same time, provide liquidity to a market that came to this situation due to a marked imbalance between supply and demand of foreign currency.

Everything confirms that, although the change of global climate complicates, the crisis here does not stop due to domestic issues. "Argentina is being more punished than other countries and it's because of local issues," said economist and former finance minister Daniel Marx to explain the impact on the real economy.

"It's true that not only does the peso fall in. The problem is that our currency falls at a faster rate and does not stop accelerating," observes economist Alejandro Minteguiaga. "But in a rarefied global context, with soybeans falling and the level reached by the twin deficits of Argentina, it must be clear that intervening in the exchange market is like paddling in dulce de leche," he says.

His colleague and consultant Alejandro Bonavita appeals to a graphic image to explain the situation: "The world lit a lighter when we were drizzled with naphtha," he says. "Given this, the only local plan is to tender the dollars provided by the IMF, it is not enough, Argentina needs dollars and you do not see the capacity to generate them: that makes the outsiders go to dollars to go and the locals buy them because they see that the peso does not pay them and promises to pay even less, "he says, alluding to the impulse that the devaluation gives to inflation.

"This shows that the oxygenation that the Government had obtained with the changes in the BCRA did not imply a change in expectations as it seems that they expected," said CeSur economist Amílcar Collante.

"The government once again relied on a market that reads the agreement with the IMF as unenforceable for an administration that aspires to have chances in 2019. That is, investors are not believing in an adjustment that orders the accounts", explained Martín Alfie , from the consultancy Radar. At the same time, Guido Lorenzo, ACM economist, corroborates that "the bullfight did not happen, it was crouched".

"You have to check recipes because theRate hike was not effective and auctions did not either. And if not, what remains to be known is what kind of change is perceived as expensive by the market: it was not the $ 25 of Sturzenegger and now it seems that that value ran above $ 30, "he continued.

The concrete thing was that the new jump of the dollar was registered in a wheel of greater movement (US $ 1017 million were operated) due to the maturity of futures, which was significant because the BCRA helped this month to expand its volume when it returned to operate ( at a loss) those instruments after almost 3 years of abstinence. That derived pesos from that spot to cash and added pressure to the dollar. "The reaction was erratic in principle, with just US $ 5 million operated, the dollar had gone up a peso, I understand that they are supporters of the flotation, but you can not let them create a problem with such a small amount that later it costs you a lot. more to disarm, "objected financial analyst Christian Buteler.

The entity decided to intervene after noon when the ticket had already taken flight: offered to sell US $ 300 million, when in the system were charged purchase positions for a similar amount. This helped the price of the ticket, which had reached a maximum of $ 29.45 at the wholesale level (came close to $ 28.10), began to converge towards the value of $ 28.9567 that arose in that auction (made after the Treasury sold the US $ 150 million it had planned at $ 29.12) and continued to go back further until the end of the day at $ 28.85.

In the BCRA they celebrated the result of this intervention because their idea is not to impose prices, but to dose market trends. "The problem is that the day before yesterday the biggest sale of the Treasury was read in response to a requirement of the BCRA to try to control the dollar and it was not like that: they sold more because they need more pesos for the payment of bonuses, but without breaching the parameters set in the agreement with the IMF, which proposed this mechanism since other countries had already used it successfully to finance the State in a context in which they wanted to help balance the market at the same time ", they explained in the BCRA.

title: Argentina  says IMF OK with  currency interventions
text:
BUENOS AIRES, June 15 (Reuters) - Argentina's Treasury and Finance Minister Nicolas Dujovne said on Friday the central bank could intervene in the spot market if needed under the country's agreement with the International Monetary Fund and that the central bank would start reducing short-term Lebac securities that have increased volatility.

"We have ratified it with the Fund. We have a floating system in which the central bank can intervene," Dujovne told a news conference a day after Central Bank President Federico Sturzenegger resigned after the peso weakened over six percent in a day.

Former Finance Minister Luis Caputo is taking over the central bank presidency and Dujovne will serve as finance minister as well as treasury minister. (Reporting by Caroline Stauffer Editing by Chizu Nomiyama)

title: ARGENTINA: Government To Announce Sale Program Of Up To US$ 7.5 Billion
text:
The Argentinean government is expected to announce soon a sale program of up to US$ 7.5 billion as part of the agreement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for budget support, said the Ministry of Finance in a press release. The move comes in the context of renewed interventions by Argentina's Central Bank (BCRA) in the foreign exchange market after launching a policy of FX floatation last Friday."The program should consist of pre-announced daily sales that should be executed through an auction mechanism carried out by the BCRA at the request of the Treasury," said the ministry, without giving details on the program.The BCRA again intervened on Tuesday with a selling participation of US$ 695 million for the first time after the agreement with the IMF and with the dollar operating a "free market" to interrupt an unchecked rise of the U.S.

currency before the arrival of a first tranche of the US$ 50 billion that the government requested from the Fund.Earlier, the managing director of the IMF, Christine Lagarde, endorsed the plan presented by the Mauricio Macri administration to close the stand-by agreement. However, the request still needs the approval of the Executive Board of the Fund. The idea is that the financing would be released on June 20, as requested by the Argentinean government.According to the IMF statement, the Argentinean government requested that one-third of this support be disbursed with the approval of the program and that half of that amount (US$ 7.5 billion) be available for budget support.

title: Argentine peso picks up after  Central Bank intervention
text:
The Argentine peso led gains among emerging market currencies on Tuesday after it was said that the central bank sold dollars to shore up the currency after falling to a record low this week.

The peso appreciated 0.8% to 25.84 per dollar at noon on Tuesday after two loss sessions. Argentina's central bank would have intervened in the currency markets on Tuesday for the first time since the announcement last week of a US $ 50 billion credit line from the International Monetary Fund.

Despite today's gains, the peso has lost almost 28% of its value so far this year, making it the currency with the worst performance in emerging markets.

As part of the agreement with the Fund, Central Bank President Federico Sturzenegger said last week that he would intervene less in the currency markets after three weeks of keeping the peso below 25 per dollar.

The Central will announce a decision on its key interest rate at 5 pm Buenos Aires time. It is expected to maintain its benchmark rate at 40 percent, according to a Bloomberg survey of 21 analysts.

The Argentine peso entry rebounds after intervention by the Central Bank was first published in La Tercera.

title: The dollar surpassed a new barrier in  Argentina
text:
Without the intervention of the Central Bank, which anticipated that it abandoned the inflation guidelines for this year and would let the dollar float to the beat of the market, the US currency increased 48 cents. According to the average made by the monetary authority, the currency traded at 25.04 pesos for the purchase and 26.01 pesos for the sale.

One day after the announcement of the agreement with the IMF and in the first round since May 14 without a bid of the Central Bank of 5000 million dollars, the currency was re-shot. The determination of the body led by Federico Sturzenegger was in line with what was announced last night, when he stressed that he would resume the exchange rate float and intervene only in an eventual manner.

In the parallel market, according to the survey carried out daily by ambito.com, the blue climbed 75 cents and reached 26.40 pesos.

It should be remembered that as Struzenegger and Finance Minister Nicolás Dujovne announced last night, the measures agreed to access the IMF loan include profound changes in the Central Bank's policy: a reform of its Charter to prohibit Treasury financing, measures additional to limit the monetary issue and a change in the composition of its liabilities to minimize the stock of Lebac.

title: UPDATE 1-EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil stocks slide, Mexico stocks and peso rise
text:
(Updates prices)
    SAO PAULO, June 8 (Reuters) - Brazilian equities extended
their recent slide amid political and fiscal worries on Friday,
while Mexican stocks and currency advanced.
    Stocks on the benchmark Bovespa stock index tumbled
across the board for a fourth straight session, as traders
continued to fret ahead of an unpredictable October election in
which market-friendly candidates have failed to gain traction,
according to recent polls.
    Recent government intervention in oil company Petroleo
Brasileiro SA has also caused traders to question the
resolve of the current government - and the ability of the next
one - to stay on a path of pro-market policies and relative
fiscal austerity.
    "It's still an uncertain scenario, without a positive
conclusion coming to light for local financial markets," said a
Rio de Janeiro-based trader.
    The Bovespa index was down 1.23 percent in late morning
trade, after falling almost 3 percent earlier in the session.
    After a punishing week for the Mexican peso, the currency
recovered on Friday, up 1.06 percent in afternoon trading.
Investors are closely watching the Group of Seven summit in
Canada and were encouraged by the fact that U.S. President
Donald Trump did not intensify his rhetoric on trade, analysts
said. 
    Mexico's benchmark index IPC was up 1.02 percent in
afternoon trading.
    In neighboring Argentina, the peso fell sharply
against the dollar after the country signed a $50 billion
standby financing arrangement with the International Monetary
Fund, causing the central bank to abandon its spirited defense
of the currency.
    "I think (the) USD/ARS upward trend should remain intact,"
said Win Thin, Global Head of Emerging Market Currency Strategy
at Brown Brothers Harriman in New York.
    "Once the IMF deal was reached in principle, I'm sure that
Argentina was asked to take FX intervention off the table. Last
thing the IMF wants to see is its program money burned away by
FX intervention."
    The Argentine peso was down 1.25 percent at 25.3 per dollar
in late afternoon trading.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil equities slide, cenbank props up  currency
text:
SAO PAULO, June 8 (Reuters) - Brazilian equities extended
their recent slide amid political and fiscal worries on Friday,
while the country's currency reversed losses as the central bank
pledged liquidity to help prop up the real.
    Stocks on the benchmark Bovespa stock index tumbled
across the board for a fourth straight session, as traders
continued to fret ahead of an unpredictable October election in
which market-friendly candidates have failed to gain traction,
according to recent polls.
    Recent government intervention in oil company Petroleo
Brasileiro SA has also caused traders to question the
resolve of the current government - and the ability of the next
one - to stay on a path of pro-market policies and relative
fiscal austerity.
    "It's still an uncertain scenario, without a positive
conclusion coming to light for local financial markets," said a
Rio de Janeiro-based trader.
    The Bovespa index was down 1.7 percent in late morning
trade, after falling almost 3 percent earlier in the session.
    Among the biggest losers on the index was food processor BRF
SA, which shed some 5.4 percent, after China said it
was slapping anti-dumping measures on Brazilian chicken.

    Shares in state-run electricity company Centrais Eletricas
Brasileiras SA, commonly known as Eletrobras, fell
5.3 percent amid ongoing setbacks to a privatization program
that now seems almost certain to be left to the next government.
    Preferred shares in Petrobras were down 4 percent after
analysts at UBS downgraded the state-controlled oil company to
"neutral" from "buy," saying the "phoenix ... (had fallen) back
down to the earth."
    Brazil's currency, however, jumped 3.4 percent on
Friday, rebounding from losses of up to 3 percent on Thursday
and 19 percent since February. 
    The currency was supported by multiple statements from
Brazilian central bank chief Ilan Goldfajn on Thursday and
Friday, saying that the bank would offer up to $20 billion in
currency swaps and ensure liquidity in the currency and interest
rate markets.
    In neighboring Argentina, the peso fell sharply
against the dollar after the country signed a $50 billion
standby financing arrangement with the International Monetary
Fund, causing the central bank to abandon its spirited defense
of the currency.
    "I think (the) USD/ARS upward trend should remain intact,"
said Win Thin, Global Head of Emerging Market Currency Strategy
at Brown Brothers Harriman in New York.
    "Once the IMF deal was reached in principle, I'm sure that
Argentina was asked to take FX intervention off the table. Last
thing the IMF wants to see is its program money burned away by
FX intervention, and so the peso needs to find its equilibrium
level somewhere north of 25."
    The Argentine peso was down 2 percent at 25.5 per dollar in
midday trade while the Mexican peso was down 0.4 percent at
20.56 per dollar.

title: ARGENTINA: Merval Climbs 4.55% On Expectations Of Agreement With IMF
text:
Merval, the main index of the Buenos Aires Stock Exchange, rose 4.55% to 30,359.26 points Tuesday, mainly driven by the shares of banks and energy companies. The good mood in the market is also related to the growing expectation for the signing of the agreement between Mauricio Macri's administration and the International Monetary Fund (IMF)."Although the figures have not yet been disclosed, the market is betting that Argentina could have access to a standby credit higher than the estimate," said Eduardo Fernandez, an analyst at Rava Bursatil.IMF's director for the Western Hemisphere Department, Alejandro Werner, said that "the negotiations are well advanced."The expectations are for the agreement to be signed in the coming days.The shares of Banco Francis (+11.76%), Distribuidora de Gas Cuyana (+9.41%), and Supervielle (+8.21%) rose sharply. The only company to close lower was Petrobras (-3.80%).Meanwhile, the locally traded U.S.

 dollar closed with a subtle drop of 0.04%, at 24.96 Argentinean pesos, with the Banco de la Nacien selling currency to avoid the USD rise in the local foreign exchange market, avoiding interventions by the Central Bank of Argentina (BCRA). The U.S. dollar keeps on rising amid expectations of an agreement between Argentina and the IMF.

title: The keys to understanding the financial crisis in Argentina
text:
For weeks, Argentines have watched anxiously how the peso falls against the dollar. The news that the liberal president Mauricio Macri seeks the help of the IMF revived old ghosts of crisis and painful adjustments. However, the government is committed to sending a reassuring message and ensures that Argentina is a solvent country. What led Argentina to the currency and financial crisis, and what does it need to conjure it? Lee: Moody's doubt Argentina crisis contagion to Latin America Chronic deficit Analysts agree that the main problem of the Argentine economy is its fiscal deficit (3.9% of GDP in 2017) and its trade balance (8,470 million dollars in 2017). For the past two and a half years Macri has been developing a program of adjustments considered "gradualist" that tries to bring the country from the protectionist model of the governments of Néstor and Cristina Kirchner (2003-2015) to one of openness.

 Among its first measures, it eliminated exchange control and negotiated with speculative funds to get the country out of default. This allowed him to finance the deficit with credits from abroad for amounts of about 30,000 million dollars per year. Lee: Central bank of Argentina performs strong intervention in foreign exchange market Ramiro Castiñeira, an analyst at the Econometric firm, argues that Macri "assumed a broken country, with great effort, he made progress, such as getting out of default, getting out of restrictions and recovering economic growth, but he could not resolve the structural: the deficit." Room for maneuver Many Argentines remember these days the economic and social crisis of 2001, which caused the fall of four presidents in a week and led the country to declare the largest default in history. And although there are similarities between the two moments, such as the accelerated depreciation of the peso and the request for help from the IMF, the experts stress that there are differences that grant a margin of maneuver to the Macri government. In 2001, the "1 to 1" rule was in effect, as was the case of the fixed-rate exchange rate policy of a peso equal to one dollar. Instead, at this time the floating exchange rate and the autonomous monetary policy "should facilitate an adjustment that prevents the currency crisis from escalating to a banking crisis and ending in an economic depression," according to Edward Glossop of Capital Economics.

"An autonomous monetary policy allows the Central Bank to increase interest rates to prop up capital flows, while at the same time weakening the currency would help stabilize, restore competitiveness and make local assets more attractive," he said. Glossop. Gradualism The motto of the Macri government has been "gradualism". That is, make adjustments little by little so as not to cause a social shock or a level of conflict that affects governance. Thus, it gradually eliminated subsidies to public services tariffs, opened the country to imports and reduced spending, but without achieving balance yet. The withdrawal of subsidies for services such as gas, electricity or water made, in some cases astronomically, the cost of households whose purchasing power is eaten by an inflation of more than 20% per year. We recommend: IMF support for Argentina is bad news, says former finance minister Marcos Peña, chief of the Cabinet, said: "We can not continue thinking that the fault lies with another, the fault of which we spend more than what we have is of the Argentines". Can you get out of the crisis? The government stresses that it went to the IMF toprevent a major crisis. Although the amount of aid that you will receive has not yet been defined, it is taken for granted that the multilateral entity will put some conditions. "The IMF is going to rethink gradualism," predicts Castiñeira. "Argentina must be aware of the situation in which it finds itself in order to make the necessary adjustment and not have to borrow abroad," he said. For Marina dal Poggetto, of EcoGo, "not depend on external credit requires a very violent adjustment, which is politically complicated." We recommend: How does the stand-by agreement that Argentina asks the IMF? Looking ahead to a 2019 marked by presidential elections and without a parliamentary majority, the task looks uphill.

title: Hundreds of Argentines protest against IMF rescue
text:
Several hundred people marched this Monday in the center of Buenos Aires against the "tarifazo ' in public services and that the Argentine government go to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in a day in which the dollar exceeded 25 pesos for sale. With phrases like "the worst is over, but the terrible is yet to come" or "we're going up, fuck, the change is coming", several demonstrators satirized the messages of the Executive, which calls for calm amid an unstoppable rise in prices of public services while the peso devalues ??and wages remain practically frozen. In view of this situation, Juan Carlos Schmid, one of the three secretaries of the General Confederation of Labor (CGT), presented his rejection of "the rate schedule", "the return to international financial organizations" and "absolutely nothing to discuss the agreements and on labor legislation ".

 We recommend: The central bank of Argentina performs a strong intervention in the foreign exchange market "No one can pay the tariff chart that has been launched," said Schmid, microphone in hand, at the foot of the iconic Obelisk. Since coming to power in December 2015, Macri has insisted on the need to update electricity or gas tariffs after years of stagnation due to being heavily subsidized during the Government of Cristina Fernández (2007-2015), which according to the Current executive caused a strong disinvestment in the energy sector. The protest on Monday also had the presence of the Argentine Confederation of Transport Workers (CATT) and the National Union Youth (JSN), the Argentine Aircraft Association or the Textile Workers Association (AOTRA), among others. Lee: IMF support for Argentina is bad news, says former finance minister In this line, the Secretary General of the AOTRA, Hugo Benítez, told Efe that he has the "hope" that the Executive "will listen to the workers' demand and that it will really open a dialogue table" in which the unions are included. , opposition and civil associations. "We are still in time for the government to listen to our claims and call us to try to see how we come out of this crisis together that really is tormenting us and a lot," he said. Under a shower of counterfeit bills of 5,000 pesos (about 200 dollars) with the face of the Minister of Mining and Energy, Juan José Aranguren, spoke to Efe Juan Pablo Brey, Secretary General of Aeronavegantes and youth secretary of the CGT, who denounced that "There are workers who have had to take credit to pay for these essential services (water, electricity and gas) for any human being." For this reason, he supported the announcement made this morning by Schmid, who assured that there will be a national strike if the Government's measures continue in this line while asking patience to have the support of all citizens. We recommend: How does the stand-by agreement that Argentina asks the IMF? "We have to organize it, we have to work on it, we are all convinced of the diagnosis we have, we are all convinced of where this government is going and where we do not want to go, but unemployment must be worked on," said Brey in support of the triumvirate. Since April 25, the Argentine peso has been abruptly devalued due to the sharp rise in rates in the United States and the consequent flight of capital to that country, which has strongly upset the Argentine political, economic and social sector and has forced the Government to start negotiating credits with the IMF and other multilateral organizations to mitigate the consequences This Monday, the Argentine currency again fell sharply: 7.59% against the dollar in the openingof markets.

title: Moody's doubts that Argentina crisis contagion to Latin America
text:

A weak economic context, the nervousness with respect to the devaluation and the preoccupation by the crop of soybean hit by the drought in Argentina are pressing to the Argentine peso, that this week fell to a historical minimum against the dollar. "It is difficult to see a contagion of Argentina's agitation in Latin America," said Mauro Leos, head of sovereign risk at the agency for Latin America and the Caribbean at a conference in London, adding the possible exception in Uruguay. title: Argentine peso is heading into the worst week since 2015
text:
The Argentine peso was heading towards its worst week since December 2015 after the International Monetary Fund said it wants to conclude talks on a possible line of credit as soon as possible.

The peso fell 3.9% to 23.6 per dollar at 1:44 pm in Buenos Aires, extending the weekly drop to 7.6%. Previously, the central bank sold dollars and bought letters from the short-term central bank, Lebacs, to stop the fall of the peso to a record of 24.1 per dollar.

Christine Lagarde, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, said on Thursday that the bank is looking for a quick solution to the talks with Argentina on the establishment of a right-of-way agreement. That did little to calm the world's worst performing currency on Friday. The peso fell 6.5% at a time before the central bank intervened, which did little to calm the nervousness.

Argentina, which would be requesting a line of credit for up to US $ 30,000 million, will resume talks with the IMF next week. The government is also in talks with the World Bank, the Inter-American Development Bank and the Latin American Development Bank (CAF) for additional lines of credit, Finance Minister Luis Caputo said Thursday night.

The central bank will face its first big test at Tuesday's auction of Lebacs, where around US $ 30 billion of bills must be renewed before they expire on Wednesday.

The central bank also stopped adding liquidity to the markets through its inverse repo of up to 47%, according to a person with knowledge of the subject. By stopping the inverse repo the additional entry of weights to the market is stopped, which prevents operators from using those pesos to buy dollars. The center of the bank's 7-day repo range of 40% is used as the monetary policy rate.

title: Argentina’s Move to Seek IMF Aid Fails to Halt Market Slide
text:
Argentina’s announcement Tuesday that it is seeking a line of credit from the International Monetary Fund failed to stem the more than weeklong slide in its currency, stocks and bonds as foreign investors continued to flee the troubled market.

The appeal to the IMF for help follows three unannounced emergency interest-rate hikes by the central bank. Argentina’s benchmark interest rate reached 40% last week following the increases, briefly pausing the currency’s slide.

The MSCI Argentina index was down 6% recently, retracing from steeper losses in early morning trading that at one point had the widely tracked equities benchmark down as much as 8% on the day. The Argentine peso weakened against the dollar, which was up 2%. JPMorgan’s benchmark Argentine bond index fell slightly, reaching its lowest level in more than a year.

Argentine equities have ​dropped 19% this month and are down 29% so far this year. The Argentine peso has weakened 10% against the dollar since the government began intervening near the end of last month.

Argentina has a history of fiscal mismanagement, government debt defaults and currency depreciation. The new administration under President Mauricio Macri has worked hard to win back foreign investors and encourage bank lending with more pro-business policies, while the central bank lowered interest rates at the start of the year in an attempt to stimulate growth.

But the plan backfired as foreign investors questioned the central bank’s independence and began selling the country’s currency.

“It’s going to be a long, tough road to regain and fully restore policy credibility, much of which was unnecessarily damaged,” said Patrick Esteruelas, head of research at Emso Asset Management.

Still, not everyone is bracing for another Argentine crisis. UBS Global Wealth Management’s chief investment office said that while Argentina’s soaring inflation and interest rates will undermine growth, it is unlikely to lead to a recession. Borrowing in Argentina had only recently begun to take off. While bank lending grew 25% in real terms last year, debt levels in Argentina remain the lowest in Latin America, at about 16% of gross domestic product 2017. That is expected to rise to 20% of GDP this year, says Charles Robertson, global chief economist at investment bank Renaissance Capital.

“Argentinians don’t borrow money; so, most people shouldn’t care about interest rates going to very high levels,” he said. “And inflation is not as important if you don’t have savings in your local currency. A big chunk of Argentinian savings have been kept offshore in Uruguay for many years because they are wary of their currency.”

Mr. Robertson said the recent slide doesn’t necessarily portend another crisis for Argentina, which hasn’t resorted to capital controls as it did in the past or seen its currency drop below the firm’s estimated fair value for the peso.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Stress levels rise as Argentina peso, Turkish lira hit record lows
text:
* Turkish lira hits record low after jump in inflation

* FX interventions fall to halt Argentina peso plunge

* Stocks fall for third day towards three-month low

* CEE digest EU budget plans, Czech central bank to hold rates

By Marc Jones

LONDON, May 3 (Reuters) - Stress levels rose in emerging markets on Thursday as Argentina's peso and Turkey's lira slumped to record lows in what looked like classic currency attacks and shares fell for a third day.

The pressure was widespread against the backdrop of a rising dollar and global borrowing rates and after more unpredictable behaviour on metal export tariffs from U.S. President Donald Trump's administration towards Brazil overnight.

It combined to push MSCI's 24-country emerging market stocks index towards a three-month low though tensions were highest in foreign exchange markets.

Argentina's peso slumped over 3 percent to an all-time low of 21.2 per dollar despite heavy intervention from its central bank just days after an emergency interest rate hike.

Turkey then saw the lira slide 0.4 percent to an all-time trough of 4.21 to the dollar, as another jump in inflation there added to jitters caused by a rating downgrade this week and government plans to up spending.

"You have this vicious circle of a deteriorating inflation outlook, a weaker currency and a central bank that is behind the curve," said ING's Chief EMEA FX and interest rate strategist, Petr Krpata.

Pressure also remained on the Central and Eastern European currencies that were some of last year's best performers in the world.

The Czech central bank was expected to keep its rates steady at a meeting later but the slide in the crown against both the dollar and the euro has boosted chances of another hike later in the year, Krpata added.

The region was also digesting news that from 2021 the European Union will cut funds paid out to member states that undermine courts and the rule of law, a move that could cost Hungary and Poland millions of euros.

Eurosceptic nationalists who have come to power in some former Communist states of eastern Europe have clashed with Brussels over what the EU describes as curbs to freedom of the media and violations of other democratic norms.

In Asia overnight, Indonesia's rupiah had fallen to its lowest in more than two years as foreign investors continued to sell their positions in the local bond and equity markets.

Indonesian stock exchange and Ministry of Finance data showed foreigners sold securities worth $684 million in equity markets and $967 million in bonds in April.

It was not all one way traffic however. The Singapore dollar and the Thai baht rose 0.25 percent and 0.15 percent respectively. The Indian rupee and the South Korean won also edged up on the day, the latter buoyed by an ongoing improvement of relations with North Korea.

In Latin America though there had been more gloomy news for turmoil-ridden Venezuela as the IMF issued a "declaration of censure" against Venezuela for failing to provide necessary economic data.

The United States cut off metals tariff talks with Brazil, contradicting an earlier U.S. announcement that the two countries had reached a permanent exemption from steel and aluminium import tariffs.

Representatives for Brazil's industry decried U.S. negotiation tactics, which the head of the association for aluminium producers, Milton Rego, called "Al Capone-like."

"You get better results by pointing a gun to the head," he said.

The action culminated on Friday in a surprise hike of the bank's key interest rate to 30.25 percent from 27.25. Monday and Tuesday were market holidays.

Argentina's local stock index rose 77 percent last year and investors even gobbled up a 100-year bond as President Mauricio Macri's strong performance in mid-term elections spurred hopes for more market friendly reforms. But investors have more recently woken up to the country's vulnerabilities.

"The forces driving the peso lower are unlikely to abate," Capital Economics said in a report on Wednesday, pointing to a current account deficit equivalent to 5 percent of gross domestic product as well as high inflation.

Local brokerage Delphos Investment said in a report the recent pace of dollar selling was not sustainable. It also said the implementation of a capital gains tax for foreign investors last month had led to a decrease in foreign capital entering Argentine markets.

Consumer prices in Argentina rose 2.3 percent in March, slightly down from the 2.4 percent increase in February. Twelve-month inflation was 25.4 percent, the same level as February. title: Argentina Puzzles Foreign Airlines -- WSJ
text:
This article is being republished as part of our daily reproduction of WSJ.com articles that also appeared in the U.S. print edition of The Wall Street Journal (December 26, 2017).

BUENOS AIRES -- Argentina's pro-business President Mauricio Macri is inviting low-cost airlines to invest in Argentina's uncompetitive air-travel market, as long as they do something they do nowhere else: keep their prices high.

That caveat is baffling not only to the companies, but also to the many Argentines, like 61-year-old Luís Segato, who badly want to see more domestic flights in the world's eighth-largest nation.

"Argentina is the strangest country in the world. We are capitalist in our rhetoric but communist in our practices," said the Buenos Aires resident, who mostly uses buses to travel around the country training firefighters. "How else can you explain why a pro-market government would tell airlines how much they can charge for tickets?"

Mr. Macri has slashed taxes, subsidies and red tape in an effort to make Argentina more attractive for investors. But when it comes to air travel and many other problematic zones of the country's economy, he has run into hard political realities. The country's powerful unions, secure in a long tradition of state protection that reaches back to the 1940s era of former President Juan Domingo Perón, are often not amused by notions of change.

The Macri administration has given Norwegian Air Argentina and Flybondi, a local startup, approval for new flights to scores of cities at lower fares -- but not too low. The newcomers say they could offer seats like those sold in Europe for as little as $15 -- a quarter the cost of a typical 13-hour bus ride -- if Mr. Macri would only let them.

The reason he isn't, government officials and industry executives say, is that allowing low-cost carriers to compete too freely might destroy bus-driver jobs and hurt dominant carrier Aerolíneas Argentinas, a state-run behemoth with about 12,000 employees.

Argentina has a long history of heavy intervention in its economy. Until last year, it set caps and minimum prices on airfares and made it hard for foreign carriers to operate here. In 2009, Mr. Macri's predecessor, Cristina Kirchner, a firebrand nationalist, expropriated Aerolíneas from a troubled Spanish travel company.

"It seems a bit crazy that in a country that's suffering from inflation you've got a company that wants to lower prices and isn't allowed to," said Julian Cook, chief executive of Flybondi, which aims to begin offering domestic and international flights next year.

Mr. Macri has feverishly overhauled the economy in two years in office, enacting drastic measures to fight double-digit inflation, lifting foreign-exchange controls and reaching a debt deal with foreign creditors. More recently, Mr. Macri moved to change Argentina's pension system, sparking violent street protests.

In some areas he faces steep resistance from strident union bosses, who say market-oriented policies displace workers and erode salaries.

Last year, after Argentina's central bank encouraged banks to start emailing digital statements instead of sending them off in paper envelopes, a truckers' union threatened to stop hauling cash to automated teller machines, citing fears that digital statements would mean less work. The central bank delayed its plans.

Such resistance highlights a constraint on Mr. Macri's ability to modernize a country where many favor state protection over market competition.

"If they let these low-cost carriers in it will be raining cadavers," said Pablo Biró, head of the pilots union, claiming budget airlines wouldn't invest properly in maintenance.

Bus-driver unions also fear the worst. Roberto Fernández, head of the UTA transportation workers union, says budget airlines would deprive long-distance buses of passengers, killing up to 10,000 ground-transportation jobs. "Macri needs to tell me where those people are going to find work," Mr. Fernández said.

Airline unions have repeatedly shut down airports nationwide, canceling hundreds of flights and leaving thousands of passengers stranded.

But carriers like Norwegian are undeterred and see opportunity in Argentina, which has Latin America's biggest middle class but where people are only half as likely to fly as residents of countries with similar income levels, according to Aeropuertos Argentina 2000, which runs 35 airports in Argentina.

"We see the Argentine market the way other markets were 20 years ago," said Ole Cristian Melhus, the regional head of Norwegian Air Argentina, which says it wants to invest up to $4.3 billion here.

Holger Paulmann, chief executive of Sky Airline, a budget carrier based in Chile, says he would offer domestic flights here -- but only if he could set his own prices.

"The minimum fare in Argentina is probably eight to 10 times higher than the lowest fare in Chile," Mr. Paulmann said.

Norwegian could eventually offer one-way tickets from Buenos Aires to Mendoza, home of Argentina's famous Malbec vineyards, for just $15, Mr. Melhus said. The government-set minimum price is currently about $58.

"We are carrying out an airline revolution, but it's a gradual process," said Guillermo Dietrich, Argentina's transportation minister.

There are other hurdles for airlines. Pilots are required to be Argentine citizens, and there aren't enough of them. Mr. Cook estimates that up to 400 Argentine pilots work abroad, and says he is trying to entice them to work for Flybondi.

Meanwhile, jet fuel costs about 15% more in Argentina than in Chile or the U.S. Duties to import a new airplane are high, Mr. Paulmann says. And a single company, Intercargo, has a nationwide monopoly on airport services, raising operating costs.

Brazil and Colombia, which opened up their airline markets, attracted millions of new passengers who never flew before, said Andy Ricover, a transportation industry expert.

"Who's opposed to that? The unions are holding back Argentina's development by opposing deregulation," he said.

Madalena Announces: Spudding of New Well; Appointment of Chairman; Board of Directors

CALGARY, Alberta, Oct. 30, 2017 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) --

Spudding of new well

Madalena Energy Inc. ("Madalena" or the "Company") (TSX-V:MVN) (OTCQX:MDLNF) is pleased to announce that their joint-venture partner Pan America Energy LLC ("PAE") successfully started operations on the spudding of a second horizontal multi-frac well (CAS.x-14) in the Vaca Muerta Shale Formation at the Coiron Amargo Sur Este ("CASE") block in Argentina. The CAS.x-14 exploration follows the earlier successful intervention into well CAS.x-15. The program includes drilling horizontally for approximately 1,500 metres in the Vaca Muerta unconventional oil resource play at a vertical depth of approximately 3,100 metres and performing approximately 60 hydraulic fracs with approximately 10,800 klb of proppant.

Total gross estimated cost of this re-entry is US$8.3 million, which includes the costs for drilling, completing and equipping the well.

The results of the last production test on CAS.x-15 yielded 125 boe per day through 3mm choke with 680 psi; Cum Oil Production of 29,200 barrels. Preliminary interpretations of the well results indicate that the well has stabilized at approximately 125 boe per day without artificial lift.
