title: Argentina  Central Bank  Chief:  Forex  Controls Are "Common Sense"
text:
BUENOS AIRES--Argentina's controversial foreign exchange controls are a "common sense" way to prevent capital flight and keep the economy growing, central bank President Mercedes Marco del Pont said Monday.

Mrs. Marco del Pont's comments come almost a year after the government began severely limiting the sale of U.S. dollars and other foreign currencies to the public. She said the controls are needed to stem capital flight outflows--which last year represented 4.2% of gross domestic product--so the government and industry have enough dollars on hand to pay debt and buy critical imports.

"It was common sense for a government like this, which aspires to embrace and consolidate this economic process of growth and [social] inclusion had to confront capital flight by Argentines," Mrs. Marco del Pont said at the central bank's annual monetary conference.

Domestic capital flight, which involves mainly Argentines withdrawing their dollar-denominated savings from local banks, has accounted for at least 3% of GDP over the past 15 years, Mrs. Marco del Pont said.

The central bank chief defended the government's interventionist policies and said that Argentina is "almost alone" in the world in its pursuit of unorthodox, stimulus-based recipes for growth.

Mrs. Marco del Pont questioned recent decisions by ratings firms to downgrade the outlook of the country's sovereign debt and the ratings of its companies and banks.

Last month, Moody's Investors Service cut its outlook on Argentina's B3 sovereign rating to negative from stable, and also lowered the outlook on 30 Argentine banks and 17 non-financial companies to negative.

Moody's based its decision on what it described as a "continued haphazard policy environment", doubts about the reliability of government economic data, and questions about the government's willingness to pay due to a lack of resolution to its debt arrears with the Paris Club.

Indeed, Mrs. Marco del Pont said not only have the ratings firms failed to properly interpret events in Argentina, but that people should view their conclusions as evidence that Argentina is pursuing precisely the right kind of policies.

"We have to be prepared to see those declining ratings of Argentina and those interpretations of Argentina as an indication that in reality we are heading in the right direction," she said.

Mrs. Marco del Pont voiced a gloomy outlook for the global economy and saw "no light at the end of the tunnel" for the financial problems in the developed world.

While economists outside Argentina are talking about "a lost decade" of economic malaise in developed nations, she said Argentina and other Latin American countries are in the position to claim a successful decade thanks to heterodox policies that stimulate growth and improve wealth distribution.

title: UPDATE: Argentina to Boost Stimulus in 2013 if Needed - Minister
text:
--Deputy economy minister says stimulus will be forthcoming if needed

--Most of the government's financing needs will be covered with domestic resources

--Deputy economy minister reaffirms government's foreign exchange policy

(Updates with background and comments about government's 2013 financing strategy) 


 
   By Ken Parks 
 

BUENOS AIRES--Argentina's federal government won't hesitate to take additional fiscal stimulus measures next year if the economy stumbles, a top policymaker said Wednesday.

President Cristina Kirchner has launched a number of stimulus measures this year to goose the country's sluggish economy. Those include tariff protection for local producers, a state mortgage program and lending requirements for banks.

Deputy Economy Minister Axel Kicillof said the government doesn't think it will need to make the same counter-cyclical spending efforts next year, but stands ready to do so if necessary.

"This government, if confronted with an [international] recessionary environment greater than that today or a continuation of global [economic] stagnation will take expansive fiscal measures because it has to; it will spend more," he said in testimony to the Lower House budget committee.

The government plans to cover its financing needs in 2013 largely with domestic resources, Finance Secretary Adrian Cosentino said at the same event.

Those sources include borrowing from the central bank and public-sector institutions such as state-run commercial bank Banco de la Nacion and the federal pension fund agency. In the case of the central bank, the government plans to borrow $7.97 billion from its international reserves to pay creditors next year.

The Kirchner administration expects Argentina's economy to grow 4.4% next year thanks to an expected recovery in the global economy.

President Cristina Kirchner's 2013 budget bill forecasts 3.4% growth this year.

If correct, her government will have to make payments of about 19 billion pesos ($4 billion) on growth-linked securities known as GDP warrants. The warrants pay out when growth exceeds 3.26%.

If the economy grows less than expected and the warrants don't pay out, those funds will be spent on infrastructure projects, Mr. Kicillof said.

"We are making provisions to pay the GDP warrants next year," he said.

Argentina's official economic statistics have been the target of considerable criticism following a purge of the national statistics agency in early 2007. The Kirchner administration is thought to significantly understate inflation and overstate growth.

Earlier this month, the International Monetary Fund gave Argentina until mid-December to improve the quality of the inflation and GDP data it reports to the fund or face possible sanctions.

Speaking on the Argentine peso, Mr. Kicillof said the government will continue its controlled float of the peso to prevent violent swings in the exchange rate or recessionary devaluations that dogged Argentina during the second half of the 20th century.

The Central Bank of Argentina regularly intervenes in the foreign-exchange market, buying dollars to build its international reserves and keeping the peso on a slow path of depreciation against the U.S. currency to help exporters.

The budget bill forecasts an average exchange rate of ARS4.53 to the U.S. dollar this year, and ARS5.10 to the dollar in 2013.

The gradual depreciation of the peso hasn't completely offset inflation that most private-sector forecasters say is between 20% and 25%. The government's latest estimate of 12-month inflation was 10%.

title: Argentina's Bonds, Stocks Close Higher; Merval Up 0.8%
text:
BUENOS AIRES--Argentina's bonds and stocks closed higher Wednesday, as investors ventured into the local market in the absence of negative news from the U.S. and Europe.

Adrian Mayoral, a trader at his family's brokerage, said assets have benefited from less volatility in offshore markets and the government's $2.2 billion payment of the Boden 2012 bond two weeks ago. But Europe and local politics are headwinds, he said.

"Uncertainty means that [asset] prices are very cheap. But we don't have a lot of conviction," he said. "We are at a good point in time to build positions with prudence."

Turnover on the local fixed-income market was 874.6 million pesos ($190 million), accounting for almost 76% of the total volume of securities traded on the exchange.

The Bonar X closed 1.4% higher at ARS520.40, yielding 4.53%

The Boden 2015 rose 1.3% to ARS585.75, and the Bonar 2013 closed 1.3% higher at ARS657.75.

The 2035 peso-denominated GDP warrant closed 0.3% lower at ARS12.859.

The peso closed at ARS4.6080 to the U.S. dollar on the MAE foreign-exchange wholesale market.

The Central Bank of Argentina regularly intervenes in the foreign-exchange market, buying dollars to build its international reserves and to keep the peso on a slow path of depreciation against the dollar.

According to the newspaper El Cronista, the dollar fetched ARS6.35 on the black market Wednesday.

The Argentine government's strict foreign-exchange controls have forced many individuals to seek dollars on the black market.

title: Fitch: Risks of Argentine Government Bank  Intervention  Remain
text:
CHICAGO--(BUSINESS WIRE)--May 09, 2012-- 

Argentina's government still maintains sufficient fiscal flexibility to avoid direct intervention in the country's private banking system, but future efforts to divert liquidity from Argentine banks cannot be ruled out. Fitch Ratings believes that a government liquidity grab, potentially taking the form of compulsory bond purchases, could ultimately lead to a crisis by weakening public confidence in the banking system.

Over the near term, we expect the government to continue its reliance on intrapublic funding, mainly from the central bank. Funds could also be moved from the state-owned pension plan administrator ANSES, as well as state-owned Banco de la Nacion Argentina, the country's largest commercial bank.

Prior to seeking cash from private banks, we believe the government would be more likely to increase intervention in other sectors of the economy, as seen recently in the nationalization of YPF S.A. Moreover, announced exchange controls and import restrictions should provide sufficient foreign currency for the remainder of the year.

According to the central bank, total deposits in the banking system at Feb. 28 totaled 482.3 billion Argentine pesos, including $13.3 billion of dollar-denominated deposits. Liquid assets, including cash, interbank loans bills, and notes issued by the central bank, represented 42.3% of total deposits. Overall exposure to the public sector among private banks is low, unlike the precrisis period at the beginning of the last decade.

We would expect any government intervention in the financial system to be viewed negatively by the public, particularly because the 2001 financial crisis was preceded by state intervention in the banking system and an increase in the banks' public sector exposure.

In addition to increasing pressure to divert U.S. dollars, we believe there is a risk that the government may consider other types of intervention. This may include directed credit or caps on interest rates and fees that could hurt bank profitability and the solvency of the banking system over the longer term.

The volatility of the Argentine operating environment is already factored into bank ratings. As a result, the current situation is not likely to lead to widespread downgrades of financial institutions. However, any change in the sovereign rating and/or an increase in government intervention in the banking system will be monitored closely and could have a negative impact on financial institution ratings.

title: Brazilian Real, Emerging Market  Currencies  Fall; Debt Little Changed
text:
--Emerging-market currencies weaken broadly

--Brazilian real erases 2012 gains on ongoing central-bank intervention

--Emerging-market debt is little changed but Argentina underperforms


 
    By Erin McCarthy 
    Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real led emerging-market currencies' fall Wednesday, while debt held steady, as concerns about the euro-zone debt crisis dominated markets and investors focused on ongoing intervention in Brazil.

Markets were anxiously gearing up for a Spanish bond auction Thursday, after Spain's borrowing costs rose in an auction earlier this week. Rising Spanish government bond yields have made the country the latest focal point of the euro-zone debt saga, especially as it struggles to rein in its fiscal deficit through tough austerity measures.

"I do get a sense that there's a little bit of nervousness as there's a Spanish auction tomorrow," said Win Thin, Brown Brothers Harriman's global head of emerging-market currency strategy.

Broader market concerns modestly weighed down emerging-market currencies like the Mexican peso and South African rand, which often takes cues from market sentiment. Emerging-market central-bank rate decisions were also in focus, with a string of policy-setting meetings this week.

The Brazilian real, however, stood out, as it erased all of its 2012 gains Wednesday on ongoing central-bank intervention. The dollar climbed to BRL1.8827, marking the real's weakest level since Dec. 29, 2011. Brazil's central bank stepped into the foreign-exchange market twice Wednesday to buy dollars. Brazil's Treasury also issued a sovereign bond denominated in reais in the international market this week, in part to help in the fight against the real appreciation.

This "more aggressive intervention" and is "not good for the currency," Thin said.

Investors also were waiting for Brazil's rate decision Wednesday night. The central bank is widely expected to cut the Selic benchmark rate by 75 basis points to nine basis points.

Elsewhere in the region, the Mexican peso slipped in line with U.S. stocks. It fell 0.4%, with the dollar buying MXN13.1616 late Wednesday, according to CQG.

The South African rand slipped 0.3% against the dollar, which traded at ZAR7.8356. Earlier Wednesday, data showed inflation in South Africa slowed to 6.0% on the year in March from 6.1% in February.

The Turkish lira, meanwhile, held up relatively well compared with other currencies' broad decline. The dollar traded flat on the day against the lira, at TRY1.7890. A more hawkish tone from Turkey's central bank provided support for the lira, analysts said.

Turkey's central bank Wednesday held all its key policy rates steady, in line with expectations, but warned it may have to tighten market interest rates more regularly to curb rising inflation spurred by higher oil prices.

Emerging-market sovereign debt, meanwhile, was little changed on the day, in line with listless trading in U.S. Treasurys. The risk premium on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Global, or Embig, widened by three basis points to 359 basis points over Treasurys. In price terms, its index slipped 0.2%.

Argentina's debt, however, weakened significantly. Its spread widened by 52 basis points to 1045 basis points over Treasurys. In price, its index dove 4%. Investors continue to move out of Argentina assets, after Argentine President Cristina Kirchner said Monday she will ask Congress for approval to expropriate a 51% stake in Argentina's largest oil-and-gas producer, YPF SA (YPF, YPFD.BA), from its controlling shareholder, Spain's Repsol YPF SA (REP.MC, REPYY).

title: UPDATE 3-Argentina says can rebuild reserves used to pay debt
text:
* Bank charter reform will free more reserves for gov't use

* Bill also aims to regulate and reorient bank credit

* "Buries" any chance of moving to inflation-targeting

* Critics say reform risks exacerbating inflation

(Recasts throughout; adds comment from former cenbank head)

By Magdalena Morales and Hilary Burke

BUENOS AIRES, March 7 (Reuters) - Argentina can gradually replenish the foreign reserves it uses to pay government debt, its central bank chief said on Wednesday, signaling the bank will keep buying billions of dollars on the local market to help keep state finances afloat.

Latin America's No. 3 economy has boomed in most of the last nine years thanks to hefty public spending, high grains prices and consumer demand fueled by an unorthodox policy mix.

As a slowdown takes hold and the trade and budget surpluses shrink, the center-left government is moving to free up more reserves to repay creditors - which critics say will only worsen double-digit inflation.

By tapping these funds for a third straight year, central bank chief Mercedes Marco del Pont said Argentina will be able to avert "brutal fiscal cuts" or costly debt issues on the global market. Argentina has not issued international debt since defaulting on some $100 billion during a 2001-02 crisis.

"(We) defend this expansion in Argentina's freedom of action ... to face this complicated world without giving up our fundamental objectives of growth and stability," she said.

This year's budget earmarks up to $5.7 billion in "excess" reserves to repay private creditors, but under current rules, there are no excess reserves left.

For that reason, the government is backing a bill to reform the central bank charter that loosens the definition of excess reserves, clearing the way for continued high spending aimed at spurring economic growth.

It also permits bilateral loans to be paid with reserves, which could augur a long-awaited deal to repay about $9 billion in debt to the Paris Club of creditor nations.

"The central bank is in a position to recover these reserves gradually," Marco del Pont told legislators as she defended the reform, which would expand the bank's mandate to include financial stability and "economic development with social justice". The reform is expected to pass Congress.

The central bank has bought roughly $2.1 billion on the local market since the start of 2012 to bulk up foreign reserves that have fallen by nearly $6 billion since hitting a record high $52.7 billion in January 2011.

In the past two years the administration tapped about $16 billion of central bank reserves to pay debt.

Critics say the use of more reserves for this purpose will exacerbate inflation estimated at between 20 and 25 percent annually by private economists. Government inflation data is widely discredited and consistently lower than private readings, at around 10 percent.

"This new charter institutionalizes the creation of a parallel slush fund within the public sector that has no oversight," said former central bank chief Martin Redrado, who quit in early 2010 when the government first proposed the use of reserves to pay debt.

"This will generate more inflationary pressures," he added.

MORE CREDIT TO FIGHT INFLATION

Under the current bank charter, "freely available" or excess reserves are defined as those that surpass the monetary base, or the level needed to back up cash in the economy.

Marco del Pont said there was no reason for reserves to be linked to money supply, saying bank officials should instead evaluate external accounts to determine what cushion is needed to keep currency volatility in check.

Argentina's central bank intervenes nearly every day in the foreign exchange market to ensure there is no abrupt swing in the value of the peso. The currency is losing its competitive edge as local production costs rise.

Responding to questions about inflation, Marco del Pont reiterated her stance that price pressures stem more from supply problems than overheated demand.

She said the charter reform would help tame price pressures by giving the central bank new tools to promote long-term lending for investment.

The bill says the bank could regulate credit conditions including loan maturities, interest rates and commissions, while "orienting" credit toward projects that boost domestic production.

The reform eliminates the requirement to present an annual monetary program. Marco del Pont said it "buries" the possibility of moving to an inflation-targeting regime, which she said was giving headaches to policymakers elsewhere.

(Additional reporting by Guido Nejamkis and Luis Andres Henao; Editing by James Dalgleish and Andrew Hay)

* Economy has boomed for years under unorthodox policies

* Analysts say high inflation not being addressed

(Adds details, context, analyst quotes)

By Hugh Bronstein

BUENOS AIRES, Dec 29 (Reuters) - Argentina's economy should expand by 4.5 percent to 7.5 percent next year, the central bank said on Thursday, warning that Europe's financial mess poses the biggest threat to growth.

According to it's freshly approved monetary program, the bank said the policies that have helped Argentina's economy boom over the last nine years will remain largely in place.

"The biggest source of uncertainty is associated with the sovereign debt crisis and financial system risk presented by the advanced economies," the program says.

Italy, the euro zone's third-largest economy, remains at the center of the debt crisis that began in Greece two years ago.

Italian Prime Minister Mario Monti pledged new efforts to boost the economy after a disappointing bond auction on Thursday underlined the country's shaky public finances.

Investors meanwhile fret that Argentine President Cristina Fernandez's unorthodox and hard-to-predict policies will leave the country vulnerable to fallout from Europe's debt woes and to slower demand from key commodities client China next year.

Argentina has roared back from the dark days of its 2001/02 sovereign debt default and shock currency devaluation. Fernandez credits her policies, and those of her late husband, Nestor Kirchner, who preceded her in office, for the rapid expansion.

But Wall Street takes a dim view of her reliance on state intervention in the economy, and Argentina has remained locked out of the international capital markets.

INFLATION

The country's economy grew 8.1 percent in October from a year earlier, beating market expectations but marking the slowest pace of growth in a year.

Inflation for full-year 2012 is seen at 9.2 percent, according to the document issued by the central bank.

Private economists say that Argentina has under-reported consumer price increases over the last five years for political gain as well as to save on inflation-linked bond payments. They say the country's inflation rate is actually more than twice the rate reported by the government.

"These figures show that the monetary stance will remain extraordinarily lax, with the central bank continuing to accommodate inflation at a very high level," Alberto Ramos, who analyses the country for Goldman Sachs, said in reference to the central bank's projections.

"This strategy is likely to lead to further erosion of the current account and add pressure on the Argentine peso to depreciate," he said.

The central bank targeted broad M2 money supply growth at an average of 26.4 percent for 2012, compared with the target for growth of 27.9 percent for 2011.

Argentina's trade surplus more than doubled in November from a year ago and the central bank projects a positive balance of $8.9 billion in full-year 2012.

(Additional reporting by Nicolas Misculin; Editing by Andrew Hay and Steve Orlofsky)

title: Argentina's Stocks, Bonds End Volatile Year In Light Trading
text:
--Argentine peso posts 7.6% year-on-year loss vs dollar in penultimate session of 2011

--Argentine government bonds were broadly higher this year

--Argentina's benchmark Merval index fell 30% in 2011


 
   By Ken Parks 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Argentina's stocks and sovereign bonds posted solid gains in the last trading session of 2011, while the local currency closed little changed against the dollar as the central bank kept the peso steady.

Argentina's stock and bond markets are closed Friday and Monday. The MAE foreign-exchange wholesale market will operate until 10:30 a.m. EST Friday, and is closed Monday.

The peso dominated financial headlines in the fourth quarter, after President Cristina Kirchner imposed foreign exchange controls in late October to limit capital flight that was slowly draining international reserves.

The Central Bank of Argentina intervenes in the exchange market almost daily to engineer a gradual weakening of the peso to help exporters.

The peso was quoted closing on the MAE at ARS4.3035 to the U.S. dollar on Thursday, bringing its year-to-date loss to 7.6%.

The bank spent billions of dollars in reserves to keep the peso steady in the run-up to October's general election, in which Kirchner won re-election by a record margin.

With a second term in her pocket, Kirchner swiftly limited the public's access to dollars by requiring all foreign exchange transactions be vetted by the tax agency.

Investors pulled more than $18 billion out of the country in the first nine months of the year on fears that annual inflation of more than 20% will eventually force authorities to weaken the peso at a faster rate to keep exports competitive.

Now that private-sector dollar demand has been suffocated, the central bank has become an active buyer of greenbacks in recent weeks. After hitting a multiyear low of $44.70 billion on Dec. 14, reserves reached $46.27 billion on Wednesday.

Carlos Lizer, director of currency trading at brokerage Puente, expects the central bank to keep the peso on a slow, but steady course of depreciation in the first quarter.

"For the end of March we expect a floor of around ARS4.40 and a ceiling of ARS4.45," he said.

The mixed performance of Argentine stocks and government bonds this year was closely tied to international events, namely Europe's unfolding sovereign debt crisis.

Events abroad will continue to drive trading in both asset classes in 2012, especially if Europe slips into recession and Argentina's top trading partners, China and Brazil, grow at a slower pace than economists currently forecast.

Most benchmark bonds posted gains this year, with the notable exception of the 33% plunge in the 2033 discount bond.

On Thursday, the Bonar X rose 0.7% in price terms to close at ARS407.00, yielding 8.88%. The Bogar 2018 closed 2% higher at ARS221.50, to yield 11.40%.

The Boden 2015 rose 1.5% to ARS449.00, yielding 6.37%.

The 2035 peso-denominated GDP warrant rose 0.8% to ARS11.54, while dollar GDP warrants closed 1.8% higher at ARS62.10.

After rallying 52% in 2010, the benchmark Merval stock index plunged 30% this year as Europe's crisis and prospects of slower global economic growth in 2012 spurred investors to exit riskier markets like Argentina.

Banks and public utilities, which are heavily weighted on the index, were the biggest losers, with shares of Grupo Financiero Galicia SA (GGAL.BA, GGAL) falling 53% and electric energy holding company Pampa Energia SA (PAMP.BA, PAM) stock shedding 29% of its value.

On Thursday, the Merval rose 1.5% to close at 2462.63 on volume of ARS35.8 million.

Deutsche Bank recommends zero exposure to Argentine stocks, though it did note in a recent report that a rally might ensue if the government were to adopt market friendly policies.

"Argentina remains the only [Latin American] market that could rally driven by policy changes given: 1) significant rerating potential, and 2) many sectors are under earning under current regulatory environment," Deutsche Bank analysts said.

title: RPT-FACTBOX-What is Argentina's peso really worth?
text:
( Repeats Tuesday story for more subscribers )

BUENOS AIRES, Nov 22 (Reuters) - Argentina's peso currency trades in several markets, and for most of the last eight years, the exchange rates in these markets have been much the same.

However, the spread, or difference, between the peso's value in these markets has widened sharply since Oct. 31, when President Cristina Fernandez slapped tough new controls on foreign currency purchases after months of brisk capital flight. [ID:nN1E79U0X9] [ID:nN1E7A80OQ]

Between August and October, when Fernandez won easy re-election, capital flight surged to an estimated $10 billion as investors bet she would allow the local currency to depreciate at a faster rate after the election.

Inflation estimated privately at about 25 percent is fast eroding the competitiveness of Argentine exports and has easily outstripped the peso's nominal rate of depreciation.

Capital flight prompted the central bank to shell out some $4.8 billion in foreign reserves in recent months to prop up the peso. Government officials fear a sudden depreciation could fuel inflation and exacerbate outflows.

Here are brief profiles of the different peso markets:

INTERBANK

This is the formal, spot market administered by the Open Electronic Market, or MAE by its Spanish initials. The main players are banks handling orders by large companies, including Argentina's grain exporters.

The central bank intervenes in this market on a near-daily basis, more recently by selling dollars to keep the peso stable despite surging demand for greenbacks amid capital flight and fast-growing imports. In the last few days, the country's monetary authority has resumed dollar purchases.

Sources at private banks said recently the government had asked big companies to keep out of the market for a few weeks to help ease pressure on the peso.

Trade volume has fallen to about $180 million per day from about $450 million before the controls on dollar purchases came into force. The formal peso <ARS=RASL> closed at a bid price of 4.2575 to the dollar, a 6.7 percent loss over the last year.

RETAIL

Operated by banks and foreign-exchange houses, this market is generally used by individual savers and small- and medium-sized companies.

Under the new controls imposed three weeks ago, tax inspectors must pre-approve all operations in the retail market. If the potential buyer has a record of unpaid taxes or is judged to have insufficient reported income, the transaction is rejected.

Government officials say the measure is aimed at combating rampant tax evasion and money laundering, but traders say it has acted as a barrier on dollar purchases. Trade volume has shrunk by about 80 percent from its pre-control levels of some $60 million per day.

In retail trade <ARSCC=>, the peso closed at 4.2400 on Tuesday, having shed 6.9 percent in the last 12 months.

PARALLEL MARKET

Under-the-counter deals are largely carried out by foreign- exchange houses, where savers and small companies go to stay off the tax agency's radar since they are generally changing money that has not been declared to authorities.

In the first few days after the currency controls were implemented, the informal or parallel peso, as measured by Reuters, slumped to a record low of 5 per dollar.

But government efforts since to tighten controls on foreign-exchange houses effectively froze the market, which tended to move about $200 million a day.

Market sources have said the government is pressuring currency traders to sell the peso at around 4.40/4.50 per dollar in the informal market, well below the roughly 4.70 per dollar reported to be sought by holders of greenbacks.

No deals of any significance have been made on the informal market since Monday, Nov. 14, when the Argentine peso fetched 4.77/4.79 per dollar <ARSB=>. That represented a 7 percent decline since the controls were put into place.

BLUE-CHIP SWAP RATE

This is the implicit exchange rate involved in buying peso-denominated assets that trade in Argentina, mainly government bonds, and selling their counterparts on the market in New York to obtain dollars abroad.

This operation, which some banks call the blue-chip swap rate, tends to reflect capital flight since investors use it to send money abroad without triggering capital controls.

As demand to get cash out of the country grows, the exchange rate for doing so tends to rise.

After the government controls were imposed, this implicit rate reached a record 5.19 pesos per dollar. It later eased back to its current level of around 4.70.

Traders said the rate cooled, thanks to state pensions agency ANSES, which heavily sold dollar-denominated bonds to reduce the gap between the price for these assets in pesos and their counterparts in dollars.

FUTURES MARKETS

There are two big futures markets in Argentina, one run by the MAE in which banks are the main actors, and the other one by Rofex, which is part of the Rosario exchange, and whose players include financial entities and agricultural exporters.

These markets move around $500 million a day, about 65 percent of which is traded on the Rofex.

As a way to avoid selling too many foreign currency reserves in the interbank market, the central bank often makes deals on the futures market as part of its bid to tame the peso's volatility.

Tuesday's close on the Rofex <0#ARS:> showed pesos for Nov. 30 settlement <ARSX11> at 4.2640 to the dollar and the peso for Sept. 28, 2012 settlement <ARSU12> at 4.8050 to the dollar.

NON-DELIVERABLE FORWARD (NDF)

These over-the-counter futures let investors bet on changes in the value of the Argentine peso and are worth about $150 million a day, with most deals concentrated in near-term contracts.

NDF's are settled in dollars, meaning no pesos actually change hands. They are primarily used to hedge, or insure, against peso-dollar exchange-rate risk.

The implied yields on peso futures in New York <ARSNDFOR=> are much higher than what is seen in the Argentine futures markets, indicating there is a greater expectation that a steeper depreciation is in store.

On Tuesday, the peso's NDFs traded at 4.3778 per dollar one month out, while six-month contracts fetched 4.9500 per dollar and 12-month deals were being made at 5.5800.

The implied yield, or return, on the 1-month peso NDF <ARS1MID=> is 33 percent a year, compared with less than 7 percent a year ago.

(Additional reporting by Jorge Otaola and Jeb Blount; Writing by Helen Popper and Hilary Burke; Editing by Jeb Blount and Jan Paschal)

title: WSJ: Tests Mount For Argentine Economy
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--President Cristina Kirchner's mixed signals about how she plans to address longstanding problems in Argentina's economy are adding to uncertainty that is causing capital flight, analysts say.

In the gap between Mrs. Kirchner's re-election last month and her December inauguration, Argentines aren't clear which policy makers are in charge and what the strategy is, the analysts say. In recent days, government policy has veered from market-intruding controls on foreign-currency transactions to market-friendly reductions in some utility subsidies to consumers.

(This story and related background material will be available on The Wall Street Journal website, WSJ.com.)

The dissonance seems to reflect internal struggles within Mrs. Kirchner's team on whether Argentina will moderate its free-spending and interventionist policies in the second term, or whether it will offer more of the same, even though fewer resources are available. The outcome of the apparent debate won't become clearer until Mrs. Kirchner announces her new cabinet, sometime closer to the Dec. 10 start of her second term.

One government official said the recent turmoil was a temporary blip, partly related to economic uncertainty in Brazil and Europe. The official said Mrs. Kirchner was politically strong, following her landslide re-election with 54% of the vote, and that there were signs in the past few days that the worst of the dollar drain had passed.

Others point to underlying problems.

"For a while, most of the decisions were easy because the government was dealing with abundance," said Gabriel Torres, an economist at Moody's Investors Service. "It was a question of, 'Do we spend 100% of the money coming in or 110%?'"

But after years of fast growth and heavy government spending, fueled by high farm commodity prices, Argentina will be hard-pressed to maintain business as usual, Mr. Torres said.

The big trade and fiscal surpluses that once provided Argentina with an economic cushion have withered. The peso, once undervalued to keep industry competitive, has appreciated against the dollar over the past couple of years.

Many Argentine savers and investors started switching from pesos to dollars a few months ago, anticipating that the government would devalue the currency after the election. But then, at the end of last month, the interventionist wing of the government moved to try and throttle the dollar outflow by requiring that foreign-currency purchases receive prior approval from Argentine tax authorities.

Overseeing the currency controls has been Guillermo Moreno, the internal commerce secretary whose zeal has prompted some in the business community to dub him "El Loco," the Crazy Man. Previously, Mr. Moreno had been responsible for enforcing price controls that are unpopular in the business community.

Mrs. Kirchner herself has tried to counter the flight to the dollar, jawboning companies to reinvest profits rather than transferring them out of the country. At the recent opening of a General Motors Co. (GM) plant, she praised the company's investment as exemplary and decried business executives who "make formidable sums of money and don't reinvest and take them out of the country."

Even though transactions on the foreign-exchange market have plummeted recently due to the exchange controls, the central bank has experienced a slow, steady drain on hard currency reserves. Reserves have fallen to $46 billion from $52 billion in August.

In part, the loss of reserves has persisted because the currency controls boomeranged and made Argentines even more jittery. Some Argentines with dollar-denominated local bank accounts have been withdrawing money to place under the mattress.

Late Friday, Miguel Angel Pesce, vice president of the central bank, said the rate of withdrawals had declined in an "important" way by the middle of last week, and that the scenario was improving. Still, Argentina lost $1.7 billion in dollar deposits, about 11% of the total, in the first two weeks after the exchange controls announcement on Oct. 28, the bank said.

The negative repercussions of the currency moves have been partially offset by initiatives this month to reduce government subsidies that have kept consumers' electricity, water and gas rates at rock-bottom levels. Those subsidies cost about 4% of Argentina's gross domestic product and are no longer affordable, economists say.

The subsidy reductions will be initially limited to industrial users and residential users located in wealthy neighborhoods of Buenos Aires, said planning minister Julio de Vido and economy minister Amado Boudou, two cabinet officials who are favored by the business community.

But other Buenos Aires residents will be required to fill out forms justifying that they actually have an economic need for the subsidies, said Mr. De Vido, who is a candidate to succeed Mr. Boudou as economy minister when the latter moves on to serve as Mrs. Kirchner's vice president in December.

It is still unclear how far the government will go in cutting subsidies among residential users, analysts say. Steep cuts would increase the utility bills paid by the mass of the population and likely cost the government political support.

Investors have been left to put their own interpretation on the mixed signals. During a recent conference call with investors, Franco Bernabe, CEO of Telecom Italia SpA (TI, TIT.MI), a telecommunications giant that is a big investor in Argentina, praised the subsidy cuts as representing "a very positive approach on problems that have been developing for over a long period of time."

Nevertheless when pressed by a stock analyst on Argentina's currency policy, Mr. Bernabe acknowledged that companies were facing "moral pressure from the government" against transferring dividends outside of the country. He nevertheless said that Argentina was on "the right track."

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

November 20, 2011 20:14 ET (01:14 GMT)

title: Fitch: Argentina Policy Options Narrow With  Forex  Restrictions
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Fitch Ratings said Wednesday that Argentina's implementation of stricter foreign-exchange controls might reduce the government's policy options as it tries to limit capital flight and defend the peso.

"Fitch Ratings sees the potential for a continuation of unorthodox economic policies as a growing risk for Argentina as it seeks to avoid a disorderly currency depreciation and rising inflation," the ratings firm said in a statement.

The government on Monday tightened controls on the local foreign-exchange market by requiring individuals and businesses to receive prior approval from the tax authority before buying foreign currency.

The new control is the latest in a series of measures announced in recent days by the administration of President Cristina Kirchner to stem capital flight that has become a slow but steady drain on Argentina's international reserves.

Last week, the government ordered foreigners buying Argentine companies and real estate to deposit the full amount of the transaction in Argentina. Oil and mining companies now must also repatriate the proceeds of export sales, while insurance companies have to bring all offshore investment home before the year's end.

The Central Bank of Argentina regularly intervenes in the local foreign-exchange market to gradually weaken the peso against the U.S. dollar to help exporters and limit inflation that is widely believed to be running above 20%.

The exchange rate is a politically sensitive issue in a country whose citizens still view the dollar as a safe-haven currency due to Argentina's long history of violent devaluations and financial crisis.

After winning re-election last month with 54% of the vote, Kirchner faces a challenging second term amid a sluggish global economy and high inflation at home.

Argentina's economy is expected to grow at least 8% this year, though economic activity will slow next year, with the government forecasting a 5.1% expansion.

Fitch expects Argentina to report its first current account deficit this year since 2001 due in part to a shrinking trade surplus.

With the outlook for agricultural commodity prices and global growth weakening, Fitch said Argentina faces a more difficult export situation that could exacerbate external imbalances and declines in dollar reserves over coming months.

Fitch said it continues to view any shift to a more pragmatic policies as generally supportive of Argentina's ratings.

"However, ratings remain heavily constrained and could become vulnerable if a disorderly exchange rate adjustment or a significant ramp up in inflationary expectations destabilizes the macroeconomic environment," the ratings firm said.

-By Ken Parks, Dow Jones Newswires; 54-11-4103-6740; ken.parks@dowjones.com [ 02-11-11 1711GMT ]

title: Argentina Stocks, Bonds Climb As Rebound Extends To Third Day
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Argentine stocks and bonds notched up the third straight day of solid gains Thursday as the local market continues to claw back some of the heavy losses suffered in recent weeks.

Argentina's benchmark Merval stock index rose 2.3% to close at 2,596.64 points. Volume was moderate at 57 million pesos ($14 million.)

The fact that local equities gained despite the weakness overseas is a good sign that "genuine investors are returning and displacing the overseas traders that caused so much damage by aggressively liquidating their holdings during the latest global sell-off," economic consultancy Estudio Ber said in a market note.

Power company Edenor (EDN, EDN.BA) and energy holding group Transaner (TRAN.BA) posted some of the biggest gains. Edenor shot up 6.5% to close at ARS1.47, while Transaner added 5.4% to close at ARS1.18.

Bonds also closed mostly higher as investors snapped up the high-yielding government debt.

Earlier Thursday Barclays Capital said the time is right to shift bond holdings from Venezuela to Argentina. Risk is up in Venezuela ahead of next year's election and Argentine bond prices are tempting after being beaten down, the firm said. Argentina "has been particularly -- and unfairly, in our view --penalized during the recent sell-off."

Barclays' pick is the short-maturity Boden 15, which "still trades at very depressed prices ... despite the rally in recent days, and offers an attractive, low price volatility combined with relatively high carry."

The Boden 15 ended the day 0.7% higher in price terms at ARS402, with the yield at 8.7%.

Meanwhile, the peso eased to ARS4.2135 to the U.S. dollar on Argentina's MAE foreign-exchange wholesale market, compared to ARS4.211. The Central Bank intervened again to stem the peso's slide.

Argentina will continue to pump foreign reserves into the currency market to stem a decline in the peso, but a significant drop is still expected next year, RBS said in a market note.

Heavy capital flight ahead of October presidential elections has drained reserves and put the peso under pressure. The government's commitment to an orderly depreciation strategy will cause reserves to fall $7 billion this year and $8 billion next, with the peso ending 2012 at ARS5.11 to the dollar, RBS says.

Central Bank reserves stand at $48.2 billion, down more than $1.8 billion from Sept 1.

-By Shane Romig, Dow Jones Newswires; 54-11-4103-6738; shane.romig@dowjones.com [ 13-10-11 2214GMT ]

title: Argentina Stocks, Bonds Extend Losses In Volatile Session; Merval Down 0.2%

Turnover on the local bond market was ARS582.50 million, accounting for about 58% of the total volume of securities traded on the exchange during the session.

The Central Band of Argentina and other public-sector institutions have stepped up their intervention in the local foreign-exchange markets in recent weeks to keep the peso steady ahead of presidential and congressional elections on Oct. 23.

title: Argentina Pension Agency Trimmed Government Bond Holdings In June
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Argentina's pension fund agency, Anses, trimmed its holdings of government securities in June compared with the previous month.

Anses's investments in public-sector debt fell 0.2% on the month to 106.5 billion pesos ($25.3 billion) at the end of June, but rose 14.2% on the year, the agency said Thursday in its monthly report on assets under management.

The U.S. dollar-denominated Bonar X bond showed the biggest decline as a percentage of the agency's government bond portfolio, falling to 7.9% from 8.5% at the end of May. The agency's holdings of dollar-denominated Boden 2015 bonds was steady at 3.4% of the total.

Anses and the Central Bank of Argentina regularly intervene in the local foreign exchange market to stabilize the peso amid growing levels of capital flight in an election year.

Local traders say Anses has taken a bigger role in the foreign exchange market in recent months, selling and buying bonds to take some of the pressure off the central bank, which has seen its reserves fall as it defends the peso.

President Cristina Kirchner is trying to avoid abrupt moves in the exchange rate that would spook voters as she seeks reelection in October. Kirchner is widely expected to win a second term after receiving just over 50% of the vote in Argentina's first open primary election in August.

But investors are speculating that Kirchner will allow the peso to depreciate at a swifter rate after the elections to help exporters, who have seen their competitiveness eroded by high inflation at home.

The peso was quoted closing on the local MAE foreign-exchange wholesale market at ARS4.2045 to the dollar Thursday, unchanged for the fourth straight session. The peso has depreciated about 5.4% versus the dollar so far this year.

Barclays economist Sebastian Vargas wrote in a report Thursday that he expects Anses to play a key role in helping the government to cover an estimated financing gap of $6.4 billion in 2012.

"In its role of underwriter of treasury debt, we continue to expect Anses to tap markets for $5 billion to $6 billion in 2012," Vargas said.

The agency could sell its Bonar X positions, which totaled about ARS8.3 billion at the end of June. But the government would have to issue additional debt to Anses during the year to bridge the gap, according to Barclays.

Anses publishes information about its investment portfolio with a three month delay to prevent market participants from speculating in Argentine assets, according to agency officials.

Anses' overall investment portfolio grew 27.2% on the year to ARS191 billion as of June 30.

The biggest gains were noted in equity investments, which rose to ARS24 billion, and financing for infrastructure and industrial projects, which totaled ARS23.6 billion.

Anses has invested in projects ranging from public housing to the completion of the Atucha II nuclear power plant as part of Kirchner's job creation policy.

Public pension systems that don't create jobs "are useless", Economy Minister and vice presidential candidate Amado Boudou said at a pension seminar earlier this month.

-By Ken Parks, Dow Jones Newswires; 54-11-4103-6740; ken.parks@dowjones.com [ 29-09-11 2312GMT ]

title: Argentina Can Easily Manage Exchange Rate Of Peso - Official
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Argentina's government can easily manage the exchange rate of the Argentine peso even if financial troubles worsen in Europe and the U.S., a top government official said in an interview this week.

"Whatever the case, whatever the situation, I don't see Argentina having any problem at all managing the exchange rate," said the official, who declined to be named. "We have enough of a cushion to keep the rate completely under control, regardless of what happens abroad."

The cushion refers to about $49.5 billion in foreign currency reserves held by the Central Bank of Argentina.

The central bank uses those reserves to intervene in the currency market, buying or selling dollars as needed to prevent the peso from fluctuating abruptly.

"The exchange rate is a particularly important variable in Argentina because of the country's history," said the official. "There's absolutely no reason for this to be an issue now or after the election in October."

Argentina holds a presidential election on Oct. 23. President Cristina Kirchner is expected to win in a landslide.

The peso currently trades for about ARS4.20 to the U.S. dollar. It has been slowly but predictably depreciating in recent years under Argentina's managed exchange-rate policy.

The peso depreciated by about 1% a month this year until August, when it weakened at an even quicker pace.

Currency traders here expect it to weaken another 10% to 11% next year, putting it at around ARS4.50.

But many economists say high inflation surpassing 20% annually is causing the peso to appreciate in real terms, crimping the competitiveness of Argentine exporters.

Some in Argentina's manufacturing sector have asked the government to let the peso slide faster. Others say letting the peso move too quickly in any direction would spook investors, especially average Argentines, who have a strong psychological aversion to a weak peso given repeated financial crises here.

"The president's job is to listen to all sectors, evaluate all the issues, and then decide to do what is best for the country as a whole. That's exactly what she's going to do," the official said.

The central bank has intervened often in the currency market since Argentina's 2002 economic meltdown and devaluation. Since 2003, the bank's reserves have risen from $10.5 billion, according to a report this week by the think tank Abeceb.

That trend began changing in 2008 during the global financial crisis and local political problems that spurred capital flight that reduced reserves by over 11%, Abeceb reported.

Last year, the bank also used $6.5 billion in reserves to make debt payments. This year it has used $9.6 billion.

Abeceb cautioned that using reserves too quickly could raise investor concern and lead people to buy dollars en masse.

"Though the macroeconomic situation is good, an increase in devaluation expectations could cause inflation to accelerate because a depreciating peso leads to higher prices," Abeceb said. "It would add volatility to the financial market."

title: UPDATE: Hochschild CEO Sees Argentina Devaluation Due To Inflation
text:
--Argentina is where Hochschild is experiencing the most cost inflation

--Hochschild fairly unhedged to Argentine peso

--Argentine peso devaluation unlikely in 2011

(Adds more details throughout beginning in the 1st paragraph.)


 
  By Alex MacDonald and Ken Parks 
  OF DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

LONDON (Dow Jones)--Argentina will have to devalue its peso as inflation drives up the costs of industrial activities like mining, the chief executive of precious metals producer Hochschild Mining PLC (HOC.LN) said Tuesday.

"Argentina is where inflation is hitting our costs the most, it's not sustainable," Ignacio Bustamante told Dow Jones Newswires. "There has to be a devaluation," he added, noting the company is keeping its exposure to the Argentine peso fairly unhedged.

In a conference call with analysts, Bustamante said he doesn't expect a devaluation to happen this year due to presidential elections in October.

President Cristina Kirchner is widely expected to win a second term after she received nearly 51% of the vote in a national primary election held earlier this month.

The Central Bank of Argentina has stepped up its intervention in the foreign exchange markets in recent months to engineer a gradual depreciation of the peso against the U.S. dollar to help exporters, but not so much as to spook Argentines who still see the dollar as a safe haven currency.

The peso was recently quoted trading on the local wholesale foreign exchange market at ARS4.1830/dlr, bringing its year-to-date depreciation to 4.9%.

But annual gains in consumer prices that most economists say exceed 20% have caused the peso to appreciate in real terms against the greenback. At the same time, Argentina's powerful trade unions have won salary increases of close to 30% this year to compensate for inflation.

Hochschild said Tuesday that unit costs per ton of ore mined rose 37% for its Argentine operations, far outpacing a 12% on average rise at its lower cost Peruvian operations.

Unit costs at its San Jose mine in Argentina rose 37% on year to $191.3/ton due to local price inflation of between 25% to 30% owing mainly to higher wages.

Prices for raw materials, most notably fuel, steel and reagent, have also risen, the company said, reiterating that it still expects to keep increases to its Argentine unit cost between 25%-30% for the full year in 2011.

Excluding royalties, unit costs rose 33% on year in Argentina during the first half, according to the company.

London-listed Hochschild operates five gold and silver mines in Latin America: three underground mines in Peru, one underground mine in southern Argentina, and an open pit mine in northern Mexico.

The San Jose mine produced 5.2 million of attributable silver equivalent ounces in the first half of 2011, resulting in $156 million in revenue and operating profit before administration, exploration and other expenses of $79.6 million or 28% of the company's total equivalent operating profit during the first half of the year.

Hochschild's shares were recently up 0.6% or 2.6 pence at 460.60p.

title: Argentina Capital Flight Picks Up Ahead Of October General Elections
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Businesses and individuals pulled money out of Argentina at a faster pace during the second quarter ahead of presidential and congressional elections in October, according to a measure of capital flight published by the central bank.

The formation of assets abroad by the nonfinancial private sector rose to $6.13 billion in the quarter, from $3.68 billion in the previous quarter and $2.24 billion in the fourth quarter of 2010, the Central Bank of Argentina said in its quarterly foreign exchange report Thursday.

The central bank attributed the increase to the "habitual behaviour of the private sector in pre-election periods" with most of the foreign currency demand coming from small savers.

Argentines frequently turn to the U.S. dollar during an election year and 2011 is proving to be no exception.

President Cristina Kirchner, whose populist economic policies have long spooked foreign investors, is still widely favored to win re-election this year even after her ruling coalition suffered big losses in local elections in Buenos Aires City and Santa Fe Province last month.

The central bank regularly intervenes in the foreign exchange markets to engineer a gradual depreciation of the peso versus the dollar to control inflation and to help exporters.

The central bank said it made net foreign exchange purchases of $2.40 billion during the quarter, down from $3.15 billion purchased in the first quarter. The central bank's international reserves totaled $50.31 billion on Thursday, compared with $51.7 billion at the end of June.

The peso has weakened about 4.2% against the dollar so far this year, closing at ARS4.1535 versus the dollar Thursday. The government has pledged an average exchange rate of around ARS4.10 per dollar in 2011.

J.P. Morgan said in a note that it expects the peso to end the year at ARS4.25 per dollar as the central bank and pension fund agency Anses likely continue intervening in the exchange market.

Argentina imposes restrictions on capital inflows and outflows, with Argentine residents limited to $2 million a month in foreign currency purchases.

Dividends and profits sent abroad by companies totaled $1.66 billion in the quarter, compared with $361 million in the first quarter and $914 million in the fourth quarter of 2010, the central bank said.

Foreign direct investment rose to $829 million in the quarter, totaling $2.56 billion for the 12-month period ended June 30. The central bank said that mining, petrochemicals, and construction were the single biggest recipients of that investment.

title: Argentina Official, Parallel  Forex  Rates Gap To Widen
text:
-Gap between official and parallel rates expected to widen on economic doubts

-Parallel rate is a gauge of confidence in Argentina's peso and the economy

-The government has sought to strangle trading in the parallel market

The gap between Argentina's official foreign exchange rate and a parallel market has narrowed in recent weeks, but traders warn it will likely widen again as investors fear a swifter depreciation of the peso as authorities struggle to address growing imbalances in the economy.

"It's a leading indicator on confidence in the forex rate," said Siobhan Morden, a fixed-income strategist at RBS Global Banking & Markets, in reference to the parallel market. "This is actual sentiment on the currency because we can't see the actual sentiment on the currency in the spot market because it's so heavily manipulated."

The Central Bank of Argentina actively intervenes in the forex market to gradually weaken the peso to help exporters. The peso was recently quoted trading at ARS4.1026/dollar on interbank markets by ICAP Plc, bringing its year-to-date loss to 3.1%.

The parallel rate is the difference between the purchase price of a local stock or bond in pesos and the implied exchange rate when that asset is sold offshore for U.S. dollars. Rates can vary considerably depending on the liquidity of the security used in the transaction, which is known as the blue-chip swap.

The trade is a perfectly legal way for individuals and businesses to get money out of Argentina, though at a substantial premium.

After reaching levels above ARS4.40/dollar in May, parallel rates have firmed to around ARS4.25 today. Traders attributed the narrowing to government intervention in the bond market and renewed investor appetite for emerging market assets following recent steps to help heavily indebted Greece.

Still, the respite could prove short lived amid doubts about economic policy after October's presidential election. President Cristina Kirchner is expected to win a second term.

"It's obvious that the market believes in, and is prepared to pay for, a bigger gap. The government's fire power means that its interventions" counter the pressure on the parallel rate, said a local trader who asked not to be named.

Argentines still see the dollar as a benchmark currency given their country's long history of financial crisis and violent devaluations. The government has pledged a stable peso this year, with an average exchange rate of around ARS4.10/dollar.

"It doesn't impact the real economy and isn't a concern," Deputy Economy Minister Roberto Feletti told reporters last week when asked about the parallel market.

But the parallel rate to some degree reflects investor expectations that a weaker peso is in the cards as well as skepticism that Kirchner will adopt more orthodox policies to tame rampant inflation.

Most private-sector estimates put annual inflation above 20% due to excessive fiscal spending, an overheated economy and an expanding money supply. Inflation as measured by the government's consumer price index was 9.7% at the end of May.

The central bank's weakening of the peso at a slower rate than inflation has caused the local currency to appreciate in inflation-adjusted terms versus the dollar, to the detriment of some exporters.

But a faster nominal depreciation of the peso would only aggravate inflation and capital flight.

Indeed, a measure of capital flight tracked by the central bank rose to $3.68 billion in the first quarter, from $2.24 billion in the previous quarter.

Trading volumes attributed to the blue-chip swap have dwindled to between $30 million and $50 million a day from more than $200 million two years ago due to a crackdown by regulators, said a trader who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

Among other measures aimed at discouraging the trade, the central bank in 2008 required that investors who buy domestic securities have to wait at least three days before selling them offshore.

"The only reason why people are afraid of talking about this is the... government is trying to stop it. But there is nothing illegal about buying and selling bonds," he said.

title: DJ Argentina's Alfonsin To Focus On Inflation, Peso If Elected - Adviser
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Argentina's leading opposition presidential candidate, Ricardo Alfonsin, would focus on fighting double-digit inflation and preventing the peso from appreciating if elected, a top adviser said Thursday.

"Inflation is creating a lot of problems," Adrian Ramos, Alfonsin's chief economic adviser, said in an interview.

Alfonsin would use a "multiple anchor strategy" to gradually reduce inflation through a combination of fiscal, monetary and tax policies, he said.

Argentina holds presidential and congressional elections Oct. 23. Alfonsin, a congressman from the Union Civica Radical party, is likely to be the top challenger to incumbent President Cristina Fernandez, if she runs.

Ramos said inflation is pummeling the poor and making it hard for investors to make long-term decisions. He also described the peso's inflation-adjusted appreciation as "unsustainable."

To help local exporters, Argentina's central bank often intervenes in currency markets to gradually weaken the peso against the U.S. dollar. So far this year, the peso has lost about 2.8% versus the dollar, following a 4.5% slide last year. But this nominal depreciation contrasts with annual inflation that most economists say is well above 20%.

Soaring inflation and the crawling depreciation have led to a de facto 15% appreciation in the currency, Ramos said.

The peso was recently quoted by Thomson Reuters as trading at ARS4.0925 to the dollar on interbank markets.

Ramos said tackling inflation would require restoring credibility at the national statistics agency, Indec.

The veracity of Indec's data has been questioned ever since President Fernandez's husband and predecessor, Nestor Kirchner, reorganized the agency in early 2007.

Kirchner replaced many civil servants with political appointees and Indec's statistics soon began diverging from private-sector estimates, leading analysts to conclude that Indec manipulates economic data for ulterior motives.

Indec officials have repeatedly denied the charges.

Ramos said another Alfonsin priority would be ensuring that Argentina has access to global capital markets.

"We won't necessarily tap capital markets, but apart from the actual decision to issue debt, we need to have the ability to do so," he said.

Ramos indicated Alfonsin might also use the central bank's international reserves to make debt payments.

"There's no written dogma saying that they can't be used," Ramos said. "But it depends on the circumstances. title: DJ Argentina Slams Brazilian Retaliation In Trade Dispute
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Argentina lashed out against its top trading partner Thursday, after Brazil slapped retaliatory trade barriers on Argentine auto parts and vehicle imports.

"This kind of behavior is an attack on the normal flow of communication between the two largest members of the Mercosur [trade block]," Industry Minister Debora Giorgi said in a statement Thursday.

The Mercosur customs union includes Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay as full members.

Brazil's move flies in the face of "the commitments made by the two presidents to balance bilateral trade and achieve peaceful industrialization between two countries," Giorgi said.

On May 10, Brazil changed auto imports from "automatic" licensing to "nonautomatic" licensing, which can result in delays at the border for up to 60 days while the country processes the corresponding paperwork, according to a Brazilian government source.

The move by Brazil, the world's fourth-largest automobile market, appears targeted at Argentina, the leading source of vehicle imports to Brazil. More than 50% of all imported cars sold in Brazil are shipped from Argentina, according to car maker association Anfavea.

Brazil's measures will affect 50% of the bilateral trade between Argentina and Brazil, Giorgi said.

Argentina is especially incensed by Brazil springing the measures on them by surprise.

"When Argentina imposed the nonautomatic licences on 200 goods last February, the government informed its Brazilian peers 10 days before the official announcement," Giorgi said.

Almost 24% of the goods, calculated by value, imported from Brazil face import barriers from Argentina, local economic research firm Abeceb.com said in a report Thursday.

Argentina has stepped up import barriers to protect local industry and preserve its still hefty trade surplus.

Argentina's attempts to block Brazilian imports during the global crisis in 2009 also provoked a trade spat between the two South American nations. Brazil retaliated with similar measures against Argentine goods, mainly agricultural products and car parts.

In the end, diplomacy prevailed and commerce between the two neighbors has since prospered, though Argentina ran a trade deficit of more than $4 billion with Brazil in 2010, according to Abeceb.com.

Brazil's latest trade measures affect one of Argentina's largest manufacturing sectors that has benefited in recent years from government financial support as well as strong demand for vehicles and parts in Brazil. Abeceb.com said that 80% of Argentina's vehicle exports and 65% of the auto part exports go to Brazil, with about $7 billion worth of goods in play.

Another significant issue affecting bilateral trade are the steep gains in Brazil's currency relative to the dollar lately. At the same time, Argentina's central bank has intervened heavily to keep the peso trading within a tight band relative to the greenback.

"It would appear that a strong real is feeding into cheaper imports, which are putting domestic Brazilian firms under pressure," Win Thin, head of emerging markets strategy at Brown Brothers Harriman, said in a note.

"It's clear that policy makers are reacting to complaints from domestic auto-parts manufacturers that are getting squeezed by the strong real. Exports have gotten more expensive, while domestic sales are getting squeezed by cheaper imports," Thin wrote.

The strong real, together with high labor, materials and transportation costs, have made imported automobiles more attractive to Brazilian consumers. More than 20% of cars sold in Brazil are imported, up from 7% just five years ago.

title: Argentina Central Bank  Steps Up  Forex Intervention  On Soy Harvest
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--The Central Bank of Argentina has stepped up its intervention in the foreign-exchange market to prevent the peso from strengthening amid an influx of U.S. dollar inflows from the country's soybean harvest.

"Last week and the first days [of this week], we are seeing average daily operating levels of $100 million. That is probably going to increase in coming weeks," Carlos Lizer, director at local brokerage Puente, said in reference to the central bank's intervention.

"As of now, the central bank is surely going to have a more important presence in the market," he said.

The central bank frequently intervenes in the currency market to keep the peso trading within a tight band relative to the U.S. dollar, but with a depreciating bias to help domestic exporters.

The central bank aims to purchase $12.5 billion in dollars in the exchange markets this year to build its reserves and weaken the peso. In the first quarter, it bought about $2.7 billion, including $1.4 billion in March alone.

Those dollar purchases are set to rise in the coming weeks as grain exporters repatriate the proceeds of their sales from the current soy harvest that runs from March to July.

This year through April 8, grain companies repatriated $5.33 billion, according to Ciara-Cec, an industry trade group that represents grain exporters and edible oil producers.

As of Thursday, farmers had harvested about 45% of the estimated 49.2 million metric tons of soybeans they are expected to produce this season, according to the Buenos Aires Cereals Exchange.

"The central bank is now buying close to the daily equivalent of soybean sales," Gustavo Quintana, a forex trader at Lopez Leon Brokers, said. "In recent days, it has been buying more than $100 million a day."

The peso was quoted by Thomson Reuters closing at ARS4.0675/dollar on interbank markets Thursday, bringing its year-to-date loss against the greenback to 2.2%, following a 4.5% decline in 2010.

President Cristina Fernandez's administration, which heavily influences the Central Bank of Argentina, has set an average exchange-rate target of around ARS4.11 and a year-end rate of ARS4.15 for 2011.

The central bank's so-called managed float of the peso has allowed Argentina to buck the trend of currency appreciation in several of its top trading partners in South America during the last two years.

Brazil's real has firmed about 5.4% versus the dollar so far this year, even in the face of a growing number of capital controls put in place by Brazilian policy makers. Chile has had more success than Brazil in taming its currency, with Chile's central bank managing to weaken the Chilean peso 1.1% after it appreciated 7.8% in 2010.

However, the expansion of the money supply as a direct result of the Central Bank of Argentina's foreign-exchange policy is contributing to inflation that most private-sector economists say has become anchored north of 20%.

A central bank spokesman wasn't immediately available for comment.

The central bank has been careful to limit the peso's gradual slide to avoid fanning inflation even more by making imported goods more costly.

Greater private-sector demand for dollars closer to general elections in October should help the central bank meet its $12.5 billion target without overshooting, said Lizer, who thinks the peso will likely end the year slightly weaker than official forecasts.

"We estimate the dollar at ARS4.25 to ARS4.30 and an average of...ARS4.15 to ARS4.20," he said.

title: DJ Argentina To Keep Capital Controls In Place--Minister
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Argentina has no plans to lift capital controls any time soon as developing nations struggle to contain the destabilizing effects of a world awash in liquidity, according to a top government minister.

"We have controls on short-term capital flows, speculative capital. We are going to keep them," Economy Minister Amado Boudou told Dow Jones Newswires at the sidelines of an event Friday night.

For years, Argentina has required that foreigners deposit 30% of any financial investments they bring into the country in a zero-interest account at the central bank for a year.

Argentine policymakers say those controls have been instrumental in keeping hot foreign money out of the country. Critics say it has discouraged foreign investment in the country's tiny domestic capital market.

The low interest rates in developed countries and lax monetary policy at the Federal Reserve have spurred investors to pour their money into commodities and the higher-yielding financial assets of fast-growing economies in Asia and Latin America.

That wave of speculative capital has led to the rapid appreciation of a number of emerging-market currencies, with serious implications for global trade.

In Latin America, Brazil has steadily expanded capital controls to halt the appreciation of the real and its detrimental effect on exporters, while Chile's central bank in January launched a $12 billion currency intervention program aimed at weakening the peso.

Argentina has enjoyed considerable success in weakening its currency even as grain exporters who are enjoying high prices repatriate billions of dollars of proceeds from the sale of their crops.

However, the Central Bank of Argentina's managed float of the peso with a bias toward depreciation has come at the cost of greatly expanding the money supply as the monetary authority prints pesos to sop up those incoming dollars.

A booming economy that is widely expected to expand more than 6% this year coupled with an increase in the money supply are fueling inflation that most private sector economists say is north of 20%.

The heavily criticized national statistics agency's most recent reading of annual inflation as measured by its consumer price index was 10% at the end of February.

An International Monetary Fund technical assistance mission is in Argentina April 4-11 to assist the agency, Indec, in developing a new national CPI amid widespread distrust of official data.

"We hope to have a report soon and will look at the possibility of putting into practice a national price index as soon as possible," Boudou said.

The administration of President Cristina Fernandez stunned investors last November by inviting the IMF to help Indec improve the way it measures inflation in a move that signaled a rapprochement between Argentina and the multilateral lender follows years of icy relations.

Fernandez had long vilified the IMF, whose free-market policies in the 1990s, she says, crippled Argentina's industrial sector and contributed to its $100 billion sovereign-debt default in 2001.

The IMF and Argentina have also been at odds over the latter's refusal to submit to a periodic review of its economic policies, a so-called Article IV surveillance consultation, that is required of all IMF member nations.

Boudou will travel to Washington DC for the IMF's spring meeting April 15-17.

Argentina and other developing nations have pushed for deep reforms to the institution, which has historically demanded wrenching economic reforms of countries that have sought its financial aid.

Boudou said recent comments by the head of the IMF to the effect that the so-called Washington Consensus of the 1990s--which called for deregulated markets and privatizations--is a thing of the past are significant.

"It's indispensable that the IMF staff be profoundly changed because that is where the rancid idea that there is only one policy for the world is rooted," he said in reference to overhauling the IMF.

-By Ken Parks and Alberto Messer, Dow Jones Newswires; 54-11-4103-6740; ken.parks@dowjones.com

title: *DJ Goldman Sachs Raises Argentina 2011 GDP Growth To 6.8% From 5.6%
text:
21 Mar 2011 15:03 EDT DJ  Goldman Sachs Lifts Argentina 2011 GDP Growth To 6.8% From 5.6%

BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Goldman Sachs on Monday lifted its forecast for Argentina's economic growth this year to 6.8% from 5.6% following a bigger-than-expected expansion in the economy during the second half of last year.

"Leading and coincident indicators show that activity remained quite strong during 1Q11, and the authorities seem bent on maintaining very strong fiscal and monetary stimulus ahead of the October presidential elections," Goldman Sachs economist Alberto Ramos said in a report.

Argentina's gross domestic product expanded 9.2% last year as the economy bounced back from what many economists say was a recession in 2009. Last year's growth was underpinned by strong domestic consumption and booming trade with Brazil.

However, an overheated economy and expanding money supply have contributed to double-digit gains in consumer prices.

Most private-sector economists say inflation is running at about 25%, while the government said last week that inflation as measured by its consumer price index eased to 10% at the end of February.

President Cristina Fernandez and her ministers have made it clear that the administration has no intentions of cooling the economy.

The credibility of national statistics agency Indec's economic data has been called into question since former President Nestor Kirchner purged the agency in 2007, which led to a sharp divergence between government data and private-sector estimates. By understating inflation, the government can also report rosier GDP figures.

Inflation has become firmly entrenched above 20%, with the Torcuato di Tella University's monthly survey of inflation expectations published Monday showing that Argentines expect consumer prices to rise 25% during the next 12 months.

The Fernandez administration has played down inflationary pressures in the economy, attributing whatever pricing pressures that might exist to the actions of greedy businessmen.

Earlier this month, the government took the unusual step of fining no fewer than three economic research firms for publishing consumer-price estimates that differ from official estimates.

The ability of labor unions to win salary increases equal to or greater than inflation as well as government subsidies to poor, informal sector workers have so far blunted the corrosive effects of rising consumer prices on the public's buying power.

However, exporters, specially in the manufacturing sector, are seeing their competitiveness undermined by rising domestic costs and a relatively stable exchange rate.

The Central Bank of Argentina frequently intervenes in currency markets to keep the peso trading within a tight band relative to the U.S. currency, but with a bias toward a gradual depreciation to help exporters but not so much as to add even more fuel to inflation.

"Beyond entrenched high inflation, the erosion of external competitiveness during 2010-2011 is another thorny issue the next administration will have to face, which, if not properly handled, could end up generating a crash- rather than soft-landing of the economy in 2012," Ramos wrote.
