title: Argentina Tells Uruguay New Import Barriers Won't Hurt Trade
text:
BUENOS AIRES -(Dow Jones)- Argentine authorities sought to reassure Uruguay on Monday that a new set of import barriers thrown up by Argentina isn't targeted toward the neighboring country and won't affect trade between the two.

Argentina's trade secretary, Eduardo Bianchi, called his Uruguayan counterpart, Sebastian Torres, on Monday to explain that imports from Uruguay "won't have problems getting into the country" and offered to set up a bilateral commission to monitor imports, Argentina's production ministry said in a press release.

Last week, Argentina expanded to about 600 from 400 the number of imported goods that have to request a Non Automatic License, affecting items such as luxury automobiles, consumer electronics, and glass and metal products.

That immediately set off alarm bells among manufacturers in Uruguay and Brazil, Argentina's top trade partner. Washington Burghi, president of Uruguay's leading industrial trade group, the CIU, criticized the move in Uruguayan daily El Pais on Friday. In 2009, Uruguay ran a trade deficit of $1.3 billion with Argentina.

Manufacturers in Brazil voiced similar complaints, and Brazilian Trade Minister Fernando Pimentel visited Buenos Aires on Friday to seek assurances that trade wouldn't be disrupted. Following the meeting, Argentine Industry Minister Deborah Giorgi said the expansion of the list of products that require an NAL was aimed at "unfair competition" from countries located outside of the Mercosur customs union, which includes Argentina, Brazil, Uruguay and Paraguay.

The administration of President Cristina Fernandez has tried to boost local industry and job creation through formal and informal trade barriers. The central bank of Argentina also regularly intervenes in the foreign-exchange market to foster a gradual peso depreciation to keep export-oriented manufacturers competitive and protect the local industry from imports. According Giorgi, those policies allowed Argentina to substitute $9.2 billion in imports during the last year and has saved 1 million jobs.

"The NALs have been applied in sectors where the country produces enough to satisfy demand and where there have been investments where it's strategic to preserve their development," Monday's press release said.

Trade between Argentina and Brazil--South America's two biggest economies--has grown tenfold in the last two decades to nearly $33 billion in 2010, although Argentina posted a $3.38 billion trade deficit with Brazil last year.

However, the trade relations between the two neighbors haven't been free of the occasional spat. In 2009, Argentina raised barriers against its top two trading partners, Brazil and China, in an effort to protect local manufacturers during the global economic crisis.

Brazil retaliated with similar measures against Argentine goods, mainly agricultural products and car parts. In the end, diplomacy prevailed and commerce between the two neighbors has since prospered, helping to fuel steep growth. Exports to Brazil have helped to underpin Argentina's booming economy, which President Fernandez said Friday expanded 9.1% last year.

Argentina is a major buyer of Brazilian tractors, automobile parts and iron ore, while Brazil imports large quantities of automobiles from Argentina and buys about 90% of its neighbor's wheat exports.

Trade barriers have also angered China in the past, and it retaliated by refusing to import Argentine soyoil for six months in 2010. That spat was eventually smoothed over, with China resuming soyoil imports and pledging to loan Argentina about $9.5 billion to upgrade its railway network and buy Chinese-made railroad equipment.

However, Argentina has continued to take actions to protect local manufacturers against Chinese imports. On Thursday, Giorgi signed a decree renewing antidumping measures against Chinese-made air-conditioning units.

-By Shane Romig, Dow Jones Newswires; 54-11-4103-6740; shane.romig@dowjones.com [ 02-21-11 2037ET ]

title: DJ Argentina Prepared To Recognize $9B Paris Club Debt - Report
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Argentina is prepared to recognize that it owes the Paris Club of sovereign creditors nearly $9 billion, but will seek a repayment period of up to six years, local daily Pagina 12 reported on Wednesday.

Citing unnamed government sources, Pagina 12 said the administration of President Cristina Fernandez will focus on obtaining favorable repayment terms, five to six years compared to the 18 months demanded by the Paris Club, rather than disputing the amount it owes.

The $9 billion includes unpaid principal on loans as well as interest and penalties accrued after Argentina defaulted on its debts with private and sovereign creditors in 2001, according to the paper, which is close to the government.

Economy Ministry officials weren't available for comment.

Finance Secretary Hernan Lorenzino is leading a technical mission to Paris this week to hammer out an agreement on the total amount Argentina owes the Paris Club.

Economy Minister Amado Boudou said Monday that he was optimistic that a repayment plan could be reached by June.

Argentina's outstanding debt was $6.87 billion at the end of 2009, according to the Paris Club's annual report for that year. Most of that is owed to Germany, Italy, Japan, the U.S. and the Netherlands.

Settling its debts with the informal group of creditor nations would reopen Argentina's access to financing and loan guarantees provided by the international financing agencies of Paris Club members.

The Fernandez administration appears to have softened earlier demands that a deal include the forgiveness of penalties and interest. Argentina has already won a major concession from the club, which waived its long standing requirement that the International Monetary Fund participate in the process. Argentina had bitterly opposed the intervention of the IMF in any debt talks with the club.

However, Argentina might have a difficult time convincing the club that it should be granted a lengthy repayment schedule given its economy grew an estimated 9% last year and the government's ability to tap the central bank's $52 billion in foreign exchange reserves to pay debt.

Earlier this month the Economy Minister borrowed $7.5 billion of reserves from the central bank to pay private creditors.

Coloring the negotiations are general elections in October, in which Fernandez is widely expected to seek a second four-year term. With that in mind, the administration might be unwilling or unable to take on significant new debt servicing commitments at the same time it ramps up spending on infrastructure projects and social programs ahead of the elections.

BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Argentina's industrial output likely expanded at a brisk pace in November as manufacturers benefited from buoyant domestic demand and exports, according to economists.

"The industrial sector continues to be supported by solid external demand, particularly from Brazil. But its competitiveness has been gradually eroded by the fact that costs are growing faster than the nominal depreciation of the peso," Goldman Sachs economist Alberto Ramos said in a note.

The national statistics agency, Indec, is expected to report that industrial production rose 8.1% from November 2009, according to the median forecast of nine economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires.

Indec is scheduled to release its report on Friday at 2 p.m. EST.

Local industry is benefiting from an economy that the government says will expand 9% this year. Argentina's largest trading partner, Brazil, is also a key export market for manufactured goods.

The automobile industry, a key manufacturing segment, produced 76,813 vehicles last month, a 36% increase from the year-ago period. Exports rose 26.4% on the month to 49,740 units.

At the same time that manufacturers are seeing robust demand for their products, they also face what many economists say is double-digit inflation that is pushing up input and labor costs. Earlier this year, unions in many sectors negotiated salary increases of between 20% and 40%.

Indec reported Wednesday that annual inflation as measured by the consumer price index was 11% at the end of November, compared to private-sector estimates of well over 20%.

The credibility of Indec's economic statistics has been called into question since former President Nestor Kirchner made personnel changes at the agency in 2007.

Consumer prices will likely rise even more in 2011, with the latest monthly survey of inflation expectations published on Wednesday by the respected Torcuato di Tella University showing Argentines expect consumer prices to rise 30% during the next 12 months.

For exporters, rising domestic costs haven't been fully offset by the exchange rate. The peso has depreciated just 4.5% versus the U.S. dollar so far this year due in large part to the Central Bank of Argentina's regular intervention in the foreign exchange market aimed at gradually weakening the local currency.

Indeed, many economists see a stable exchange rate as one of the few mechanisms keeping inflation from accelerating even further in the face of profligate government spending, a consumer spending boom fed by wage rises, and a central bank that has aggressively increased the money supply.

title: Argentina Could Be Dragged Into  Forex  Fight On Inflation, Brazil
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Argentina has largely sat on the sidelines of the so-called global currency war thanks to capital controls and its closely managed float of the peso, but rampant domestic inflation and moves by its biggest trading partner, Brazil, to limit the appreciation of the real could soon pull it into the fray.

Central Bank of Argentina President Mercedes Marco del Pont said earlier this week that capital controls requiring foreigners to deposit 30% of any financial investments they bring into the country in a zero-interest account at the central bank for 12 months have been instrumental in keeping hot foreign money at bay.

"We are very calm because what the central bank continues to buy everyday as it accumulates reserves are commercial dollars, dollars from foreign trade. Speculative capital still hasn't shown up in Argentina," she said in prepared remarks at the Senate.

Argentina's checkered economic history has also served to discourage both financial and direct investment in the country. Argentina took a hard line with creditors following its default on about $100 billion of sovereign debt in 2001, offering just 33 cents on the dollar in two debt swaps in June this year and in 2005. Like Nestor Kirchner, her recently deceased husband and predecessor as Argentina's head of state, President Cristina Fernandez has also voiced little faith in private enterprise and pursued statist economic policies of price controls and heavy government spending.

The low interest rates in developed countries and lax monetary policy at the Federal Reserve have spurred investors to dump U.S. securities in favor of commodities and the higher-yielding financial assets of fast-growing economies in Asia and Latin America.

That wave of speculative capital has led to the rapid appreciation of emerging-market currencies, with serious implications for global trade.

Leaders of G-20 nations, in a summit in South Korea that wrapped up Friday, pledged to move toward more market-determined exchange-rate systems and avoid competitive currency devaluations.

The Central Bank of Argentina regularly intervenes in foreign-exchange markets to foster a gradual peso depreciation to keep export-oriented manufacturers competitive and protect the local industry from imports.

Currently trading around ARS3.9625 to the dollar, the peso has weakened nearly 13% against the greenback since the start of 2009. President Cristina Fernandez's 2011 budget proposal assumes an exchange rate of ARS4.10 vs. the dollar at the year.

However, Mercedes del Pont faces an increasingly difficult balancing act of counteracting the natural tendency of the peso to appreciate amid massive inflows of dollars from soybean and cereal exports, while at the same time trying to keep inflation from accelerating if the peso were to slide too much.

For exporters, the gradual weakening of the peso coupled with the appreciation of Brazil's real have proven to be a boon. Exports to Brazil grew 36% on the year to $10.5 billion in the January-September period, led by shipments of industrial goods like automobiles, which surged 42% to $7.28 billion, according to national statistics agency Indec. Even so, Argentina posted a trade deficit of $2.18 billion with Brazil in the first nine months of the year.

The real has gained more than 30% against the dollar since early 2009, leading Brazilian policy makers and industry executives to express concern in recent months that a strong currency will hurt exports.

In October, Brazil raised its financial operations tax on foreign investment in fixed-income securities and a separate tax on margin deposits for derivatives transactions in an effort to curb investment inflows. Central Bank of Brazil Deputy Governor Luiz Awazu said on Nov. 2 that additional measures might be necessary.

For Enrique Mantilla, president of exporters association CERA, exchange rates are less of a concern to exporters than the strength of the Brazilian economy and galloping inflation in Argentina that is pushing up operating costs.

"What is most important is that Brazil grows," he said in a telephone interview. "Inflation needs to be better controlled. The rate of inflation today is bad."

According to Indec, Argentina's annual inflation was 11.1% at the end of October. However, private sector economists say inflation is actually more than double the official rate as a result of heavy government spending, a booming economy that could grow 9% this year and hefty wage increases negotiated by unions. The respected Torcuato Di Tella university's recent monthly poll showed that Argentines expect annual inflation of 30% during the next 12 months.

The Fernandez administration, which blames inflation on greedy businessmen and supply bottlenecks resulting from a lack of private investment, regularly denies accusations that it manipulates Indec data.

Compared to its main trading partners, Argentina's wages continue to be "competitive," Marco del Pont told senators.

Morgan Stanley economist Daniel Volberg said inflation is slowly eroding the competitiveness that Argentine exporters have enjoyed from a weak nominal exchange rate and Brazil's strong real.

"There's a question mark about whether Brazil is going to see a weaker currency. But if they do, depending on the magnitude of the weakness, it could have important repercussions for Argentina both for industrial exporters and also for those industries that have been helped by the weak exchange rate regime to give them protection from import competition," he said in an interview.

-By Ken Parks, Dow Jones Newswires; 54-11-4103-6740, ken.parks@dowjones.com

Mercedes Marco del Pont has said those mechanisms were adopted as public policies by emerging markets and give Argentina autonomy in the globalized world. [ID: nN02222834]

Marco del Pont said the central bank's role will be key given the global context "where capital flows are provoking a lot of damage -- not only creating a bubble effect but also appreciating currencies."

title: ANALYSIS-Inflation casts cloud over modest Argentine rebound
text:
* Inflation expected to speed to 20 pct as growth picks up

* Central banker seen backing state spending, depreciation

* Price rises hit president's support base hardest

By Helen Popper

BUENOS AIRES, Feb 10 (Reuters) - Argentines may have tolerated inflation of 20 percent when the economy was booming, but with only modest growth seen this year, rising prices look set to aggravate President Cristina Fernandez's economic woes.

In a nation of steak lovers, the surge in beef prices is making headlines and economic analysts are warning of a more generalized spike in inflation. Any such spike will likely fuel pay rise demands and take its toll on Fernandez's support base among the poor.

Her appointment of a pro-government economist, Mercedes Marco del Pont, to head the central bank earlier this month suggests Fernandez is determined to press on with expansionist policies whatever the inflationary cost.

"We've left the wolf to look after the sheep. (Marco del Pont) talks about devaluing the peso, increasing the money supply and she has played down the inflationary problem ... it sends a horrible message," said Nicolas Salvatore, an economist from the University of Buenos Aires.

Some analysts fear a weaker peso <ARSB=> and cheaper credit would make for an inflationary cocktail in Latin America's No. 3 economy, where prices rose by an estimated 15 percent in 2009 even as the economy slowed following a six-year boom.

Most private surveys expect a tentative recovery of 3 percent or 4 percent growth this year to be accompanied by inflation of about 20 percent.

INDEC, the official statistics bureau which is widely seen as underreporting inflation over the past three years, said prices rose 7.7 percent last year.

Economy Minister Amado Boudou has dismissed the surge in steak prices as "an adjustment of relative prices," saying livestock shortages were due to recent rains that meant ranchers were leaving animals out to graze. For full story, see[ID:nN02139634]

"I don't see an inflationary process in Argentina," he told the Pagina12 daily in an interview on Monday.

But powerful trade union leader Hugo Moyano, a close government ally, said inflation is "a reality no one can deny," raising the specter of tensions over consumer prices.

CENTRAL BANK

Marco del Pont replaces former central bank chief Martin Redrado, who Fernandez sacked earlier this month because he opposed her plan to use $6.6 billion in foreign currency reserves to help pay this year's rising debt obligations.

The plan, which critics called inflationary because it would have let the government maintain high levels of public spending, was blocked by the courts. But the government is lobbying to resuscitate the plan by winning support in Congress. [ID:nN08146410]

With a close ally installed at the central bank, Fernandez may be able to tap the currency reserves after all, which would further increase the money supply.

If former Central Bank President Martin Redrado did little to stem soaring prices -- the monetary authority does not set a benchmark lending rate or an inflation target range -- Marco del Pont will do even less as she focuses on boosting growth.

"It's likely that the new authorities will focus on a vigorous increase in private credit," Buenos Aires-based consulting firm Prefinex said in a report, adding that it expected government pressure on banks to lend and fewer sales of central bank notes and bills that absorb peso liquidity.

Marco del Pont is expected to continue Argentina's long-time policy of maintaining a relatively weak peso <ARSB=> through daily central bank interventions in the foreign exchange market, to keep Argentina's exports competitive.

January's inflation data is due to be reported on Friday, and analysts expect the official data to only partially reflect a jump in food and drink prices and in tourism expenses over the Southern Hemisphere summer holidays.

Observers also say an acceleration in inflation will make it harder for Boudou to pursue his effort to restore credibility to the INDEC data by gradually narrowing the gap between official figures and private price surveys.

"The only thing an acceleration in inflation will do is widen the gap that was narrowed last year ... and prolong the distortion," said Gabriel Martini, an economist at Buenos Aires consultancy Abeceb.com.

WAGE DEMANDS

Any surge in inflation will pile pressure on the president to hike public-sector wages, pensions and welfare payments at a time when she can ill afford to.

Fernandez faces a widening fiscal deficit and debt repayments of some $15 billion this year -- up to $7 billion of which must still be funded. She will be loath to cut spending in the run-up to a presidential vote next year.

Her approval ratings have dropped to about 20 percent and support for her administration remains strongest among the poor, who are hardest hit by rises in food and drinks prices, which INDEC said climbed 1.6 percent in December.

Rather than sacrifice growth, Fernandez is more likely to resort to the unorthodox price controls, subsidies and export curbs used to tame prices in recent years.

But with her government weakened, she and ailing husband Nestor Kirchner -- her predecessor in the presidency and seen as the architect of her economic strategy -- may find such controls harder to enforce.

Farmers have threatened to resume strikes and protests to demand an end to intervention in the wheat market and business leaders may be more willing to rebel against price watchdog Guillermo Moreno, the domestic commerce secretary.

"Moreno doesn't scare like he used to," said pollster and analyst Sergio Berensztein. "But for as long as Nestor Kirchner doesn't want to sacrifice short-term growth to lower inflation ... I think we'll get more of the same."

title: FACTBOX-Key risks to watch in Argentina
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Feb 5 (Reuters) - Argentina's government is trying to clean up lingering damage from its massive 2002 default and woo back investors so it can sell debt on global markets and ease a financing crunch.

President Cristina Fernandez, whose approval ratings have slipped to about 20 percent, faces another tight financing year but she will be reluctant to put the brakes on public spending in the run-up to a 2011 presidential election.

Here are some of the issues investors are watching:

DEBT SWAP

The government says it will soon launch a swap to mop up $20 billion in defaulted bonds, offering investors a steep discount. A prompt and successful completion of the swap, which has been delayed repeatedly, is crucial for Latin America's No. 3 economy to return to global credit markets for the first time in eight years. [ID:nN04130847]

A positive outcome could let Argentina sell bonds in global markets at lower rates and would reduce the risk of lawsuits by holders of untendered bonds.

If the swap collapses or gets put on hold indefinitely it would likely send Argentine bond prices tumbling. <AR/BONOS> A failure would also worsen a tight financing outlook and could force the government to borrow even more heavily from state agencies or tap central bank reserves.

What to watch:

-- Rate of acceptance by bondholders. Markets will see a rate of less than 60 percent as disappointing.

-- Impact of swap outcome on debt yields and whether they would fall low enough to encourage new bond issues.

CASH CRUNCH

Argentina faces debt obligations of about $15 billion this year, most of which come due in the second half of the year, and for now it cannot turn to global markets for fresh funds.

That will likely mean a deepening of the fiscal deficit, which reached $1.8 billion last year, and could force the government to find ever more creative ways to maintain the primary budget surplus, which measures how much money the government has to make debt payments.

Fernandez sought to tap $6.6 billion from foreign currency reserves to help pay debt, but the courts have blocked the plan. She may try to revive it in Congress, or could look for other funding sources such as central bank profits. [ID:nN28182949]

What to watch:

-- Efforts to revive the reserves fund plan in Congress.

-- Deepening of fiscal deficit as debt payments come due.

-- Creative accounting to maintain primary budget surplus.

PROTESTS, SOCIAL UNREST

A wave of strikes and street protests erupted late last year and demands could increase in 2010, especially if inflation rises and erodes living standards. [ID:nN13365378]

Such protests put particular pressure on Fernandez because her eroded support base is mainly concentrated among the poor living on the outskirts of the capital, many of whom have benefited from hikes in welfare payments and pensions.

The conflicts also reflect splits in the ruling Peronist party and the trade union movement, which have deepened since the government was defeated in mid-term elections last year.

Signs of an economic rebound could help ease unrest, but only if job creation and wage rises outpace inflation.

Farmers remain disgruntled with agricultural policy and more hardline leaders have threatened to resume strikes and protests if their demands for lower export taxes are not met.

What to watch:

-- Resumption of farmer protests, possible impact on key grains shipments.

-- Further erosion of government popularity.

-- Prolonged unrest that could fuel demand for dollars, capital flight. <ARSB=>

-- Any sign government is losing backing of CGT umbrella union and powerful mayors in Buenos Aires suburbs as rival Peronist factions jostle for position ahead of the 2011 election.

INFLATION

Despite a sharp economic slowdown, inflation clocked 7.7 percent last year and private forecasts put it at twice that. As the economy rebounds, consumer spending is picking up again and many analysts warn inflation will surge this year.

Controversy over consumer price data compiled by the INDEC national statistics agency continues. Economy Minister Amado Boudou has vowed to restore creditability to the figures, and the gap between official numbers and private estimates narrowed slightly last year, but that will be far more difficult if inflation picks up.

Brisk public spending is not expected to slow in the run-up to next year's presidential vote, stoking inflation.

What to watch:

-- Gap between official price data and private surveys.

-- Any sudden surges that could hit poor and spark unrest.

-- Public sector wage demands.

PRESSURE ON BUSINESS, INSTITUTIONS

Fernandez's government has nationalized several public service companies and is currently threatening to intervene in leading phone operator Telecom Argentina in an anti-trust ruling against parent Telecom Italia .

She has also appointed a close ally as head of the Central Bank, which might let the government increase its already tight control over the monetary authority. [ID:nN04152202]

Several high-profile court rulings have gone against the government in recent weeks, blocking the use of reserves to pay debt and suspending Telecom Italia's forced sale of its holdings in Telecom Argentina. [ID:nN02246176]

What to watch:

-- Any changes to Central Bank statutes to cut its autonomy.

-- Possible nationalization of Telecom Italia holdings.

-- Government effort to regain influence in the courts. (Editing by Kieran Murray)

title: Argentina to seek G20 measures on policy reversals
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Argentina's central bank chief on Wednesday said G20 members should seek coordinated measures to address potential adverse consequences of a reversal in stimulus policies once the global economy rebounds.

"We'll need to coordinate, for example, solutions for a potential tightening in monetary policies in developed countries on international trade and on capital flows," Martin Redrado, the central bank president, told Reuters.

Finance chiefs from the Group of 20 top developed and emerging economies will discuss the unwinding of emergency economic stimulus packages introduced over the last year when they meet in Scotland later this week.

Near-zero interest rates in the United States, Europe and portions of Asia have helped trigger a massive shift in global asset allocation, with investors favoring emerging markets.

But Redrado warned that a rapid "reversal of (low interest rate) policies could lead to financial outflows" in emerging markets such as Argentina.

Argentine bonds rallied more than 60 percent on Buenos Aires markets in the first 10 months of this year and the country's benchmark stock index <.Merval> gained more than 90 percent in local terms in the period.

Demand for higher-yielding local assets in emerging markets has been so heated that central bankers in other emerging market countries such as Brazil started to contemplate measures to hold back capital.

Brazil last month implemented a 2 percent tax on financial inflows to stem the rapid appreciation of its currency.

While no similar follow-up by Argentina is in the cards, Redrado said the tax was "very important" for the neighboring country. The central bank closely reins in foreign exchange trading in Argentina and intervenes regularly on markets to prevent volatility in the currency.

Argentina, Redrado said, is more interested in the development of financing products such as "liquidity buffers" as an insurance against violent swings in capital flows.

Argentina's economic officials are also expected to meet with representatives of the International Monetary Fund during the G20 meeting and discuss a possible economic review of the country by the Fund, according to local papers. (Reporting by Guido Nejamkis; Writing by Vivianne Rodrigues; editing by Leslie Adler)

title: S&P: Weaker Econ, Fiscal Outlook Could Harm Argentina Rating
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Argentina's government has time to change its economic policies without having to take drastic action, but a weaker economic and fiscal outlook means time is running out, according to ratings agency Standard & Poor's.

"Perhaps the biggest risk for Argentina's rating is that the government might not use the limited capacity it still enjoys for changing economic policies in the coming months," said S&P analyst Sebastian Briozzo in a report published Wednesday.

President Cristina Fernandez's ruling party suffered a major setback in June 28 midterm Congressional elections, which many analysts and opposition politicians have said provides an opportunity for the government to change direction, and drop some of its more unorthodox and interventionist policies.

If the government sticks to its guns, which S&P said seems most likely at this stage, it may not be able to control the worsening economic and fiscal outlook, which, from the agency's point of view, could hurt the country's single-B-minus speculative grade sovereign rating.

"Deteriorating economic and fiscal performances and the continuing lack of access to voluntary debt markets could put additional pressures on the ratings in the future if corrective actions are not implemented," Briozzo said.

The government seems to have its 2009 obligations to private-sector bond investors covered, but there's less certainty about 2010, Briozzo said.

The Argentine government must repay about $13.5 billion in the second half of 2009, of which $6 billion is due to private investors, the report said. The government has plenty of room to tap other government sources of cash, such as the pension system, state-owned Banco de la Nacion and the central bank, while multilateral lenders "could still add as much of $800 millions to the treasury."

For the whole of 2010, the government owes about $13.2 billion, of which $7.2 billion is estimated to be in private hands. It's possible to imagine the government muddling through, Briozzo said, but there are other, more preferable alternatives.

"The government's ambition is to be able to access voluntary markets in 2010, but this will depend on improving economic policymaking," he said.

'Voluntary' refers to tapping investors through the capital markets to raise funding, rather than by turning to 'involuntary' sources within the government system.

Investors will be watching to see whether President Fernandez gives the incoming economy minister, Amado Boudou, a mandate to begin rebuilding relations with international financial markets.

Argentina has been unable to turn to overseas funding since its mammoth $100 billion default of late 2001, and a subsequent debt restructuring in 2005. Investors holding about $30 billion in bonds rejected the offer of about 30 cents on the dollar, and have been fighting in court every since.

Added to that, the government's relations with the International Monetary Fund have soured, blocking a plan to settle defaulted debts with the Paris Club group of government creditors, another obstacle to overseas funding.

Compounding these problems are allegations that since 2007 the government has interfered directly in the government statistics institute, or Indec, primarily to manipulate inflation data. Indec says inflation is running at about 5.5% per year, while private-sector economists say the real figure could be three times that number.

Settling the dispute at Indec would quickly help restore links with the IMF and Paris Club, which would be a "positive shock" for expectations about Argentina's economy, S&P said.

"Despite how emblematic intervention of the Indec has become, making the institute more transparent should not be considered a very ambitious task," Briozzo said. "Reforming the inflation index should be easier now that private sector and official estimates of inflation have started to converge because of the economic slowdown in Argentina."

As well as these concerns over sources of financing, the analyst said there are two other possible default scenarios which have to be considered.

The first is that the government launches a liability management operation to exchange existing debt, possibly of the Boden 2012 bonds, which, depending on the terms, S&P "could interpret as a distressed exchange and therefore characterize as a default."

The second possibility is that the government makes another grab for cash along the lines of the seizure of the private-sector pension funds at the end of 2008.

"Although it is difficult to predict what types of measures those could be, what seems more likely is that these potential actions, taken in a context of deteriorating political support, declining economic activity, and vulnerability to capital outflows, could end up accelerating financial instability," Briozzo said.

"Drastic and unanticipated measures...could lead to a run on deposits and the currency that would set the basis for a default on the government debt, despite the modest debt payments due over the medium term," Briozzo said.

While Argentina may be struggling at home, the improving global economy, particularly growth in China, India and, most importantly, neighboring Brazil, should help.

"If Brazil continues to enjoy [economic] growth, it will improve the regional environment in which Argentina operates and provide opportunities for the country's business sector," Briozzo said.

title: ANALYSIS-Argentine inflation not top worry but still needles
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Dec 30 (Reuters) - Although inflation worries have lost ground to recession fears since Argentina's booming economy hit the skids several months ago, the problem of rising prices won't vanish next year.

Annual inflation of around 20 percent this year is seen falling by between 5 and 10 percentage points in 2009, with one optimistic analyst forecasting a single-digit increase.

Consumer spending and investment are cooling fast as a global downturn breeds caution among everyday Argentines and business executives. Sinking prices for the country's commodities have eased inflation pressures but also thinned the once-padded pockets of the country's farmers.

"While many forces point to a reduction in inflation next year, namely lower global commodities prices and lower activity levels, inflation persistence in the form of wage pressures and the peso's depreciation will still keep inflation high," said Sebastian Vargas, the Argentina economist at Barclays Capital.

Growth in Latin America's No. 3 economy averaged 8.8 percent a year from 2003 through 2007 but is seen slowing to 7.0 percent this year. The economy will grow at much lower rates in 2009, and could even contract, analysts say.

High growth has been accompanied by high inflation, obscured by accusations of systematic data manipulation at the national statistics office, INDEC.

Consumer groups, economists and even some state statisticians have accused the government of intervening in INDEC to under-report inflation, both for political gain and to lower payments on inflation-adjusted debt.

Officials strenuously deny any tampering, but government figures are widely discredited.

INDEC reported 7.9 percent annual inflation through November <ARECI09>, with private estimates near 20 percent.

Marina Dal Poggetto, director of consulting group Estudio Bein & Asociados, expects annual inflation to fall to 12 percent next year from around 19 percent in 2008.

While prices for tradable goods have stagnated, the cost of services -- such as private education and health care -- will rise in direct proportion to wage hikes next year, which she said are unlikely to dip below 15 percent.

"Inflation a little above 10 percent is not a major problem. The country will be focused on other priorities, but we won't have price stability either," Dal Poggetto said.

CURRENCY DILEMMA

One of the factors that could aggravate inflation next year is the continued depreciation of the Argentine peso <ARSB=>.

"Inflation should fall ... but the risk is that the currency depreciates faster than expected or the government pursues a dangerously expansive macroeconomic policy," said Bertrand Delgado of New York-based IDEAglobal consultancy, who forecasts 2009 inflation at between 12 percent and 15 percent.

Argentina's central bank intervenes in the foreign exchange market nearly every day to avert abrupt changes in the peso's value. Local industry leaders want a weaker peso since neighbors such as Brazil and Chile have let their currencies fall sharply against the dollar amid the global downturn.

But in a country hit by a freez on bank deposits and a massive devaluation in 2002, analysts say the central bank cannot permit a steep depreciation without sparking further capital flight -- and stoking inflation.

"If fiscal pressures emerge, one possible way to close a potential fiscal and current account gaps would be to let the peso depreciate more rapidly, which would stoke inflation and allow the government to continue to collect a large 'inflation tax' from the economy," Goldman Sachs said earlier this month.

The people who would pay the highest price in this scenario are the poor, who make up about one-third of Argentina's 40 million people, according to private estimates.

"Rising unemployment and high inflation is the worst mix the poorest segment of the population can have," Vargas said.

title: Argentina Bonds Dn On Fitch Rating Cut; Stocks Dn, Peso Unch

BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Argentine bonds were generally lower Thursday following a downgrading of Argentina's debt by Fitch Ratings, while stocks broke an 11-day run of gains to close lower on profit-taking.

The peso closed unchanged against the dollar as strong demand from exporters seeking to turn their dollars into local currency was balanced by Central Bank intervention.

"Lower economic growth, falling commodity prices and limited funding sources have increased the risk of Argentina facing difficulties in meeting significant fiscal and external financing needs over the next two years," Erich Arispe, associate director in Fitch's Latin America Sovereign Group, said in a press release Thursday.

The downgrade followed the release earlier in the day of gross domestic product numbers that indicated a slowdown in growth. The pace of Argentina's economic growth in the third quarter was up 6.5% on the year, and up 1.3% from the previous quarter, the national statistics agency INDEC said. That follows growth of more than 8% in each of the past five years.

The government also revised upward its second-quarter GDP year-on-year growth estimate to 7.6%, from 7.5% previously.

The benchmark discount bond in pesos fell 4.39% in price terms to close at ARS49 ($14.38). The discount bond is yielding 21.21%.

title: UPDATE 2-Argentina industrial output growth slows in October
text:
(Updates with comment from economy minister, head of industrial business group; adds byline)

BUENOS AIRES, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Argentina's industrial production rose just 2.6 percent in October from a year earlier and fell from September, hurt by a sharp slowdown in the automotive sector, the government said on Monday.

The year-on-year figure came in well below the 4.9 percent median forecast in a Reuters poll of eight analysts, whose non-seasonally adjusted estimates ranged from 2.4 percent to 5.6 percent.

The automotive sector, one of the main drivers of industrial growth in the last five years, grew 6.2 percent in October from a year earlier, but saw output fall 7.8 percent compared with September.

Growth in that sector topped 22 percent in the first 10 months of the year when compared with the same period of 2007.

Several carmakers have started cutting back workers' hours and are negotiating lower wages with unions to try to avoid firing people as demand for vehicles starts to shrink.

The textile industry also took a beating in year-on-year terms, sliding 10.4 percent, while output in rubber and plastics fell 10.8 percent.

Overall factory output fell 1.9 percent from September, according to the government's seasonally adjusted data.

The global financial crisis has started to cool the Argentine economy and analysts are now forecasting a sharp slowdown, or possibly even a recession, next year.

Economy Minister Carlos Fernandez on Monday rejected the possibility of a recession, however, and said growth may just slow from previous high rates.

Latin America's No. 3 economy grew by at least 8.5 percent in each of the last five years and is seen expanding about 7 percent in 2008.

Business executives gathered at an annual meeting of the Argentine Industrial Union, or UIA in Spanish, urged the government to help revive the sector's competitive edge, focusing particularly on the exchange rate.

The head of the UIA, Juan Carlos Lascurain, reiterated that the Argentine peso should be allowed to depreciate further against the dollar, saying "we need to resolve this in light of how other currencies in the region have moved."

The local currencies in Brazil and Chile have fallen much more sharply against the dollar than the Argentine peso in recent months, thanks to near-daily intervention by Argentina's central bank in the foreign exchange market.

Argentina's industrial production grew 5.8 percent year-on-year in September and 9.7 percent in October 2007 <ARECI10>. (Additional reporting by Hilary Burke; editing by Gary Crosse)

title: Argentine business gloomy over government controls
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Nov 11 (Reuters) - Government intervention in everything from Argentina's foreign exchange market and private pension funds to auto factories has heightened business uncertainty even more than the global financial crisis.

President Cristina Fernandez and her husband and predecessor Nestor Kirchner have long used price controls to try to fight high inflation, and businesses tolerated the measures as the economy boomed from 2003 to 2007.

But with manufacturing slowing and consumer spending expected to drop, business leaders complain that the government is focused on arm-twisting companies rather than taking measures to shield the local economy.

"We can't do anything about the international situation, but on the local level the government could do things to prepare the country for what's coming, but all they do is waste time," said an executive at a local bank who asked not to be named as did all the sources who spoke to Reuters for this story.

The Kirchners are center-left leaders who have maintained a fiscal surplus and some pro-business policies, but Fernandez often makes strong speeches against unrestrained capitalism.

The labor minister has asked car manufacturers not to lay off workers as orders sink from their main market, Brazil.

Meanwhile, the agency that oversees agricultural exports has added layers of red tape that have slowed farm shipments.

"It's absurd, it's beyond belief," said a meat exporter about shifting rules that lost him sales to China. He has scaled back buying in Argentina, one of the best-known beef producers in the world, in favor of Paraguay.

Many business leaders are also angry about the government's alleged manipulation of inflation data, but they normally complain about government policies in private because many fear time-wasting criminal investigations.

Argentina's central bank, which spent $2 billion of its reserves in October to keep the peso from depreciating steeply, last week tightened controls on dollar purchases.

Banking sources said the central bank asked banks and foreign exchange houses for more information about big clients and sent official monitors to some trading floors.

The peso firmed last week to 3.3 per dollar from almost 3.4 per dollar as local media reported that Domestic Commerce Secretary Guillermo Moreno had threatened tax audits of foreign exchange houses that did not reverse large orders for dollars.

Reuters was not able to independently confirm the reports.

Moreno is the main enforcer of government price controls, imposed upon companies under threat of fines.

"The bad mood that seized the financial system last week and the outlook for a complete loss of transparency in the foreign exchange market sadly confirm the mistaken economic policy Argentina is now following," said an editorial on Monday in La Nacion, which often criticizes the Kirchners.

JUMPY

Central Bank President Martin Redrado says his priority is to stabilize the currency because Argentines are so jumpy from past economic crises that they could make a run on banks if the currency depreciates too fast.

Fernandez's announcement last month that she would nationalize the country's $25 billion private pension fund system also unnerved the business community because it was a complete surprise and could give significant government control over companies that issue public stock and bonds.

Local bonds and stocks fell sharply after the announcement, which was interpreted as a desperate move by the government as it faces more than $20 billion in debt obligations next year.

However, the bill has met little public protest since the pension fund managers are widely considered inefficient, and it is expected to pass through Congress easily.

At the same time as it announced its takeover plans, the government launched investigations of fraud at the pension fund administrators and installed auditors at the funds.

The government is also in a tense confrontation with private Spanish company Marsans over terms of a state buyout of the country's biggest airline, Aerolineas Argentinas.

Fernandez has met with executives from Spain, Argentina's biggest foreign investor, to send the message that the pension funds nationalization does not mean that Argentina is threatening private property in general.

But the message has not traveled far.

"Business people are asking themselves what is next to be grabbed by the government," said a business sector officer at one foreign embassy. (Editing by Kieran Murray)

title: Argentina  Stks Dn, Bonds Mixed, Peso Up on Govt  Intervention
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Argentine stocks ended the day moderately lower after rising in line with Wall Street in the morning and following it lower in the afternoon.

Bonds were mixed, with most closing lower on continued uncertainty, while the peso inched higher on government intervention.

The Merval index of leading shares fell 0.97% to close at 1,085.87 points. The index was up as high as 3.84% in early trade and was down as much 2.75% in the afternoon.

The early gains were led by steel tube maker Tenaris (TS), which benefitted by rising oil prices, but Tenaris gave back some of that ground in the afternoon to close just 2.6% higher at ARS41.35 ($12.53).

BBVA Banco Frances (FRAN) ended 1.96% lower, at ARS3.50, despite reporting third-quarter net earnings at the end of trade of ARS117 million ($30 million), up 60% from ARS73 million a year earlier.

Bonds were mixed, with continued uncertainty over the country's economic prospects and amid Senate debate of the government's plan to nationalize the private pension fund system.

The Boden 2012 dollar denominated bond rose 0.49% in price terms to the dollar equivalent of ARS154.50. The benchmark discount bond in pesos fell 1.59% to ARS46.50.

The House passed the nationalization bill last week and President Cristina Kirchner is pushing hard for a fast vote from the Senate.

Amid the international financial crisis, confidence is falling and Argentine private sector bank deposits fell 2.8% in October, Goldman Sachs analyst Pablo Mora said in a market note.

"The government's decision to seize the private pension funds...further fueled such loss of confidence," Mora said.

"Unless confidence is restored, deposits are likely to continue falling and people are likely to continue seeking refuge in the U.S. dollar, placing continued pressure on the exchange rate," Mora said.

However, the peso gained a little ground due to government intervention. The peso closed at ARS3.3 to the dollar, up from ARS3.305.

Volume was very low, with the exchange rate set by the monetary authority's intervention, brokerage Portfolio Personal said in a market note.

The government's "monitoring of transactions and the slowing of currency purchases has resulted in the private demand for dollars being temporarily replaced by government activity," Portfolio Personal said.

title: Argentina  Peso, Bonds Dn Despite  Intervention ; Stocks Rebound
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Argentine stocks made late gains to pull the index into the black at the end of trade Wednesday, while bonds and the peso slipped ahead of Thursday's bank holiday, which will see markets closed. Shares moved higher in the last two minutes of trade as the government's Banco de la Nacion stepped in to buy, said a trader who asked not to be named.

The Merval index of leading shares rose 1.12% to close at 1,135.79 points. The index was down as much as 2.56% during the last hour of trade before late buyers stepped in.

Banco de la Nacion stepped in to buy late in the session partly to support battered share vales and partly as an investment decision, said the trader.

With the Merval down from about 2,200 points in June, some investors also did some buying to take advantage of the "extraordinarily low" share values, said Cohen Financial Services Group analyst Jaqueline Maubre.

Yet confidence remains weak due to the international financial crisis and a series of market-unfriendly decisions made by the government recently.

That lack of confidence was reflected in falling bond prices Wednesday after solid gains posted since last Friday.

The government stepped in to buy back its own debt Tuesday, purchasing ARS150 million of Boden 2012 bonds, a trader said. While the government was expected to continue its secretive buyback program, the lack of purchases on Wednesday led to sharp declines.

"No one excepts the government is interested in buying bonds right now," the trader said.

The Boden 2012 dollar denominated bond fell 3.61% in price terms to the dollar equivalent of ARS156.15.

The peso also eased on Wednesday despite heavy intervention from the Central Bank.

The peso closed at 3.30375 to the dollar, down from 3.29125

The Argentine Central Bank on Tuesday made the unprecedented move of forcing currency exchange houses to overturn market transactions that had already occurred as part of its bid to steady the peso, said Hector Blanco, a trader with ABC Mercado de Cambios.

Traders say the inspections are tantamount to currency controls and are a roundabout way of pushing banks and exchange houses to work within certain limits.

A Central Bank official on Wednesday would neither confirm nor deny that it had reversed transactions. He said the bank is simply "trying to guarantee that traders are complying with new rules" issued Monday that impose a minimum three-day holding period on the purchase of stocks and bonds.

Investors had been buying foreign stocks and bonds here and then immediately selling them in New York, where they could deposit U.S. dollars obtained from the deal. This allowed them to get dollars quickly without having to deal with burdensome Central Bank regulations in Argentina.

Argentine Central Bank officials, together with officials from the Argentine Securities Exchange and the national tax agency, AFIP, have been auditing exchange houses and trader operations at banks since Monday.

Blanco said the Central Bank has also been pushing exporters to sell their dollars in the market to alleviate pressure on the peso.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Economic fears hit stocks, debt;  FX  mixed
text:
* Emerging assets plunge on forced liquidation

* Commodities drop hit LatAm markets

* EM stocks fall sharply on the back of recession fears

* Currencies mixed amid intervention

(Updates prices, adds funds data)

By Manuela Badawy

NEW YORK, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Emerging market assets plunged on Friday as investors unwound positions in previously profitable though risky markets on fears of a global recession.

Emerging economies are being hit by fears about the world's worst financial crisis in 80 years, falling commodity prices and the unraveling of hedge fund positions.

Government bonds of emerging economies have lost 27.75 percent of their original price so far this year, and 23.8 percent in October alone, according to JP Morgan's Emerging Markets Bond Index Plus (EMBI+) <11EMJ><.JPMEMBIPLUS>.

Emerging sovereign debt spreads, the premium that investors demand for holding securities riskier than U.S. Treasuries, widened above 900 basis points over Treasuries for the first time in six years, before narrowing to 855 basis points later in the day.

Benchmark emerging stocks have lost 60 percent this year and are down 38 percent this month. Morgan Stanley Capital International's emerging markets stock index <.MSCIEF> on Friday was down 7.8 percent, while the MSCI Latin American stock index <.MILA00000PUS> fell 7.04 percent to levels not seen since August 2005.

"Emerging market valuations continued to violently adjust weaker this week, no surprise given the asset class was the star performer over the past 4-5 years and is now underperforming core markets on the downside," RBC Dominion Securities said in a note.

"The EM de-coupling myth is clearly proving flawed with the key three pillars of emerging market support: liquidity, growth, and commodity prices -- now all simultaneously and abruptly moving in reverse mode."

Commodity prices continued their fall, hurting most of Latin American markets, which have commodity-based economies.

Oil prices <CLc1> fell as far as $62.69 a barrel, a 17-month low to close at $64.15 a barrel, as OPEC's agreement to cut 1.5 million barrels per day of supply failed to halt a price slide fueled by concerns about falling demand in a global economy headed toward recession.

Copper prices were down 24 percent for the week and have slumped over 50 percent since July's record high of $8,940 a tonne. Gold ended up snapping a three-day losing streak, as safe-haven buying emerged on fears that global stock markets were heading into a free fall. Sugar and coffee prices slid to multi-month losses and risked further falls.

The market is seeing "forced liquidation and this money flow has been hitting every commodity," said Bill O'Neill, managing partner at Logic Advisors in New Jersey.

"Even if you have good assets that you would like to hold, such as some commodities perhaps, you are being forced to sell because of the liquidation pressure and margin calls, etc, along with the fact that the dollar is rallying.

"You look at these markets, whether it is agricultural or industrial commodities -- we are not trading on fundamentals, we are trading on money flow."

Investors pulled cash out of equity and debt funds in the week ended Oct. 22, with emerging market sector funds hit hardest, EPFR Global data showed on Friday.

Latin American-focused funds suffered their 20th straight week of outflows, losing a net $134.8 million to redemptions.

Europe, Middle East, and Africa funds had outflows of $189.1 million. Emerging market debt funds suffered losses for the 11th straight week. Outflows totaled $854.8 million. Long-only dedicated equity funds had outflows of $752.6 million.

STOCKS FALL, CURRENCIES MIXED

Peru's stock exchange <.IGRA> closed down nearly 7 percent weaker despite a four-hour trading halt, the latest in a series of stops called by the exchange during bouts of intense volatility.

The IGRA index fell further after trading reopened to close at 6,364.91 points. The bourse has lost some 50 percent of its value since June.

Brazil's Bovespa index <.BVSP> closed down 6.91 percent at 31,481 after touching its lowest level in five years.

Mexico's IPC index <.MXX> shed 4.6 percent to 16,978 points, its lowest since June 2006. Argentina's MerVal index <.MERV> fell more than 8 percent breaking the 900 points barrier, lowest level since June 2004. The index lost 26 percent this week and 46 percent so far this month.

Chile's blue-chip stocks <.IPSA> closed 2.22 percent lower. Chile's all-market IGPA index <.IGPA> fell 2.05 percent, while Colombia's IGBC stock index <.IGBC> lost 5.6 percent, its lowest since June 2006.

Emerging currencies were mixed as some investors liquidated positions, dragging the local currency down while central banks intervened to offset a sharp fall.

Argentina's peso weakened 0.77 percent to 3.2775/3.2800 per dollar <ARS=RASL> in formal interbank trade, its lowest level since the January 202 devaluation. In informal trade between foreign-exchange houses, as tracked by Reuters, Argentina's peso lost 2.38 percent at 3.42/3.43 per U.S. dollar <ARSB=>, its lowest level since December 2002, despite a strong liquidity injection from its central bank.

Brazil's currency, the real <BRBY>, closed down 0.94 percent at 2.327 per dollar even after Brazil's central bank sold about $752 million in dollar swap contracts in a bid to counter a surge in demand for the U.S. currency.

The Mexican peso <MXN=><MEX01> rebounded after four days of steep losses to close 2.1 percent higher at 13.4175 per dollar.

Chile's peso <CHILJ><CLP=CL> closed down 2.8 percent to end the session at 670 per dollar, the lowest in more than five years. Its peso fell 8.7 percent against the dollar this week, bringing year-to-date losses to 25.7 percent.

Colombia's central bank placed "call" options to sell $180 million in a measure to control volatility of the peso <COP=RR> currency, which has weakened 13.64 percent in the last month and is down 17.19 percent against the greenback so far this year. The peso traded at 2,371 per dollar, up 1.94 percent on the day.

title: Argentina  Ctrl Bk  Intervenes  As Peso Dives On Pension Reform
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--The Argentine Central Bank intervened heavily in early foreign exchange trading in Buenos Aires Tuesday as the peso dropped on concern about an expected nationalization of the pension fund system.

Traders cited as much as three big, dollar-selling interventions within the first hour as the central bank sought to contain the peso's decline.

Jose Nogueira of ABC Mercado de Cambio said the central bank had offered dollars for pesos on three occasions to a total of $240 million. Others cited a figure of $150 million.

Nogueira said the central bank offered dollars at ARS3.2320 in its last intervention. But, he said, "that price won't satisfy the market," which dropped as low as ARS3.25 to the dollar in volatile moves. The local currency closed at ARS3.2275 to the dollar Monday.

The last quoted price on the Argentine Electronic Market put the peso at ARS3.2420. Separately, Reuters reported that the peso had initially dropped as far as ARS3.33 to the dollar in the "informal" over-the-counter market.

President Cristina Fernandez is scheduled to make a statement at 5:00 p.m. local time (3:00 p.m. EDT) Tuesday where she is expected to announce a planned transfer of the entire balance of funds in Argentina's nine private pension funds, known as AFJPs, into the state-run social security system, ANSES.

"The news generated uncertainty and currency short-covering," said Gustavo Quintana, a trader at Lopez Leon Brokers.

Quintana said the medium-term effect of the reform would depend on its implementation, but he added, "the AFJPs are very powerful institutional investors that fuel a lot of the trade volume. The market is going to shrink."

title: Argentina  Peso, Bucking Trend, Ends Up After  Intervention
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--After a dramatic last-hour rally that followed repeated heavy interventions throughout the day, the Argentine peso reversed a big earlier slide that had been fueled by retail selling.

In the end, it closed stronger than its Thursday close, remarkably bucking another sharp fall in the currency of its giant neighbor, Brazil.

At the close of interbank trading at 3 p.m. local time (1800 GMT), the peso was at ARS3.2225 to the dollar, a full centavo stronger than the ARS3.2325 level it finished with on Thursday. Earlier in the day, it weakened as far as ARS3.27 as the Brazilian real went into yet another freefall and Argentines began pulling money out of banks.

As the initial slide took hold, the Argentine Central Bank conducted repeated interventions, traders said. Hector Blanco, of ABC Mercado de Cambio, estimated that the monetary authority offered $539 million in total while the actual amount transacted was between $450 million and $500 million.

For most of the day, these dollar sales contained the peso's descent but did not reverse it. Then, traders said, the sudden surge came at the end and was driven not by central bank demand for pesos but by a small number of banks seeking peso liquidity in preparation for a long holiday weekend. The five-centavo jump in the local currency corresponded to a mere $40-50 million in dollar sales, Blanco said.

Long lines were seen through the day at local banks, with many customers switching into dollars. This meant that in contradiction with the wholesale interbank rate, the price for dollars at the retail level ended higher on the day, with the greenback offered at ARS3.27, compared with ARS3.24 on Thursday.

Faced with this worrying sign, the Argentine Central Bank is trying to demonstrate that it won't let the exchange rate be driven by external forces, Blanco said. This is in keeping with Bank President Martin Redrado's promise not to undermine stability in the banking sector.

"They want a gradual depreciation, not fast depreciations to match Brazil's," he said. However, he added that this may not be sustainable, given that the currency of Argentina's biggest trading partner has lost more than a quarter of its value since September amid the massive global flight to quality caused by the current financial crisis.

The weakness in the real and other emerging market currencies puts the central bank in a bind.

On the one hand, it creates a competitiveness challenge at a time when Argentina must also contend with a sharp drop in the international price for its agricultural commodities. But on other hand, it cannot let the peso-dollar rate drop too far because of inflation risks and the historically important role that the exchange rate plays in the confidence of Argentine savers.

Years of past crises have led many Argentines to treat the peso-dollar rate as the single most important indicator of financial stability, regardless of what harm its strength might do to the underlying economy's capacity to generate foreign currency earnings.

-By Michael Casey, Dow Jones Newswires; michael.j.casey@dowjones.com; 54-11-4590 2428 [ 10-10-08 2000GMT ]

title: Darling of Argentine industry, autos see downturn
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Oct 10 (Reuters) - Argentina's flourishing automotive sector is girding for a slowdown as fallout from the global credit crisis combines with high inflation and a local currency that is losing its competitive edge.

Union leaders are warning of possible layoffs in Latin America's third largest car-manufacturing nation, and companies such as General Motors Corp and PSA Peugeot Citroen have cut shifts this month to trim what has been extraordinary growth in production in the last six years.

At the same time, the industrial lobby is upset over the recent sharp depreciation of the Brazilian real, which could make Argentine goods comparatively less competitive if -- as the central bank has said -- the Argentine peso is held firm.

Brazil is the top market for Argentine-made vehicles, so a downturn in the Brazilian economy would also spell trouble.

"We have to look very closely at the availability of credit, especially for commercial sectors ... and the impact this crisis has on Brazil's economy," said Enrique Alemany, president of Ford Argentina, an arm of Ford Motor Co .

"We'll see if we can turn this growth in Argentina's automotive sector into a great opportunity for the future or if it was just a phase and we'll have to shift gears at some point," Alemany told a business seminar this week.

The Ford executive said the Argentine auto industry's total production has grown fivefold from 2002 and will reach a record of 620,000 vehicles this year. Land vehicle exports account for about 9 percent of the value of Argentine exports.

Sales of locally made and imported vehicles, originally forecast at as many as 650,000 units, is now estimated at 600,000 -- which is still a record high.

Dealerships are offering discounts to lure buyers as the rosy outlook recedes.

"The automotive industry's latest figures are negative in terms of slower growth. Uncertainty is causing companies to reduce or suspend investment plans," Juan Carlos Lascurain, head of the Argentine Industrial Union, told local media.

"The very significant currency devaluation seen in our regional partner (Brazil) could imply a serious risk for some sectors," he added.

TOO MUCH INVESTMENT?

The Brazilian real <BRBY> has shed 29 percent against the dollar since Aug. 1, rebounding slightly this week thanks to central bank intervention.

Meanwhile, the head of Argentina's central bank has vowed to ensure demand for the peso <ARSB=> and keep the currency from tracking the real's steep drop. The peso has weakened by nearly 9 percent since the start of August.

Asked how this could affect Argentine-based firms, Labor Minister Carlos Tomada told reporters: "The companies will analyze this, and we'll be watching how this productive process unfolds to see if employment is affected."

Tomada said, however, that the reduction in working hours at some automotive plants was due to decisions made at corporate headquarters abroad, and did not necessarily reflect a deterioration in Argentina's market conditions.

The automotive industry grew 24 percent year-on-year in the first eight months of 2008, compared with a 6.2 percent rise in overall industrial production.

But the sector's growth has slowed. August's output rose 8.0 percent from a year ago and fell 6.6 percent from July.

Meanwhile, high inflation -- which private estimates put at between 20 percent and 25 percent in the last year -- has sparked increasingly contentious wage negotiations.

Most recently, the SMATA labor union kicked off negotiations with car dealerships by demanding an annual raise of 50 percent -- which the dealerships said was completely out of step with current conditions.

Higher production costs are squeezing profits in the industry. But Aldo Abram of Exante consulting group said carmakers should have seen the downturn coming.

"Companies made investments in recent years that I believe were out-of-proportion ... they were clearly banking on growth in Argentine demand that won't come through, and on greater exports to Brazil, which won't happen either." (Additional reporting by Juan Bustamante; Editing by Derek Caney)

title: ANALYSIS-Latam central banks go it alone to curb crisis fallout
text:
SANTIAGO, Oct 9 (Reuters) - Far from coordinating their efforts, Latin American policy-makers will likely continue to go it alone as they seek to stabilize their currencies and prevent the banking crisis in industrialized countries from undermining the health of emerging market economies.

Central banks in Brazil, Mexico, Chile and Colombia had been raising interest rates this year to curb inflation, but may now have to follow Europe and the United States in cutting rates as tumbling prices for energy and food undermine the value of the region's exports and threaten five years of steady economic growth.

While Latin America's government budgets and current account balances are in much better shape than they were a decade ago during the Asian and Russian crises of 1998, the policies and problems of the region's countries are different enough to prevent much coordinated regional action.

"I'm not surprised that we haven't seen concerted action. I'd be very surprised if we get it," said Rafael de la Fuente, chief economist for Latin America at BNP Paribas in New York.

"One reason is that despite the trade ties between these countries, they're still not that integrated," he added. "Most of these are open economies, but they're open to areas other than Latin America ... on the whole."

There is no tradition of policy maker coordination in Latin America, and some say there is still likely bad blood from unilateral actions during past crises.

"Brazil's measures to try to improve competitiveness, and certainly the (depreciation) of the real, has an impact on Argentina. It's raising a lot of concerns in Argentina," said Daniel Kerner, a Latin America analyst with Eurasia Group.

"You don't have the institutional mechanisms of dialogue and revision. The problems each country faces are individual and the solutions are also for the most part individual."

Caught off guard by the scale of the worst global financial crisis since the Great Depression, some central banks ditched U.S. dollar purchases and scrambled to inject dollars into their markets. Even Mexico overcame initial hesitation and defended its currency this week.

CURRENCIES, LIQUIDITY FIRST

"That's the first line of defense," said Igor Arsenin, head of Latin America strategy at Credit Suisse in New York. "They are going to use their quite substantial foreign exchange reserves to try to smooth currency volatility."

Analysts say Brazil's central bank may need to consider halting a series of interest rate rises, and dig deeper into its more than $200 billion foreign reserve stockpile to help keep the real above the 3-1/2-year lows seen this week.

Brazil's central bank has sold foreign exchange swaps and dollars on the currency market and eased mandatory reserve requirements to free up bank lending.

As fears of a deep U.S. recession mount, amid what has been dubbed as the 'perfect storm', Mexico's central bank is also under pressure to relax monetary conditions soon for the first time since April 2006.

Analysts increasingly expect Colombia's central bank to cut rates in November or December, with President Alvaro Uribe keen for lower rates to foster growth which is seen slowing to around 4.0 percent this year from more than 7.0 percent in 2007.

But it is still too early to say whether Latin American central banks or governments will have to take even more drastic measures such as creating money, widening guarantees of deposits, or taking over banks, analysts said.

The spreading crisis forced Chile's central bank into an abrupt policy turnaround last week, calling an early halt to an $8 billion foreign exchange intervention introduced earlier in the year to counter a sharp peso appreciation.

It has instead embarked on steps to inject dollars into the banking system -- currency swaps, domestic currency repurchase agreements and auctions for dollar-denominated tax revenue.

While Brazil, Mexico, Chile and Peru all enjoy investment-grade sovereign debt status, other regional economies could be harder hit by the crisis.

"(We must) rethink the role of international coordination on monetary policy and finance. It is essential to take measures, but clearly in this case we have to be careful," Argentine Central Bank President Martin Redrado told a business seminar this week.

Argentina had already resorted to exchange rate intervention and price controls on goods and services after it was battered by deep economic crisis in 2001-2002 and is now in its sixth year of strong growth. But it is seen as having less flexibility in its reserves and finances. (With reporting by Elzio Barreto in Sao Paolo, Hugh Bronstein in Bogota, Noel Randewich in Mexico City, Lisa Yulkowski in Santiago and Hilary Burke in Buenos Aires)

title: Argentina peso hits three-month low, bonds slide
text:
(Adds bonds, stocks)

BUENOS AIRES, Sept 10 (Reuters) - Argentina's peso fell on Wednesday to its weakest level against the dollar in three months, while bonds slipped as investors ditched riskier emerging market assets.

The peso took a beating as the U.S. currency continued to firm against counterparts around the globe, with low foreign currency inflows from exporters exacerbating the peso's slide.

It closed down 0.57 percent to 3.0725/3.0750 per dollar <ARS=RASL>, in formal trade between banks, its weakest close since June 2.

In informal trade between foreign exchange houses, as measured by Reuters, the peso fell 1.52 percent to 3.1250/3.1300 per dollar <ARSB=>, its lowest level since June 17.

On world markets, the dollar <.DXY> scaled a one-year peak against the euro, its rise fueled by retreating crude oil prices and by U.S. investors cashing out of emerging markets positions and bringing their money home.

"Investors still prefer having foreign currency positions, and covering those positions is continuing to drive up the dollar," said one Argentine trader.

Argentina's central bank intervenes regularly in the foreign exchange market and traders said they expected it to step in to level the market.

On the local debt market, Argentine bonds <AR/BONOS> closed down for a second straight session, falling by 1.1 percent on average due to greater risk aversion amid fears over the health of the U.S. economy, traders said.

Among the day's biggest losers was the dollar-denominated Boden bond, maturing in 2014, which slumped 4.1 percent.

However, Argentine stocks closed with a gain of 0.61 percent, ending a run of four losses.

The benchmark MerVal <.MERV> index closed up 0.61 percent at 1,604.84 points, lifted by energy-related stocks, which rose despite falling crude prices on Wednesday due to a surprise OPEC decision to cut production.

Gainers were led by Tenaris , the world's top producer of seamless steel tubes for the energy industry, up 4.96 percent to 67.7 pesos per share.

title: Latin American  currencies  stage steepest fall in months
text:
NEW YORK, Aug 8 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies staged their sharpest fall in several months on Friday as concerns grew that the slowing global company could further weaken the prices for the region's raw materials exports.

Russia's military action in Georgia on Friday also heightened investor aversion to risky investments in emerging markets, analysts said.

"The ongoing process of the U.S. dollar strengthening in the last couple weeks, combined with the news of the conflict in Georgia, has scared people, increasing risk aversion, weakening emerging markets," said Nick Chamie, head of emerging markets research in Toronto at the Royal Bank of Canada.

On global markets, the U.S. dollar surged Friday, on track for its biggest weekly rise in 3-1/2 years, helped by a slide in oil prices stemming partly from the slowing global economy.

As a result Latin American currencies fell across the region early Friday.

On Friday, Brazil's currency, the real <BRL=> <BRBY> tumbled 1.6 percent, its fifth straight day of losses. Mexico's peso <MXN=> <MEXO1> peso fell nearly 1.4 percent, its sharpest one-day fall in two years.

Colombia's peso <COP=> fell 1.9 percent, Chile's peso <CLP=> fell 1.3 percent; Peru's sol <PEN=> slid 0.9 percent.

Commodity prices continued to fall on Friday also as the U.S. dollar rose, increasing concern about economic growth in Latin America, which is a major exporter of food and fuel to world markets.

Year-to-date, Latin American currencies had posted strong gains this year as central banks in the region aggressively raised interest rates to combat inflation, running at the highest annual pace in several years.

The rate rises drew in a flood of "carry trade" investors who borrow in low interest rate currencies and invest the proceeds in currencies offering higher yields.

Brazil, whose benchmark 13 percent interest rate is one of the world's highest after discounting for inflation, took steps to slow capital inflows as a result.

RED BALANCE OF PAYMENTS

But the lure of Brazilian interest rates is now being undercut by worries over Brazil's current account balance of payments, which recently has turned decisively into a deficit after years of hefty surpluses.

"We are nearing the point when the long Brazilian trade trade will be driven more by prospective exchange rate changes than carry considerations alone, as the risk/reward is increasingly defined by trends and a turn in the balance of payments," said RBS foreign exchange analyst Flavia Cattan-Nasalusky who is based in Greenwich, Connecticut.

Brazil's current account deficit in January through June hit $17.4 billion, the highest ever for the first half of the year since the central bank began tracking the data in 1947.

"The broadening global slowdown carries serious risks for emerging export markets," wrote RBS' David Simmonds. "In Brazil the current account surplus has evaporated despite the positive terms of trade shock from high commodity export prices."

On Friday, the Brazilian real Friday tumbled about 1.6 percent to 1.618 per dollar in Brazilian spot trade.

At the session low the real weakened about 1.8 percent day, the worst one-day drop since March 14.

COPPER POUNDS CHILE

In Chile the peso fell 1.3 percent to trade at 517.50/518.00 as prices for its main export, copper, hit a six-month low.

Peru,also a major exporter of copper and other minerals, saw its currency fell about 0.9 percent to 2.835 to the dollar.

Colombia's peso dropped 1.9 percent to 1,830 pesos to the dollar At session lows, the peso fell as far as 3.6 percent.

Banco de Bogota analyst David Rivera blamed the weakening emerging market currencies on the growing awareness that the U.S. economic slowdown was spreading around the world.

"The market had been counting on that the economies outside the United States were more resilient and data is now showing that is not the case," he said. "As this happens optimism falls in emerging markets."

MEXICAN "SUPER PESO" LOSES SHINE

In Mexico the peso <MXN=> <MEX010> fell 1.38 percent to 10.1275 per dollar, its sharpest one-day fall since July 2006.
