title: With New Bank Rule, Argentina Ctrl Bk Adds More Fuel To Peso
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Having spent billions of dollars to defy wary investors and drive the Argentine peso to a two-and-a-half-year high, the Argentine central bank this week briefly gave it more fuel with a surprise change to bank accounting rules.

When the monetary authority told local banks last week that they would have to count their clients' foreign exchange holdings in their own "global currency position" - making them subject to the same limits - an unwinding of dollar positions ensued.

Accordingly, the peso strengthened by two centavos to close at a new two-and-a-half-year high of ARS3.0175 to the dollar Tuesday, a level it again held Wednesday.

Thursday saw a sudden reversal, with the peso closing at ARS3.0275 to the dollar. But this was still a far cry from the ARS3.19 lows of one month ago, when the peso was going through its weakest moment since 2003 as a bitter farm crisis stirred fears of financial turmoil.

Hopes now exist that Congress will find a face-saving solution to the intense dispute over a grains export tax, ending three months of protests and blockades by farmers and truck owners. But there is no guarantee that the crisis will be resolved. Meanwhile, economic reports, such as one this week showing a 0.3% on-month decline in May industrial production, clearly points to economic damage.

With Argentines still nervously drawing down their peso deposits - and shifting into dollars at the attractive rates the central bank is delivering - most traders and analysts are convinced the exchange rate has become a weapon in the government's battle with the farmers.

"The gain cannot be seen in terms of economics; it's a political phenomenon," said Noelia Lucini, an analyst at Capital Markets Argentina.

The central bank disputes such claims, saying its intervention is about preventing volatility, and claiming it doesn't target exchange rates. At a conference last Thursday, bank president Martin Redrado defended the expenditure of almost $3 billion in reserves in two months, arguing that it would have been "absurd" not to tap its $50 billion war chest to defend the peso during this crisis.

But why overshoot by so much? A rally of the magnitude seen this past month had not occurred since the end of the 2002 financial crisis, largely because the central bank's diligent, daily dollar purchases had stopped the peso from following other currencies' gains versus the greenback.

So regardless of what the central bank says, the market is reading what seems like blatant exchange rate signals. The talk now is that the monetary authority is targeting ARS3.00. And the change in bank accounting rules seems to confirm that.

Yet it's not clear how long this can last without Redrado's institution spending more money or without hurting the financial system. Indeed, the accounting rule also prompted a decline in money market rates and, while this was no doubt also desired by a central bank worried about stress to the financial system, it could also make the peso inherently less attractive to investors and savers. Thursday's one-centavo reversal of the prior days' gains could prove indicative.

As the dollar positions were unwound on Monday and Tuesday and as money flooded into the Central Bank's three-month Nobac certificates - a benchmark peso-based security - their nominal rate fell by more than 350 basis points this week, according to a research report by Barclays analysts.

Before the regulatory change, relatively low implied rates on peso-dollar hedges in the non-deliverable forward, or NDF, market had made the three-month Nobac's 17.6% nominal yield an attractive play, Barclays said.

But after it dropped to 13.48% while the accompanying price jump delivered a tidy capital gain to anyone who had taken advantage of the spread, it was time to get out, the bank's analysts concluded.

"(We) believe the interest rate move in our direction is likely to be short-lived, and prefer to take profits," they wrote.

Initially at least, the local banks' unwinding of both their spot dollar positions and their offsetting NDF hedges helps the central bank - which was exposed in the forwards market due to the locally traded futures contracts it had used in lieu of even more spot market interventions.

But as Barclays analyst Eduardo Levy-Yeyati pointed out, the new phase of interest rate equilibrium - the narrowing in the spread between the implied NDF and the nominal Nobac rates - could give way to new selling pressure on peso securities.

Lower nominal rates means greater peso liquidity and to the extent that those fresh pesos go chasing dollars, the central bank will again have to use reserves to prop up the exchange rate.

Such flight remains a distinct possibility when concerns about political and economic stability remain. Many observers expect voter-wary lawmakers to break their allegiance to President Cristina Fernandez and amend her contested tax bill - a move that should prevent a return of farmer protests. But the process is not going smoothly.

There have been altercations in the plaza outside the Congress, where pro- and anti-government protesters have set up competing tents. Inside the building, pro-government lawmakers in the ruling majority have frustrated opposition counterparts with stalling tactics.

Just last week, a survey by Poliarquia put Fernandez's popularity rating at a mere 20%, while Torcuato di Tella University said its consumer confidence index had dropped to its lowest level since March 2003.

In fact, the farm crisis is only a small part of what's unnerving Argentine consumers and bank clients. Of bigger concern, arguably, is the threat of inflation.

With annual price gains thought to be running as high as 25% - and with surveys showing that virtually no one believes the official consumer price index reading of 9.1% - economists warn that any measures making interest rates even more deeply negative in real terms will further dissuade Argentines from keeping their savings in pesos.

Although he believes the new rules will lead banks to stop offering dollar deposits as an alternative to such peso accounts, Macrovision economist Esteban Medrano warns that savers won't simply go back to peso deposits. Instead they'll put their money in an investment option that Argentines often use at such moments, one of little benefit to the financial system: safety deposit boxes.

-By Michael Casey, Dow Jones Newswires; 54-11-4590 2428; michael.j.casey@dowjones.com [ 26-06-08 1912GMT ]

title: Argentina  Peso Firms As  Intervention  Changes Bets; Bonds Firm
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--The Argentine peso firmed more than a centavo against the dollar Friday, despite an entrenched farm conflict, as days of heavy central bank dollar selling appeared to push currency speculators to change their bets in favor of an even-stronger peso.

The peso closed at ARS3.10 against the dollar in interbank trading, from Thursday's close at ARS3.1125. That marked peso's strongest point since June of last year, and a sharp turnaround from the five-year weak point of ARS3.1825 it hit amid farm-crisis concerns on April 22. To push the peso, the central bank has had to sell some $1.4 billion in reserves, a move traders say is more political than logical monetary policy.

"It's a show of strength, a response to the farmers" who have been protesting a grain export tax hike since March, said Hector Blanco, a currency trader with local brokerage ABC Mercado de Cambio. For nearly five years, the government has regularly bought dollars to maintain a weak peso that favors exporters. Currency traders think this deliberate strengthening of the peso by the central bank is a way to show cereal exporters just who is in charge.

The central bank was apparently not buying peso bonds Friday as it had in previous sessions in a bid to shore up local debt prices, said local fixed-income analyst Noelia Lucini of Capital Markets Argentina.

Still, demand was strong for peso notes, with the price of the Discount rising 2.8% to ARS102.70, with a yield of 10.34%, while the Par in pesos ended 2% higher at ARS33.15, with a yield of 9.65%.

In a report Friday, Barclays Capital said it expects that the Argentina government's offer Thursday night to rework grain export taxes will weaken and splinter farm protests, despite initial farm leader rejection of the new measures.

That's because subsidies for small and medium farmers will make them less likely to protest as time goes on, while the planting season represents a time constraint.

"We find these arguments convincing enough to believe that, after the announcement of the government's proposal, the farmers' conflict will gradually dilute into non-disruptive demonstrations and media rhetoric," Barclays wrote.

Barclays recommended dollar notes, the Discount in dollars and Boden 2012s. The local Discount in dollars ended 0.75% lower at ARS263, while the Boden 2012 rose 0.36% to ARS282.

On the Buenos Aires Stock Exchange, the benchmark Merval Index slid 0.81% on farm-crisis uncertainty to 2,205.72 points. Among losers, Banco Frances BBVA (BFR) slid 5.73% to ARS6.41 in heavy trading, while Grupo Financiero Galicia (GGAL.BA) ended 4.81% lower at ARS1.78.

title: Argentina Markets Slide As Farm Talks Stall;Peso At 5-Yr Low
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Argentine stocks and bonds slid Tuesday on a spike in investor uncertainty fueled by news that key farm talks were suspended, a further sign that disruptive farmer roadblocks will resume next month.

Meanwhile, the peso reached its lowest point since March 2003 to close at ARS3.1825 against the dollar in interbank trading, slightly weaker than Monday's close at ARS3.18. The peso had weakened as far as ARS3.1875 by mid-afternoon, but recovered some ground amid apparent central bank intervention.

In New York, Argentina was by far the worst performer on JPMorgan's Emerging Markets Bond Index Global Diversified, dropping 25 basis points to 585 basis points, for a negative 2.56% return. The broader EMBIGD was 2 basis points wider with a 0.07% negative return. Argentina's 2033 discount bonds late Tuesday were down 1 13/16 at 74 7/16 bid, while the 2038 par bonds were still off 1/2 at 36 even, according to Reuters.

"There's been negative sentiment toward Argentina for a week or so now," said a New York-based emerging markets debt trader, adding that the latest headlines aren't helping. "People need something positive that they can sink their teeth into, and they're not getting it," he added. The credit has also been hurt by recent news that a U.S. federal judge has frozen Argentine bonds with a face value of up to $17 billion ahead of a hearing next week involving investor "holdouts" who rejected the harsh terms of the nation's 2005 debt restructuring.

In the local Argentine debt market, concern this week has come from the sense that "the farm conflict talks are closer to failing than reaching an agreement," said fixed-income analyst Paulino Seoane, also of Lopez Leon Brokers. "That adds to worry that there isn't any real or sustainable measure to contain inflation," which undermines debt value.

Farm group leaders Tuesday stepped up threats to resume roadblocks after a 30-day truce launched on April 2 expires, while news emerged by late afternoon that the day's key wheat talks between farm group leaders and government officials had been suspended.

A three-week farm strike last month led to food shortages in the Argentine capital, and helped accelerate inflation that economists already saw running at 20% on the year. Farmers launched the strike in response to a government increase in soybean export taxes.

The benchmark Discount in pesos neared its record low of ARS100, seen during last summer's subprime crisis. "But yields are at a record now, higher than last year, due to inflation index adjustments," Seoane said. The Discount closed at ARS101, with a yield of 10.35%, while the Bogar 2018, another peso note linked to inflation, fell to ARS134.65, with a yield of 11.45%.

Investors also are concerned about the sliding peso, Seoane added. "It's still not clear if the central bank is going to hold the peso or let it weaken further," he said.

Daniel Bou Kahir, a currency analyst at local Banco de la Pampa, said the central bank apparently sold about $100 million during the final 15 to 20 minutes of trading in a bid to shore up the currency.

Bou Kahir said this week's rise in political uncertainty has boosted demand for dollars from institutional investors and banks, as well as at the exchange house level as individuals seek more dollars and euros.

He said the heavy late-session intervention could put the breaks on the local currency's slide, although it is clear that the central bank is comfortable with a weaker peso. "There is some speculation that it could go to ARS3.20," Bou Kahir said.

On the Buenos Aires Stock Exchange, the benchmark Merval Index, which had been resisting local political noise in recent sessions amid a mild upswing, dropped 2.48% to 2,147.00. Volume was a very heavy ARS342.9 million ($107.7 million).

Among the losers, Tenaris (TS) ended 1.67% lower at ARS88, while Grupo Financiero Galicia (GGAL) slid 5.96% to ARS2.05.

"It's not just the farm sector" and a sliding peso that has shaken investors, said stock analyst Juan Jose Vazquez of local Bull Market Brokers. He also attributed rising uncertainty to some newspaper rumors of a Cabinet shakeup that could replace Cabinet Chief Alberto Fernandez and Economy Minister Martin Lousteau.

title: ANALYSIS-Argentine peso still bucks regional trend, for now
text:
BUENOS AIRES, March 4 (Reuters) - The Argentine peso has become Latin America's great anomaly, holding steady against the U.S. dollar as the currencies of neighboring countries have risen in the past year.   

The government's persistent intervention to sell the Argentine peso and buy U.S. dollars has managed to keep the currency weak, an effort that may have been made easier by high inflation surpassed only by Venezuela in the region.   

The weak peso has helped the government foster an export boom, and take advantage of soaring international commodity prices, to stimulate economic growth and refill its coffers after a debt default and currency devaluation in 2002.   

Growing global inflation pressures may force the Argentine government into letting the peso appreciate to help contain rising consumer prices, but such a change in monetary policy would undermine government's export-led growth strategy -- and some analysts predict instead further nominal depreciation.   

Currencies in Brazil, Colombia, Peru and Chile have hit multiple-year highs against the U.S. dollar in recent months, as the greenback sinks against free-floating currencies worldwide.   

But Argentina, like China and other protectionist countries, intervenes heavily in the foreign exchange market to keep its exports competitive. The Argentine peso <ARSB=> slipped 2.7 percent last year and has traded stable against the U.S. dollar since late December.   

"It could be that the peso should appreciate, that's the theory held by scholars and technocrats," said Fernando Izzo, director of currency brokerage ABC Mercado de Cambios.   

"But the theory doesn't hold in Argentina, where the exchange rate is controlled and moved up and down by the central bank."   

President Cristina Fernandez, who succeeded her husband in office three months ago, touts the role of a weak peso in stimulating "re-industrialization" after a one-to-one peg to the U.S. dollar shut down factories in the 1990s.   

The government has held the peso steady at roughly 3.0 per dollar for nearly four-and-a-half years, mainly by having the central bank buy dollars and then issue debt to neutralize the inflationary impact of expanding the monetary supply.   

As a result, the country's foreign reserves have surged to some $49.3 billion from $10.3 billion five years ago.   

Rising currency reserves are not unique to Argentina. Many emerging market governments are stockpiling foreign exchange reserves as commodities prices boom.   

The hitch is that surging grain and crude oil costs are also stoking inflation globally. And one way for governments to ease price pressures linked to imports is by letting their currencies appreciate.   

EXPORT FIESTA   

Inflation is a stubborn problem in Argentina, where the official annual rate of around 8.0 percent is widely discredited and private estimates go as high as 25 percent.   

Fernandez, like her husband, rejects anti-inflation tactics such as monetary tightening and backs instead unorthodox measures like price caps and export bans.   

"The (foreign exchange) policy is interventionist and protectionist, favoring industry and jobs," former central bank chief Rodolfo Rossi said. "If the peso were allowed to float freely, this would have a huge impact on the workforce."   

Investment bank  Bear Stearns said that strong export-related inflows could overpower Argentina's ability to keep the peso weak without worsening inflation.   

"Unless grain prices fall materially as the year evolves or the public sector decides to save much more money ... authorities will likely be forced to accept at least some nominal currency appreciation this year -- perhaps all the way towards the 2.9 per dollar level," the bank said last month.   

Some other analysts disagree, noting that industry groups are lobbying for an even weaker peso as inflation and hefty salary rises erode their competitive edge.   

They also say the export boom benefits the government, too, thanks to heavy taxes on soy, grain and fuel sales abroad.   

An analyst at Hallgarten & Company consultancy called Argentina's currency regime unsustainable and said a large hedge fund investor like George Soros could try to force the peso to strengthen.   

But Izzo said capital controls and other regulations would make such a move difficult, and Rossi agreed this was not likely but said Argentina should stay vigilant to prevent it.   

One point in Argentina's favor is that the central bank has been making fewer dollar purchases in recent months, and has issued less debt, as the Treasury taps its fiscal surplus to help sustain the peso.   

"That's more genuine because it doesn't imply money injection," said Pablo Morra, an economist at  Goldman Sachs. "The government's policy approach is facing some challenges, but in the very near future I think it can still succeed, particularly if the Treasury helps."

title: Argentina boosts repos to curb 'unjustified' rates
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Sept 17 (Reuters) - Argentina's central bank said on Monday it was stepping up its intervention in the local interbank money market to curb what it termed an "unjustified" jump in short-term rates fueled by global credit turmoil.   

The central bank said it would offer up to 1 billion pesos ($313.2 million) on Monday of seven-day repurchase agreements, double the amount it had offered for sale at auctions during the last month.   

This measure "will inhibit unjustified increases on interest rates for loans," the central bank said in a statement.   

The repos offer an 11 percent fixed annual interest rate.   

Since July, Argentina's short-term interbank lending rates have surged to as high as 25 percent, a four-year record, fueled by instability in global markets, initially sparked in the United States by investments in risky U.S. mortgages.   

The interbank rates were in single digits before the volatility began.   

"The central bank considers that we have significantly reduced the repercussions ... of the strong volatility in world markets," the bank said.   

Instead of auctioning the repos, as it has since mid-August, the central bank said that banks on Monday would be allowed to buy them in proportion to their share of deposits.   

The bank also said it would continue auctions to buy back up to 500 million pesos a day of notes and bills it had previously sold.   

In informal trade between foreign exchange houses, as measured by Reuters, the Argentine peso <ARSB=> was trading 0.16 percent firmer at 3.1900/3.1925 per dollar at midday.   

It was steady though at 3.1350/3.1375 per dollar <ARS=RASL> in formal interbank trade, where the central bank intervenes.

title: Argentina Ctrl Bank  Forex  Policy Questioned At Bank's Event
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--The Argentine Central Bank's two-day conference, which ended Tuesday, featured heavyweight monetary chiefs and private economists, some of whom took issue with their host's unorthodox foreign exchange policy.   

The speaker list included four current members of the European Central Bank, as well as the ECB's former Chief Economist, Otmar Issing, the presidents of the Russian, Indian and Chilean central banks, and the chief economist of the  Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Joseph Tracy. The line-up also included big-name university economists such as Columbia's Joseph Stiglitz, Harvard's Richard Cooper, Chicago's Raghuram Rajan and Stanford's Ronald McKinnon.   

How did Argentina's central bank, hardly a world behemoth, afford the gala event?   

The answer can be found in the Central Bank's balance sheet, in an item that was in fact the focus of a polemical debate in the conference: its foreign reserves.   

Since Martin Redrado succeeded Alfonso Prat-Gay as the Central Bank's president in September 2004, reserves have grown from around $18 billion to more than $40 billion, even after accounting for a $9.6 billion withdrawal to pay off International Monetary Fund in early 2005. Those holdings explain a big chunk of the Bank's 6.5% return on investment, a figure Redrado cited in opening remarks Monday.   

But as some speakers pointed out, Argentines could be paying a high price for this expansion in reserves, which stem from the Central Bank's heavy, daily dollar-buying in the foreign exchange market. These interventions have kept the peso more or less unchanged at around ARS3.00 to the dollar for three years, in line with the oft-stated objectives of the federal government.   

As he always does, Redrado described the policy as one of "reserve accumulation," thus sidestepping the critique that his ostensibly independent institution is following the policy guidelines of the federal government.   

Building reserves, he said, provided a "prudent" buffer against external shocks and volatility, so long as the Central Bank's monetary objectives are met. These targets, defined this year as an expansion in the M2 monetary base of between 11.7% and 18.7%, have been repeatedly attained while the real growth in money supply has been brought to below that of GDP for the first time since the country's financial crisis of 2002, Redrado said.   

But other speakers turned the logic on its head, treating reserve growth as a byproduct of a de facto fix in the exchange rate, not a policy in itself. And this currency fix runs the risk of generating sustained inflation and financial instability over the medium term, some warned.   

"Now, I don't want to offend anyone, but Argentina is targeting its exchange rate," said Stanford University's McKinnon. "They say they have a money supply rule or something like that, but in fact the exchange rate is stable...so, it is as if the money goal was the instrument but the target is the exchange rate."   

By preventing the peso from naturally appreciating, McKinnon said, the Central Bank has postponed the real, inflation-adjusted exchange rate's return to the purchasing power parity it had before the crisis. The continued differential between the undervalued nominal exchange rate and that equilibrium rate has undermined the effectiveness of the banking system, where credit growth is weak, and has left the economy with pent-up inflation, McKinnon added.   

Admitting that he doesn't have "a clean solution" for restoring equilibrium at this late stage, the economist said the delay in nominal exchange rate appreciation had put the Central Bank in a bind.   

It can't simply tell the world it will now allow the peso to gradually appreciate, he said, because "the announcement effect" will attract a massive inflow of "hot money" capital seeking to reap the guaranteed exchange rate gains, he said. As with the problems that China faces with its gradualist yuan appreciation strategy, these inflows would complicate the Central Bank's ability to manage the growth in Argentina's monetary base, McKinnon said.   

As it is, the Central Bank's policy of buying up almost all the dollars coming into Argentina is already creating monetary policy problems.   

Its foreign exchange interventions are paid for with large-scale injections of pesos into the system, which the Central Bank must then turn around and "sterilize" through absorption operations. The result has been an ever-expanding portfolio of short- and medium-term money market liabilities. This creates a constant refinancing treadmill, where the task of maintaining investor demand without jacking up interest rates is challenged by the inflationary environment.   

Esteban Medrano, an economist at local consultancy  Macrovision, said the offsetting issuance of Central Bank securities means the reserve accumulation policy is better described as "reserve borrowing" policy. It's effectively financed by loans from the financial sector.   

The rates paid on the longer-term liabilities are considerably higher than the interest earned on reserves, since Argentine inflation is high by world standards, he noted. The consumer price index is up 8.8% year-on-year in official terms but real inflation is thought to be well above 10%, given widespread mistrust of the government data.   

Medrano said the negative spread between the rates paid on the Central Bank's liabilities over its assets will sooner or later put an end to the profitability helping to pay for events such as this week's conference.   

The only way to stop this vicious cycle, many economists say, is to rapidly revalue the real exchange rate. That can be done via the nominal currency, which would seriously hurt both domestic exporters - whose tax payments form a crucial pillar in the government's fiscal surplus - as well as employers in the import-competing industries that have blossomed in the post-crisis era. Alternatively, the country can inflate its way to real exchange rate equilibrium, creating financial stability that deters both savings and investment.   

But judging from his closing remarks Tuesday, Redrado has no intention of changing course.   

In an apparent critique of McKinnon, who compared Argentina's situation to the better-managed policies of South Korea after its 1998 crisis, Redrado said "simplistic comparisons between...diverse countries...can result in totally erroneous recommendations."   

Citing the Chilean experience as a model, Redrado lauded that country's use of an "exchange rate anchor" in its initial transition to an inflation-targeting regime. He also argued that Argentina's experience showed that "there is nothing more procyclical than an appreciated local currency," which stokes both private and public consumption.   

-By Michael Casey, Dow Jones Newswires; michael.j.casey@dowjones.com; 54-11-4313 1918 [ 06-06-07 2000GMT ]

title: FOREX  VIEW:  Argentina  Peso Seen Weaker On  Intervention
text:
Drew Benson 
   A Dow Jones Newswires Column 
   

BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--The Argentine peso is expected to continue its slide against the dollar in 2007, pushed weaker by continued heavy dollar buying by the Central Bank.  

The Central Bank's latest survey of economists, out last week, sees the peso closing 2007 at ARS3.18 against the dollar, a 3.5% decline from last year's close at ARS3.07.  

That nominal depreciation will likely be more than offset by inflation, which the Central Bank survey sees rising by 10% during the full-year, leading to a real appreciation of the peso this year.  

The Central Bank buys dollars on a regular basis, making the peso one of the least volatile currencies in the region. While there are occasional blips stemming from movements in the Brazilian real and other neighboring currencies, the outlook for the peso depends mostly on an analysis of the Central Bank's capacity to balance the effect of its daily foreign exchange interventions with the effects they have on monetary conditions.  

Officially, the Central Bank says it buys dollars regularly to build reserves, but it is widely seen as a de facto industrial policy, one that is implemented to offset real appreciation from inflation and maintain a relatively competitive peso in favor of Argentine exports.  

Inflation came in at 9.8% last year after jumping to 12.3% in 2005, representing a loss of competitiveness over that time. As of Thursday's close, the peso was at ARS3.08 against the dollar, while reserves were at $32.57 billion.  

Since daily dollar buying pumps pesos into the money supply, the Central Bank must use various "sterilization" measures to reabsorb the excess currency out of the system so as to avoid runaway inflation.  

The extent to which it succeeds in this effort could, in the long run, become a factor in the strength of the currency. If monetary expansion were to get out of control, a loss of confidence in the peso itself could transpire, which could leave the Central Bank facing the opposite problem: a vicious spiral in which rising prices and rapidly falling exchange rates feed off each other.  

For now, though, the monetary authority looks to have the key variables relatively well controlled.  

The Central Bank does not target inflation, but instead sets money supply targets based on M2, which is comprised of currency in circulation plus checking and savings deposits.  

The Central Bank's 2007 monetary plan, presented to legislators last month by bank president Martin Redrado, sets an 11.7%-to-18.7% target expansion range for M2 money supply. That's marginally narrower than last year's 11.7%-to-21.2% goal, and puts the upper-end band slightly below the actual 2006 expansion rate of 18.9%. Even so, it still leaves a wide target for the bank to hit.  

Most observers say money expansion should, much like last year, come in just under the upper end of the target in 2007, closely following nominal GDP growth. It suggests inflation will remain high compared with other countries but comfortably close around the relatively benign 10% figure.  

Still, the Central Bank is not without challenges. One problem lies in the dwindling choices it has for sterilizing the pesos it injects into the system with each dollar purchase.  

With commercial banks improving their balance sheets, the Central Bank will soon be unable to count on one unique source of monetary absorption that has greatly aided its monetary control efforts: a regular transfer from the banks in repayment of discount loans issued during the 2001 and 2002 financial crisis.  

That leaves it with fewer sterilization tools. One option still available if money growth gets too fast, would be to announce another hike in reserve requirements. But that would push effective money market interest rates higher - a politically unpopular move - at a time when an expected slowdown in emerging market economies might not warrant such a tightening.  

More likely is the use of bigger weekly auctions of Nobac notes and Lebac certificates.  

The Central Bank already did so this week with the introduction of a three-year Nobac that pays 2.5% above the 30-day moving Badlar average of Argentine certificates of deposit. A positive market response to that issue suggested that it currently has little to fear if it wants to adopt a more aggressive sterilization program.  

The three-year Nobacs, of which just $25 million were initially offered, drew a record 2.8 billion pesos ($908 million) in bids, prompting the Central Bank to issue ARS324 million in the new notes.  

But such strong results, partially a function of the seasonal boost in liquidity that comes in January with the conclusion of the holiday and bonus period, won't always be possible.  

Demand for Central Bank notes could also dry up, said Sebastian Di Nucci, a portfolio manager in Buenos Aires with FDI consultants, if other investment assets become more attractive.  

"Before stocks and bonds began sliding in May of last year, there were weeks during which the Central Bank struggled to place notes," Di Nucci said.  

If that scenario reemerges, the Central Bank may also have to hike rates to get its Lebacs and Nobacs out to market. Aside from contradicting an official government policy against rate hikes, this could also draw in foreign capital and compromise the exchange rate goals, requiring more dollar-buying intervention and putting the Central Bank on a difficult, accelerating treadmill.  

This threat is one reason why economists see the Central Bank maintaining a relatively lax approach to the M2 goals.  

"The only way to balance all of the policy goals is to come in closer to the upper band of the target," said Pablo Morra, an economist for Latin America with Goldman Sachs in New York. "That will allow them to intervene and sterilize at the lowest cost in terms of interest rates."

title: Argentina  Peso Weaker On  Intervention ; Bonds Mixed
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--The Argentine peso weakened Monday for a second straight session as heavier central bank intervention sent the market a signal that the government plans to maintain a weak peso.  

Meanwhile, bonds were mixed amid steady trading.  

The peso ended the day at ARS3.0775 against the U.S. dollar, weakening from Friday's close at ARS3.0725. The peso's slide "was a consequence of anticipation that the central bank will intervene and not permit the dollar to further weaken," said Carlos Lizer, head currency trader at local brokerage Puente Hermanos. The central bank regularly intervenes in the local market, buying dollars to build reserves while maintaining a weaker peso that favors Argentine exports.  

But stronger demand for pesos from overseas investors seeking locally traded bonds this month gave the peso a sharp boost against the dollar. From October's close at ARS3.09 against the dollar, the peso had strengthened to ARS3.0675 last Thursday, Nov. 9.  

Lizer said he expects that the peso reached a ceiling, and will remain weaker than ARS3.07 to the dollar for the remainder of the year.  

In the local bond market, the price of the benchmark Discount bond in pesos continued to gain ground, recently reaching ARS134.60, up from Friday's close at ARS134.40, while the Par in pesos was down slightly to ARS50.70 from ARS50.80.  

So-called GDP warrants, which were stripped out of restructured debt late last year, were also mixed, with the peso warrant at ARS11.05, down from ARS11.20, and the dollar coupon under New York legislation at ARS38.40, up from ARS38.15.  

Argentina's Economy Ministry announced Friday that the peso-denominated gross domestic product-linked securities will pay ARS0.65 per ARS100 of notional, while dollar-warrants will pay ARS0.62.  

The December payment uses 2005 as a reference year.  

The peso coupon "is paying less than expected," said Alejandro Barros, an analyst with local Banco Piano. Barros had expected an ARS0.67 payment for the peso warrants.

title: IMF raises Latam growth on domestic demand, exports
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 14 (Reuters) - Latin America's economy should expand 4.75 percent this year, up from a prior forecast of 4.3 percent, on firm domestic demand and high prices for key export commodities, the International Monetary Fund said on Thursday.  

But the region with the world's second-largest oil and gas reserves has for the most part failed to capitalise on a doubling in crude prices in the past two years to either boost output or invest, it said in its twice-yearly review of the global economy.  

Brazil, however, is reaping the benefits of long-term investments by Petrobras which have turned a country that had long been an energy importer into a self-sufficient one in 2006.  

Gross domestic product in the region's biggest economy should expand 3.6 percent this year and 4.0 percent in 2007, both increases from the IMF's April forecast, while inflation should slow from 4.5 percent in 2006 to 4.1 percent next year.  

Two weeks ago Brazil's central bank cut its benchmark lending rate by 0.5 percentage point to a 20-year low of 14.25 percent, the 10th consecutive rate cut since September 2005. It is targetting inflation at 4.5 percent in 2007 and 2008.  

"In rapidly growing Argentina, the monetary policy stance has been gradually tightened in response to double-digit inflation but remains accommodative," the IMF said.  

Argentine inflation should be 12.3 percent this year before slowing to 11.4 percent in 2007 while growth is forecast to be 8.0 percent in 2006 and 6.0 percent next year.  

"The use of regulatory counter-measures will need to be supported by a further tightening of macroeconomic policies to contain inflation," it added.  

The IMF urged "adequate foreign exchange rate flexibility" in managing foreign currency inflows and warned that sustained sterilised intervention would have heavy "quasi-fiscal" costs.  

Argentina's central bank buys dollars to build reserves and keep the peso weak for exports at around 3 per dollar while Venezuela fixes the bolivar at 2,150 per dollar.  

Officials in Caracas last month said they were analysing a possible restructuring to cut up to three zeros off the bolivar.  

The IMF openly chided Venezuela and Mexico for low rates of investment in their energy sectors and for only beginning to address governance issues. Both have state-owned energy firms.  

Venezuela, the world's fifth-largest oil exporter, should grow 7.5 percent this year and 3.7 percent in 2007. Inflation should speed up from 12.1 percent in 2006 to 15.4 percent in 2007.  

Mexico, which only recently boosted investment to make up for dwindling output at its largest oil field, should see GDP growth of 4.0 percent in 2006 and 3.5 percent next year, it said.  

Mexican inflation should be 3.5 percent this year and 3.3 percent in 2007 while the current account deficit should narrow to 0.1 percent of GDP in 2006 and widen to 0.2 percent next year.  

Most South American countries should have current accounts in surplus except for Colombia where the deficit should be 1.2 percent of GDP this year before growing to 1.7 percent in 2007 and Uruguay where it should narrow from 4.3 percent in 2006 to 3.2 percent next year.  

Government spending has increased over the past two years across the region and the IMF said it was concerned that not all of it was well targeted.  

Some countries have renewed reform efforts after the financial crises in the late 1990s and beginning of this decade and the IMF urged greater openness to trade across the region's economies.

text:
BUENOS AIRES, Sep 06, 2006 (DJCS via Comtex) --  

The Argentine peso continued to lose ground on the dollar Wednesday, as the central bank bought more dollars to edge the local currency deeper into a three-year weak spot.  

The peso closed at ARS3.1050 against the dollar, after hitting the ARS3.1000 point on Tuesday.  

"The central bank's strong interventions continue," said Carlos Lizer, head currency trader with local brokerage Puente Hermanos. "This is basically in line with our estimate that by the end of the year we'll see a dollar between ARS3.10 and ARS3.13."  

The central bank habitually buys dollars to build reserves and maintain a weak peso that favors Argentine exports.  

The end of the annual soy harvest, which brings heavy dollar inflows from exporters, has made it easier for the central bank to weaken the local currency.  

Wednesday's close marks the peso's weakest point since mid-March 2003, when the local currency slid as far as ARS3.1250 against the dollar.  

In the local bond market, prices were "mostly down, possibly on some profit taking after yesterday," said Diego Zavaleta, an analyst with local Besfamille Sociedad de Bolsa. Volume was weak for a second day, he added.  

Among sliders, the benchmark Discount in pesos was down to ARS126.50 from ARS126.90, while the Par in pesos was down to ARS49.30 from ARS49.80.  

Earlier Wednesday, the Economy Ministry called an auction for $500 million in new seven-year, dollar-denominated BONAR VII bonds.  

Bids for the new 2013 BONAR VII bonds will be accepted until 2 p.m. (1700 GMT) Thursday, with an issue on Sept. 12. The sale will include competitive and noncompetitive bids. The BONAR VIIs come due in 2013 and carry a 7% coupon. The auction follows a this year's BONAR V series of five-year 2011 bonds. The BONAR V program authorizes $1.5 billion in issuance, with two separate tranches of $500 million each coming to market so far.  

"There is room for shorter-term dollar bonds," Zavaleta said. "There is the Boden 2012 and beyond that the long-term Pars and Discounts in dollars." Argentina initially issued $15.5 billion in Boden 2012s during the nation's 2001-02 financial crisis.

title: DJ REPEAT&CORRECT: Argentina Peso Hits ARS3.10/Dlr; Bonds Up
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Sep 05, 2006 (DJCS via Comtex) --  

(The item "Argentina Peso Hits ARS3.10 On Intervention; Bonds Up -2-" published at 3:47 p.m. EDT, omitted paragraphs 1-5.)  

The Argentine peso hit the ARS3.10 mark against the dollar Tuesday, its weakest point in three years, on heavy last-minute dollar buying by the central bank.  

Meanwhile, locally traded bond prices were higher across the curve, albeit amid mild volumes.  

The peso closed at ARS3.10, weakening from ARS3.0950 on Monday, amid normal volumes. Tuesday's close marks the peso's weakest point since mid-March 2003, when the local currency slid as far as ARS3.1250 against the dollar.  

The central bank habitually buys dollars to build reserves and maintain a weak peso that favors Argentine exports. Officials, including Economy Minister Felisa Miceli, have recently reiterated their defense of this plan.  

Although the central bank stopped reporting its daily dollar buying in July, local currency trader Hector Blanco of local brokerage ABC Mercado de Cambio estimated that the central bank bought roughly $80 million during the last 15 minutes of the session to push the peso into weaker territory.  

Miceli said Monday that regular dollar buying will continue, estimating that without steady intervention the peso would strengthen to ARS2.30 against the dollar.  

In addition to recovering the $9.5 billion that the government tapped in January to entirely pay down its debt with the International Monetary Fund, daily intervention will likely increase total reserves on the year as President Nestor Kirchner heads toward his 2007 re-election bid, Blanco said.  

The central bank's late dollar buying Tuesday came after the monetary authority sold dollars earlier in the day.  

"It sold cash dollars at ARS3.0950, ARS3.0960 this morning and then at the last minute paid cash at ARS3.0990," Blanco said. "There must have been some financial transaction that isn't clear at the moment."  

Total volume in the local currency market reached $237 million.  

In the local bond market, "prices are generally all up," said Paulino Seoane, an analyst in Buenos Aires with Lopez Leon Brokers.  

The benchmark Discount in pesos was up to ARS126.85 from ARS126.60, while the Par in pesos was up to ARS49.75 from ARS49.60. At the shorter end of the curve, the Bocon Pre 12, another peso note, was also higher at ARS176.20 from ARS175.50.  

Peso notes are linked to inflation. The government announced late in the session Tuesday that the consumer price index rose 0.6% in August, higher than a 0.5% increase predicted last week by economists surveyed by Dow Jones Newswires.  

Among dollar notes, the Boden 2012 was up to ARS287.80 from ARS287.40.  

"There's not much volume, as usual," Seoane added.

title: Argentine stocks steady with volume at 3-year low
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (Reuters) - Argentine stocks ended steady Monday and trade volume dwindled to a three-year low in the absence of guidance from U.S. markets, closed for the country's Labor Day holiday, traders said.  

The benchmark MerValindex of 12 leading shares closed just 0.02 percent lower at 1,677.49 points. MerVal shares are up 8.7 percent since the start of the year.

BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Locally traded Argentine bonds were little changed Monday, while the peso closed flat on the day at ARS3.0950, as local markets saw little activity due to the U.S. Labor Day holiday.  

"It is very calm," said Alejandro Barros, a financial analyst with local Banco Piano. "Some notes are down slightly, but there isn't much happening."  

The benchmark Discount bond in pesos was recently quoted at ARS126.65, off slightly from Friday's close at ARS126.75, while the Par in pesos was unchanged at ARS49.55.  

The Discount saw just over ARS4 million in volume traded Monday, well below the ARS20 million that normally exchanges hands.  

Peso bonds linked to inflation, such as the Discount and Par notes, could take a hit this week following Tuesday's release of August inflation data. Inflation is expected to have shown more signs of moderation in August, and a Dow Jones Newswires survey produced a median forecast of a 0.5% increase in the consumer price index. That forecast comes in below the 0.7% estimated in a month-old survey conducted by the central bank.  

In the foreign exchange market, the central bank apparently abstained from its daily dollar buying.  

The central bank habitually buys dollars to build reserves and maintain a weaker peso.  

Economy Minister Felisa Miceli again defended that policy Monday, saying that regular dollar buying will continue. Over the weekend, Miceli estimated that without steady intervention, the peso would strengthen against the dollar to ARS2.30.

The Argentine peso hit the ARS3.10 mark against the dollar Tuesday, its weakest point in three years, on heavy last-minute dollar buying by the central bank.  

Meanwhile, locally traded bond prices were higher across the curve, albeit amid mild volumes.  

The peso closed at ARS3.10, weakening from ARS3.0950 on Monday, amid normal volumes. Tuesday's close marks the peso's weakest point since mid-March 2003, when the local currency slid as far as ARS3.1250 against the dollar.  

The central bank habitually buys dollars to build reserves and maintain a weak peso that favors Argentine exports. Officials, including Economy Minister Felisa Miceli, have recently reiterated their defense of this plan.  

Although the central bank stopped reporting its daily dollar buying in July, local currency trader Hector Blanco of local brokerage ABC Mercado de Cambio estimated that the central bank bought roughly $80 million during the last 15 minutes of the session to push the peso into weaker territory.  

Miceli said Monday that regular dollar buying will continue, estimating that without steady intervention the peso would strengthen to ARS2.30 against the dollar.  

In addition to recovering the $9.5 billion that the government tapped in January to entirely pay down its debt with the International Monetary Fund, daily intervention will likely increase total reserves on the year as President Nestor Kirchner heads toward his 2007 re-election bid, Blanco said.  

The central bank's late dollar buying Tuesday came after the monetary authority sold dollars earlier in the day.  

"It sold cash dollars at ARS3.0950, ARS3.0960 this morning and then at the last minute paid cash at ARS3.0990," Blanco said. "There must have been some financial transaction that isn't clear at the moment."  

Total volume in the local currency market reached $237 million.  

In the local bond market, "prices are generally all up," said Paulino Seoane, an analyst in Buenos Aires with Lopez Leon Brokers.  

The benchmark Discount in pesos was up to ARS126.85 from ARS126.60, while the Par in pesos was up to ARS49.75 from ARS49.60. At the shorter end of the curve, the Bocon Pre 12, another peso note, was also higher at ARS176.20 from ARS175.50.  

Peso notes are linked to inflation. The government announced late in the session Tuesday that the consumer price index rose 0.6% in August, higher than a 0.5% increase predicted last week by economists surveyed by Dow Jones Newswires.

"There's not much volume, as usual," Seoane added.

text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--The Argentine peso weakened slightly as the central bank resumed dollar buying Wednesday, pushing the currency back to its weakest point against the dollar since March 2003.  

Meanwhile, bond prices rose and volume nearly doubled as investors took positions after a recent slide.  

The peso closed at ARS3.0975 against the dollar, weakening from Tuesday's close at ARS3.0950. Total volume was also higher in the local foreign exchange market, reaching $319 million. The peso was further weakened as banks sought dollars to close positions at the month's end, Quintana said.

"Longer-term dollar bonds are doing especially well," he added. Among these, the Par bond under U.S. jurisdiction was recently quoted at ARS135, up from ARS132.00 at Tuesday's close.  

Among peso notes, the Bocon Pro 12 was at ARS175.75, up from from ARS175. "The Pro 12 is seeing the day's biggest volume after being punished in recent sessions," Salvucci said.  

The local bond market took its lead from U.S. government securities, which saw prices rally after the successful auction of $14 billion in five-year Treasury notes.

title: DJ  Argentina  Bonds Mixed; Peso Weaker On More  Intervention
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Aug 23, 2006 (DJCS via Comtex) --  

Argentine bond prices were mixed Wednesday amid mild volumes, while the peso continued to slide against the U.S. dollar on steady central bank intervention.  

The peso slid to ARS3.0875 against the dollar, weakening from ARS3.0850 on Tuesday.  

The local bond market early last week saw stronger prices and a return of foreign investors on better-than-expected U.S. economic data and a growing belief among investors that the Fed's two-year tightening cycle was over.  

After light profit-taking during the past few sessions, the local market lacked a clear tendency, said Sebastian Di Nucci, a portfolio manager with local FDI Consultants.  

The restructured par in pesos stood out as the day's best performer, albeit amid thin trading. The par in pesos was recently quoted at ARS49.20, up from ARS48.70.  

Di Nucci said the local market will remain in a lull until it becomes clear where the U.S. economy is going. "Although the Fed stopped raising interest rates this month, I think they could continue to raise them again next month," he said.  

Among local sliders, the discount in pesos was at ARS126.45, down from ARS127.10, while the dollar-denominated Boden 2012 was at ARS285.50, from ARS285.66. The Bogar 2018, a peso note, was up slightly to ARS147.20 from ARS147.10. These three note typically account for about half of the local market volume.  

In the local foreign exchange market, "it was similar to yesterday, with total volume reaching about $256 million," said Gustavo Quintana, a currency trader with local Lopez Leon Brokers.  

The central bank bought dollars in the final half hour of the session Wednesday, pushing the peso into slightly weaker territory against the dollar, he added. Quintana sees intervention pushing the peso to the ARS3.1000 against the dollar, with the exchange rate possibly hitting ARS3.0900 by week's end.

title: IMF: Argentina Needs Tighter Budget To Cut Inflation
text:
WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--Consumer price inflation in Argentina will probably accelerate if Argentina's government doesn't restrain public spending and tighten monetary policy, the International Monetary Fund said Wednesday.  

Though the economy appears likely to continue expanding rapidly as it has since Argentina began recovering from a financial crisis in 2001, inflation "remains high," the IMF said in a press summary of its annual Article IV review of Argentina's economy. Argentina needs to control public spending, raise real interest rates above zero and allow "for a greater upward flexibility in the exchange rate," the IMF said.  

The IMF "regarded current inflation as more a consequence of aggregate demand growth that was not being met by a sufficiently rapid supply response than as a temporary phenomenon arising from a delayed relative price adjustment after the 2002 crisis," the IMF said. "Achieving a soft landing for the economy requires a different macroeconomic policy mix as well as reforms to promote investment and supply, especially in areas where bottlenecks are of macroeconomic significance."  

The IMF noted that core inflation is now running just above 12%, and formal private-sector wages are rising.  

Argentina's recovery from crisis, which has included sharp declines in unemployment and poverty, a strengthening banking system, rebuilding of foreign exchange reserves and repayment of IMF obligations, coincided with a massive adjustment in the government's budget. The overall public sector posted a budget surplus of 2.4% of gross domestic product in 2005, compared with a deficit of 5.9% in 2001.  

Public spending is now rising, stimulating demand. Non-interest government spending rose by 11% in real terms, eroding the primary surplus as a share of the economy. Provincial spending has been growing 19%, adjusted for inflation.  

"Early indicators imply that current trends are set to continue this year," the IMF said. "Public sector capital spending continues to rise rapidly, growing at a real rate of 70% in the 12 months to May."  

Argentina's interest rates are "accommodative," the IMF said. The IMF "underscored that all of the available policy instruments should be brought to bear to allow for a soft landing with sustainable growth and low inflation."  

The value of Argentina's currency has been stable, amid sustained intervention by the central bank, the IMF said. A strengthening peso could also help damp demand and keep prices in check.  

Some IMF directors suggested government price controls can help contain inflation expectations, but the benefits are only temporary, the IMF said. Most IMF directors believed the price controls will ultimately worsen inflation because they make supply shortages worse.  

"Most directors advised that such administrative measures should be dismantled as soon as possible, since repressing prices in regulated industries, selective price agreements, and export restraints would ultimately exacerbate capacity constraints in key sectors and undermine the business climate," the IMF said.  

-By Elizabeth Price, Dow Jones Newswires; 202-862-9249; Elizabeth.Price@dowjones.com [ 09-08-06 1800GMT ]

title: Argentina  Bonds Mixed; Peso Weaker On  Intervention
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Argentine bonds remained mixed Monday, as longer-duration bonds continued to see higher prices, while investors moved away from shorter notes linked to inflation.  

Meanwhile, the peso closed at ARS3.0725 against the dollar, slightly weaker than Friday's close at ARS3.0700.  

Dollar instruments continued to do well in the local bond market, with the Boden 2012 bond recently quoted at ARS286.75, up from ARS286 Friday. So-called GDP warrants in dollars under U.S. jurisdiction were at ARS29.00 from ARS28.60, while dollar warrants under Argentine law were at ARS25.89 from ARS25.60.  

The benchmark Discount bond in pesos was also higher, reaching ARS124.30 from ARS124. At the shorter end of the curve, however, peso notes linked to the consumer price index continued to fade after the government reported last week that the CPI rose by 0.6% in July on the month. "With inflation waning, people are losing interest in (inflation indexed) bonds," said Alejandro Barros, an analyst with local Banco Piano.  

In part, investors are moving from shorter-term bonds to floating-rate Nobac notes that the central bank auctions on a weekly basis. Meanwhile, a recent change in reserves requirements has led banks to offer more attractive interest rates on longer-term accounts to draw depositors from checking and other current accounts, Barros said. As of Aug. 1, banks are required to hold 19% of depositors' checking and savings account funds in reserve at the central bank, up from 17% for these "sight," or current, accounts.  

In the local foreign exchange market, the peso weakened on late central bank intervention. Overall volume was around $250 million, said Carlos Lizer, head currency trader with local brokerage Puente Hermanos.  

Demand for pesos from cereal exporters repatriating overseas dollar earnings has begun to wane now that the annual soy harvest has wrapped up, Lizer said.

title: DJ  Argentina  Bonds Mixed; Peso Flat On  Intervention
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Aug 04, 2006 (DJCS via Comtex) --  

Argentine bond prices were mixed Friday, as longer-duration notes followed U.S. Treasury prices higher while shorter-term notes slid on lower-than-expected Argentine inflation data for July.  

Meanwhile, the peso ended unchanged on the day at ARS3.0700 as the central bank again bought pesos to offset demand for the local currency.  

Volumes remained generally thin in the local bond market, however. Among gainers, the dollar-denominated Boden 2012 was recently quoted at $70, up from $69.70 at Thursday's close.  

The government made principal payments on the Boden 12 Thursday, and many investors were apparently reinvesting in the note, said Adolfo Zuberbuhler, an analyst at local Banco Finansur.  

"I think we are going to see more appetite for dollar bonds than for shorter-term (inflation-linked) peso notes," Zuberbuhler said. Investors seeking peso investments will likely move from short-term peso bonds to the floating-rate Nobac notes that the central bank auctions on a weekly basis, he said. Argentina's statistics agency, Indec, announced Thursday that the consumer price index rose 0.6% in July on the month. That came in below expectations, making the inflation-linked bonds less attractive, Zuberbuhler said.  

Among shorter-term losers Friday, the Bocon Pre 9 was down at ARS110.05 from ARS110.40, while the Bocon Pre 8 was at ARS191.00, down from ARS192.10.  

The benchmark Discount bond in pesos was higher, however, rising to ARS125.40, up from ARS124.00, as emerging market debt benefited from tame U.S. employment data out Friday.  

In the local foreign exchange market, the central bank bought dollars to offset peso demand and rebuild reserves that the government tapped for this week's Boden payout.  

Meanwhile, the overnight call money rate eased some Friday, to around 8.5% from 9% Thursday. Liquidity tightened this week after a reserves ratio hike went into place Tuesday.  

Beginning Aug. 1, banks must hold 19% of depositors' checking and savings account funds in reserve at the central bank. The reserve ratio for these "sight," or current, accounts had been 17% since March, when it rose from 15%.  

Before the change tightened liquidity, the overnight call money rate had been around 7.5%. The rate rose as high as 9.5% on Tuesday.

title: DJ  Argentina  Bonds Continue Climb;  Intervention  Softens Peso
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Jul 20, 2006 (DJCS via Comtex) --  

Locally traded Argentine bonds continued to rebound Thursday as U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke made dovish comments for a second straight day.  

Meanwhile, the peso ended at ARS3.0825 against the dollar, slightly weaker than Wednesday's close at ARS3.0800.  

The local bond market didn't immediately react to the release of the minutes to last month's Fed meeting, which failed to trigger more U.S. Treasurys gains.  

Earlier Thursday, bonds rose after Bernanke testified to the U.S. House after briefing the Senate on Wednesday. He echoed dovish comments regarding inflation, adding that there has been some reduction in U.S. demand for oil, warning that there could be significant consequences on inflation and growth if oil prices rise much more.  

Local gainers included the Discount bond in pesos, last quoted at ARS120.40, up from ARS119.50, and the Par in pesos, which rose to ARS47 from ARS46.70. The Bogar 2018, another peso note, was at ARS145.10, up from ARS144.60 in stronger volume.  

"I don't know if the higher volumes correspond to the new rule allowing AFJPs (pension funds) to buy the Bogars, but volumes have been improving," said Sebastian Di Nucci, a portfolio manager with local FDI Consultants.  

Earlier Thursday, Argentine Economy Minister Felisa Miceli called on Mercosur trade bloc nations to join Argentina and Venezuela in a plan to issue a "Bond of the South."  

Miceli spoke in the Argentine provincial city of Cordoba, where economy ministers from the region were meeting ahead of a Mercosur presidential summit on Friday.  

"We offer interested countries to join us in this action, which will be concluded by the end of September," Miceli was quoted as saying.  

Argentine and Venezuelan officials first announced the "Bond of the South" plan earlier this month. The plan has been met with skepticism by some fund managers, who are waiting for more details about how the bonds will work.  

Di Nucci compared the hypothetical bond to the Boden 2015, which wasn't trading on Thursday. The Argentine government issued the Boden 2015 earlier this year in a direct sale to the Venezuelan government. Such bond issues represent a more political than financial strategy, Di Nucci said.  

Such issues, "augment the Argentine government's debt, but aren't attractive to individual investors for the lack of liquidity they have because they are so concentrated in the hands of one creditor," Di Nucci noted.  

In the local foreign exchange market, the peso edged slightly lower on central bank dollar buying. The peso gained early, leading the monetary authority to start buying dollars at ARS3.0785, said Hector Blanco, a trader with local brokerage ABC Mercado de Cambio.  

Peso demand also ebbed somewhat as cereal exporters eased repatriations of overseas dollar earnings, Blanco added.

title: ANALYSIS-Argentina's Redrado eyes reserves, not rates
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina, June 8 (Reuters) - Compared to other central bankers, Argentina's Martin Redrado spends very little time talking about interest rate policy.  

Redrado told a conference on Monday that "the power of classic monetary policy instruments (like interest rates), is reduced" in Latin America's third largest economy, which has a "financial market without sufficient depth."  

Inflation is running at about 12 percent per year after more than three years of fast economic growth, and rising prices are now a concern, especially as hyperinflation is a recent memory.  

But many economists agree that raising interest rates would have little effect on tackling inflation in a country where credit stands at a relatively low 10 percent of gross domestic product, as the banking system is still recovering from economic collapse in 2001-2002.  

"It's true Argentina has no reference rate for (monetary) regulation, but rather the amount of money issued," said Aldo Abram, head of the Exante consultancy.  

According to the latest available figures from the first quarter, the central bank was to keep the money supply, using the commonly watched M2 yardstick, within a target range of 116.3-126.2 billion pesos ($37.5-40.7 billion).  

CONCERNED OVER COMMODITIES  

Harvard-educated Redrado was deputy foreign minister when he replaced Alfonso Prat-Gay, a former J.P. Morgan executive who was seen as market friendly. A former chair of the National Securities Commission, the markets took Redrado's appointment in their stride.  

In a recent newspaper column, Redrado said he was more concerned over Latin America's vulnerability to shifts in demand for commodities from China, India and Russia than international interest rates.  

In that situation he preferred to prepare for possible external shocks with a "counter-cyclical" policy of building up reserves and a budget surplus.  

Since Argentina payed off the final $9.6 billion it owed the International Monetary Fund in January, the central bank has boosted its reserves by some $5.6 billion by buying up dollars flooding the country due to strong demand abroad for its commodities.  

"With its policy of boosting reserves, the central bank is building real anti-crisis insurance against our recurring external vulnerability," wrote Redrado, whose six-year term began in September 2004.  

Some economists worry that the bank's policy of paying for dollars by issuing bonds may check inflation in the short term, but makes it vulnerable to investors taking fright and opting to cash in rather than renew paper.  

"It isn't credible to think the bank can maintain that level of debt forever," said independent economist Fabian Prieto. "They must give the money back some time, and I don't know what will happen when the monetary base expands again."  

Neil Dougall, head of emerging markets research at Dresdner Kleinwort Wasserstein in London, was concerned the central bank has been effectively softening the peso to help exporters and this could itself stoke inflation.  

Dealers say that frequent mopping up of dollars by the central bank increases the supply of pesos to the foreign exchange market and tends to either make the local currency weaker or prevent it from rising against the greenback.  

"At a time when underlying inflation is on the rise, one tool that could be used to dampen inflationary expectations would be to let the currency appreciate," he said.  

"If you get a path of rising inflation, that's something that's also potentially destabilizing to the currency," he added.  

Argentina's peso <.ARSB=> has traded at close to 3.00 to the dollar since late 2003 amid repeated central bank intervention.

title: DJ UPDATE: Argentina  Bonds Rebound, Peso Flat On  Intervention
text:
BUENOS AIRES, May 16, 2006 (DJCS via Comtex) --  

(Updates 5th paragraph with central bank intervention data.)  

Locally traded Argentine bonds rebounded strongly Tuesday, following the lead of other emerging market assets, as some hopeful news on U.S. inflation helped end a recent sell-off.  

The Argentine peso, meanwhile, remained in a state of isolation from the rest of the world. Just as it failed to fall in sympathy with the Brazilian real and other currencies when they were suffering capital flight in recent days, on Tuesday the peso failed to join their recovery. It closed the day unchanged at ARS3.0425 to the dollar.  

The main reason for the peso's stability in a sea of volatility, traders said, is the persistent intervention policy of the Argentine central bank.  

The monetary authority's heavy dollar-buying interventions have left the Argentine currency so undervalued relative to the real and other competing currencies that speculators resisted selling it during the recent phase of emerging market jitters.  

On Tuesday, the intervention - at $80 million, according to the central bank - had the opposite effect. It kept the peso from rallying, even as the regular movement of exporter funds continued to flow into the country.  

"Argentina is an isolated country, just as it has been for some time," said Hector Blanco, a trader at ABC Mercado in Buenos Aires.  

But that isolation wasn't so apparent in the fixed-income market.  

After heavy selling last week and on Monday, Argentine bonds rebounded strongly Tuesday. Investors followed the lead from other countries, where the mood was bolstered by the U.S. April producer prices report, which wasn't so harsh as to ramp up the risk of a bigger hike in U.S. interest rates. And the fact that Argentine bonds had sold off even more strongly than other emerging markets only enhanced their appeal Tuesday, said Noelia Lucini, an analyst at Argentine Capital Markets in Buenos Aires.  

"The market was searching for a floor," said Lucini. "So, today we have seen a very strong rebound that is practically across the length of the (yield) curve."  

The benchmark discount bond in pesos, which fell about 1% on Monday, was quoted late Tuesday at ARS127.70, up 1.31%. And the discount bond in dollars issued under New York jurisdiction was up 2.01% at a dollar-equivalent ARS96.3.  

The dollar-denominated Boden 2012, meanwhile, rose 0.54% to a dollar-equivalent ARS286.40. It was helped by news that Venezuela will buy another $200 million of this issue.  

And the peso-denominated Boden 2008 was last quoted at ARS129.40, up 0.33%.

title: DJ UPDATE: Argentina  Peso Gains Amid  Intervention ; Bonds Lull
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Mar 15, 2006 (DJCS via Comtex) --  

(Updates with intervention data.)  

The Argentine peso edged stronger Wednesday, despite central bank intervention, as exporters and banks sought the local currency.  

Meanwhile, bonds hit a lull as prices held flat or inched into weaker territory amid low volume, following in part rising U.S. Treasury rates.  

The peso ended the day at ARS3.0725 against the dollar compared with Tuesday's close at ARS3.0775. The local currency has slowly strengthened against the dollar this week, gaining a full centavo from Friday's close at a three-year weak-point.  

The central bank reported later Wednesday that it bought $30 million and EUR40 million during the day's session. The central bank held off on its habitual dollar buying on Monday and Tuesday, but surprised the market Tuesday by purchasing EUR50.5 million. "It's a sly strategy because the market watches dollars," said trader Fernando Izzo of local ABC Mercado de Cambio.  

Buyers were mainly investors, exporters repatriating overseas dollar earnings and private banks, he added.  

Liquidity has tightened this week, with the overnight call money rate reaching 10.5% Wednesday.  

Analyst Javier Salvucci of local Silver Cloud Advisors attributed the call money rate rise to an announcement from the Argentine Central Bank Monday night. The monetary authority hiked minimum reserve requirements for bank's savings and checking deposits and ended the practice of paying interest on those funds.  

In the local bond market, volume was thin, with notes at the shorter end of the curve losing some ground. Among sliders, the Bocon Pre 12, a pre debt-swap peso note, was down to ARS179.75. Restructured longer term notes in pesos were unchanged, with the discount steady at ARS52 and the par at ARS127.  

Salvucci said shorter-term bonds could be losing on some arbitrage to long-term Nobac certificates auctioned weekly by the central bank. The long-dated Nobac notes have rates tied to the "Badlar" average of 30-day certificate of deposit rates and are expected to benefit from Monday's reserves requirement change.  

In Tuesday's certificates auction, the 728-day Nobac paid 5.0206% over Badlar, or 12.9581% in absolute terms, compared with 12.6773% last week.  

The rising Badlar reflects a move by banks to attract more savers to its longer-term fixed deposits. That rate is expected to rise further once the new reserve requirement rules come into effect April 1.

title: UPDATE: Argentina  Bonds Begin Turnaround; Peso Stronger
text:
(Updates with central bank intervention data.)  

BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Locally traded Argentine bonds, taking a lead from U.S. Treasurys, began to recover amid low volumes Tuesday after a recent wave of profit taking.  

Meanwhile, the peso continued to slowly firm against the dollar, strengthening to ARS3.0775 from Monday's close at ARS3.0800.  

"It looks like the market has hit bottom and some bonds are beginning to pick up," said Paulino Seoane, a fixed-income analyst in Buenos Aires with Lopez Leon Brokers. Among restructured gainers, the discount in pesos was last quoted at ARS127.00, up from ARS126.70 on Monday, while the par in pesos was unchanged at ARS52.00. Some dollar notes were also improving, with the Boden 2013, a pre-debt swap bond, up to ARS264.01 from ARS263.80.  

Trading was still somewhat thin, however, as local investors looked to get a better read on where the U.S. market is headed, Seoane said. U.S. Treasury prices rallied across the curve Tuesday as investors moved from bearish positions after the government released mixed reading on retail sales.  

In the local foreign exchange market, trading was also thin, with weak central bank intervention, according to trader Hector Blanco of local ABC Mercado de Cambio. "The bank bought sporadically, but it wasn't a very aggressive intervention," Blanco said. He said that total volume was around $110 million. The central bank reported later Tuesday that it didn't buy any dollars, but instead bought a solid EUR50.5 million.  

The central bank regularly buys dollars to maintain a weaker peso and rebuild reserves tapped in January to pay down Argentina's entire $9.5 billion debt with the International Monetary Fund. The constant pumping of pesos into the market has led to some concerns about inflation. In a move that could ease those concerns somewhat, the Argentine Central Bank announced late Monday that it increased minimum reserve requirements for bank's savings and checking deposits and ended the practice of paying interest on those funds. The change is expected to tighten liquidity conditions and could promote longer-term saving and lending.  

According to a central bank statement, banks are required as of April 1 to hold 17% of their checking and savings deposit funds in reserve. Savings and checking account reserve ratios had been cut to 14% from 15% in December in a bid to boost liquidity for the summer vacation period.  

All fixed term deposits, or certificates of deposit, will maintain their reserve ratios at existing levels. These ratios range from 14% for CDs of up to 29 days to 1% for CDs of between 180 days and 365 days in length. For any deposits held for more than a year, banks are free of any reserve requirement.  

The Central Bank said that the increase in reserve ratios implies an additional monetary absorption from the financial system on the order of ARS1.35 billion.  

-By Drew Benson and Kim-Mai Cutler, Dow Jones Newswires; 5411-4311-3127; andrew.benson@dowjones.com [ 14-03-06 2222GMT ]

BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--The Argentine peso held at a three-year low for a second-straight session Friday, with the central bank engaging in last-minute dollar-buying to offset a mild uptick in demand for the local currency as foreign investors returned to the local bond market.  

Locally traded bonds gained ground as U.S. Treasurys began to recover from an early session slide on strong U.S. jobs data for the month of February.  

The peso ended at ARS3.0825 against the dollar, after reaching ARS3.0800 just 10 minutes before market close.  

"The central bank came in at the last minute to hold the peso," said currency trader Gustavo Quintana of local Lopez Leon Brokers. Although official data wouldn't be available later, Quintana estimated that the monetary authority bought on a par with Thursday's $41 million intervention.  

Quintana attributed renewed demand for the peso to returning investors. "The stronger (Brazilian) real also helped," he said.  

In the local debt market, bonds went on the upswing after a week of profit-taking. Among rebounders, the restructured par bond in pesos was recently quoted at ARS52.40, up from Thursday's close at ARS52.00. Also, the discount in pesos, the heaviest traded note Friday, was up at ARS127.40 from Thursday's close at ARS126.40.  

Overall, volume was up on the day but remained moderate, according to analyst Leonardo Chialva of local Delphos Investments.  

"I believe in the next week we're going to see a bond market that is recuperating from its recent fall," Chialva said. "We'll see the market revalue these bonds."

title: UPDATE:  Argentina  Bonds Fall, Peso Down On  Intervention
text:
(Updates in ninth paragraph with intervention data from the Argentine Central Bank.)  

BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Locally traded Argentine bonds dropped slightly Monday as market participants took profits from the strong rallies they posted last week.  

Meanwhile, the peso weakened slightly to close at ARS3.07 to the dollar, down from ARS3.0675 on Friday, after last-minute intervention by the central bank.  

"There was a bit of profit-taking but volumes were pretty good," said Noelia Lucini, an analyst at Capital Markets Argentina. She said last week's rallies in Argentine sovereign debt, when bonds were helped by a strong auction of 30-year U.S. Treasurys and later by a rally in Brazilian bonds on the back of a buy-back announcement, gave way to "corrections" Monday.  

Moreover, she said, expectations for a moderation in consumer prices following last week's confirmation of an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in Argentina, which is expected to drive down beef prices, have softened peso-denominated inflation-indexed bonds.  

The discount bond in pesos was last quoted at ARS130.85, down 0.34% on the day. The par in pesos had fallen even further, sliding 1.12% to ARS53.15. Both bonds are indexed to an inflation indicator known as CER.  

Dollar bonds, which were especially helped by the Brazil-led narrowing in Argentina's yield spread to Treasurys last week, were more stable. The Boden 2012 was down just 0.04% at a dollar equivalent ARS285.00.  

In the foreign exchange market, trading was confined for most of the day to a very narrow range in thin volumes, holding tightly to the ARS3.0675-to-the-dollar level it had closed at Friday.  

Then, in the last few minutes, traders said, the Argentine Central Bank entered the market with bid for dollars whose size exceeded the market's total offering. This pushed the peso to a weaker close of ARS3.07.  

After the close, the Central Bank said it bought $54.5 million in the open market Monday and EUR1 million.  

Ever since Argentina tapped $9.5 billion in reserves to pay down its debt to the International Monetary Fund in early January, the Argentine Central Bank has vowed to use interventions to recuperate reserves.  

Still, traders were surprised to see it enter the market at such late notice Monday. The peso remains close to three-year lows, which means the central bank is paying a high price for its dollars. Moreover, the weak valuations mean the basic objective of the federal government - for a competitive exchange rate - has already been met, they say.  

Hector Blanco, a trader at ABC Mercado, said interventions such as Monday's added to the unpredictability of policy. And that, he said, has driven participants out of the market, pushing down volumes.  

"No one wants to take positions in this market," Blanco said.  

-By Michael Casey, Dow Jones Newswires; michael.j.casey@dowjones.com; 54-11-4313 1918 [ 13-02-06 2145GMT ]
