title: Argentina Ctrl Bk Head Defends Policy,Lauds Credit Growth
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Argentine Central Bank President Martin Redrado used an op-ed article heralding the long-awaited recovery of bank lending in the country to defend his institution's policies Monday.  

In an article published by business daily El Cronista, Redrado said bank credit, which was severely depressed after the financial crisis of 2001 and 2002, had marked its "definitive" recovery in recent months.  

He attributed this to the Central Bank's policy of providing incentives for lending while at the same time maintaining a "firm control of risks in the financial system."  

These policies, he said, had been accompanied by the necessary precondition of a "prudent monetary policy" marked by a rapid accumulation of international reserves.  

Redrado's defense of his institution's policies comes as criticism of it rises among private economists.  

Critics argue that the Central Bank's reserve accumulation policy is the flip-side of a federal government-backed policy of keeping the peso weak through foreign currency-buying interventions.  

This, they say, has helped fuel rising prices in Argentina as it has promoted imported inflation and has resulted in mass issuance of domestic currency that has expanded the money supply in an inflationary way.  

The Central Bank's failure to achieve its inflation target for 2005 - consumer prices rose 12.3% last year, more than four percentage points above the ceiling rate for the Central Bank's target band - reflects a loss of independence in policy-making, these critics say.  

Redrado did not directly address these criticisms in his article but he nonetheless made a strident defense of his policies.  

He argued that policy positions at the Central Bank that have encouraged a reduction in banks' exposure to government debt have reduced the "crowding out" factor from government borrowing, promoted private sector lending and at the same time inherently bolstered the Central Bank's independence.  

"The financing of government constitutes one of the criticisms that has always been leveled when the independence of central banks in emerging countries is evaluated," Redrado said. "In such countries, excessive holdings of public debt on the part of banks implies an assumption of risks that can result in perverse behavior once the moment to reduce position arises."  

Rerado said banks' exposure to public sector debt has fallen from 40% to 31% of the total sector's assets over the past 12 months, which he said was accompanied by a sharp increase in lending to the private sector.  

While he welcomed this development, Redrado said more work was needed to get lending rates above the low 10% of gross domestic product currently seen in Argentina.  

Separately, the Central Bank announced new measures on Sunday aimed at boosting housing loans. The measures would expand the collateral banks can use as guarantees against lending for home construction.  

Banks can now accept rights to structured trust fund vehicles that invest in construction projects in lieu of direct mortgages over a piece of property.

title: UPDATE 2-Argentina trade surplus thins despite record exports
text:
(Adds details, quote and 2006 forecasts)  

BUENOS AIRES, Argentina, Jan 31 (Reuters) - Argentine exports climbed to a record high in 2005 on rising prices for natural resources, but the trade surplus shrank due to strong import growth in the country's third year of sizzling economic expansion, according to government data released on Tuesday.  

President Nestor Kirchner is seen winning political points with the export boom, billed as a result of his government's policy of maintaining a weak peso currency <ARSB=> to favor exports and win new markets.  

The trade surplus narrowed last year to $11.32 billion from $12.11 billion in 2004 on exports of $40.01 billion and imports of $28.69 billion, the Economy Ministry said in a report.  

In December, the trade surplus rose to $1.03 billion against $854 million in the same month a year earlier, beating analysts' median forecast of $879 million in a central bank poll on Jan. 4.  

Rising prices for Argentina's agricultural products, fuels and copper boosted exports in the month by 19 percent over December 2004 to $3.53 billion, also above analysts' median estimate of $3.44 billion.  

In all of 2005, exports swelled both in terms of revenue and volume as Argentina's economy, Latin America's third-largest, grew by an estimated 9 percent.  

Analysts said the big story in last year's 16 percent export growth was the growing presence of the manufacturing sector.  

" Cars have grown a lot due to an accord with Mexico and some sales to Brazil as well. The steel sector has also grown due to prices, not just volume," said Maria Castiglioni, an economist with Asesores Economicos consulting firm.  

"With this exchange rate, there are industrial sectors that are going to continue to do well and export," he added.  

With intervention of the Central Bank in the foreign exchange market, Argentina has prevented the currency from strengthening, keeping it at roughly 3 per U.S. dollar. The peso closed at 3.07/3.0725 per dollar on Tuesday.  

The Economy Ministry said exports that grew the most in terms of absolute value in 2005 were vehicles and vehicle parts, followed by seed and soybean sales, mainly to China.  

Imports in Argentina have been gradually recovering from a near-freeze in 2002 when prices on foreign goods shot up because of a currency devaluation.  

Imports in December jumped 18 percent to $2.49 billion and in the year imports climbed 28 percent to $28.69 billion, both slightly below forecasts.  

The ministry said imports grew in all economic sectors last year, but values rose most for goods related to the automotive industry, cellular phones, data processing equipment and fuels such as natural gas.  

The central bank estimates a 2006 trade surplus of $11.5 billion, according to a report in December.  

The government forecasts economic growth this year of 4.0 percent while the central bank puts its expansion at 6.2 percent.

title: Argentina  Peso Stronger As  Intervention  Lulls; Bonds Up
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--The Argentine peso gained ground on the dollar for a second-straight day as the central bank apparently continued to abstain from its almost daily intervention in the open market.  

Meanwhile, a handful of inflation-linked peso bonds were gaining in an otherwise quiet market.  

The peso ended the day at ARS3.0525, stronger than Tuesday's close at ARS3.0600. "Demand for pesos hasn't changed," said Carlos Lizer, the head currency trader with local brokerage Puente Hermanos. Instead, "yesterday and today the central bank and (state-run) Banco de la Nation have not been present," he said.  

Overall, trading remained thin in the foreign exchange market. "January, especially during the first two weeks, has lower-than-normal volume," Lizer added. Despite its temporary absence, the central bank is expected to return to regular dollar buying to rebuild reserves the government tapped to pay down its $9.5 billion debt with the International Monetary Fund last week, and to maintain a weak peso that favors Argentine exports.  

The central bank's steady intervention, which pumps new pesos into the market, comes as Argentina struggles with rising inflation that increased by just over 12% for the full year in 2005. Part of the central bank's strategy to pull pesos out of the system is its weekly auction of short-term Lebac and Nobac certificates. The central bank reported late Tuesday that this week's 1.2-billion-peso ($392.15 million) Lebac auction was oversubscribed, although there was again a heavy concentration of bids in the shortest end of the rate curve.  

Meanwhile, the total ARS1.333 billion amount accepted was insufficient to roll over all the ARS1.527 billion in Lebacs expiring this week. Based on the discounted value of bids accepted, some ARS205 million in excess liquidity was not absorbed. Last week, the central bank failed to roll over ARS324 million in expiring Lebacs, after a ARS1.35 billion auction drew bids worth just ARS1.174 billion. Yet again this week, the central bank again seemed reluctant to let interest rates rise in order to draw in more buyers in all but the longest-dated instrument.  

Rising consumer prices, in turn, have continued to fuel demand for locally traded bonds linked to inflation. During Wednesday's session, investors focused on a handful of inflation-linked peso bonds, said Adolfo Zuberbuhler, an analyst with local Banco Finansur. Among gainers, the restructured discount in pesos was last quoted at ARS120.90, up slightly from 120.00, while the pre-debt swap Bogar 2018 was up to ARS141.60 from ARS141.40, and the Bocon Pro 12, another pre-restructuring peso note, was at ARS181.00 from ARS180.50.  

Beyond these three bonds, "the rest of the market is calm," Zuberbuhler said.  

-By Drew Benson, Dow Jones Newswires; 5411-4311-3127; andrew.benson@dowjones.com [ 11-01-06 2119GMT ]

(Updates with central bank intervening to buy $70 million)  

BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--The Argentine peso ended slightly weaker against the dollar Wednesday as the central bank continued to buy dollars to offset demand for the currency from investors seeking locally traded bonds.  

The peso ended the day at ARS3.0400 against the dollar, off slightly from Tuesday's close at ARS3.0375.  

Currency trader Fernando Izzo of local brokerage ABC Mercado de Cambio said the central bank bought dollars throughout the day's session. The central bank reported later that it bought $70 million during the day's session, bringing total reserves to $18.673 billion.  

The continued intervention, which pumped some ARS213 million pesos into the system on Wednesday alone, came a day after the central bank's weekly auction of short-term Lebac and Nobac certificates was undersubscribed due to high year-end liquidity needs and low interest rates.  

The central bank has struggled with its weekly auctions, raising worries about its ability to control inflation. The government's statistics agency reported after the local foreign exchange market close that the consumer price index rose by 1.1% month-on-month in December, bringing full-year inflation to a whopping 12.3%.  

Many analysts see monetary policy becoming more difficult to manage since the central bank plans to use steady daily intervention to recover the $9.5 billion in foreign reserves it tapped on Tuesday to entirely repay Argentina's debt with the International Monetary Fund.  

Meanwhile, bonds "have begun the new year very well," said Noelia Lucini, an analyst with Capital Markets Argentina. "This has more to do with better Treasury rates, which have helped emerging markets in general," she said. The inflation data, which were leaked at midday to a local television news channel, also helped boost demand for peso-denominated bonds linked to inflation, Lucini added.  

Among gainers, the restructured discount bond in pesos was last quoted at ARS120.30, up from ARS119.30 on Tuesday, while the par in pesos was at ARS50.50, up from ARS50.20. title: DJ  Argentina  Peso Gains On Dlr Despite  Intervention ;Bonds Up
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Dec 22, 2005 (DJCS via Comtex) --  

The Argentine peso gained on the dollar Thursday, boosted in part by investors seeking the local currency to buy locally traded bonds, which also saw gains.  

The peso ended the day at ARS3.0225 against the dollar, a full centavo stronger than Wednesday's close at ARS3.0325. Hector Blanco, a currency trader with local brokerage ABC Mercado de Cambio, said that the market has recovered from last week's announcement that the government plans to entirely pay down its $9.8 billion debt with the International Monetary Fund. With business returned to normal, "traders are struggling to determine where the central bank has set its target to intervene in the market," he said.  

The central bank's intervention trigger will likely remain weaker than ARS3.00, based on what President Nestor Kirchner told a group of industrial business leaders Wednesday. Kirchner said the peso would trade between ARS3.00 and ARS3.05 to the dollar in 2006, weaker than the ARS2.95-2.98 rate pegged in the government's budget proposal for next year.  

The Kirchner administration has actively maintained a weaker peso in a bid to boost exports, which sparked Argentina's economic recovery in 2003 and remain strong. Many analysts believe the peso is undervalued and would strengthen significantly without almost daily central bank intervention.  

Blanco estimated that the central bank bought between $15 million and $30 million Thursday, up from $12 million on Wednesday. Official data would be available later in the day.  

During Kirchner's Wednesday meeting, he also asked the industry leaders to keep prices steady and to continue increasing investment. Inflation, projected to hit 12% by year-end, has become the administration's top macroeconomic concern.  

In the local bond market, "just about everything was up, although volumes were thinner," said Alejandro Barros, a financial analyst at local Banco Piano. Investors are coming back to the local bond market after initial concerns about the IMF debt paydown announcement because "the economy is doing well and next year looks to be another good year, although inflation remains a concern."  

Among gainers, the restructured discount bond in pesos was last quoted at ARS117.80, up from ARS116.00 on Wednesday, while the par in pesos was at ARS48.80, up from ARS48.00. Moving to the middle of the curve, the peso-denominated Bogar 2018 was up at ARS145.85 from ARS145.60, while shorter-term bonds were largely unchanged, Barros said.  

Markets will be open Friday, although it is a holiday for government employees. Traders expect very thin volumes.

title: UPDATE: Argentina  Peso Weaker On  Intervention ; Bonds Mixed
text:
(Updates third graf with central bank buying $100 million during session)  

BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--The Argentine Central Bank intervened heavily in the market Thursday to weaken the peso to ARS3.0150 against the dollar, delivering a clear message that the monetary authority has set the previously off-limits 3-to-1 mark as the new ceiling for the local currency.  

Meanwhile, the local bond market saw mixed results amid sluggish volume.  

The peso weakened nearly two full centavos from Wednesday's close at ARS2.9975. The central bank reported that it bought $100 million, just up from Wednesday's intervention of $99 million.  

"Clearly (the central bank) doesn't want the peso stronger than ARS3," said Daniel Bou Kahir, a trader with local Banco de la Pampa. "The band between ARS2.90 and ARS3.00 no longer appears to be the (Economy) Ministry target." Operating volume was strong, with cereal exporters stepping in to repatriate overseas dollar earnings in heavier numbers once the peso crossed ARS3.00, he added.  

The central bank buys dollars to maintain a weaker peso that favors Argentine exports. But stepping up the dollar buying just as inflationary concerns begin to take off should do little to ease analysts' concerns about where the economy is headed. Inflation rose 1.2% on-month in November and it is expected to come in above 12% for 2005.  

In the local bond market, longer-term bonds were down, while short-term notes saw some gains, said analyst Javier Salvucci with local Silver Cloud Advisors.  

Among losers, the restructured discount bond in pesos was down to ARS118.50 from ARS119.10 on Wednesday, while the par in pesos was at ARS48.60 from ARS49.00. On the upside, the pre-debt swap Bocon Pro 11 was at ARS177 from ARS176.50, while the Bocon Pre 8 was at ARS193.80 from ARS193.30.  

The losses on the longer end of the curve likely followed on lower U.S. Treasurys prices, while inflation-adjusted bonds on the shorter end continued to do well on continued increases in the consumer price index, Salvucci said. Just how far inflation can rise before the CPI-linked bonds lose their luster is "the million dollar question," Salvucci said.  

Meanwhile, there was only muted reaction to late-session news from the national statistics agency, Indec, that gross domestic product rose 2.3% in the third quarter from the second quarter and was up 9.2% on the year, Salvucci said.  

On an accumulated basis, growth was also 9.2% for the nine months to the end of September compared with the same nine-month period in 2004.  

Economists had expected to see an 8.5% year-on-year growth rate for the quarter. And an earlier one-month economic activity index for September that acts as an initial proxy indicator of GDP had estimated the growth rate for the accumulated nine-month period at 9%.  

The result puts Argentina on target to achieve economic growth of around 9% for the third consecutive year in 2005 since its financial crisis of 2002.  

-By Drew Benson, Dow Jones Newswires; 5411-4311-3127; andrew.benson@dowjones.com [ 15-12-05 2238GMT ]

title: UPDATE:Argentina Peso Sees Light Gain; Ctrl Bk Caps Rally
text:
(Updates with central bank intervention.)  

BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Argentina's peso strengthened a touch against the dollar Wednesday, with the central bank wading into the session to keep the local currency from extending its one-day rally too far.  

The peso ended local trading at ARS2.9925 to the dollar, just stronger than its ARS2.9975 level a day earlier. Tuesday's session had ended a three-day decline against the U.S. currency that saw the peso slip past the psychologically important level of ARS3.00.  

Trader Daniel Bou-Kahir of Banco de la Pampa said the peso had been gradually gaining against the dollar for most of the session before the monetary authority entered the market to buy pesos, seeking to keep the local currency around recent levels. Ten minutes before trading closed, the peso had been at ARS2.99.  

The central bank bought $44 million Monday and $43.5 million Tuesday. Official data showed the monetary authority bought $41 million Wednesday, on par with levels seen earlier this week.  

Meanwhile, liquidity remains healthy as a result of last week's central bank measure to lower minimum cash ratios.  

"We see that many companies still have liquidity and are not requiring credit for their (end-year) payments," Bou-Kahir said.  

The end of the year traditionally bolsters the peso, as companies needing liquidity to pay bonuses and settle accounts creates higher, seasonal demand for the local currency.  

Meanwhile, in the local fixed-income market, worries over consumer prices continue to drive investors into peso bonds that are adjusted for inflation. The discount bond in pesos was quoted at ARS120, compared with ARS119.9 a day earlier. The par bond in pesos, another inflation-linked note, was ARS48.30, just higher than ARS48.20.  

Analyst Alejandro Barros of Banco Piano said fixed-income investors have largely shrugged at the government's efforts to broker price accords with specific sectors such as supermarkets, seeing these agreements as ineffective.  

The primary concern remains the government's commitment to its monetary policy and whether the central bank will continue buying dollars to maintain the exchange rate around ARS3.00, which the government favors to keep exports competitive.  

"If there's an issue that keeps getting thrown out there with regards to inflation, it's the exchange rate," Barros said. "The dollar should theoretically be at ARS2.40, ARS2.50. To maintain the dollar at ARS3.00, (the central bank) has to bring a lot of pesos to the market."  

Last week, the peso's decline sent dollar bond prices higher and put light pressure on peso bonds. Barros said dollar-denominated bonds were seeing some minor declines Wednesday, though prices should hold steady in the near term.

title: UPDATE:  Argentina  Bond Rally Steams Along; Peso Steady
text:
(Updates with intervention data, central bank raising repo rate) 
   

BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Locally traded Argentine bonds continued to rally Friday, with investors snapping up GDP warrants, the special coupons tied to economic growth that stripped out restructured bonds this week.  

The peso closed the trading day virtually unchanged at ARS2.9825 against the dollar, little changed from ARS2.9800 on Thursday.  

"Bonds are trying to reach levels seen before (former Economy Minister Roberto) Lavagna's exit" was announced on Monday, said Hernan Korin, a local portfolio manager with Supervielle Asset Management. "I think there was an overreaction to his departure and now bonds are recovering. Investors are especially interested in the GDP coupons today."  

Before trading separately on Wednesday, the peso-denominated coupons had traded in the gray market around ARS4.60. But they slid to ARS4.20 on the news that Lavagna would be replaced by former Banco de la Nacion President Felisa Miceli. The market perceived Miceli, whose credentials and experience aren't as strong as Lavagna's, as being easily manipulated by Argentina's populist President Nestor Kirchner.  

Among gainers Friday, the restructured discount bond in pesos was last quoted at ARS118.00, up from ARS116.60, while the par in pesos was at ARS47.80 from ARS47.60. The GDP coupons, meanwhile, were higher at ARS5.00.  

Korin warned that market volatility will remain a concern in the near term. "The market is very sensitive to rumors right now," he said. Chief among them has been swirling talk that Central Bank President Martin Redrado plans to step down after being passed over for the economy minister job.  

In the foreign currency market, it was a slower day as cereal exporters didn't repatriate much of their overseas dollar earnings, said Claudio Arar, a currency trader with Banco Itau in Buenos Aires. "Some days are just busier than others," Arar said. He said that the central bank apparently stepped in to buy some dollars. The monetary authority reported later that it bought $50.5 million in the open market, up from $44 million Thursday.  

The central bank's varied activity this week - from selling dollar futures to stop a run on the peso in the wake of Lavagna's exit announcement to buying dollars to check the peso's recovery - which shows that the monetary authority wants the local currency between ARS2.97 and ARS3.00 against the dollar, Arar said. "That's the range that the central bank seems pleased with," he said.  

After the currency market close, the Argentine Central Bank raised its reference rate for transactions in the securities repurchase, or repo, market at the same time that it took the somewhat contradictory action of easing liquidity conditions for banks by lowering minimum cash ratios.  

Although the news emerged about 15 minutes before the local bond market closed, Supervielle's Korin said the reaction was negligible. He speculated that the move could free up more money to buy bonds - especially inflation-linked shorter-term notes that are expected to draw investors. Argentina's statistics agency Indec is slated to release November consumer price index data on Monday. The central bank's most recent consensus forecast predicts a 0.8% month-on-month rise from October, although Korin said some are expecting a figure closer to 1.0%.

MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--Argentina's central bank president defended his bank's foreign exchange intervention policies and said they are not creating inflation pressures in his country.  

Martin Redrado, at a conference held by the Bank of Mexico in Mexico City Tuesday, said, "I don't see there is a conflict there as long as we sterilize" the bank's moves to buy dollars to build up his nation's foreign exchange reserves.

He added, "we are exactly on track" in terms of the bank's monetary policy goals.

The peso weakened late last month on emerging market pessimism that has since cleared. The central bank was to report its daily intervention data later Tuesday. [ 08-11-05 1944GMT ]

title: RPT-Argentina post-election economy: more of the same?
text:
(Repeats to additional subscribers)  

BUENOS AIRES, Argentina, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Argentine President Nestor Kirchner is likely to keep playing hard ball with the IMF and big business after a resounding victory in Sunday's mid-term elections, but may soon face some tough decisions to sustain the country's recovery.  

Kirchner bolstered his support in Congress and wrestled power away from a rival faction of the Peronist Party in a vote that centered on a Senate race between his wife and a former first lady to represent Buenos Aires, the country's heavyweight province.  

On the campaign trail, Kirchner won crowds with his habitual sharp-tongued attacks on the International Monetary Fund and foreign investors, including giant Western European utility companies, while taking credit for a three-year economic rebound he said was possible because of snubbing the standard free market policies pushed by Wall Street.  

While Argentines wondered whether their leader would adopt a more moderate stance once the election was out of the way, analysts say he will likely continue with an approach on the foreign front that appears to have worked so far.  

"He's convinced he did things right and as a result we have this economic recovery ... So why would there be any need to change course?" said Aldo Abram, an analyst with Exante consultancy.  

Kirchner needed to triumph in the polls after taking office in 2003 with just 22 percent of the vote when his runoff contender quit.  

With 97 percent of the ballots counted, his wife, Cristina, thumped her foes by winning 46 percent, 26 points more than wife of former President Eduardo Duhalde. The president's left-of-center Peronist camp clinched 43 percent of seats in the lower house.  

Kirchner was helped by an economic boom now in its third year after a devastating 2001-2002 economic crash that forced a currency devaluation and massive debt default. The economy is growing at around 9 percent for the third year running.  

SLEEPLESS IN BUENOS AIRES  

But now runaway inflation is menacing that recovery. Kirchner admitted in a radio interview last week he is "losing sleep" over price hikes and Economy Minister Roberto Lavagna is expected to make fighting inflation a top priority.  

There is also growing unease about Argentina's monetary expansion and central bank intervention to keep the peso from strengthening, which critics say is inflationary. A stronger peso could reduce the price of imported goods, but at the cost of making Argentine goods less competitive abroad.  

Consumer prices are headed this year toward 10 percent growth -- the first bout of double-digit inflation in three years, a troubling prospect for the 38 percent of Argentines living in poverty.  

To combat inflation, Kirchner may have to backtrack on some policies and stifle labor demands for higher wages or allow the peso to appreciate, economists believe.  

"The prolonged bout of inflation above 10 percent is not stable: it is likely to lead to a dangerous inflationary spiral if the monetary and fiscal authorities do not move to contain it," said Gray Newman, economist at Morgan Stanley in New York.  

And it is still not clear whether a poltically fortified Kirchner will agree to immediate loan talks with the IMF or speed up stalled negotiations with disgruntled utility companies to end a 2002 rate freeze.  

Major utility companies, such as Suez of France, have opted to pull out of Argentina over the rate conflict and others like Spain's Telefonica and Telecom Italia are still negotiating.  

"There won't be an accord with the IMF, there won't be any utility rate increases and on the inflation issue, he will continue to put pressure the price-makers but not act on the monetary and foreign exchange policy," said Buenos Aires political analyst Rosendo Fraga.  

But Credit Suisse First Boston analyst Carola Sandy said in a report last week a Kirchner victory is a "positive or neutral market event" that signals a possible fiscal and monetary tightening and renewed interest in negotiations with the IMF, which it owes $11 billion.  

Argentina suspended talks with the IMF last year to concentrate on restructuring $100 billion in defaulted debt. The lender has repeatedly said in the past few weeks it is ready to meet with the Argentines and Buenos Aires is expected to respond in the coming days. [20051024 170132 GMT]

title: Milei would not encourage diplomatic ties with China, but neither would he stand in the way of its investments.
text:
The leading candidate in Argentina's presidential elections, the libertarian Javier Milei, did not deviate from his ideals and said that in mining and metals he would leave the markets to their fate.

In his first interview with foreign media Javier Milei promises to pay Argentina's debt and close the Central Bank.

The government has been working to prevent Latin American resources from suffering the same fate again and is trying to turn Argentina's lithium rush into a local electric vehicle battery manufacturing industry. When asked if he would abandon those efforts, Milei said he would not pick winners and that batteries should be made where people want to make them.

Milei indicated in an interview Wednesday at Bloomberg's Buenos Aires offices that he would not encourage diplomatic ties with China because of what he called encroachments on personal freedoms. But neither would he stand in the way of trade and investment between China and Argentina. China is a major buyer of Argentina's soybeans and unprocessed beef, and a leading developer of its Andean lithium deposits.

The candidate argued that he would eliminate state intervention in the country's giant agricultural industry to unleash an export boom.

Milei, a free-market devotee, promised to quickly end the policies that have held back agricultural investment this century. He would unify exchange rates, eliminate export taxes and quotas, and end direct meddling in food prices.

"It's part of our deregulation program," Milei told Bloomberg. "Those are all the regulations we have to get rid of as quickly as possible."

Argentina is one of the world's leading suppliers of beef as well as soybean meal and corn to feed livestock in other countries. But farmers have been unable to fully tap the potential of the vast plains due to years of market intervention designed to boost tax revenues and quell inflation. Milei says Argentina's high poverty rates prove the policy has been a failure.

Given that he plans to reduce government spending and end inflation by getting rid of Argentina's currency, interventions, in addition to running counter to his libertarian values, would, in theory, be redundant. A free market system could achieve an explosion in agricultural activity, according to Milei's manifesto.

Still, the path to such radical change is likely to be difficult: if there are street protests or dissent in Congress, that could stop investors in their tracks.

Agricultural exports surged during former President Mauricio Macri's government's brief experiment with market-oriented policies. But Milei would take things a step further by eliminating billions of dollars in annual taxes on soybean exports.

In a transition period, farmers would pay soybean taxes in exchange for lower income tax collections, Milei said. They would become so wealthy under Milei, they would even be willing to fund their government, he said, a notion that is anathema to them under the current administration.

In the oil sector, Milei said investors should have no doubt that he would re-privatize YPF S.A., which was nationalized in 2012 to spearhead the development of Patagonia's shale riches. But privatization would not happen for about two years, as a Milei government would need time to prepare for the shift to freer energy markets.

"We need YPF and Enarsa to finish adjusting the imbalances in the energy sector," Milei said.

Argentina's booming shale oil industry has been constrained by capital, price and export controls that Milei aims to banish. Restrictions on cash flows recently led Exxon Mobil Corp. to put its shale assets up for sale, according to the governor of Neuquén, the country's oil heartland.

title: Candidates duck inflation issue on eve of Argentina election
text:
It is on the lips of the people, but not so much on the lips of those who want to govern them. Inflation, which daily eats away at Argentines' wages and adds to the ranks of the poor, is a topic that the country's leading presidential candidates have sought to dodge ten days before the primary elections.

Deeper discussions on the problem, which would require unpopular measures, have been left for later on the candidates' agenda. Instead, they have chosen to prioritize possibly more fruitful agendas in terms of votes, such as public safety and job creation.

On the streets, however, rising prices are the number one cause of angst cited by voters of any political preference or region, different surveys indicate. A July survey by the University of San Andrés found that 55% of Argentines say inflation is Argentina's biggest current obstacle. Insecurity comes in second, mentioned by 38% of the population.

"Before we could have a barbecue on the weekends, now the money isn't enough," complains Miguel García, 56, a janitor outside his building in an affluent Buenos Aires neighborhood. And what do the candidates intend to do about it? He shrugs: "I don't know, they just promise and never deliver."

On the Peronist side, Sergio Massa has avoided the topic as much as possible, since he has been economy minister for more than a year and has so far failed to halt the devaluation of the peso. On the opposition right, Buenos Aires Mayor Horacio Larreta and former Security Minister Patricia Bullrich - who are vying for a seat in the first round - repeat the mantra of lowering spending, but do not detail how.

"Neither of the two largest coalitions is able to address the issue as an advantage, because both doubled inflation in their governments," says Artemio López, director of consultancy Equis, referring to the administrations of Republican Mauricio Macri (2015-2019) and the current president, Peronist Alberto Fernández.

The exception is the ultra-liberal Javier Milei, who uses the country's economic malaise as his main political springboard, but does not expose concrete plans on his proposal to dollarize Argentina, according to analysts. "It's the issue that Milei can lean on the most, but he can't pin down a government project, he proposes interventions on specific issues," says López.

The primaries in Argentina, called Paso (Primary, Open, Simultaneous and Compulsory), are usually seen as a major national poll for the first round on October 22. This time, however, they could also change the course of the election, depending on who wins in the opposition coalition Juntos por el Cambio. Larreta is more center-leaning, and Bullrich is more to the right.

So far, the scenario is one of great uncertainty, with polls showing a close race between the two, who register something close to 15% of voting intentions. Together, they account for about a third of voters, while the Peronist coalition Union for the Homeland is close behind. Milei has lost steam in the last month and registers figures ranging from 12% to 20%, depending on the survey.

There is also a significant portion of the population that has not decided on a candidate, such as Miguel, a janitor, or intends to vote blank or null. The feeling of "I'm fed up" and disillusionment with politics is a hallmark of this election, after successive governments failed to contain the escalation of inflation and avoid the country's third major economic crisis in 40 years of democracy.

Prices have risen 116% in the last 12 months, considering the accumulated index until June - the second highest figure in Latin America, behind Venezuela. Some of the causes are an insistent deficit, high foreign debt, a currency without credibility and a lack of dollars in public coffers. Four out of ten Argentines are below the poverty line.

"The solutions include eliminating subsidies, cutting public services and other measures that are unpalatable in an election campaign, which is why the candidates shy away, even though they all have studies on the path they intend to take," says economist Juan Telechea, director of the ITE (Institute of Labor and Economics of the Germán Abdala Foundation).

Peronist minister Sergio Massa, for example, has focused his speeches on national industry, and always sides with workers: "Two models of country are at stake, one that bets on national production, genuine employment and the sale of Argentine labor to the world, and another that seeks only financial speculation," he declared at a rally this week.

Horacio Larreta, meanwhile, is banking on his experience running the capital Buenos Aires, saying "we're going to do it because we've done it before". To the sound of hopeful or heroic songs, he is one of those who lists the most economic proposals, talking about spending control, tax cuts and boosting exports, but without going into detail.

He also advocates more conservative measures in the area of security, as does Patricia Bullrich. Macri's former minister talks about "putting order" in the country and encourages polarization with Peronism. On finance, she also advocates ending the limit on the purchase of dollars and an independent central bank, but has recently been the target of jokes for statements in which she showed ignorance of the area.

Milei's campaign, on the other hand, stands out from the lukewarm tone of the other candidates. To the sound of rock music, wearing a leather jacket and always surrounded by a crowd of young people, the libertarian talks about ending the Central Bank and radically cleaning up the state against corruption. His slogan, always in bold letters, is a little more direct: "Long live freedom".

title: More spending adjustment, dollar  intervention  and new reserves target: what  Argentina  agreed with the IMF - By Melina Manfredi
text:
On the verge of the July maturity date, the Government and the IMF reached an agreement that will unblock a disbursement of US$ 7.5 billion that Argentina was waiting for to cancel part of the debt with the multilateral organization, as well as to strengthen international reserves and provide predictability.

The discussion was long, much longer than expected, and the parties had to compromise on some issues. Although the Government succeeded in getting the IMF to acknowledge the impact of the drought and not to ask for further cuts in the deficit for this year, Sergio Massa had to accept some conditions in exchange.

In the communiqué issued by the IMF are the first clues of what the Government promised to the organization to unblock the discussion. "Given the economic challenges, the authorities agreed to firmly implement the policy package in the coming weeks and months, and to adapt proactively to the evolution of external and domestic conditions," said IMF officials following the Argentine case.

The cuts committed to by Sergio Massa

According to the IMF communiqué, the fiscal deficit target for this year remains at 1.9%. However, at the current pace of the public accounts, economists assure that it will be very difficult to meet.

The IMF itself acknowledged that "meeting the target requires a further tightening of fiscal policy in the second half of this year supported by a series of agreed revenue and expenditure measures, protecting priority social and infrastructure programs".

In this sense, the agency highlighted that, on the revenue side, the Government has already implemented new taxes on imports and an extension of the agricultural dollar. On the expenditure side, meanwhile, the IMF said that efforts are still needed to:

Contain wage bill growth.

Update energy tariffs to better reflect changes in production costs, while improving the progressivity of the system.

Strengthen spending controls through better targeted social assistance and further rationalization of current transfers to provinces and state-owned enterprises.

On the other hand, the IMF remarked that the Central Bank will not have to issue more pesos to comply with the agreement. "The agreed fiscal path does not imply additional reliance on direct monetary financing of the fiscal deficit," it said.

How the foreign exchange market will be managed after the agreement with the IMF

Regarding official intervention in alternative dollar markets, the IMF stated that "it will remain a key instrument to contain market pressures, with interventions in the parallel and currency futures markets focused on addressing situations of disorderly conditions."

However, it asked Massa that official involvement in the bond segment should focus "on ensuring the normal functioning of the market, while protecting the Central Bank's balance sheet."

On the other hand, the IMF reminded that it is essential to harmonize and strengthen the foreign exchange market. At the same time, the organization acknowledged that the rate of devaluation of the official dollar will continue to be managed to preserve competitiveness and support reserve accumulation objectives.

Reserve accumulation, a little more flexible

A relative victory for the Government in the negotiation was in the net reserves accumulation target, which went from US$8 billion to US$1 billion at the end of this year, due to the impact of the drought on the exportable balance.

However, it is still a challenging target, given that today the BCRA's net reserves are negative by about US$7 billion. This means that, even if the IMF lowered the bar, the Government will have to raise the same amount of dollars as originally planned.

"This accumulation is expected to be supported by improvements in the energy balance (resulting from the completion of the first phase of the gas pipeline) and by the expected recovery from the drought starting in the latter part of this year," the IMF stated.

What will happen to the fixed term rate

In order to sustain the demand for pesos and address high inflation, the Argentine authorities committed to the IMF to ensure that the interest rate remains in positive territory in real terms.

Currently, the fixed term rate is above 8% per month and is above the last two inflation data recorded.

title: Effects of the "yuanization" of the  Central Bank : between loans to import and ill-informed  intervention
text:
As the days of July went by, certain discrepancies began to be noticed between what the Central Bank of Argentina reported to the press about its intervention in the foreign exchange market and what was later confirmed by the Central Bank itself.

Doubts were raised in the market, but it was not known for sure what was really happening, because the monetary authority misreported its intervention, and mainly with favorable numbers for the entity in the press releases.

From here we will try to give a description of what is happening and how to analyze the Central Bank's future press releases. The origin of the problem

On June 28 we witnessed the first major deviation from what was to be a confusing data collection that generated uncertainty as to how the exchange rate scenario was turning out for the Central Bank, and what scenario was taking place.

From that moment on, the errors started to be not only more frequent, but there were also -accumulating for the time being-, intervention underestimates for u$s835 million.

Why is this difference? It basically arises from an unannounced change in the way of communicating the Central Bank's interventions in the foreign exchange market, since previously the data was reported to the press in a unified manner. That is to say, whether dollars or yuans were sold, the data was netted and condensed into a dollar amount.

But the gradual "yuanization" of the foreign exchange market led the monetary authority to intervene mainly in two currencies, dollars and yuans. So far, the Central Bank has used yuan for about u$s3,600 million (between exchange intervention and payment to the International Monetary Fund), of which it has approved for free availability u$s5,000 million, and another tranche authorized for use (which is not the same as conversion) for another u$s5,000 million. In addition, the Chinese swap is for US$ 18 billion.

What do these numbers mean? That since May so far, it has been used for: 72% of authorized amount of free availability. 36% of the amount authorized so far. 20% of the total amount of the swap.

So far in July alone, yuans have been sold for u$s910 million in foreign exchange intervention, while, if only the dollar figure is analyzed, the Central Bank is a seller of u$s47 million. Such a huge difference denotes a clear will of the Central Bank to release yuans (at the cost of assuming debt with the Asian country) instead of getting rid of the so precious dollars.

Therefore, in order to analyze in correct terms the intervention that the monetary authority must make in the foreign exchange market to meet the demand for foreign currency, not only the dollar figure should be included, but now also the yuan figure.

There you will find the answer to how much it is costing the Central Bank to maintain an exchange rate like the current one, and at the same time, a brief look at how the yuan is playing an interesting role in the foreign exchange market. Yuanization of the foreign exchange market

We are witnessing a displacement of operations carried out in dollars, to be replaced by yuans. Why? Precisely because dollars are in short supply -and in short supply-. Net reserves are around u$s7,300 million negative, and the Central Bank does not stop getting rid of foreign currency every day.

Here comes the People's Bank of China to offer a "rescue", logically under its own interests, offering a foreign currency loan whose terms are located in a thick fog of sub-information, but which in any case allows giving some temporary relief to the current situation at the cost of worsening it in the future, or at least contracting a loan whose repayment we do not know if it will be economically feasible or convenient.

Therefore, although the dollar scenario in July is not exaggeratedly bad, it is bad if analyzed in net terms, adding the intervention via the Asian currency. In only 10 rounds of July, a net u$s950 million have been sold, a few dollars away from surpassing the maximum sold in the seventh month of each year with the cap.

At the same time, imports from China are implicitly encouraged through these operations, knowing that, for the time being, the allocation of foreign currency is at least somewhat more flexible than if it were in dollars. Let us recall that this year's trade deficit with the Asian country (in goods) accumulated up to May was u$s 3,150 million.

In short, China would be financing Argentina's exports, or Argentina would be requesting a loan from China to be able to import from there. But like any loan, such obligation will mature and Argentina will have to pay. How? Probably with dollars .

In the meantime, not only the sales of foreign currency are underestimated here , but also the consequences of financing them.

title: Argentina hopes to close IMF staff deal by Friday
text:
Argentine authorities hope to close a team-level deal with the International Monetary Fund by Friday after months of negotiations over the $44 billion program, according to Economy Ministry officials.

Economy Minister Sergio Massa held talks with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva on Sunday, according to one of the officials, who asked not to be identified.

Argentina will send a delegation to Washington on Monday evening to speed up the negotiations, they added, although a trip has been suggested several times in recent weeks by ministry officials, then postponed.

As of Sunday evening, some Argentine government officials had not yet been told whether they would fly on Monday, according to one person. Three weeks ago, Massa promised a deal would be announced in "hours" but that has not happened.

The Argentine government needs to pay about $2.6 billion to the IMF by the end of July to stay in good standing with the multilateral lender. The country's central bank made a similar-sized payment in June, using its IMF special drawing rights and yuan from a currency swap line with Beijing.

Massa wants to revise the IMF deal amid a record drought affecting the country's agricultural sector and "political setbacks". At the same time, negotiations have been stalled for political reasons because Massa is now the ruling party's presidential candidate.

Massa and his team are trying to receive advances from the IMF after the drought destroyed $20 billion in agricultural exports. They are also pressing the IMF to allow Argentina to use some of the money to intervene in foreign exchange, an economic policy the IMF has criticized in the past.

An IMF spokesman declined to comment when reached on Sunday. Julie Kozack, the IMF's communications director, declined to give details of the talks at a news conference last week, noting that the two sides were working "intensively".

Argentines will go to the polls to choose a new president, congressmen and governors of several provinces on October 22.

title: Dollar at 500 pesos
text:
In contrast to the historic gain of the Mexican super currency under the administration of President Andrés Manuel López Obrador, we can see that in the south of the continent they are no longer feeling the hard way, but the hard way. In view of the delay of an agreement with the International Monetary Fund and the almost null firepower of its central bank to intervene in the market, Argentina's peso broke the barrier of 500 units per dollar yesterday in the informal exchange round. We are reminded that when Alberto Fernandez's government started the parity was at 60 Argentine pesos, that is, the currency is already worth a small fraction than at the end of 2019. With inflation at over 100% and just one month away from the primary elections to determine the candidacies in national positions for the presidential and legislative elections of October 2023, they explain to us that the problem is not that Argentina lacks dollars, but that there is a furious excess of pesos.

The sabotage continuesWe are told that there is no end to the sabotage between the two most important telecommunications companies in Mexico. So much so that, in the ring, the company that seemed to be on the side of the technicians became rude just like its main competitor. We are told that users have already detected that when Telmex's Infinitum service starts to fail, it is certain that, in the following days, the same thing will happen with Izzi, which is managed until August by Jose Antonio Gonzalez Anaya. We are told that everyone knows that it is the same workers of both companies who cut the cables to cause the interruption of the Internet service and, incidentally, the landline and cable TV service, and no one stops them.

There is a Mexican Jetta for a whileDespite the fact that several automakers have decided to stop manufacturing vehicles that sell well in the Mexican market, such as the Aveo, and instead bring them from China, we are informed that Volkswagen, headed by Holger Nestler, plans to continue manufacturing the Jetta model at the Puebla plant. We are assured that Volkswagen de México is not considering importing this model, which is, in fact, the car with the highest historical production volume for the German company in the country, with more than 6 million units made by Mexican hands. So there is a Jetta for a while in the domestic market. We are told that Chinese brands no longer only manufacture for North American or European assemblers, but now export to the country vehicles of their own brands such as Chirey, Omoda, Jetour, MG and JAC, whose sales have multiplied over the last few years.

20 years financing car purchasesWe are informed that this week, Nissan Mexicana's finance company, Credi Nissan, headed by André Medeiros, is celebrating 20 years of operation. In these two decades, the finance company has served 3 million drivers, placing it in first place in the automotive credit sector. The company offers financial options for entrepreneurs, companies that require fleets, SMEs, people who cannot prove income, leasing for corporations and students who want to buy their first vehicle, among others. They tell us that now, the company's focus is to make its credit process 100% digital. It currently has a portfolio of 441 thousand active contracts and the most financed cars are NP300, Versa and Sentra.

title: Record  intervention : the government used the largest monthly amount of its entire administration to contain the dollar
text:
In May alone, the Government used US$ 759 million of the scarce reserves of the Central Bank of Argentina (BCRA) to intervene in financial dollar rates and contain the exchange rate gap. This was the highest monthly amount of the entire Alberto Fernández administration, in which more than US$ 4,500 million were used for the same purpose. According to the official view, keeping calm in the exchange market is the key to control inflation until the elections, even at the cost of putting even more pressure on the weakened coffers of the monetary authority.

In the midst of the April run, which took the blue dollar to the $500 level, the Minister of Economy and presidential pre-candidate of the ruling party, Sergio Massa, ordered the BCRA to begin to carry out operations with bonds held by the entity in order to cut devaluation pressures. This decision went against the request made by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) during the review of the Argentine program corresponding to the first quarter and reinstated a practice that was used in the times of Martin Guzman before the 2021 elections.

In detail, the monetary authority used US$ 115 million in April to contain the gap, but in May the number shot up to US$ 759 million. Romano Group economist , Salvador Vitelli, pointed out that this amount was a new maximum for Alberto Fernández's administration. The fact that net reserves are negative today is partly due to this," Vitelli pointed out.

Beyond the picture that May left, economist Fernando Marull stated that the Government used almost US$ 4,500 million to contain the parallel dollars. With those dollars 1.5 gas pipelines could have been built, such as the Néstor Kirchner pipeline which was inaugurated this Sunday", detailed the consultant.

The big question going forwardis what will be the margin Sergio Massa will have to contain future exchange rate pressures, even more so in a context of elections in which the dollarization of portfolios tends to accelerate and a second semester in which the supply of foreign currency falls seasonally. In addition, the drought will mean a US$20 billion drop in income from agricultural exports this year. The truth is that the BCRA's firepower is decreasing and negotiations with the IMF to obtain an advance of disbursements continue to be delayed.

In this regard, Cohen's chief strategist, Martín Polo, commented: "Specifically, in the last week, the BCRA sold more than US$500 million in the foreign exchange market -a much larger amount than reported so far- with the agricultural sector liquidating only US$233 million. These operations, added to the net debt payments of US$750 million, implied a decrease of US$1,314 million in the international reserves, which closed the week with a gross stock of US$26,612 million, while the net reserves extended the negative balance to US$6,600 million. Let us remember that US$ 3.4 billion more remain to be paid until the PASO and, with the dynamics of the exchange market, they could reach -US$ 11 billion. Although we believe that the panic will act as a "disciplinarian" to find a point of agreement, this context challenges more and more our scenario of no exchange rate jump during the electoral process?

Sergio Massa's team has a simple calculation: in April, the run-up in inflation peaked at 8.4%, while the record interventions in May allowed a deceleration of the CPI to 7.8% per month. This hypothesis does not take into account the fiscal and monetary imbalances accumulated by the local economy. Econviews consulting firm estimated that the monetary authority used US$ 100 million in June to curb financial exchange rates.

So far in July, the exchange rate gap has remained low, as reviewed by the consulting firm Ecolatina: "In the last week the alternative dollars remained relatively stable. While the blue dollar ($492) and MEP ($485) remained practically at the same levels in the last week, the CCL showed an advance of 2.6% ($495). Consequently, the average exchange rate gap ended the week at 88%, slightly lower than last Friday's 89.4%?

Let us remember that keeping the exchange rate gap contained is an essential part of the?Massa plan? and a transversal challenge to the ?dollar front?, the ?peso front? and the ?price front?: currently, a jump in the parallel dollars filters more easily the inflation (as we already saw in the April figures) and increases the devaluation expectations, reducing even more the net supply of foreign currency? concluded Ecolatina.

title: An agreement that is being discussed until the last minute due to the use of dollars
text:
Leandro Gabin

eleconomista.com.ar

"The Fund and Argentina are like those marriages that are cheating on each other and they both know it. But they are still together because neither of them would like to separate". That is the definition that the Government has of its relationship with the organization at the gates of a new agreement that Sergio Massa (with his traditional effervescence) said was "imminent" and would be known in a matter of hours.

The truth is that one of the points to be deciphered in the new understanding, which will be until the next government takes office, is the use of dollars to intervene in the exchange market and whether or not there will be an advance of funds. The Central Bank reserves are negative and it is believed in the market that Miguel Pesceintervenes using (even) the bank reserve requirements in dollars (as stated by the opposition economist Luciano Laspina).

The desperation of the economic team to reach the PASO and afterwards, consists in just that: how to avoid a devaluation of the official exchange rate or a jump of the alternative dollar.

Some voices in Washington indicate that even part of the delay of the agreement between Massa and the Fund has to do with the use of dollars. The minister and now the only candidate of the Kirchnerist party had been asking that the new agreement should contemplate that Argentina should use foreign currency to control the dollar.

The IMF does not want to be tied to that (something that would violate its own statute) but neither does it want an implosion of the country.

As they say in Casa Rosada, fights of a married couple that lives deceiving each other. The truth is that the new understanding does not seem to have anything outstanding beyond incorporating the fact that Argentina failed to meet all the goals due to the drought.

Disbursements and measures

Will there be money up front? Anker Latinoamérica, Luis "Toto" Caputo's consulting firm, says that Massa's candidacy "reinforces the view that the chances of the IMF validating a relevant disbursement advance without demanding measures in exchange (particularly regarding the exchange rate) are very low".

"On the one hand, it would be even more difficult for the organization to advance funds without demands to the candidate of the ruling coalition, given the political implications that this could entail. On the other hand, given that the current minister could be the President with whom the IMF would have to negotiate as of December, there would be no technical reason to justify the postponement of measures aimed at macroeconomic order", states Anker.

Alejandro Werner, former IMF, agrees with this view: "It is unlikely that the program will have significant additional resources for Argentina to be able to use them to intervene in the foreign exchange market".

The former official of the organization believes that if there are any, they will be few because the IMF knows that it is lending them to a program that does not make sense and also because they will be used for electoral purposes. "Besides, he knows that between December and February he will have to negotiate with a new government that will probably also ask for new resources", said the Mexican who has always catalogued as a "bad agreement" what was signed between Alberto Fernández and the organization.

For Werner, what will be seen will be an agreement with very low demands from the Fund, given that the current Government is ending its term and does not have the margin to face a comprehensive program that includes a reform package to sustain it. In any case, the outcome of the Massa-IMF affair remains to be seen.

Confidence for what is to come

For the time being, there is some hope in the private sector that the coming economy will be better. From the foreign bankers grouped in ABA, they said that "the challenging context we are going through in 2023 should be, at the same time, the kick-off for the long-awaited take-off of our country in 2024".

"Even in the midst of the macroeconomic instability resulting from the fiscal imbalance, the scarcity of international reserves, the strong commitments assumed with multilateral credit organizations and the drought that affected the main productive sector, it is possible to glimpse the mechanisms for the recovery of the activity, the creation of formal employment and a strategic insertion in the world, for which -as expressed by the economic swords of most of the candidates-, an economic or stabilization plan of the macroeconomic variables is required", requested the bankers whose visible face is Claudio Cesario.

Carlos Melconian, who recently presented his team and economic program of the Fundación Mediterránea (for the use of the candidates) said, in his own way, something similar. "I see a lot of light for next year. Soybean, gas, lithium...everything is going for the better", he pointed out.

But, true to his style, he clarified: "Let's not be fooled either. Are those who are coming the cow tied up? Never say that in Argentina. But we will be better off if we do things right".

The country that was not. The country that will be?

title: Dollar, inflation and debt: the economic variables that drove Martin Guzman out of office remain in crisis one year after his resignation
text:
"The first time I spoke to Argentina as Minister of Economy of the Nation, I said that our goal was to calm the economy. This concept may not generate much enthusiasm for many people, but it always seemed to me (and it seems to me) that calming the economy would be a true epic". With these words, expressed in a letter he shared on his Twitter account exactly one year ago, Martín Guzmán left his post as Minister of Economy amidst strong questioning from the hard-line Kirchnerism. His departure triggered an institutional crisis within the Government and also a strong economic and financial volatility.

After a few days of uncertainty, Silvina Batakis took over the management of Argentina's economic destiny. She even met with the Managing Director of the IMF, Kristalina Georgieva. However, she did not manage to stabilize the markets and was only in office for 24 days. As of July 28 last year, she was replaced by the now presidential pre-candidate, Sergio Massa.

The merit of the current minister had to do, above all, with stopping the exchange rate run that had been unleashed when he took office, but he did not manage to avoid a deterioration of the main economic variables, despite the measures he took.

What happened to the dollar since the departure of Martín Guzmán and the measures taken by Sergio MassaIn the weeks prior to Guzmán's departure, alternative exchange rates had started to overheat. On Friday, July 1st, the last day of his administration, the blue dollar closed at $239, while the MEP was quoted at $248.03 and the cash with liquidation was $252.22.

Throughout this year, all these quotes continued to rise. The blue dollar closed this Friday at $494, which represents an increase of 106.7% in the last year. Financials also rose. The MEP dollar rose 94.54% and the cash with liquidation increased 103%.

On the official side, the devaluation of the peso continued, at different rates: some months it matched inflation and others it was somewhat below it. However, the price of the wholesale dollar went from $125.45 to $256.75, which resulted in an increase of 104.6% in 12 months, similar to that of the blue.

In order to try to contain the gap, a variety of measures were taken in the last year. Some of these decisions sought to contain demand. Among them, we can mention:

The creation of the Qatar dollar, to apply a more expensive exchange rate to consumption abroad. The surcharge on luxury goods and the so-called cultural dollar, for international shows coming to the country -called Coldplay dollar- were also implemented.Restrictions on the purchase of some products in foreign platforms (e.g. gift cards).Greater restrictions to operate with the MEP dollar and cash with liquidation.Making some imports more difficult.Companies and provinces were forced to refinance their debts in dollars.What happened to the reserves and the IMF agreement?Other key issues for the Ministry of Economy -both in Guzmán's and Sergio Massa's administration- have to do with the accumulation of reserves and the maintenance of the agreement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

When Massa arrived at the Treasury Palace, he insisted on the need to create a "dollar factory" to allocate BCRA reserves. Under that objective, he implemented a series of rules that tried to increase the supply of foreign currency:

The three soy dollar schemes (the last one also included other agricultural products) to give exporters a more competitive exchange rate.Monotributo tech, to favor the liquidation of dollars in the country by freelance workers rendering services abroad. This initiative was approved by the Chamber of Deputies and has been approved by the Senate, but is still awaiting approval.Differential dollar for tourists arriving in Argentina, in line with the MEP price instead of the official one, to prevent those foreign currencies from escaping to the illegal market.In any case, reserves dropped by more than US$14 billion in the last year -if Friday's last cut is taken as a reference, where reserves closed at US$27,933 million- and several payments to the IMF are still pending for the remainder of 2023, in addition to the amortization of a bond for around US$1 billion in July.

The accumulation of reserves is one of the pillars of the agreement with the IMF -in addition to the reduction of the fiscal deficit and the control of the BCRA's assistance to the Treasury-, which after Guzmán's departure also underwent some changes.

Already with Massa in Economy, the Government moved forward in the removal of subsidies to the tariffs for the higher income sectors, started audits on the delivery of the Potenciar Trabajo plans and suspended the assistance to some 160,000 people.

However, this year it failed to comply with the planned guidelines -so far this year, the BCRA transferred $670,000 million and the primary deficit accumulated $1.2 trillion during the first five months of the year-, so that since April the economic team has been negotiating a modification of the understanding under the argumentation of the losses caused by the drought.

In addition, one of the last conditions that the Fund had imposed on Argentina was the impossibility of intervening in the financial market with the BCRA reserves, but after the run that left the blue dollar on the verge of $500, the Government rejected this requirement and resigned part of the reserves to avoid a more abrupt jump in the exchange rate front.

What has happened to inflation since Martín Guzmán resigned?The last inflation figure for Martín Guzmán's administration was 5.3% monthly in June, which translated into a year-on-year increase of 64%. Although these were high numbers, they continued to rise after his departure.

Over the last 12 months, the government achieved some monthly decreases, but the price index accelerated monthly since the beginning of this year and reached a monthly high of 8.4% in April. On the other hand, year-on-year inflation never stopped rising and according to the latest INDEC data, between June 2022 and May this year, prices rose 114.2%.

The measures taken by the Government to try to curb the price increase were based on agreements with the private sector, but they proved to be insufficient. It also appealed to monetary decisions.

Precios Justos (Fair Prices) was launched to replace the former Precios Cuidados (Cared Prices) program, with a basket of grocery and cleaning items at prices whose monthly increase is capped. It is available in large supermarkets.In the same spirit, a seasonal basket of fruits and vegetables was added, which changes every month, and an attempt was made to bring a similar version to local stores.Fuel increases were also limited and work is being done to renew the price agreement for white goods, clothing and electronics until after the PASO.The Central Bank raised the interest rate by 45 percentage points to try to increase the attractiveness of peso deposits. Thus, the reference yield went from 52% to 97% since the resignation of Martín Guzmán until now.

title: Imports: USD 512 million in yuan paid this year and expected to accelerate in coming months
text:
As a result of the window opened to pay imports with yuans in the midst of the scarcity of reserves, so far this year Argentina has paid more than USD 500 million of purchases of inputs directly to China with that currency and has committed to use, in terms ranging from 30 to 90 days, about USD 2,400 million more.

According to official information, throughout the year, the equivalent of some USD 512 million of imports were paid directly in renminbi currency, and almost USD 800 million since 2020. The figure is clearly low compared to the rhythm of imports from China every month, but there are two elements that mark the official dispatches as a trend: firstly, that in the last weeks there has been an acceleration that they qualified as "exponential". As an example: the first two weeks of June have doubled the figure for the whole of May.

Secondly, as the yuan payment scheme progresses and consolidates, this number will find a monthly floor of operations much higher than the current one. According to the latest figures of the Secretariat of Commerce, the SIRAs authorized for companies seeking to import paying with Chinese currency exceeded an amount equivalent to USD 2.4 billion.

Although these authorizations will be activated as these waiting periods are met, the Government has already committed to importers half of the first tranche of the currency exchange with the Chinese People's Bank, which was for an amount equivalent to USD 5 billion.

There are maximum hypotheses circulating in official offices, with the numbers of commercial exchange with China in hand. So far this year, monthly imports from China have been between USD 920 million and USD 1,100 million.

A first objective set by the Ministry of Economy had been to be able to pay between 700 and 800 million dollars of these imports directly with Chinese currency. An official with direct incidence in the authorizations points out that, if the scheme were sufficiently oiled in the next months, the Government could be able to pay all purchases from China with the Chinese currency.

According to official data, there are some sectors that have a special preponderance in foreign trade with China and have started to look for a mechanism to pay for their purchases of inputs with yuan. Nearly one third of the authorized requests belong to the electronics sector, which has an industrial pole in Tierra del Fuego and imports its main inputs from Asia.

With disaggregated data up to the end of May, the electronics sector concentrated an equivalent of USD 762 million of import payment authorizations in yuan, followed by electrical equipment (USD 304 million), general-purpose machinery (USD 222 million) and chemical products (USD 201 million).

With the acceleration of the use of yuan for the payment of imports, the renminbi futures market, a segment of the Rofex - the derivatives market that concentrates approximately 90% of the volume traded in dollar futures in Argentina - in which agents, importers and financial entities that have operations in Chinese currency participate, re-emerged, albeit timidly.

"The operations that the BCRA has been carrying out are key to develop this market and are aimed at offering foreign exchange risk hedging to local importers that operate in that currency. RMB yuan futures contracts are traded in Argentine pesos and are settled through daily differences in pesos, so they do not imply the transfer of yuan between the parties", official sources indicated.

According to Rofex data, there is an open interest in the renminbi futures market equivalent to some 123 million dollars, which would imply almost 900 million yuan. This is a figure, of course, much lower than the amount of dollar futures traded daily.

"The operations that the BCRA has been carrying out are key to develop this market and are aimed at offering exchange risk coverage to local importers that operate in that currency", the monetary authority assured.

The Government offered as a carrot to importers, in order to tempt them with the possibility of paying for these purchases with renminbi, that the terms in which the access to foreign currency at official prices is approved is shorter, since while those operations made with US dollars take an average of 180 days from the approval until the importer actually has access to the foreign currency, in the case of payment with yuans it is 90 days, and according to the Executive Power, shorter terms for SMEs.

The acceleration in the use of this tool for the payment of purchases abroad and the marked shortage of foreign currency forced the Central Bank to seek an extension -within the limits of the current swap amount, over USD 18 billion- of the use for foreign trade. That was one of the main objectives of the economic team's mission to China last week, which ended with a consensus to add another USD 5 billion for that purpose.

What the BCRA said on the subject.

"The availability of the currency swap with the People's Bank of China allowed a growth in commercial operations conducted in local currencies, reaching payments for CNY 3,650 million in the course of the year. Since April, SIRAs in yuan were authorized for an equivalent of US$ 2.9 billion, which will enter the market 90 days after being issued, on average", informed the monetary entity.

"The use of yuan in trade was CNY 1,075 million in May and CNY 2,045 million in the first ten rounds of June, showing the rapid acceptance among economic agents."

In parallel to the use in trading, "the Central Bank of Argentina (BCRA) has been actively intervening since October 2020, promoting the RMB yuan futures market, which is gaining depth and development in the country. The higher volume of operations that has been registered in the last months, added to the interest shown by agents, financial entities and companies for this instrument, promise to accelerate the development of the RMB yuan futures market."

"Also, the BCRA may carry out operations in yuan for financial stability purposes. The Central Bank of the Argentine Republic has its own holdings of yuan, in addition to the CNY 35 billion freely available from the currency swap for a global amount of CNY 130 billion renewed this month", he specified.

"As part of the agreements, the process of extending the special activation for an amount of up to 35 billion yuan renminbi was initiated, which will be released in favor of the BCRA as the use of the first 35 billion is completed and as the financial and reserve strengthening needs require it", he indicated.

"The operations that the BCRA has been carrying out are key to develop both the foreign exchange market and the futures market, where foreign exchange risk hedging is offered to local importers that operate in that currency. RMB yuan futures contracts are traded in Argentine pesos and are settled through daily differences in pesos, so they do not imply the transfer of yuan between the parties."

"The active participation of the Central Bank of the Argentine Republic is in line with the meetings that the president, Miguel Ángel Pesce, held in China with representatives of financial entities based in Beijing, where they discussed the need to develop in the Argentine capital market spot and futures operations in RMB yuan and in which the BCRA committed itself to support the development of such market."

"Also in that sense, and with the specific purpose of disseminating the operation of import payments with yuan, the BCRA organized in May a virtual meeting with the participation of agencies, entities and different foreign trade referents. Most of the operations are carried out in the Matba Rofex, the derivatives market that concentrates approximately 90% of the volume traded in yuan futures in Argentina", he concluded.

After the swap, the Government will once again tender debt to renew 1.2 trillion pesos per month until the PASO (the Presidential Elections).

The payment of the half Christmas bonus adds more pressure to a free dollar that is once again close to 500 pesos.
