38. FERROSUR ROCA S.A. CONCESSION AND RELATED RAIL SERVICES

On March 11, 1993, Ferrosur Roca S.A. obtained the concession of the General Roca National Cargo Railway Network with the exception of the Altamirano-Miramar corridor and the urban sections, through the approval of the concession contract formalized by National Executive Branch Decree No. 2681/92, after the presentation made through a national and international tender and formalized to that effect. The area of influence is concentrated in the center and south of the province of Buenos Aires, north of the province of Río Negro and Neuquén. It has access to the ports of Buenos Aires, Dock Sud, La Plata, Quequén, and Bahía Blanca.

Ferrosur Roca S.A. is indirectly controlled by the Company, through Cofesur S.A.U. which owns 80% of the interest, 16% of which belongs to the National State and the remaining 4% belongs to the workers of Ferrosur Roca S.A. through a trust created for this purpose.

The term of the concession is 30 years, which expires in March 2023, and originally provides for an extension of 10 additional years.

Ferrosur Roca S.A. requested the above-mentioned extension in due time on March 8, 2018, and in line with the bidding terms and conditions and the concession agreement. The concession extension request was reiterated on March 1, 2019.

On November 7, 2018, Decree No. 1027/2018, which regulated Law No. 27,132, was published in the Official Gazette. The relevant subjects were: readjustment of existing concession contracts with the possibility of extending them for a term not greater than 10 years, full implementation of an open access system on the day following expiration of the last concession contract (of the three private concessions existing at present), including extensions, with the possibility of initiating this modality in the branches that allow it when the planned investments are made; revision of technical standards; revision of the sanction regime, and creation of the registry of operators.

On March 29, 2021, through Resolution No. 219/2021, the National Commission for Transport Regulation ("CNRT") approved the Rules and Regulations of the National Registry of Railway Operators and granted such capacity to Ferrosur Roca S.A. and the other railway concessionaires and, through Resolution No. 211 of the Ministry of Transport, published in the Official Gazette on June 28, 2021, and rejected the request for an extension of the concession contracts duly submitted by all the private railway concessionaires. Therefore, the railway concession operated by the Company will expire at the end of its original term, that is, on March 10, 2023. The purpose of the National State is that the national railway network be based on a mixed modality combining public and private cargo operators, where the National State will manage the infrastructure and control the related investments, thus allowing any registered railway operator to provide railway services regardless of who owns or possesses the facilities at the point of loading or destination.

As a consequence, the Group understands that, at the end of its concession, it will continue to provide the cargo transport rail services it currently provides but as a cargo operator under the terms set forth in Resolution No. 211, Law No. 27,132, and Decree No. 1027 dated November 7, 2018. To this end, the Group will have to readjust various operational issues once it hands over control of the railway infrastructure linked to its current concession to the National State. The Group's Management understands that the intention of the National State is to prioritize the continuity of the current operators for each of the existing services and businesses, thus guaranteeing the best use of the experience they have acquired.

On November 14, 2021, the mid-term general legislative elections took place, and the outcome was contrary to the governing party, with a nationwide differential of almost nine points with respect to the main opposition alliance, and a loss of almost fifteen points as compared to the votes obtained in the 2019 presidential elections. After the electoral result became known, President Alberto Fernández anticipated the sending and treatment at the National Congress of a bill articulating the multi-year economic program, including the agreement with the International Monetary Fund ("IMF").

During the first quarter of 2022, Argentina and the IMF reached an agreement where fiscal and monetary targets were set, and existing debt maturities were refinanced. In the second semester, after the resignation of Economy Minister Martín Guzmán, the main macroeconomic imbalances were contained, especially the fiscal imbalance. With the new Economy Minister Sergio Massa in office, the fiscal deficit slowed down and the target set with the IMF for 2022 were met with some margin. In addition, the Central Bank of the Argentine Republic ("BCRA") stopped direct monetary assistance to the treasury (via temporary advances), although since October 2022 it has intervened steadily in the secondary market of government securities.

Argentine economic activity has performed better than expected in 2022 and is expected to reach about 0.2 annual growth in 2023 according with the IMF.

Although the BCRA reserves increased at the end of 2022 thanks to the strong contribution of the "soybean dollar" for more than USD 7,000 million, they continue to be restricted by the commercial commitments and debt payments that the country has to meet. In addition, in 2023 the Argentine economy is expected to be highly impacted by the prolonged drought that affects the agricultural sector and entails significant losses that will affect both the level of exports and tax revenues, along with a federal budget deficit that may be difficult to curb in an election year.

The national consumer price index published by INDEC accumulated 94.80% in 2022 (as compared to 50.94% in 2021), while the depreciation of the Argentine peso against the US dollar was 72.5%.

There is a challenging curve of public debt due dates in pesos during 2023 that the government will have to face, considering the difficulties to obtain long-term financing, and the drought that is reducing the yields of the wheat, corn, soybean and other crops, and agribusiness in general.

title: What is the 'blue dollar' and why is its value high in Argentina?
text:
BUENOS AIRES - Anxiety, lack of prices and lack of goods in stores are generalized in Argentina due to the rise of parallel exchange rates, in a population accustomed to follow the 'blue dollar' (black market) due to the strong restrictions applied by the Government to access the official one.

The rise in the value of the US currency, which is in its second week, is followed up to the minute in portals and TV channels, in a country accustomed to use the dollar as a thermometer of economic crises.

What is the 'blue dollar' in Argentina?In Argentina there are several types of dollar exchange rates. The BBC explains that there is the official dollar and the blue dollar.

The official dollar price is determined by the Central Bank of Argentina. And it has the lowest quotation, in addition to the fact that only financial and foreign trade entities have access to this official dollar.

But the real king is the blue dollar, notes the BBC: for many people in Argentina, such as traders, it is the most important reference. Its value is higher than the official dollar.

The price of the 'blue dollar'"In the moments of rise and fall of the 'blue dollar', some stores stopped selling, because they could not establish a sale price", since "the fabrics are all imported" and "the jeans stores changed the price three times in a period of two hours", Cecilia Weingardt, administrative employee of a textile importer that sells wholesale fabrics, told EFE.

Situations like this, the immediate increase in prices or the absence of the value on the menus of restaurants and supermarket shelves, so as not to have to change them several times a day, explained those establishments, are becoming commonplace.

For example, on Tuesday, April 26, María José Boga bought a stove online and explained to EFE that, in the period in which she completed the purchase process, "the price increased by 3000 pesos", to almost 53,000 pesos (241 dollars at the official exchange rate, 113 at the parallel rate).

The 'blue dollar' touched 500 pesos this Tuesday, in the second week of exchange tension triggered by a higher than expected inflation (104.3 percent annual in March), when there was already a shortage of foreign currency and net international reserves at minimum levels, deepened by a historic drought that reduces agricultural exports by some 20 billion dollars and a fiscal deficit financed with monetary emission in an economy that demands little local currency.

Waiting for the opening of the market this Wednesday, the 'blue dollar' is down to 473 pesos per unit, "there is nobody buying", added Weingardt.

Those who sell non-essential products see how sales have come to a standstill: "People say it is very expensive," Belén Lizzi, who sells scented candles, told EFE.

Blue dollar' soars in ArgentinaThe soaring parallel exchange rates fuel expectations of a jump in the official exchange rate, despite the fact that the Central Bank has accelerated the daily depreciation, since it quotes 221.54 pesos per unit for sale, with a 106 percent gap with the so-called financial dollars.

The decision of the Minister of Economy, Sergio Massa, on Tuesday to use "all the tools" to order the exchange rate situation is bearing fruit on Wednesday, since the "cash with liquidation" dollar (CCL, which consists of buying locally with Argentine pesos stocks or bonds and selling them in dollars on Wall Street) is down 2 percent, to 456.72 pesos per unit.

In spite of the fact that the President ratified the President of the Central Bank, Miguel Pesce, the Treasury increased its interference in the exchange rate management, as a result of Massa's decision, and managed to contain the rise.

Argentina's political weaknessThe economic fragility has a political component, because the ruling Peronism has internal differences and manages with the only common vision of reaching the primary elections of next August and the presidential elections of October without an explosion.

The head of state, Alberto Fernandez, resigned last Friday to run for reelection and, very weakened, blames the speculation of "the right wing" of the opposition for this rise of the last days, while the vice-president, Cristina Fernandez, will only appear in public this Thursday.

Massa was negotiating concessions from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), with whom the country agreed a program to refinance a debt of 45 billion dollars.

The minister notified the IMF of his decision to intervene in the parallel exchange markets, since it implies not complying with the "restrictions" that weigh on Argentina, which call for avoiding such interventions by the Central Bank, something that Massa said he plans to "change in the rediscussion" of the program.

The economic team will travel this week to Washington to negotiate with the IMF, since Argentina intends to receive the quarterly disbursement despite not having met the net reserves and fiscal deficit targets for the first quarter, while seeking access to more foreign currency.

Despite the IMF's predisposition to maintain a "constructive" work with Argentina, the Peronist government's management is difficult until the elections, which adds to the usual search for coverage in election years.

Additionally, the proposals of the opposition candidates to dollarize the economy or to quickly end the restrictions (cepo) to operate in the official exchange market further fuel the purchase of dollars, increasing the exchange rate uncertainty.

title: Faced with lack of  foreign exchange , Massa activates swap with China
text:
After Tuesday's exchange run, the Government seeks to reduce dependence on the dollar by switching trade with the Asian giant to yuan. It seeks to speed up imports to mitigate the effect of shortages on inflation.

The Minister of Economy, Sergio Massa, announced yesterday that an agreement was reached -with the participation of the People's Bank of China, the Central Bank and a group of Argentine companies- whereby an import authorization system with shorter terms will be implemented and imports will be paid directly with yuans, thus avoiding Argentina the use of dollars to finance those purchases abroad.

The announcement was made at the Treasury Palace, in a ceremony attended by the Chinese ambassador in the country, Zou Xiaoli, and a group of Argentine officials, including the president of the Central Bank of Argentina (BCRA), Miguel Pesce, the secretaries of Economic Policy, Gabriel Rubinstein, and of Trade, Matías Tombolini, and the head of the General Directorate of Customs (DGA), Guillermo Michel.

Tranquility

The minister said that this "allows us for the coming months to work on the possibility of bringing forward the pace of imports, the vast majority of these authorizations were worked at 180 days and with the yuans they are worked at 90 days, and to schedule a volume of imports in yuans for more than US$1 billion as from next month, which replace the use of dollars from Argentina". He further assured that "this improves Argentina's reserve outlook in terms of net reserves" and "gives us greater freedom".

In these troubled days, he said that the agreement "adds operating capacity from the Central Bank [when] we had to make the decision to intervene against those who, thinking that we did not have economic capacity as a State, speculated and overspeculated", he affirmed.

He also stated that "somehow it also allows us to maintain the level of activity, the volume of imports, the rhythm of trade between Argentina and China, and the levels of economic operation that Argentina needs".

"This release of payment obligations of the Central Bank, not only of a stock but of the flow, is greater strength for the reserves, greater capacity of State intervention, greater freedom of our economy and above all it is the guarantee to continue producing with intermediate goods that are imported from China and that also no longer suffer the triangulation process that in some cases we had detected", he concluded.

The Chinese vision

For his part, Chinese Ambassador Zou Xiaoli assured that this agreement will aim "to continue strengthening cooperation between China and Argentina and reflects the strategic relationship and complementarity between Argentina and China, that was reflected in the visit of President Alberto Fernandez to China."

"China pays a lot of attention to bilateral trade with Argentina. We attach importance to the swap we have been working on, wishing to work together to protect and develop our global markets and companies so that they can use local currencies and reduce risks and costs", mentioned the Chinese government representative.

"In 2020, the People's Bank and BCRA signed the new agreement to establish new swap tranches. We have been working closely to exchange data and information. We are confident that Argentina can maintain its economic and financial stability", he concluded.

Some numbers

Since the implementation of customs inspections, the import request monitor, the Import System of the Argentine Republic (SIRA) managed by the Federal Administration of Public Revenues (AFIP), the Secretariat of Commerce and the BCRA, there has been an increase in the use of yuans for the payment of imports from China itself. That number increased eightfold. "So far in April alone, SIRAs were authorized in yuans for the equivalent of US$217 million, compared to US$29 million in January", official data show.

Similarly, the number of SIRA procedures in yuan also increased, from 206 in January to 325 in February, 388 in March and 517 in April, accumulating 1,436 procedures so far this year. In 2023, 4,803 destinations for US$287,781,648 of imports of goods manufactured in China and re-invoiced in European countries have been analyzed.

Put in numbers, the new tranche of the swap announced by the Ministry of Economy implies the payment of imports with yuans for an equivalent of US$1,040 million for May, and that in the next months there will be a minimum of purchases from that country paid in yuans for a value equal to some US$790 million per month.

The blue dollar fell after two days of "fury". Yesterday, Wednesday, was a day of calm in the exchange market because the price of the free dollar fell, after the escalation that took it to almost $500 on Tuesday. "We had to intervene before those who overspeculated, this will give us more freedom", said Massa.

The blue registered a drop of 22 pesos and showed the first important drop after a week of extreme tension in the exchange market. Thus, the parallel currency cost 473 pesos, after touching 500 pesos on Tuesday.

Yesterday, it dropped as low as $467 in the selling segment and finally closed six pesos higher; for purchase it ended at $468. The exchange gap between the parallel and official dollars dropped to 114.4%.

The sharp fall of the US currency in the illegal market occurred after the Central Bank of Argentina (BCRA) intervened on financial dollars, reducing the price of the MEP dollar by 0.20% this Wednesday, to $446.43.

To do so, the BCRA used bonds and reserves, as indicated, managing to position the gap in the case of the stock exchange dollar at 101.3%, while the cash with liquidation (CCL) dropped to $458.11 and the spread with the official dollar is at 106.8%.

In this way, the national government managed to stop the rise of the blue dollar, which started on April 10 and has been going up since Tuesday of last week. This maneuver meant to violate the agreement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and to put an end to the main aid available.

title: La Repregunta. Axel Kaiser: "If Argentina had free trade, 70% of the caste would disappear immediately".
text:
"You destroy democracy by annihilating economic freedom: people don't want to live under a system that condemns them to misery and prevents them from getting ahead," he says. "Democracy has to be liberal. Otherwise, it has no advantage over any dictatorship of the worst kind," he argues. "There are Central Bank models that are more responsible than others and it has a lot to do with the idiosyncrasy of each country", he analyzes and develops: "Argentina cannot have an independent Central Bank because it will never be allowed". "The Chilean Constitution forbids the Central Bank to buy public debt. It is totally forbidden to finance the government. In the new Constitution, they wanted to eliminate that restriction," he details. "In Chile, an example that is not as dramatic as Argentina's, in the last few years, there were 80 billion dollars of capital flight. Why? Because we have started to follow a path more similar to Argentina's," he is alarmed.

 "In Latin America, the Central Bank is used politically to finance public spending", he says and adds: "The Central Bank is used by the mafia that governs our countries and ends up destroying the quality of life of the people". "The Argentine political class and elites are rapacious," he questions. "The Central Bank is very tempting for politicians", he continues.

"There is a consensus among libertarians that the Central Bank should be eliminated," he concludes.

Argentina is a parasitic society where all interest groups try to live at the expense of everyone else," he defines. "The political caste are those who have decision-making power and who govern for their own interest and the interest of those who support them", he specifies. "Milei is the only one who denounces the great problem of Argentina as it has to be", he believes.

"It is a fallacy to say, as Eva Perón used to say, that where a need is born, a right is born: needs are not rights", he challenges.

Poverty is overcome with economic growth, not with distribution", he believes. "In Argentina, the State is the cause of people being in poverty," he criticizes. "There may be limited and focused aid policies, but they do not imply the conception that every need is a right," he clarifies. "The notion of needs is extremely broad and endless," he warns.

"If you want to use the State to satisfy unlimited needs with scarce resources, you will end up with a completely ruined country", he explains.

The State has to support groups that were left out of progress, but not with the logic that every need is a right", he insists and concludes: "in Argentina, everything is a right and that is why the country is broken". "When taxes are high, productivity tends to fall", he analyzes. "Taxes have to be as low as possible and that gives a gigantic incentive for the creation of wealth", he stresses. "The classical liberal tradition allows us to argue in favor of a limited state that charges very low taxes," he points out. "It is very important that the state does not affect the right to property and protects it," he warns. "When there is no competition and there is private property, there is a fascistization of the system," he analyzes. "Mercosur should not matter and should be integrated, as Chile has done, to different economic blocs", he compares.

"Democracy is not an end in itself", he warns,

"Democracy can produce a frightening result", he warns. "Democracy has to be liberal to be worthwhile," he argues. "Compared to Bolsonaro, the progressive left put in religious criteria of this postmodern morality that is completely destructive and pathological," he posits. "If you have the right to life, you have the right to bear arms and defend your life," he asserts. "Boric's government wants to take all the weapons away from citizens while we have the highest homicide rate in the history of Chile", he specifies.

"The discourse against guns seems to me the most dangerous", he assures.

The respected Chilean intellectual Axel Kaiser, one of the most influential voices in the Latin American liberal and libertarian world, was in La Repregunta. Kaiser is president of the Foundation for Progress in Chile. He holds a PhD in Philosophy and Political Economy from the University of Heidelberg, Germany, and is a lawyer from the Universidad Diego Portales, Chile. He is the author of numerous books, the latest, El economista callejero. 15 lessons in economics to survive politicians and demagogues, presented by Javier Milei in Buenos Aires.

When libertarian ideas gain ground in this election year, questions arise: Does every libertarian want to dynamite the Central Bank? Are we all libertarians, including Javier Milei? Why do libertarians like Trump? Kaiser made his analysis.

In the libertarian utopia, can there be a Central Bank-For a country to achieve libertarian ideas in the economic field, does it necessarily have to dynamite its Central Bank

-There is a great discussion among economists of libertarian inspiration also in this matter. But there is a consensus among libertarians that the Central Bank should be eliminated. The reason why it should be eliminated is that it has a task that is impossible to do, which is price calculation. The Central Bank, and let us not forget that this is one of the proposals in the Communist Manifesto among the 10 points of Marx and Engels, not only determines the quantity of money but also, at the same time, the rate of interest. There are conflicting ideas among economists on this matter but those who are closer to the libertarian or classical liberal school propose the abolition of the Central Bank and its replacement by a system of calibre banking, competition of currencies and, in countries like ours, dollarization which, ultimately depends, of course, on a Central Bank that is in the United States. At least, it puts a brake on our central banks. The problem is that, in Latin America, the Central Bank is used politically to finance public spending. Then you have gigantic inflations like those in Argentina or Venezuela. Throughout history, in the whole region, we have had periods of shortages and inflation. But there is a deeper point, in addition to the discussion about the independence of the Central Bank, which also reaches the United States and Europe because they do not seem to be independent there either. The more fundamental problem is that the Central Banks cannot make the calculation they are supposed to make of how much money the economy needs at any given minute and what the level of interest rates should be. That is the reason why socialism fails: because they cannot calculate prices. The price system is an extremely complex system. That is why Central Banks do not know how to allocate resources from one side to the other, how much of each thing is missing... This is a process that is determined by the demand and supply of products among us, human beings who exchange every day. And with money it should be no different. That is a more technical argument. The political argument is that the Central Bank ends up being used by the mafia that governs our countries to finance public spending and ends up destroying the quality of life, especially for the poorest people

-In Argentina, we know this version of a Central Bank tied to political decisions and financing the fiscal deficit. But this is not the case in all the economies of the region. In Chile it has been independent. In Peru, despite the enormous political instability, the Central Bank, headed by Julio Velarde, has been the stable economic authority that has been allowing a reasonable Peruvian economy in fiscal terms and with growth.

Italso shows positive results in Brazil, where it has managed to maintain a certain independence from political power by setting certain rules. Is the problem a Central Bank co-opted by politics and not the Central Bank in general? Could there be a Central Bank that functions with that independence that is required to fulfill its role in a liberal society or in a liberal or libertarian political organization?

There are Central Bank models that are certainly more responsible than others. And it has a lot to do with the idiosyncrasies of each country. In Chile, the history of the Central Bank is disastrous. It is a history of chronic inflation until the late 80's and early 90's when a much more independent institution was set up, anchored, moreover, in the Chilean Constitution, which prohibits the Central Bank from buying public debt. In the new Constitution, they wanted to eliminate that restriction. A couple of exceptions were introduced, but it was one of the strictest constitutions in the world in terms of how our Central Bank operates. It is totally forbidden to finance the government. If a country has something like that and a more sensible and more responsible political class, capable of enforcing that independence, and a technocratic culture that goes after that goal, that country could have a better functioning Central Bank. Clearly, the case of Chile is an example. But even so, we still have double digit inflation. Chile is not in the best of all worlds in terms of monetary policy either.

better than a Central Bank would be to have a system of free issuance, free banking, as we had in the past. It worked much better than the history of the Central Bank.

Better than aCentral Bank would be to have a system of free issuance, free banking, as

we had in the past.It worked much better than the history of the Central Bank. In the United States, the Central Bank also finances the government deficit and the public debt. So does the European Central Bank. They are an embarrassment from the point of view of their independence. That is why they also have rampant inflation and high levels of debt. Now, Argentina cannot have an independent Central Bank because it will never be allowed that independence. The only way out is dollarization, as Ecuador, Panama, El Salvador did. Because the political class, the Argentine elites, are predatory, they form interest groups that will always do everything possible to exploit the rest with the resources at their disposal and the Central Bank is very tempting for politicians. In Chile, we almost lost the independence of the Central Bank in the new Constitution because our politicians wanted to get their hands on the banknote printer.

Are we all castes and so is Javier Milei?-In his vision of the Argentine political class as very focused on rapacity, the notion of caste that Javier Milei insists on is implicit. Now, there are problems with that notion of caste: who defines who is a caste and what is outside the caste?

-Yes, it is a political argument. Political arguments are difficult to qualify. When you are in a campaign in a country that is suffering economic ravages, as Argentina is, you cannot make the most sophisticated, academic analysis. I recently spent a couple of months living in Argentina. But what is clear is that Argentina is what in political economy is called a "limited access order", that is, it is a rent-seeking society, a parasitic society where all interest groups try to live at the expense of everyone else. A dynamic of extractivism is generated from the connections that certain groups have with the State. And I am not only referring to businessmen who expect all production to be national and free trade to be closed, or to politicians who live off the State and who employ their friends and who, in addition, do all kinds of corrupt things with public works. There are also sectors of society that get used to receiving transfers from the State and end up being a captive vote. So, which is the caste? Those who have decision-making power and who, instead of governing for the common good, govern for their own interest and the interest of those who support them. This is something very old in philosophy. Aristotle distinguished between different governments. When the monarchy ceases to be concerned with the common good and becomes an instrument at the service of those in power, it becomes a tyranny. The same happens with aristocracy: when it no longer cares about the common good, it is called oligarchy. And what you have today in Argentina is an awful oligarchy that has destroyed the country. This context means that if you do not play within those rules, even if you do not want to, you cannot survive. And that is the big problem Argentina has. And the only one who denounces it as it should be is Javier Milei

-I completely understand the point, but the problem of the definition and scope of the concept of caste still remains. One of the reproaches made to Milei, for example, is his relationship with businessman Eduardo Eurnekian, to whom he provided professional services for some years. In the composition of place that you raise, he could be considered as one of these businessmen who advocate for their interests in society unbalancing that more virtuous process of a libertarian or liberal society. So, again, is there anything left outside the caste? That question persists because not even a libertarian like Milei can show a trajectory free from the game of caste. That is, a caste society has, in a way, castes everywhere, as is clear from his explanation. It is a structural problem of

society-what defines caste is not that it seeks its interest. Everything was looking for our interest and that's fine. Everywhere in the world, even in the most economically free countries like New Zealand and Switzerland, businessmen, of course, look for their interest. We all do. We go to work because we want an income. That's the normal thing to do. The problem is when you use influence and the power of the State, from networks built in an institution that is supposed to serve the common good, to serve itself. As far as I know, Javier Milei has never done that

,but if he works for a business that works according to those rules, isn't that a questionable point?

No, it depends on the company in question. I don't know it. I don't have the slightest idea of the details. But in the end one lives in an ecosystem. So, by that logic, we would all be entering a caste whether we want to or not. But

thatis exactly the point that my question questions: that when someone defines that there is a caste in society, that systemic structure of castes ends up placing us all within a caste, including the libertarian who fights against

caste-No, because you are not exercising influence and power so that this parasitic system deepens, remains and benefits you-If

someone advises a prominent member of this functioning, he is contributing to consolidate

it- We would have to look at the specific case. The

definition of caste has to do with the definition of oligarchy: it is a small group of people who have closed the system. They have closed the system to benefit themselves at the expense of others and the rest of us have no choice but to live in that ecosystem, or we have to leave the country.

-Let's leave the personal cases. Let's talk in general. Let us suppose that there is a business sector that functions as a caste, as you describe it, and there is a politician who claims to be anti-caste and who has worked advising this business sector so that its profitability grows. Is that politician not contributing to the consolidation of a caste system?

Not necessarily, because a person who is working for that businessman manufacturing something or cleaning the company's corridors is not contributing to a caste system. The definition of caste has to do with the definition of oligarchy: it is a small group of people who have closed the system. They have closed the system to benefit themselves at the expense of others and the rest of us have no choice but to live in that ecosystem, or we have to leave the country.

But one thing is an anonymous worker, who is very far from the apex of the pyramid of that caste, and another very different thing is an advisor on economic and business issues. In direct dialogue with the vertex of the pyramid of that caste, that advisor is consolidating the perpetuation and growth of that caste

. It depends on the advice you give. If you are lobbying for that company to benefit from the State, to be given subsidies, for example, or special privileges or to be protected from competition, you are clearly helping to consolidate the caste. But I have absolutely no doubt in my mind that Javier Milei has never done anything like that. If you are simply doing accounting or marketing analysis, you are not making any contribution to consolidate the caste. What you are doing is that a productive unit more or less sustains itself, especially with the problem of legislation and regulations that exist at the State level. In a corrupt system like that, after all, there are still jobs. Therefore, the way to solve the problem of that functioning is to go upwards and change the regulations. All this is produced only and exclusively by State regulations: only by that. If there were free trade in Argentina, 70% of the caste would disappear immediately. If there were transparent systems for awarding public works, another percentage would disappear. Chile is 29th in the ranking of economic freedom; we used to be much higher, but we have been breaking it. Even so, we have problems, but as it is a country so integrated to the world from the free trade point of view, we can handle it. Argentina is among the last 10 or 20 in the world in terms of economic freedom. When a country has a system of institutions that is completely corrupt, that has to be fixed at the level of the Constitution and at the level of legislation. And the only way to do that is to have a government willing to make those changes and a citizenry willing to face the cost. Because there is a cost to pay for a while, at least, so that the country can take off afterwards. That is what Chile did. In the early 1970s, Chile was one of the poorest countries in Latin America because we had a caste led by socialists and led by people from the right. That caste extracted the wealth of the country, did not allow free trade; there was a system of import substitution, all national production. Finally, in 1973, we ended up going bankrupt in an inflation and we know the rest of the story. We have to be careful with the analysis. If they do not make a deep, institutional transformation, Argentina is completely lost.Wherethere is a need, is there a right?-A key discussion in Argentina and in the world, and which particularly crosses libertarian ideas, has to do with the role of the State and the role of the market. In El economista callejero, you explain the issue of scarcity of resources versus the logic of the expansion of rights. Could you develop the arguments on that point?

-Yes, it is very important for the discussion in Argentina, a country I love and admire very much. There is no awareness among citizens in general, nor among the political elite and many people in the media that there is a basic principle: that there are scarce resources. Those scarce resources have to be produced by people who go to work, who invest, develop their talent and risk their capital. Therefore, if you want to temper that scarcity of resources, you have to provide all the incentives to make it easy for the people who produce them. If you tax them too much, put regulations that kill them, distort the currency because politicians spend more than they have and finance them with the Central Bank, the result will be the depredation of resources. Therefore, the human capital and wealth of that country will flee. In Chile, an example that is not as dramatic as Argentina's, in the last few years, there have been 80 billion dollars of capital flight. Why? Because we have started to follow a path more similar to that of Argentina. In Argentina there is much more that could be inside and is not. Those dollars would generate employment, innovation, increase wages, we would all be better off. They would pay more taxes for production and economic activity than what they are generating. It is a fallacy to say, as Eva Perón said, that where there is a need, a right is born. Needs are not rights. And as long as Argentines do not get out of their heads that Peronist mental infection with the idea that "I have the right to get everything for free", they will not get ahead. That conception is a call to populisms of all colors to distribute and kill the goose that lays the golden eggs.

They will bemuch better off getting ahead by their own means in an environment of freedom

- I am conceptually interested: why is need not a right? I imagine a child born in poverty, whose parents do not have enough money to feed him/her because they were born in that poverty that reproduces itself. Is that need for food not a right of childhood?

Let's suppose you have a very well-to-do neighbor who lives in the same neighborhood and sends her children to the most expensive school in Argentina. That's her lifestyle. It always has been until one day she goes bankrupt and can no longer afford the school or the luxurious apartment, which for her and her family is a necessity.

Ithas been her way of life all her life. Does she have a right to take part of your income to finance her children's schooling?

No: one thing are unsatisfied basic needs and another thing are needs that are close to a luxury

- it is not a luxury to give your children a good education. It is an ideal that we all want to achieve. In other words, public schools are a disaster in Argentina. You can see it in the results of international tests. Now, the question is: can anything be done to help that family? Yes, first of all, economic growth: poverty can be overcome with economic growth, not with the distribution that has been going on for 80 years in Argentina and that leads to a poverty rate of 45 percent,

but the problem of economic growth cannot be reversed quickly

:economic growth is improved by changing three things that the oligarchies in Argentina do not want to change in order to achieve it. Argentina was the richest country in the world in terms of per capita income in 1896. There was no redistributing welfare state. And poverty was falling at a rate never seen before in the history of mankind until then. So don't tell me that Argentina needs the State to lift people out of poverty. The State is the cause of people being in poverty in Argentina. Going back to your point, of course there can be limited and focused aid policies. But we must not confuse targeted policies with the idea that every need is a right. You may have a need for an operation that costs 500 million dollars and you can only have it done at the Mayo Clinic in the U.S. Do you have the right to have the whole world finance 500 million dollars for you to have the operation there? If you continue with that logic, you end up with a country like Argentina, completely ruined

-then the problem is the expansion of that notion to other types of rights. One could establish basic rights such as food, the right to education, two rights, for example.

-No. There could be education systems financed by vouchers, with taxpayers' money. I resist a mentality: to think that you have a right because you need something. Because the notion of need is extremely broad and endless. One of the rules of economics is that resources are scarce while needs are unlimited. If you use the state to satisfy unlimited needs with scarce resources, you are going to end up in a completely ruined country.

If there were two basic needs, education and food for children and adolescents, would you agree that that is reasonable in a liberal society?

I agree that there are margins in which you can use taxpayers' money, because we pay for it with our taxes, to support groups that have been left out of a process of general progress when you have high economic growth and capital investment. In that case, yes, you could do that. But I don't agree with justifying it as a right because it becomes unstoppable: why education and food and not health or clothing

-those would also be rights-

and why not transportation, housing, vacations or retirement? They have all that in Argentina and that is why the country is broken, because everything is a right in Argentina. So, the mentality that it is a right is different from saying: here there is a problem, let's look for a specific public policy and help to solve that problem without using it, in addition, to win votes and generate welfare networks, one of the main problems you also have in Argentina: the destruction of labor morale with state interventionism. And you can see this even in cases like Sweden. When the state starts giving things away, people lose the work ethic. Even if they have opportunities to work, many people, not all, but many people lose the work ethic.

High taxes, a perverse logic.-In The Street Economist, you make a very refined reading of the incentives to go out to work and make an effort and increase the wealth of a household.What are those incentives and how, according to your perspective, high taxes undermine that incentive.

-If we are taxed 100 percent on our income, we are going to stop going to work and we are not going to produce anything, zero. I'm taking the example to the extreme. In other words, there is a point at which, when taxes are levied, productivity tends to fall. From that point on, you cannot collect more taxes than you are collecting because productivity starts to fall, and therefore, the stock of wealth in society falls and, therefore, less employment starts to be generated, you have more unemployment, more poor people, and so on. And also, the State collects less because, as you have less economic activity, less taxes are paid, so it can also make less social policy, so you have to indebt the State. And when you can't get it into debt, you have to go out and use the banknote printer. And people face inflation of around 100 percent. Taxes have to be low, as low as possible. That is going to give a gigantic incentive for wealth creation, for people to come from all over the world to invest in your country, for people to get ahead, to hire, to have entrepreneurship. That is the formula for success. It is true that there are European countries with high taxes, but notice that corporate taxes in countries like Sweden, Denmark and others are lower than in most Latin American countries: they charge 21 percent, while in Chile we are almost 45 percent

.A liberal State could charge taxes if there was an appropriate measure that would not produce collateral effects such as the disincentives you point out?

The classical liberal tradition, indeed, allows arguing in favor of a very limited State that charges very low taxes, with very general and open regulations for entrepreneurship, investment and innovation and with a very limited redistribution. Now, the anarcho-capitalist vision, no: the anarcho-capitalist vision affirms that the State is the problem because it acts on the basis of aggression on third parties. And that is true and that is why we have to keep it limited. Because what is the essence of the State? It is the monopoly of physical violence, that is what defines the State from the sociological point of view. They don't ask you for taxes, please: you pay them or they put you in jail or confiscate you to pay fines. The state, which is the political group that controls the public apparatus, penalizes you. They have the power to extract from your pocket. In this respect, classical liberalism is a slightly more pragmatic position than anarcho-capitalism, which is absolutely principled.

From the Central Bank to privateproperty-is this very reduced State accompanied by a notion of markets which, by its virtuous logic, regulates itself autonomously?

No, there has to be a fundamental regulatory framework, for example, the right to property. The State establishes a property right that is safeguarded in the Constitution at a high level and by the legislations. That is already a regulatory framework that establishes that you have the right to private property; if someone takes it away from you by force, he commits a crime; or you have the right to exchange it. Having that regulation, you can add other very general ones. Ideally, people, who know that what they have is theirs, will exchange it with other people and will enter into what we call the market. As Adam Smith said in The Wealth of Nations, there is a natural tendency of man and that is to exchange. Besides, we want to survive and improve our quality of life and that of our family. That is why we undertake and get ahead. With this type of general regulations, we will do well. It is very important that the state does not affect the right to property and protects it

- I completely agree with the institution of private property and how important it is to protect it. To challenge the logic of the most extreme libertarian ideas, just as there is a vogue for overthrowing the Central Bank because it does not fulfill its role and distorts the functioning of a society, why don't libertarians argue that private property should also be overthrown in cases of corrupt businessmen who collide all the time with the State in spurious alliances in order to maximize their profits?

Within a system that protects private property, rules that open competition are also needed. That is another important element: when there is no competition and there is private property, the system becomes fascistized. Fascism, a system very similar to what Argentina has today, is a corporatist system. This was very strongly introduced by Perón in Argentina. It implies that unions, businessmen and politicians agree to close the system to their benefit. So, there can be private property, and that is better than having a Soviet-style economy where everybody is starving like Cuba or North Korea, but it is a lousy system. Private property assumes, as a principle, that all people inside and outside a country can freely dispose of their property and exchange it. When limits are placed on international exchange with industrial protectionism for national production, the exercise of the right to private property of both Argentines, who cannot exchange what they produce for something that someone else freely produced abroad, and the right to private property of foreigners, who cannot send you their product so that you can exchange it

,

is being restricted.

When the State does not function in a virtuous way, it is planned to overthrow it but there is no question of overthrowing the right to private property in cases where that private property is the result of complicity with a corrupt caste.

-What happens is that private property is a general principle and therefore it cannot be overthrown because there are people who take advantage of regulations created by the State which is the one that allows them to abuse private property. What can be done in case of collusion is, for example, to sanction the persons responsible. If we follow your approach, it is like saying that if there is a soccer player who dopes, the problem is soccer and soccer players. The doping player is sanctioned, but the rest of the game goes on with the rules, which are transparent and honest,

but the Central Bank is not sanctioned, it is brought down, and the corrupt capitalist is not,

butthe soccer referee who is corrupted to favor a team is removed. And that is the example of the Central Bank: it is not a private entity, it is a state entity and it is not acting neutrally.

Itis playing the game in favor of the politicians who control it

: with that logic of the libertarians, the company is playing in favor of its own enrichment. Shouldn't private property be taken away, following that logic:

theproblem is systemic when you have a country in which everything is closed and you have no international competition. I insist, Argentina must open up to the world. Mercosur should not matter and it should integrate, as Chile has done, to different economic blocs. Chile is among the most integrated countries. There you would see how they are doing: much better. The problem is systemic. The problem is not the businessman who colludes. If the businessman is given the signal that the law obliges him to collude or that he earns more if he colludes, it is obvious that he is going to do it. We have seen it in Chile. Before, they were all colluding because the law ends up forcing you to take that path because there was no international competition.

Libertarians, are they in favor of democracy or not so much?-When one listens to libertarians in Argentina, it is difficult to be clear about their assessment of liberal republican democracy. When Milei was asked, for example, if he believes in democracy, he answered: "I believe that democracy has a lot of errors, for example, I ask you the question the other way around: do you know Arrow's impossibility theorem? What is Arrow's impossibility theorem and what does this theorem imply for liberal democracy

?The problem derived from Arrow's impossibility theorem is that it is difficult for democracy to end up being a faithful reflection of the preferences and wills of the majorities that are supposed to be represented in the elections. It is impossible to really arrive at a democratic system in strict rigor, in which the wills of those who have voted are represented. But it seems to me that democracy, and this is a very old tradition in classical liberalism, is not an end in itself. If democracy is understood as the electoral system by which the majority decides, it can produce appalling results, a dictatorship of the majority over the minorities, for example, and it can produce concentration camps. To be worthwhile, democracy has to be liberal. It has to go with that liberal name. Liberalism has to be a substantial ingredient to democracy. Otherwise, democracy has no advantage over any dictatorship of the worst kind. If a democracy does not respect human rights, fundamental rights, it becomes an excuse not only to concentrate power but also to create a system of plundering and robbery as it is in Argentina. In such cases, people will ask themselves at some point why they have to trust in such a system, which only exploits them. I am a firm believer in liberal democracy. The Constitution guarantees fundamental rights and restrains the power of the State and also that of the majority or organized minorities to prevent them from taking away fundamental rights such as property or the right to life and liberty. If this does not happen, without this liberal surname, democracy has no advantage over tyrannical systems. There must also be a system of freedoms that allow progress because otherwise it frustrates the great majorities. Democracy is destroyed by annihilating economic freedom: people do not want to live under a system that condemns them to misery, poverty and prevents them from getting ahead. That's also part of liberal democracy.

From Bolsonaro to Trump-Whydo libertarians feel more comfortable with illiberal right-wing populism like that of Jair Bolsonaro or Donald Trump?

-Idon't know if all libertarians feel more comfortable. But also, more comfortable compared to what? If you compare Donald Trump with Bernie Sanders, clearly you are going to be more comfortable with Donald Trump because Sanders is a socialist who admires Cuba, beyond all the criticisms he makes of Trump. And that's not just true for libertarians; it's also true for the majority of Americans who voted for him. If you prefer someone, you prefer him to someone else, that is, Bolsonaro or Lula, Bolsonaro or Cristina

-I put it to you in these terms: Bolsonaro or Fernando Henrique Cardoso?

-It depends on public policies. There has been a lot of hysteria about Bolsonaro. What happened to many of his supporters when they entered government palaces was disastrous. There are also very brainless people behind these movements. But it all depends on what he stands for. Trump was going to be the great demon who was going to create World War III, he was going to put everybody in concentration camps and he didn't do any of that. He lowered taxes, he lowered regulations. And he's probably going to be the next president of the United States. I've never been a fan of Trump but if you give me a choice between a Democratic administration that has brought us almost to the brink of theThird World War with Russia, because it has been handled very badly according to several experts; it also has the worst migratory crisis in decades, which Trump had solved; it also has a debt issue, which Trump also left badly, obviously I do not vote for the person but I vote for the ideas and practices that he will carry out and each thing in its own context. America has strong institutions. It is completely absurd to think that Donald Trump is going to become a dictator in the US. There is nothing more ridiculous than to hear people on the left say that. The U.S. has strong institutions that would make such a thing impossible. And that was demonstrated in all the somewhat ridiculous claims that Trump made that they had the election stolen from them: he had to leave and now he's trying to come back. And if he comes back, it will be just another government and he will not be able to concentrate power in his hands. In the case of Bolsonaro, everybody said he was going to be a kind of Mussolini. What did Bolsonaro do so seriously? Did he persecute homosexuals, as it was said that he was going to put them in concentration camps? No, he did not do that.

-WithBolsonaro, a discourse came to Brazil that introduced religious criteria in personal decisions of the family and individuals. The

progressive left did much worse because it introduced religious criteria of this postmodern morality that is completely destructive and pathological and turned it into legislation everywhere. In part, Brazilians rebelled against that too when they elected Bolsaron. Let's not forget that he didn't lose by much the last lesson. And Lula is a criminal, an organized crime guy. On the issue of gun carrying, I am all for it. Decent and honest people have the right to defend themselves. If you have the right to life, you have the right to defend your life. The other thing is to let criminals enter your house, rape your children, massacre you and you cannot defend yourself. In Chile, the Boric government and the Communist Party, which to this day openly defends Cuba and Venezuela, want to take away all weapons from citizens. Meanwhile, we have the biggest security crisis in history and the highest homicide rate in Chilean history. And Boric himself has to surround himself with Carabineros because the popularity of the Armed Forces and Carabinero is soaring in the polls and Boric's is plummeting. In this context, they want to leave us at the mercy of the criminals. What good is it that the Constitution guarantees the right to life when your police do not work and, on top of that, the same State that does not protect you forbids you to defend yourself? The discourse against guns seems to me to be most dangerous, especially in countries like ours. Obviously, it has to be regulated and limits have to be set. Not just anyone should be able to have weapons, not just any caliber

ofweapon

. Education. PhD in Philosophy and Political Economy from the University of Heidelberg in Germany

? Professional development. He is president of the Foundation for Progress in Chile

? Books. His new book is El economista callejero. 15 lessons of economics to survive politicians and demagogues; he also wrote: The Pope and Capitalism and The Neoinquisition, among others.

title: The Fed's lock-up generates doubts in all markets
text:
Luis Varela

eleconomista.com.ar

The reopening of the markets came with two major news items: The US has just announced that it created fewer jobs in March than in February (236,000 jobs against 311,000 the previous month). And the $300 agricultural dollar started (it will continue until May 31 for soybeans and until August 30 for other regional economy products).

This comes after the banking collapse in the US and Europe, with a massive distribution of dollars by the Fed to stop a domino fall of entities. And Massa's new agricultural dollar expects foreign currency liquidation for US$ 9 billion to add reserves, but exports will take away product supply in the domestic market, at a time when the drought left a pronounced shortage of supply.

More inflationary pressures

What is the combination of helicopter raining dollars in the US and product supply shortages in Argentina? Simple: both decisions, here and in the north, will generate another inflationary pressure. And this scourge that is flooding the world with poor people and global tension was encouraged last week by another chess move in the world war in which the planet is submerging: the oil producing countries added more fire to the fuse.

OPEC, which controls 40 percent of the world's oil supply, was on the way to cut supply by two million barrels per day as of May. However, several of its members announced additional "voluntary" reductions, i.e. without a binding agreement, which will run until the end of 2023. In total, over and above what they were already going to cut, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, UAE, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria and Oman will withdraw no less than 1.15 million barrels per day from supply.

What is the impact of this shutdown? Last week the WTI variant finished at US$ 80.47 (up from US$ 65.60 in mid-March) and the Brent variant finished at US$ 84.94 (up from US$ 71.40). Since mid-March, crude oil has risen by an average of 20% worldwide, and so far in April it has risen by 6.3%.

In other words, we find ourselves with more dollars in the US to save the banks, less supply of products in Argentina and global oil prices, which, according to experts, will mean upward inflationary pressure everywhere. Within the US, the CPI had peaked at 9% per year and due to the Fed's rate hike it flattened to 6% per year in the last data of February, but this week it will be known how much prices rose in March.

The same thing will happen in Argentina: next Friday, at 4:00 p.m., after the market close, the Indec will release the national CPI. The consulting firms that have already made their calculations have been quite heated, with an average estimate of 7.5%, the Creebba of Bahía Blanca calculated no less than 8.1%, the index of the City of Buenos Aires measured 7.1%. And the REM (Relevamiento de Expectativas de Mercado - Market Expectations Survey) prepared by the Central Bank gave 7% for March (and 110% annual rate).

The direction of rates

All these data, which seem to be separate indicators, have just turned a key global thermometer. Before the banking collapse and the OPEC adjustment, the US long rate had been falling, but last week's short rate has just turned around. In October 2022 the US 10-year rate reached 4.3% p.a. (a 12-year high), from there it dropped to 3.25% and now it has just bounced back to 3.4%.

With a latest inflation figure of 6% p.a. and with the recent massive distribution of dollars for the equivalent of 1.5 of Argentina's GDP, investors believe that US inflation will be a tough nut to crack. A 3.4% rate against 6% inflation is a negative investment, hence last week's growing abandonment of the global dollar, at a time when China is also seeking to de-dollarize the world by handing out swaps left and right.

As a result, the short week prior to Easter showed a general weakening of the greenback: down 1.1% against the Swiss franc, 0.7% against the pound, 0.5% against the yen and the euro and 0.1% in Brazil, all down. The dollar only remained unchanged against the yuan and rose 2.7% in Chile, with a flood of Chileans traveling to Mendoza for the long holiday, but not only for tourism: they took the trunks of their cars full of things they bought in supermarkets 40% cheaper on this side of the Andes.

The challenge of reservations

In Argentina, meanwhile, a completely intervened market, the Central Bank loses an average of US$100 million per day with its reserves runaway.

Before knowing the fine print of the small print of the agro dollar, analysts began to put numbers to the scope that this new patch of Economy may have. And they calculated that in the first 45 days of the agricultural dollar (between the dollars coming in from exports with a better exchange rate and imports that continue at full steam due to an official dollar at least 35 points behind) there will be a net increase of US$ 3 billion in reserves and a net issuance of $1 billion.

But the issue is inflation. Dairy farmers warned that the agro dollar will make domestic inputs more expensive, which will cause an increase in the costs to feed the cows, so the opening of April came with two surprises: strong rises in the price of milk, increases in cases of complaints about the arrival of watered milk and food companies that withdraw the supply of milk at Fair Prices, deciding to use it to produce hard cheeses, with which they get more profitability.

More weights in the market

As a result, a number of voices from the countryside (from organizations and producers) came out to say that the agricultural dollar that is now starting as the third version of the soybean dollar is "bread for today and hunger for tomorrow", since this preferential exchange rate generates more inflation and does not solve the underlying problems. Moreover, it will flood the domestic market with newly issued pesos.

And here are the key questions of the moment: where will the new pesos that will enter the market go? Will they be placed in fixed term deposits with negative rates? And analysts affirm that they will go to more consumption (more inflation) and at the end of the goods exchange channel they will end up becoming more demand for dollars.

title: Financial day: the Argentine stock market was isolated from Wall Street's rebound and deepened its downward slide
text:
Finally, inflation in Argentina exceeded 100% again after more than three decades. INDEC reported that February CPI reached 6.6%, with an increase of 102.5% compared to the same month of 2022. This bad "macro" data was associated with a response from the financial side, with the fourth downward session for stocks and the seventh negative session for the Central Bank, which continues to sell liquid reserves in the foreign exchange market.

Although foreign markets showed a rebound after the collapse of the last rounds, due to the banking crisis that forced the US government to intervene to protect depositors, the improvement did not extend to Argentina, where the relaxation of the goals of the agreement with the International Monetary Fund, far from clearing the financial horizon, awakened investors' concern. It is clear that the Government will not seek to balance the public accounts or strengthen the reserves for the remainder of the term. Therefore, there will be more inflation and deterioration of the economy in an already unstable year due to the presidential elections.

The leading benchmark S&P Merval in Buenos Aires climbed more than 3% in the morning. However, at the close it fell 2.1% to 220,447 points. The panel of leading stocks has thus recorded a loss of 12.2% in pesos -and 15% in dollars "contado con liqui"- in four consecutive downward rounds. In 2023, the Merval retains a gain of 9.1% in pesos, below inflation, and in dollars, a loss of 4.1%.

Argentine ADRs and stocks on Wall Street turned mostly negative. YPF fell 1.3 percent to USD 9.78, and Grupo Galicia dropped 2.3 percent. The state-owned oil company was particularly hit by the 4.4% drop in the international price of crude oil, to USD 71.54 a barrel in Texas.

On the New York stock exchanges, the Dow Jones index rose 1.1%, and the technological Nasdaq rose 2.1%, after it was announced that February inflation in the US was 0.4%, in line with analysts' expectations.

Emiliano Anselmi, Chief Economist at Portfolio Personal Inversiones, said: "It would seem that there is more calm, after the Federal Reserve encapsulated the problem and prevented it from spreading beyond Silicon Valley Bank. On the other hand, within this context, the possibility is also being priced in that the Fed may not dare to raise rates by 50 basis points and may end up raising them by 25 basis points or even leave them unchanged. If this were to happen -and if a flight to quality phenomenon does not occur-, it would be something that would be very good for emerging markets and would take pressure off Argentine bonds, which are with a weighted average parity of USD 27.4, from the USD 35 they were able to reach in January".

"Clearly, it is difficult for local bonds to have a big rally in the short term. Even if we were to have an electoral trade, it would be with less intensity than in 2015, because the reality is that that memory is still fresh and it was not the best. Today it takes more than expectations. External investors have not had a good time with Argentina several times and are quite more disbelieving. Also because the macro starting points are more challenging than before: from inflation, to the stagnation of economic activity and other drivers. We can say that very challenging adjustments are required," Anselmi added.

title: Argentine cenbank offers dollars at 2.36 to 2.40 peso.
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina, March 12 (Reuters) - Argentina's Central Bankintervened in the foreign exchange market on Tuesday afternoon to offer dollars at between 2.36 pesos to 2.40 pesos to prop up the peso, traders said. 

 The intervention comes as Argentina's peso weakened 7.20 percent against the dollar to trade at 2.48/2.50 (buy/sell rate) per dollar for large-scale transactions in the foreign exchange market , compared with Monday's close of 2.30/2.32. 

 The peso was pegged at par to the dollar for more than a decade until January when the cash-strapped government of Latin America's No. 3 economy devalued the currency through a dual exchange system and then fully floated it in February. 

 Argentine President Eduardo Duhalde said on Tuesday the Central Bank should intervene in the foreign exchange market to keep the peso currency within "adequate margins".

text:

to overseas suppliers.

title: Argentina seeks blns in aid to survive crisis.
text:
BUENOS AIRES/WASHINGTON, Feb 13 (Reuters) - On its second day of talks with multilateral lenders in Washington, Argentina on Wednesday tentatively estimated it needs $22 billion to $23 billion in aid to get back on its feet, but the IMF said it was "premature" to talk numbers. 

 "Normally these crises require about 12 percent of economic output, which in our case is 22 to 23 billion dollars, and in some cases they have required more," said Argentine Deputy Economy Minister Jorge Todesca in Buenos Aires. "That doesn't mean we're negotiating these numbers with the agencies," he told a local radio station. 

 But while Todesca said that no "specific number" was yet on the table in negotiations with the International Monetary Fund that he predicted could drag on for four to six weeks, his tentative estimate jibed with those of other Argentine officials. 

 In Washington, Economy Minister Jorge Remes Lenicov said an IMF mission may travel to Argentina as soon as next week to formally start negotiations on a new economic program. 

 "We have a good image of having met people who want to help Argentina and we are prepared to continue making all the changes needed to revert this crisis," Remes said, adding the government still needed to clarify its position on tax reform, bank sector restructuring and revenue sharing with provinces. 

 IMF Managing Director Horst Koehler said both sides agreed to the need for a comprehensive plan for sustainable growth. 

 "This was a good start to a new relationship, and there was broad agreement on the analysis of the economic and social situation," Koehler said in a statement. 

 The Argentine government on Wednesday heeded IMF and U.S. Treasury warnings against bankruptcy law reforms passed by Congress last month and vetoed a controversial clause that would have forced banks to write down loans that were not renegotiated within 90 days. 

 It also decreed a 20 percent tax on oil exports. 

 News of the cordial talks combined with the successful flotation of the peso earlier this week provided Argentines a breather from relentlessly news of recession. 

 Since December when deadly riots forced out two presidents in succession, shaking one of Latin America's firmest democracies to its core, Argentina has defaulted on part of its $141 billion public debt and devalued its peso currency after being fixed at par to the dollar for over a decade. 

 Officials say President Eduardo Duhalde is leery of sending a "shopping list" of funding needs, especially since his country swallowed up billions of dollars in assistance last year and still could not avert the massive debt default in December. 

 Argentina also overshot its IMF-agreed public sector deficit goal last year of 6.5 billion pesos by 2.587 billion pesos, the Economy Ministry said late on Wednesday. 

 Argentines' savings are still restricted by limits on cash withdrawals, imposed to stop a record run on banks last year. Since the public sector and local businesses have no access to credit, many shops and factories have been forced to close, driving up unemployment. 

 LIFE ON HOLD 

 While the peso finds its feet and President Duhalde's government tries to patch things up with wary multilateral lenders, everyday life is on hold for millions of people. 

 With unemployment now estimated at 22 percent conversation here centers on jobs lost and dollar savings forcibly converted to pesos and locked up in the banks. For many, personal plans like weddings and birthdays have been canceled or scaled down. 

 "I had saved up $7,000 to move out on my husband and get a divorce," laments Rosa, an unhappy Buenos Aires hairdresser. 

 As he bought dollars at a foreign exchange house, Antonio, a 75-year-old Argentine pensioner who lives in Spain, said that he had only come to see his daughter for Christmas, but his cash was stuck in the bank and he could not buy a ticket home. 

 "I was supposed to have left a 1-1/2 months ago," he said. 

 Others scramble to get around the economic shackles. 

 Speculators, who locals call "arbolitos," or little trees, stand on street corners offering black-market dollars to those who cannot face the long lines at exchange bureaus. 

 But the lack of cash to buy dollars meant the feared dive in the peso's value with Monday's full flotation did not materialize. The country had a dual system for just over a month with a fixed peso for exports and a floating peso for the public. 

 Confounding forecasts, the peso has strengthened from its lows right after devaluation to close on Wednesday at 1.95 to the dollar on the retail market and 1.98 for large-scale deals. Some had predicted it would fall as low as 5 to the dollar. 

 But traders agree the relative stability is due to the cash crunch rather than any newfound faith in the peso from people who have always stashed away their savings in U.S. dollars. 

 HYPERINFLATION FEARS 

 While prices on imported goods rise, fueling fears of a return to the hyperinflation of the 1980s, barter markets offering goods and services from food to plumbing have spread. 

 Bankers say Argentina has a month to secure foreign aid before it falls into the grip of hyperinflation. 

 January's 2.3 percent rise in consumer prices in a country accustomed to zero inflation for years and mindful of the daily and even hourly price rises seen back in the 1980s, showed how panic-inducing a real bout of hyperinflation would be. 

 Meanwhile, the economy is at a standstill. The run on the banks until cash limits were imposed in early December emptied the system of a quarter of its deposits. 

 The problems have also spilled over into neighboring Uruguay, where knock-on liquidity woes at Banco Galicia Uruguay, a bank owned by Argentina's largest private-sector bank, prompted intervention by the Central Bank. 

 Ratings agency Fitch reported that losses to the Argentine banking system in 2001 may exceed 18 percent of gross domestic product, or 50 billion pesos. 

 In a television interview late Tuesday, Duhalde put a brave face on the daily protests against the cash crunch and growing unemployment, saying: "It's ridiculous to believe a president will step down because of protests. I'm even less likely to step down if the crisis gets worse." 

 Attributing his determination to his Basque roots, the stocky former vice president from the Peronist Party promised that within "two months these things that bother people like roadblocks will disappear and things will calm down." 

 (With reporting by Charles Froggatt in Buenos Aires and Anthony Boadle in Washington).

text:

 stocks)

 The Central Bank said it would intervene in Banco Galicia Uruguay SA - wholly controlled by Argentina's Banco Galicia y Buenos Aires SA - and force a total suspension of activity for 90 days after the bank lost roughly a third of its deposits so far this year. 

 Officials from Uruguay's second-largest private bank said they may gradually return deposits in quotas or fixed-term deposits to clients, the vast majority of whom are Argentines seeking refuge from a devastating banking crisis at home.

 As shares in the group that controls Galicia fell, economists said Uruguay's banking system - widely seen as an foreign financial haven for Argentines - was still very stable but did face some limited danger of capital flight. 

 "For now, this is a lack of confidence specifically in the name Galicia rather than a systematic problem that could extend to other deposits in Uruguay," said Hernan Fardi, an analyst for the Maxinver.com consultancy in Buenos Aires.

 Analysts said the liquidity problem may also result from transfers by Galicia Uruguay to its Argentine headquarters. 

 But Uruguayan officials played down fears Argentina's problems could further affect banks in the mostly agricultural country, one of the few in Latin American to enjoy "investment grade" status from ratings agencies. 

 "Banks are strong," said Ramon Diaz, former president of Uruguay's Central Bank. "This isn't going to even come close to spreading to the rest of the system."
