title: UPDATE 1-Argentina seeks blns in aid to survive crisis.
text:
BUENOS AIRES/WASHINGTON, Feb 13 (Reuters) - On its second day of talks with multilateral lenders in Washington, Argentina on Wednesday tentatively estimated it needs $22 billion to $23 billion in aid to get back on its feet but the IMF said it was "premature" to talk numbers. 

 "Normally these crises require about 12 percent of economic output, which in our case is 22 to 23 billion dollars, and in some cases they have required more," said Argentine Deputy Economy Minister Jorge Todesca in Buenos Aires. "That doesn't mean we're negotiating these numbers with the agencies," he told a local radio station. 

 But while Todesca said that no "specific number" was yet on the table in negotiations with the International Monetary Fund that he predicted could drag on for four to six weeks, his tentative estimate jived with those of other Argentine officials. 

 In Washington, IMF External Relations Director Tom Dawson said it was "premature to be talking about numbers. There are no packages on the table." 

 He called the contacts so far "quite positive," but said real negotiations do not typically begin until an IMF mission visits a country. In Argentina's case, no date has been fixed for such a visit, Dawson said. 

 Argentine Economy Minister Jorge Remes Lenicov's meetings with the IMF, U.S. Treasury, World Bank and InterAmerican Development Bank are off to a good start, officials say. 

 That news combined with the successful flotation of the peso earlier this week provided Argentines a breather from relentlessly bleak news of recession and misery. 

 Since December when deadly riots forced out two presidents in succession, shaking one of Latin America's firmest democracies to its core, Argentina has defaulted on part of its $141 billion public debt and devalued its peso currency after being fixed at par to the dollar for over a decade. 

 Officials say President Eduardo Duhalde is leery of sending a "shopping list" of funding needs, especially since his country swallowed up billions of dollars in assistance last year and still could not avert the massive debt default in December. 

 Argentines' savings are still restricted by limits on cash withdrawals, imposed to stop a record run on banks last year. Since the public sector and local businesses have no access to credit, many shops and factories have been forced to close, driving up unemployment. 

 LIFE ON HOLD 

 While the peso finds its feet and President Duhalde's government tries to patch things up with wary multilateral lenders, everyday life is on hold for millions of people. 

 With unemployment now estimated at 22 percent conversation here centers on jobs lost and dollar savings forcibly converted to pesos and locked up in the banks. For many, personal plans like weddings and birthdays have been canceled or scaled down. 

 "I had saved up $7,000 to move out on my husband and get a divorce," laments Rosa, an unhappy Buenos Aires hairdresser. 

 As he bought dollars at a foreign exchange house, Antonio, a 75-year-old Argentine pensioner who lives in Spain, said that he had only come to see his daughter for Christmas, but his cash was trapped in the bank and he could not buy a ticket home. 

 "I was supposed to have left a 1-1/2 months ago," he said. 

 Others scramble to get around the economic shackles. 

 Speculators, who locals call "arbolitos," or little trees, stand on street corners offering black-market dollars to those who cannot face the long lines at exchange bureaus. 

 But the lack of cash to buy dollars meant the feared dive in the peso's value with Monday's full flotation did not materialize. The country had a dual system for just over a month with a fixed peso for exports and a floating peso for the public. 

 Confounding forecasts, the peso has strengthened from its lows right after devaluation to sell on Wednesday at 2.0 to the dollar on the retail market and 1.95 for large-scale deals. Some had predicted it would fall as low as 5 to the dollar. 

 But traders agree the relative stability is due to the cash crunch rather than any newfound faith in the peso from people who have always stashed away their savings in U.S. dollars. 

 HYPERINFLATION FEARS 

 While prices on imported goods rise, fueling fears of a return to the hyperinflation of the 1980s, barter markets offering goods and services from food to plumbing have spread. 

 Bankers say Argentina has a month to secure foreign aid before it falls into the grip of hyperinflation. 

 January's 2.3 percent rise in consumer prices in a country accustomed to zero inflation for years and mindful of the daily and even hourly price rises seen back in the 1980s, showed how panic-inducing a real bout of hyperinflation would be. 

 Meanwhile, the orthodox economy is at a standstill. The run on the banks until cash limits were imposed in early December emptied the system of a quarter of its deposits. 

 The problems have also spilled over into neighboring Uruguay, where knock-on liquidity woes at Banco Galicia Uruguay, a bank owned by Argentina's largest private-sector bank, prompted intervention by the Central Bank. 

 Ratings agency Fitch reported that losses to the Argentine banking system in 2001 may exceed 18 percent of gross domestic product, or 50 billion pesos. 

 In a television interview late Tuesday, Duhalde put a brave face on the daily protests against the cash crunch and growing unemployment, saying: "It's ridiculous to believe a president will step down because of protests. I'm even less likely to step down if the crisis gets worse." 

 Attributing his determination to his Basque roots, the stocky former vice president from the Peronist Party promised that within "two months these things that bother people like roadblocks will disappear and things will calm down."

text:
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina, Feb 1 (Reuters) - The Argentine Central Bankintervened in the foreign exchange market for the 14th straight session on Friday, selling U.S. dollars at 1.75 pesos each to prop up the peso, the bank said. 

 The bank did not say how many dollars it sold. 

 The peso traded at an average 1.93/1.95 per dollar for large-scale transactions in the foreign exchange market on Friday. The 1.95 peso sell rate equals a 49 percent fall from the pre-devaluation one-to-one peso-to-dollar rate maintained for a decade. 

 Argentina has an official fixed exchange rate of 1.40 pesos per dollar for foreign trade and priority transactions as designated by the government, and an unofficial floating peso for cash deals. The government plans to ditch the dual exchange rate and fully float the peso in the coming months. 

 The floating-rate peso has weakened as companies and people have sought the safe haven of dollars due to fears that the peso will depreciate even further amid a deep recession now in its fourth year.

title: Argentina 's Peso Ends At ARS1.95/Dlr; Ctrl Bk  Intervenes
text:
BUENOS AIRES -(Dow Jones)- Argentina's peso lost ground against the dollar Thursday as the central bank offered greenbacks at their highest rate since the peso began free trading Jan. 11. 

 Commercial banks quoted the peso closing at a midrate of ARS1.95 to the dollar. Spreads were quoted at ARS1.90 to ARS2.00. Spreads for the interbank rate were ARS2.05/ARS2.07 to the dollar. 

Currency traders from large banks said the central bank intervened in the market early Thursday, offering dollars at ARS1.80. The bank has usually offered the dollar at ARS1.65 and has offered them as low as ARS1.60. 

 The central bank dictates that banks that purchase dollars from the monetary authority not mark them up by more than 7% when reselling the dollars. 

 The higher rate also hinted that the bank is out looking for dollars after having tapped into precious foreign currency reserves to prop up the peso. 

Currency traders said that many Argentines are buying dollars head of Saturday's announcement of new economic measures. The government, which is currently gearing up to fully negotiate with the IMF and other lenders for up to $20 billion in aid, may free float the currency to help clinch the deal. 

 The Fund has been lukewarm on Argentina's use of a dual exchange rate. 

 As for the interbank rate, traders said that companies have been buying dollars to pay bills and buoy their accounts against further devaluation of the peso. 

 Some companies were also seen buying dollars to pay debts after Congress passed a new bankruptcy law after lawmakers scrapped an amendment from the bill prohibiting many companies from transferring money abroad to meet their debt payments. 

 The bill will now go before President Eduardo Duhalde for signature. It isn't clear if Duhalde will sign the bill into law or veto it. 

 Some indebted Argentine companies have blamed bank and wire transfer curbs for not being able to meet their debt obligations.

The central bank will continue to sell dollars indefinitely to keep the peso from depreciating further, Aldo Pignanelli, a central bank director told Clarin newspaper in an article published Friday. "There are sufficient reserves" to continue selling dollars, Pignanelli said. 

 When Argentina devalued the currency on Jan. 6, it established a dual exchange rate system. An official rate of ARS1.40 to the dollar is in place for trade, while other transactions will be subject to the floating rate. 

 Pignanelli said the central bank's intervention is aimed at keeping the free-market peso's value close to the fixed rate. 

 The central bank, in continuing efforts to prop up the peso has mandated that banks that buy central bank dollars not mark the currency up more than five cents, or 7%, when the commercial banks sell the bills. 

 The band, "has given excellent results," to help maintain and improve the peso's price, Pignanelli told Clarin.

title: Chile peso slides on Argentina woes.
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile, Jan 25 (Reuters) - Chile's peso slid on Friday, completing a week of volatile trade which is expected to continue while financial instability reigns in neighboring Argentina, traders said. 

 The currency closed at 671.50/672.00, a depreciation of 0.40 percent compared with 668.80/669.30. 

 "The exchange rate will continue to be volatile from here to March, fluctuating between 660 and 680 pesos," said Andres Perez, finance manager of BCI brokerage. 

 "The volatility will be due to the situation in Argentina, where they have announced first one measure, then another, then these are withdrawn. All this creates a lot of confusion and that has repercussions on the Brazilian real and the Chilean peso," Perez added. 

 Argentina devalued its peso currency just over two weeks ago after a decade of a currency pegged at one-to-one to the dollar. The devaluation has fuelled civil unrest and sent shock waves through regional markets. 

 Frequent interventions by Argentina's Central Bank to buoy the floating peso have contributed to doubts about the country's economic future. 

 Unlike other analysts, who expect Argentina's economic problems to smooth out after March, Perez says the political and social crises could worsen, bringing further problems for Chile's currency.

title: Argentina 's Peso Closes 1.95/Dlr; Ctrl Bk  Intervenes  Again
text:
BUENOS AIRES -(Dow Jones)- Argentina's peso (ARS) held its ground Monday in thin trading resulting from the U.S. holiday and the country's partial banking freeze that is keeping larger companies from entering the local forex market. 

 Traders said intervention from the central bank, which in the past week traders said has spent $50 million to $70 million selling dollars, kept the peso from losing ground. 

 Banks quoted the interbank midrate at ARS1.95 to the dollar, versus an open of ARS2.00 to the dollar. 

 On Friday foreign exchange houses quoted the peso closing at a midrate of ARS1.93 to the dollar. 

 As Argentina's peso has only been floating freely against the dollar since Jan. 11, banks have had to set up foreign exchange trading. In the interim, foreign exchange houses were the primary source for peso prices. 

 While traders said the interbank market was technically operational, volume was scarce and there was still some confusion about trading. 

 "The interbank market is practically not operating," said one forex trader with a locally based bank, referring to scarce volume. 

 Argentina's banking withdrawal restrictions, in place since early December, are making it difficult for large companies to participate in the market. "There is a scarcity of pesos," that is making the market more illiquid and keeping the price of the peso from weakening further, said the trader. 

 Meanwhile, the country's financial institutions are having to build a foreign exchange trading system from scratch. Traders said there is still some confusion about market operations. 

 On Monday, the central bank issued a communique asking foreign exchange houses to submit detailed activity reports to the bank, as well as to tax agencies. 

 On the retail side, foreign exchange houses quoted the peso closing at a midrate of ARS1.75. 

 Retail peso sales have kept the Argentine currency from further weakening. 

Foreign exchange houses in downtown Buenos Aires had a steady flow of customers, anxious to sell dollars they had socked away under mattresses and in safety deposit boxes. Banking restrictions, which limit cash withdrawals to 1,500 pesos a month, are forcing them to sell the stored up greenbacks. 

 "I have to buy pesos to pay my bills," said one man standing in a two-block-long line outside a foreign exchange house on Florida Street, a busy downtown pedestrian walkway. A steady-flow of small volume customers seeking to buy pesos have kept the currency from losing too much ground, traders said.

title: IMF To Send Debt, Fiscal Team To Argentina: Krueger
text:
SANTIAGO -(Dow Jones)- The International Monetary Fund's first deputy managing director Anne Krueger said Friday that  the IMF is preparing a second Argentina technical mission to focus on fiscal and debt issues that could arrive in Buenos Aires as early as next week. 

 The Argentine government has not yet formally requested funding, but does plan to do so, Krueger told reporters at a  press conference before a World Bank seminar in Santiago. 

 An IMF technical mission focusing on banking issues departed for Argentina on Monday. 

 Krueger said the second mission was scheduled to arrive in Argentina early next week, but might now be delayed by a couple of days. 

 Krueger riled members of Argentina's new government last  week, implying that the administration's plan to devalue the currency and pull the country out of a four-year recession lacked coherence. 

 Until President Eduardo Duhalde's administration devises  a comprehensive and coherent economic strategy "there is no point in our talking about a fund support program for them," she said. 

 The IMF suspended a previous multibillion dollar loan program for Argentina in December. 

 On Friday, Krueger said the lending agency has given Argentina a broad outline of what must be done to regain IMF  support. Argentina must address issues such as restoring the banking system, balancing the budget, and negotiating with creditors some acceptable solution to their debts, she said. Argentina is in default on its $141 billion sovereign debt. 

 Krueger also said, echoing comments made last week, that  Argentina must formulate a new monetary policy based on a unified exchange rate. 

 Argentina officially devalued its currency earlier this month, cutting the peso loose from a long-standing 1:1 dollar peg and introducing a dual exchange rate regime in an  effort to ease the transition to a floating currency. A fixed exchange rate of ARS1.40 to the dollar will govern large commercial transactions and some financial transactions, while a parallel, free-floating rate was introduced for retail transactions 

 Within a few days of the devaluation, Argentina's Central Bank sold dollars into the foreign exchange market to prop up the local currency. 

 Krueger said Friday that while Argentina might make a case for small interventions meant to smooth out fluctuations, large scale intervention in the foreign exchange market might be questionable. 

 -By Andrea Welsh, Dow Jones Newswires; 562-460-8547; chile@dowjones.com

title: UPDATE 2-Courts step up bank probe as IMF warns Argentina.
text:
(Adds EconMin trip to Washington, call to Brazilian 

 president, markets update.) 

 By Gilbert Le Gras 

 BUENOS AIRES, Argentina, Jan 18 (Reuters) - Argentine courts on Friday stepped up their probe into the exodus of bank deposits that helped set off Argentina's current crisis, while foreign banks, Moody's and the IMF sounded new alarms about the state of the battered banking system. 

 As the Central Bank continued to prop up the peso in the foreign exchange market, the International Monetary Fund said heavier intervention would be "questionable" and warned the government not to expect fresh aid to support the banking system. Moody's rating agency said on Friday banks were facing insolvency after this month's currency devaluation. 

 Argentine Economy Minister Jorge Remes Lenicov and Foreign Minister Carlos Ruckauf will travel to Washington at the end of January to meet with IMF and U.S. of???o help the crisis-ridden economy, a government spokesman said. 

 Meanwhile, tension in Buenos Aires a???s was palpable. Police numbers were bolstered at government buildings as protests welled, threatening a return of the violence that toppled the government and left 27 dead last month. 

 In the latest daily demonstrations against the government's freezing of most bank savings, hundreds of small businessmen staged a demonstration in front of the Central Bank building in Buenos Aires. 

 On Thursday, the authorities raided the local offices of banks, including London-based HSBC Holdings New York-based Citigroup's local unit, and Banco Frances, owned by Spain's Banco Bilbao Vizcaya Argentaria 

 The raids were part of an investigation into the wave of funds sent abroad late last year that led to unpopular government curbs on cash withdrawals. 

 "Those bringing the complaint say possible crimes include misappropriation of funds (and) fraud within the public administration," Norberto Oyarbide, one of the judges heading the probe, said Friday. 

 ALARMS SOUNDED 

 With an estimated four out of every five Argentines opposing limits on cash withdrawals, analysts warned that banking restrictions were infuriating foreign-owned banks and threatening to cripple the sector. 

 Spain's biggest bank, Santander Central Hispano, which sources have said could leave Argentina if new restrictions are not revised, said it was "pessimistic" about the situation and called for a "credible" government plan. 

 The Wall Street Journal Friday reported that FleetBoston Financial Corp. was considering leaving the country after a government decree that would force banks to convert dollar-denominated loans into devalued pesos. FleetBoston later said it was not planning strategic changes in Argentina. 

 Speaking in neighboring Chile, the IMF's first deputy managing director, Anne Krueger, said there was no money in the pipeline in the short term. 

 "It would be very difficult to have anything within a month." she said. 

 Echoing previous statements about Argentina, U.S. President George W. Bush spoke by telephone on Friday to President Eduardo Duhalde, telling him that help was at hand for Argentina after the government committed to a sustainable economic plan. Duhalde also spoke with Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso on Friday to thank him for Brazil's cooperation. 

 Krueger said that, while a case could be made for the Central Bank's "small" interventions, any large-scale intervention would be questionable. 

 Even after Argentina named a new Central Bank chief with close ties to the IMF Thursday, Krueger's comments suggested the appointment would not pay easy dividends beyond an agreement to delay for a year a $933 million loan repayment. 

 Adding to foreign investor doubts about the government's plans, Moody's criticized the Argentina on Friday for, "the lack of coherent monetary and banking policy ... coupled with paralysis in the local financial markets." 

 On the Argentine stock market, which reopened Thursday after being closed for most of the past month, local blue-chip shares soared again on Friday, as investors sought refuge from a plunging currency and the curbs on cash withdrawals from banks and a partial freeze on savings. The MerVal leading share index ended up more than 11 percent. 

 The free-floating peso ended at 1.90/1.95 to the dollar after the Central Bank sold dollars between 1.65 to 1.85 pesos, down about 49 percent from the one-to-one rate in effect for the past decade. Duhalde devalued the currency earlier this month, days after Argentina defaulted on its $141 billion public debt. 

 The government has said it would ease its bank curbs to allow withdrawals of dollar savings up to $5,000 if they were first turned into pesos. 

 But savers can only convert the dollars at the 1.40-peso fixed exchange rate set for official government transactions and exports - meaning they will lose a big part of their savings. And any funds exceeding that limit will remain in fixed-term deposits for at least a year. 

 Duhalde, Argentina's fifth president in only two weeks, has described the bank curbs as a "time bomb," but says rising poverty is an even greater evil. About a million people joined the ranks of the poor in the 1990s, and 650,000 fell into poverty around Buenos Aires alone last year. 

 So far, Argentine retailers have generally resisted raising prices to offset a near 50 percent decline in the value of the peso, while swank downtown restaurants in the capital - until recently one of the most expensive places in the world - experimented with cheap fixed-price menus. 

 But some multinationals were brutally honest about how the devaluation was going to affect their customers. 

 "Are we going to raise our prices in pesos? Yes," automaker Ford Motor Co. said in a full-page newspaper advertisement on Friday. "(But) we are dropping them 26 percent in dollar terms. 

 "You may insult us, you may agree with us, but you will never be able to say Ford hid when times were tough."

title: Brazil Real Ends Up On Invest,Bush's Argentina Aid Pledge
text:
BRASILIA -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's real ended stronger Wednesday amid a boost from continued strong foreign investment inflows and a pledge from President Bush to work with the International Monetary Fund on assistance for Argentina. 

 The real ended at a midrate of BRR2.365 per dollar on a spread of BRR2.364 to BRR2.366. 

 The currency ended at BRR2.375 per dollar Tuesday. 

 "We've had more investment inflows than outflows and with hope for assistance in Argentina, the real saw a recovery," commented a trader in Sao Paulo. 

 The real traded as low as BRR2.397 early in the session but then rebounded with the entrance of fresh investment and announcement of the U.S.' intentions to intensify aid efforts for Brazil's southern neighbor. 

 The market Wednesday reportedly saw proceeds from a large portion of a $100 million overseas debt offer by the local Votorantim group through Banco Santander. 

 Investors also took note of a market interventions by Argentina's central bank to boost the peso that should aid regional liquidity as well. 

 With more good news locally and renewed hope for a resolution to the Argentine crisis, traders here said they expected the real would continue to change hands at below the BRR2.40 per dollar mark in coming days.

title: Argentina's Peso Opens Unchanged At ARS1.85/Dlr
text:
BUENOS AIRES -(Dow Jones)- Argentina's peso opened unchanged Wednesday after the central bank intervened late Tuesday to contain further weakening of the currency. 

Foreign exchange houses quoted the peso opening Wednesday at a midrate of ARS1.85 to the dollar. Spreads were ARS1.75 to ARS1.95 to the dollar, unchanged from Tuesday's close. 

 Argentina's central bank injected $8.8 million into the new free-floating foreign exchange market Tuesday, selling dollars at ARS1.7 as private banks covered positions. It was the first time the monetary authority injected dollars into the market to contain further depreciation. 

 The peso has weakened 45.9% in just three sessions. 

 The dollar reached an intraday low of ARS2.05 before the central bankintervened, a move that pushed the currency back to a midrate of ARS1.85 to the dollar just before foreign-exchange markets closed. 

 "We still don't see a clear direction on where the market is going," a currency trader said. 

 Friday was the first day the peso floated freely against the dollar in nearly 11 years, as the government abandoned Argentina's convertibility policy, which pegged the peso to the dollar at a 1:1 ratio.

title: Chile stocks down a notch, on Argentina instability.
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile, Jan 16 (Reuters) - Chilean stocks inched lower on Wednesday as confusion and anxiety prevailed over neighbor Argentina's fledgling foreign exchange system, traders said. 

 The IPSA index of the top 40 stocks slid 0.25 percent to 96.18 percent while the general index was down 0.29 percent to 5,278.69. 

 The stock market ended flat on Tuesday after strong gains early in the session were neutralized when Argentina's Central Bank intervened in the floating currency market to defend the peso, which had crashed to 2 pesos to the dollar. 

 That instability continued to weigh on the local bourse on Wednesday. 

 "The scenario in Argentina is still so unclear. Every day they announce new plans and new interventions to try and alleviate the crisis," said Jorge Tolosa, analyst with Ugarte brokerage in Santiago. 

 Trade was heavy in energy group Enersis , which faces a drastic drop in revenues from its Argentine operations under a new peso tariffs system. Standard & Poor's downgraded Enersis on Wednesday to "negative" from "stable" and the utility announced the creation of an internal "crisis unit" to steer it through the turbulence in Argentina. 

 Nonetheless, its shares fell just 0.67 percent to 148 pesos after being driven to rock-bottom levels in recent weeks. 

 "The market was expecting the devaluation in Argentina but it did not take fully into account the impact it would have on local companies," one trader said. 

 Traders said the market shrugged off news that the Chilean central bank cut is 2002 growth forecast on Wednesday to 3.3 percent from 5 percent. The revised outlook had long been discounted, they said.

title: Emerging Debt-Drifts lower amid LatAm  currency  jitters.
text:
NEW YORK, Jan 16 (Reuters) - Emerging market sovereign bond prices drifted slightly lower on Wednesday as investors nervously surveyed the major currencies of Latin America and wondered if Argentina's economic crisis may yet throw a wet blanket over the region. 

 "Everything feels heavy. People are just taking profits now," one emerging debt trader said. "The (Brazilian) real and the Chilean peso have been under pressure and now we're starting to see it in Mexico. That's causing some nervousness." 

 While those three currencies have bounced off the lows seen early this month, analysts said they remain vulnerable to fallout as recession-plagued Argentina struggles to stabilize its peso. 

 Weaker currencies increase risk for foreign investors and make it more difficult for countries to service their international debt. 

 Brazil C bonds slumped 3/8 to bid 77-3/8, Mexico DISC bonds were flat at a bid of 99 and Argentina FRBS fell 1 to bid 27. 

 "The jitters are over local markets. Yesterday Brazilian bonds followed the real one for one," said Sara Zervos, head of emerging markets fixed income strategy WestLB, the German investment bank. 

 "Brazil and the rest of the local markets in Latin America can still be affected by Argentina," she said. 

 The Argentine Central Bank intervened in the foreign exchange market for the second straight day on Wednesday, selling U.S. dollars at 1.70 pesos to prop up the local currency. 

 The bank did not say how many dollars it sold. 

 "The market considers the central bank to be throwing money out the window because there is no way they can defend the exchange rate," Zervos said. "It is very likely they are going to go from a plan of floating the exchange rate in five months to floating it soon. I don't think it will last a month." 

 Argentina has a dual currency rate - an official fixed rate of 1.40 pesos per dollar for foreign trade and banking transactions, and an unofficial floating peso for cash deals. 

 Debt traders agreed Argentina's new currency system is a big source of anxiety now that the government has broken the peso's 10-year link with the U.S. dollar. 

 "There had been the expectation that there might be some relief once the peso started trading," one emerging debt trader said. "But no one believes this exchange rate is real or that there's a legitimate handle on what's going on." 

 Argentina, suffering from a recession now in its fourth year, has defaulted on part of its $141 billion debt and devalued the peso in the last month. 

 SPREADS FLAT 

 Emerging market bond spreads, as measured by JP Morgan's Emerging Markets Bond Index Plus, were more or less flat by midday at 734 basis points over U.S. Treasuries. The bond spreads of Mexico stood one basis point tighter at 320, after a small rally on Tuesday when Fitch upgraded the country's credit rating to investment grade. 

 The move by Fitch increased expectations that Standard & Poor's would promote Mexico to investment grade, as Moody's Investors Service did nearly two years ago. 

 But a top S&P official said Tuesday that the ratings agency would take it's time analyzing Mexico's recently-passed tax reform package and meet with government officials before deciding whether or not to grant an upgrade. 

 Higher credit ratings indicate a reduction in the risk of default. Hence, the higher the rating, the lower the cost of borrowing money. 

 By granting Mexico investment grade status, Fitch and Moody's have confirmed the country's economic integration with its North American neighbors, distinguishing it from most Latin American nations which are still in the "junk bond" category. 

 Many investment houses require portfolio managers to hold bonds that carry the investment grade stamp of approval from Moody's and/or S&P. Fitch is seen by the market as less influential in that regard. 

 "The boost that Mexico got yesterday from Fitch's upgrade was simply because it was seen as increasing the odds of an S&P upgrade," one Wall Street analyst said. "But the S&P upgrade is an open question. It may not happen until the second half of the year."

title: Chile stocks close flat on Argentine peso jitters.
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile, Jan 15 (Reuters) - Chile's stocks closed flat on Tuesday, neutralizing important early gains after Argentina's central bank intervened to break a steep fall in the neighboring country's new floated currency, analysts said. 

 On the Santiago Stock Exchange, the index of the 40 top stocks rose 0.04 percent to 96.42 points while the general index slid 0.14 percent to 5,294.18 points. 

 In the morning, stocks recovered ground lost over recent days but could not hold these gains in the afternoon as nervous investors reacted to a decision by Argentina's central bank to sell dollars in the currency market to prop up the peso, which had weakened to nearly 2.0 pesos to the greenback. 

 "The stocks held firm until the afternoon, buoyed up by purchases of key stocks at good prices. But nearly all these gains were lost due to the renewed turbulence in the Argentine economy," said Jorge Tolosa, analyst with Ugarte brokerage. 

 Argentina last week launched a dual exchange rate regime consisting of a fixed devalued peso of 1.40 per dollar and another floating peso. The floating rate is expected to converge with the fixed rate but has been highly volatile, obliging the central bank to sell dollars on Tuesday at a rate of 1.70 pesos to the dollar. 

 The day's stock market performance was a reminder to Chileans that its economy has not completely decoupled from the Argentine crisis, as stated by members of the government over recent weeks. 

 "This confirms the outlook that Argentina continues to be very fragile and could get worse. This is what the (Chilean) market interpreted it as and that led to the cutback in the gains," Tolosa said. 

 Among the heavyweights, energy group Enersis gained 1.36 percent to close at 149 pesos per share, while its distributor Endesa rose 2.21 percent to 208 pesos. 

 Copper manufacturer Madeco , which on Friday became the first Chilean company to scale back operations in Argentina, lost 11.76 percent to 135.01 pesos, which resulted in the suspension of trading of its stocks. 

 ($1=663 pesos).

title: Chilean peso slips to new low on Argentine woes.
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile, Oct 5 (Reuters) - Chile's peso plunged to new historic lows on Friday on a worsening financial crisis in Argentina, despite renewed intervention from the central bank, traders said. 

 The currency closed at 709.90/710.10, a depreciation of 1.2 percent from the 701.40/701.70 on Thursday. 

 Traders said the day's trading was characterized by a high demand for dollars, especially from two multinational companies in the power and telecommunications sectors. 

 "The demand for dollars in the last two days has been so high that the central bank's interventions have not prevented further falls in the peso," said one trader. 

 According to a survey carried out by Reuters, the bank pumped $40 million into the market. The bank has now injected $410 million into the market since mid-August, when it broke with a two-year hands-off policy. 

 Traders said the financial problems in Argentina would continue to pressure the peso in the long term. 

 Argentina's chronic debt woes have also affected its principal trading partner Brazil, adding additional uncertainty to regional markets. 

 "I would expect the peso rates to hold in the short term due to the uncertainty over Argentina's economic future. At the same time I think the Central Bank should clarify its exchange rate policy," said Gabriela Clivio, analyst at Santiago brokerage.

title: WRAPUP 1-LatAm markets split - Wall Street slide hits Mexico.
text:
SAO PAULO, Brazil, Sept 17 (Reuters) - Latin American markets were split on Monday as a sharp drop on Wall Street on the first day of trading since Tuesday's devastating plane attacks battered Mexican shares while investors snapped up already pummeled stocks in Brazil and Argentina. 

 But players said trading regionwide was erratic and volumes were razor-thin with many investors reluctant to put their capital at risk until the United States' shell-shocked markets set a clearer trend. 

 Mexican stocks, also trading for the first time since hijacked planes demolished New York's World Trade Center and hit the Pentagon near Washington, were off 1.9 percent, following a sharp fall on the Dow Jones Industrial Average .DJI) and the tech-heavy Nasdaq .IXIC). 

 In Argentina and Brazil, stocks that took a beating last week in the wake of the attacks climbed as investors seized cheaply priced companies and cheered the U.S. Federal Reserve's decision earlier Monday to knock 50 basis points off interest rates. 

 "There is a lot of bargain hunting going on," said Walter Molano, Latin American economist at BCP Securities in New York. "But the prices we are seeing on the screens are very preliminary and are not very indicative." 

 MEXICO TRIMS LOSSES AFTER SHARP DROP 

 Mexico's benchmark IPC index .MXX) of 35 most liquid stocks pared losses after initial panic at the outset sent it down about 4.5 percent. 

 But Wall Street's later climb off its worst lows eased jitters in Mexico. By late morning, the IPC, led by media and telecom shares, was trading at 5419.24, or 1.9 percent, below its close in an abbreviated session on Tuesday. 

 "In (the) short-term we will see a lot of volatility as some bail out of the market, but we are trying to be more objective and are recommending to our clients to stay put as we await a clearer picture," said Rogelio Gallegos, portfolio manager at Actinver in Mexico City. 

 Mexico sends 85 percent of its exports to the United States and its economic fortunes and foreign investment inflows are closely tied to its northern neighbor's economy. 

 In the currency market, the Mexican peso MEXO1) firmed 8.65 centavos to 9.4580 against the U.S. dollar from Friday's close, after shedding nearly 2 percent last week. 

 Argentine and Brazilian benchmark bonds moved slightly lower in minute trading volumes. 

 BOTTOM FISHING 

 Elsewhere in the region, stocks gained as investors sought for bargains in the wake of last week's sell-off that hit emerging markets particularly hard. Players feared the attacks would accelerate a slowdown in U.S. and global economic growth and tension mounted over a possible military response for the attacks that left thousands of people dead or missing. 

 On Brazil's Sao Paulo Stock Exchange's benchmark Bovespa index .BVSP), the region's largest, pummeled telephone stocks and oil giant Petrobras lifted shares off two-year lows. 

 The index rose 5.1 percent to 10,542 after shedding 18 percent last week to levels not seen since August 1999. Phone companies Telemar and Brasil Telecom rallied. 

 Jetmaker Embraer, however, mirrored the slump in global airline shares, dropping 3.7 percent on fears the U.S. attacks would slash air travel and reduce airlines' profits. Analysts said Continental Airlines' announcement that it would default on some financing agreements and lay off staff pushed Embraer even lower. Continental makes up about 50 percent of Embraer's order book. 

 "The shares are falling on fears Continental Airlines could suspend aircraft orders or cancel orders that were already made," said Rafael Quintanilha, an analyst at BES Securities. 

 But Brazil's real currency BRBY), which has lost more than one-quarter of its value against the dollar this year, was swept up in the buying wave, strengthening to 2.667 reais per dollar from 2.673 reais Friday, when the Central Bank intervened to prop up the ailing currency. 

 WIDESPREAD GAINS 

 In Argentina, where a recession and financial crisis have been temporarily overshadowed by global market turmoil sparked by the attacks in the United States - the benchmark Merval index .MERV) gained 3.2 percent to 274.470 in wafer-thin trade. 

 "From the market perspective, we are already at lows not seen in a decade, and clearly the moment has come where you have to start thinking about the actual value of shares," said Ruben Pasquali, a trader at Mayoral brokerage. "I don't know if we can logically go down much more." 

 The Merval is already down 35 percent this year. 

 Chilean and Venezuelan shares posted moderate gains, also on bargain hunting, traders said. Chile's benchmark IPCA .IPCA) index added 1.2 percent to 106.78. Caracas' benchmark IBC index .IBC) rose 1.3 percent to 7195.54. 

 The Chilean peso slumped versus the dollar following the U.S. Fed rate cut, opening at 699.50/700, but later recovered after the Chilean Central Bankintervened in the market.

title: Brazil Real Ends Stronger On Argentina's Sigh Of Relief
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO -(Dow Jones)- The Brazilian real got a lift Friday from a central bank intervention and signs that Argentina is securing increasing political support for a crisis-fighting austerity plan. 

 Traders added inflows, and the expectation of more dollars entering the Brazilian market next week also cheered the local currency. 

 The real ended at a midrate of BRR2.452 per dollar on a spread of BRR2.451-BRR2.453 after hitting a high of BRR2.433 per dollar after the central bank sold dollars on the market to prop up the real. 

 This compares with the real's Thursday's closing mark of BRR2.508 per dollar. 

 The central bank confirmed it intervened in the market but didn't say how much it sold. 

 Traders said about $140 million from Volkswagen (G.VOW) export contracts entered the forex market Friday, giving the real a boost. 

 "Investors are also expecting dollars from the Petrobras share offer to come into Brazil next week, as well as dollars from Petrobras's insurance policy for the P-36," said a Rio de Janeiro based trader, referring to a Petrobras oil rig that sank in March. 

 On Thursday, Brazil's National Development Bank BNDES said it raised a total of BRR1.73 billion from the sale of 41.4 million nonvoting shares it had in oil giant Petrobras for $19.50 per share. 

 Out of that total, $596.7 million make up the share offer's international portion, which is expected to enter the market next Tuesday. 

 Moreover, the market also expects Petrobras to receive an expected $496.75 million from an insurance contract for the loss of its P-36 oil platform. 

 Meanwhile, the central bank said international reserves were slightly lower at $36.008 billion on Thursday, from $36.018 billion Wednesday. International reserve figures are available on the central bank's website www.bcb.gov.br("http://www.bcb.gov.br/") with a one-day lag.

title: Brazil's Real Ends Stronger On  Argentina ,  Intervention
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's real ended sharply stronger Tuesday after an early central bank intervention got a bounce from Argentine President Fernando de la Rua's clinching of political support for deficit-cutting plan. 

 Expectations of a hike in Brazil's basic interest rate Wednesday added to the strengthening, traders said. 

 The real ended at a midrate of BRR2.498 per dollar on a wide spread of BRR2.496-BRR2.500. 

 Monday the real closed at BRR2.581, after uncertainties about De la Rua's negotiating skills with opposition parties forced the real beyond BRR2.60, setting a new record for weakness. 

 "The central bank's early intervention had a big impact (on the real) because of Argentina's political developments," said a Sao Paulo trader. 

 The central bank has a policy of not confirming interventions, but the monetary authority has been selling dollars daily on the market to prop up the real for about the last two weeks as part of a $6 billion plan to protect its currency. 

 Market players, said although De la Rua has mustered the support of Peronist governors to make spending cuts needed to pay debts, it remains to be seen if the cuts will be big enough or if Argentina's economy can be turned around. 

 A Dow Jones Newswires survey of 14 economists forecasts Brazil's central bank will hike its basic interest rate between 50 and 675 basis points Wednesday. The basic rate is currently at 18.25%. 

 Rating agency Fitch's announcement Tuesday that it changed Brazil's credit outlook for its sovereign rating to negative from stable had little impact on the currency, traders said.

title: Colombia holds rates on Argentina worries-FinMin.
text:
BOGOTA, Colombia, July 13 (Reuters) - Colombia's Central Bank opted against lowering its money market intervention rates on Friday due to ongoing economic troubles in Argentina, Finance Minister Juan Manuel Santos said. 

 "In the meeting (of Central Bank directors) we were going to lower rates, but given the situation in Argentina we decided not to lower them," Santos said as he exited the meeting. 

 Fears that Argentina's woes could end in a debt default have rattled markets across the world, battering Latin American currencies as investors fret over a potential 1998-style emerging market meltdown. 

 Colombia's Central Bank has not lowered rates since March 12 - when it cut all money market intervention rates by 50 basis points. Analysts have said a rate cut would have helped spur growth in Latin America's fifth largest economy.

title: Chile's Peso Ends Weaker At 665.70/Dlr, Back From 674.20
text:
SANTIAGO -(Dow Jones)- Chile's peso ended at a record weak point of CLP665.70 against the dollar Thursday, after hitting an historic intraday low of CLP674.20 at the open on fears that Argentina's economic crisis will end in currency devaluation or debt default. 

 Traders said the peso bounced back from its intraday low on mounting expectations that Chile's Central Bank will make another move to support the currency, after temporarily halting the peso's slide by announcing plans last week to float $1 billion in debt on local financial markets. 

 Despite the modest rebound, the peso ended 0.3% weaker against the dollar than Wednesday's CLP664.00 close, and 13.8% weaker from the beginning of the year. Economists attribute the currency's steady depreciation largely to contagion effects from Argentina. 

 Traders attributed the peso's early decline to lack of confidence in economic emergency measures announced by Argentine President Fernando de la Rua and Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo. The pair promised late Wednesday to balance Argentina's budget by making severe spending cuts and enlisting banks to improve tax collection. 

 Traders in Chile said the peso began to rebound in afternoon trading, as growing expectations that the Central Bank will intervene stemmed the rush to dollars. 

 "Argentina's dead. It's no longer the relevant point now that the peso is at the 670-level," said one local trader, adding that market players were pinning their hopes for Central Bank action on a monetary policy meeting scheduled for late Thursday. 

 Many economists, though, are still cautious about guessing what action the Bank might take. 

 Jose Ramon Valente, an economist with local consultancy Econsult, shrugged off market talk that the Bank will either tap its reserves to pump dollars directly into the market or double back on a six-month easing bent to raise its benchmark interbank lending rate from 3.50%. 

 "The Bank's best option is to intensify the measure taken last week and increase the quantity of dollar-denominated bonds it will place," said Valente. "The Bank should also give a strong signal to the market that the situation in Argentina is short-term, and that buying dollars (at the current exchange rate) could be risky," he added. 

 The Bank is expected to adjourn its monthly policy meeting after markets close Thursday.

title: Brazil real at new low close on Argentine fears.
text:
SAO PAULO, July 12 (Reuters) - Brazil's embattled currency chalked up its third new record low close in a row Thursday, despite intervention as players took a dim view of Argentina's latest bid to pull itself out of the recessionary quagmire, traders said. 

 The real weakened to 2.552 per dollar from Wednesday's previous record low close of 2.50 per dollar, leaving the currency nearly 31 percent below where it began the year. Earlier it hit a new record intraday level of 2.58 per dollar. 

 The new historic close came despite the Central Bank's seventh intervention in the market this month. Traders say the bank has sold some $50 million to bolster the real in each of the last six sessions. 

 The real plunged this week as a fresh wave of fears of Argentine fiscal insolvency and debt default swept through the market, adding to existing concerns about the impact of the U.S. economic slowdown and local energy shortage crisis. 

 Traders said the Argentine government's latest pledge late Wednesday to eliminate the budget gap for the rest of the year by cutting spending and fighting tax evasion had done little to lift the cloud of over the neighboring economy.

title: ANALYSIS-Turk politics place hugh strain on IMF-rescue plan.
text:
ANKARA, July 12 (Reuters) - Turkey and the IMF look set to solve a row that has delayed the payment of an urgent loan, but domestic political rifts may still keep interest rates sky-high, putting a heavy strain the country's IMF-backed rescue plan. 

 A 10-day deadlock with the IMF - ostensibly over the composition of the board of landline monopoly Turk Telekom, but really a test of Turkey's commitment to reform - has eroded much of what market confidence remained in the country's fractious three-party coalition, analysts say. 

 "The government's obstinacy with the IMF over the Telekom issue hurt market confidence a lot," said an economist with a foreign bank based in Turkey. "Everyone reckons a similar crisis could emerge any time, in a week, in a month." 

 The IMF and World Bank are expected to release more than $3 billion in loans on Thursday when they meet to review steps Turkey has taken to meet fund demands on bank reform and the grooming of Telekom for privatisation. 

 The dispute over the make up of the Telekom board highlighted hostility in the government's nationalist wing to Economy Minister Kemal Dervis, who brokered the rescue deal with the IMF and World Bank. Markets see the Nationalist Action Party (MHP) increasingly as an opposition within the government. 

 CRIPPLING INTEREST RATES 

 Turkish government debt yields - what it costs the country to borrow - are now punishingly high at around 100 percent, reflecting the market's lack of appetite. Investors have seen the value of lira-denominated bonds tumble as the lira has lost almost half its value since the February crisis struck. 

 Such yields, if sustained over coming months, could raise the country's debt burden to levels making the rescue programme unsustainable. 

 The domestic debt stock more than doubled to 84,500 trillion lira by end of May from 36,400 trillion lira at the end of last year and total interest payments will now account for upwards of 85 percent of government revenues in 2001. 

 Yet the crisis recovery plan, backed by $15.7 billion in IMF and World Bank loans, is predicated on a steady fall in rates. 

 "The current interest rate levels reflect investors' risk premiums. It's not because of high inflation expectations but lack of confidence in the programme's future," said Yarkin Cebeci, chief economist at Ottoman Bank. 

 Turkish wholesale inflation was 52.4 percent in June, while the most traded bond yields swing around 90-100 percent. 

 BLAME PUT ON LIRA FLOAT 

 A report by Nomura Equity Research was even gloomier. 

 "Turkey's economy is now clearly falling into severe financial stress. Higher bond yields are now a given, driving the currency lower in a vicious circle. 

 "Inflows of fresh forex receipts from the tourism industry (this summer) are masking what is a very ugly dynamic. Once these tail off in September, unfortunately just in time for the opening of parliament, yields are likely to explode and the lira will head south." 

 Fears of an Argentinian debt default have also added to the economic pressure on Turkey. The IMF appears reluctant to consider any further intervention to shore up Argentina, fund sources arguing political damage is of the country's own making. The warning might apply also to Turkey, which is seen to be unlikely to receive a third international bail-out in under 12 months after packages in November and February. 

 Some analysts argue the floating currency rate system, introduced when Turkey was forced to abandon a crawling currency peg regime in February, is the real cause of the current high interest rates. 

 "Investors cannot guess where the exchange rate can go, so they ask for high risk premiums for their lira investments, pushing interest rates to levels higher than those under a system where exchange rates are predictable," wrote Ercan Kumcu, an economist and columnist at the daily Hurriyet. 

 Overnight interest rates, the only instrument the central bank can use to intervene, are anchored at 63 percent. The bank cannot change the rate, since a cut would prompt dollar demand, and a rise would put a greater burden still on the treasury. 

 "It's true the floating rate puts pressure on interest rates," said Cebeci of Ottoman Bank. "But, if we were still in the crawling peg system, central bank reserves would disappear in a week under such political fears." 

 The central bank has lost about $6 billion of its international reserves since the February crisis. They now stand at $16.5 billion. 

 FLIGHT OF CONFIDENCE 

 Some other analysts argue interest rates should have fallen even under the floating exchange rate system with rising exports, falling inflation and a rosier current account balance. But that premium has been squandered by the politicians. 

 "With confidence so badly torn at home and abroad, we could not even enjoy those benefits the floating rate system could have brought," the foreign bank economist said. 

 The lira briefly traded at a new record low of 1,345,000 against the dollar on Thursday on the central bank-brokered spot market - a fall of almost a half since February's float. 

 Turkish banks and investors still seek solace in dollars, as a safe haven in crisis periods. Banks have recently closed their open foreign currency positions after an $8 billion debt swap, and seem reluctant to turn to lira instruments again. 

 The high dolarisation in the system, makes restoring confidence in the lira much harder, analysts said. According to the latest central bank data, 83 percent of its liabilities are now in foreign currencies. 

 "We are at a turning point," said Funda Gungor, chief economist at Demir Bank. "If the government meets all commitments to the IMF, the programme may have a chance to survive, though hanging by a thread."

title: Brazil's Fraga: Ctrl Bk's Hands Not Tied On  Forex  Policy
text:
NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- Central Bank of Brazil President Arminio Fraga said Wednesday the monetary authority reserves the right to intervene in the foreign-exchange market beyond the $6 billion the bank recently earmarked for spot market intervention through the end of the year. 

 "We haven't tied our hands at all," Fraga said at a news conference. "We can do (foreign exchange) intervention directly or through other instruments," such as dollar-linked bonds. 

 Fraga noted that the $6 billion is designed to "irrigate" the market and smooth the country's balance of payments. 

 "The spot market we feel needs a little clarity and we're going to stick to $6 billion," he said. 

 Asked if more could be spent on the spot market if conditions warrant, he said, "It's not our intention to change but I don't think I want to go as far as saying never." 

 The central bank unveiled its new foreign-exchange intervention plans last week, saying it would spend roughly $50 million a day on the spot market. 

 Market participants question whether the $6 billion figure would be enough to stabilize the currency, particularly given the ongoing volatility in Argentina. They also criticized the central bank for specifying its intervention strategy, as it could spark speculation against the real. 

 Despite several interventions since the plan was announced, the real has continued to lose ground. On Wednesday, the currency hit an all-time low of BRR2.570 to the dollar. 

 Fraga is in New York for a series of meetings with investors and bankers. He said the goal of the meetings is to confirm the commitment of Brazilian officials to economic stability and to explain the country's policy approach amid the market turmoil. 

 The real recovered from its earlier lows to close at BRR2.50 per dollar Wednesday, following a direct intervention on the spot market and a central bank sale of dollar-linked debt. The finishing mark was, however, the weakest ever close. 

 Fraga downplayed the market criticism of the latest central bank moves, saying it's impossible to determine how effective the new intervention plan has been, but that it's also impossible to know what would have happened if the measure had not been announced. 

 Fraga, who spoke to 80 market participants at a luncheon sponsored by J.P. Morgan, said that the response among investors has been favorable, noting that many had doubts about the foreign exchange intervention policy. 

 "He really clarified a lot with respect to what they're doing on the interventions," said one fund manager for a European bank, who asked not to be identified. "I would say I'm a bit more confident" in how the central bank is handling things. 

 Fraga, for his part, said the reforms put in place over the last two years have prepared Brazil to weather the current turbulence caused by weakness in Argentina and an energy crisis at home. 

 "While I think the short-term problems we are going through are very serious, I also feel very strongly that all the policies we have put in place...have given us a chance to look at these problems as temporary problems we will be able to address," Fraga said. 

 Brazil's central bank projects economic growth of 2.8% in 2001, down from 4.5% last year. This year's figure was originally expected to surpass 4%, but an energy crisis has led economists to slash their forecasts. 

 As for inflation, the central bank recently projected a 5.8% rate for 2001. That's near the top end of the central bank's target range for the year of between 2% and 6%. 

 Fraga declined to comment on whether the continued weakening of the real had further eroded the outlook for inflation, saying that the matter would be studied at next week's monetary policy committee meeting. 

 The central bank - which has raised its key rate a cumulative 300 basis points since March - is widely expected to have to hike rates next week given the surge in inflationary pressure caused by the weak currency. 

 Fraga was hesitant to express much optimism about Argentina's prospects for recovery, though he said he welcomed news that Argentina was planning to implement spending cuts. 

 Argentine Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo is expected to soon announce austerity measures. 

 "I see Argentina trying to respond to its difficulties," Fraga said. "The feeling I have is that they want to get things done." 

 Asked about the impact of increased bickering between Argentina and Brazil on the trade front, Fraga said he wasn't particularly concerned. 

 Early last week, Argentina announced that it had cut import tariffs for certain products coming from countries outside the Mercosur trade bloc - which includes Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay. Brazil said the measures violated existing agreements and said it would suspend bilateral trade talks with Argentina. 

 "During these last few years, with problems in Brazil and now in Argentina, I think it's natural that you get this sort of discussion," Fraga said. "We're committed to staying at the table, talking through each case." 

 "I'm confident that that won't be a major issue in this picture at all," he added. 

 Elsewhere on the trade front, Fraga said Washington could help out Brazil by committing to opening up the U.S. market to Brazilian products. 

 "We feel in Brazil very strongly that the model we have been developing requires open markets for our products," Fraga said. "We're ready to sit at the table. We need a clear signal from the American government that this is for real, that we're gonna open markets." 

 -By Stephen Wisnefski, Dow Jones Newswires; (201) 938-5692; stephen.wisnefski@dowjones.com

title: Chile may take measures to soften Argentine impact.
text:
VALPARAISO, Chile, July 11 (Reuters) - The Chilean government said on Wednesday it might take extra economic measures to counter the harmful effect on the local economy of an economic and political crisis in neighboring Argentina. 

 The main impact in Chile of Argentina's chronic instability has been a steady depreciation of the Chilean peso . The local currency sank to a fresh historic low on Wednesday of 664 pesos to the dollar, losing more than 13 percent of its value against the U.S. currency so far this year. 

 "We do not rule out any measure," Finance Minister Nicolas Eyzaguirre told reporters, without specifying what steps it was considering. 

 "If there are speculative tendencies that bring the value of the currency to levels beyond what the fundamentals of the Chilean economy can withstand, then the authorities will have a say in the matter," he added. 

 Regional and global financial markets were rattled on Wednesday by renewed fears that Argentine will default on its massive debt or devalue its currency amid a worsening political and financial environment. 

 Argentine Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo vowed on Tuesday to shrink the country's hefty budget deficit to zero to pull it out of a three-year recession and restore investor confidence. 

 Last week, the Chilean Central Bank, which is independent of the government, said it would inject $1 billion into the market over the next six months via by issuing dollar-denominated promissory notes to help shore up the peso, pummeled by uncertainty over Argentina. 

 It was the institution's first intervention since it free-floated the peso in 1999. 

 The peso firmed slightly on the news before tumbling again on Argentina's ongoing quandary. 

 SOME EXPECT DOLLAR SALES TO BOLSTER PESO 

 Local market players speculate the central bank's next move will be a more aggressive intervention along the lines taken by its Brazilian counterpart, selling dollars directly in the market to prop up the peso. 

 To date, however, the Chilean Central Bank has shown no signs of taking that route. 

 The Brazilian real, also driven to record lows on Argentina, has continued to slide despite repeated attempts by the country's Central Bank to sell dollars on the market to break its fall. 

 "I think it is often inconvenient to try to manipulate the market," said Eyzaguirre. "But I also said very clearly that we are not going to let ourselves be manipulated by the market." 

 The Argentine crisis has spilled over into Chile at a time when the former star economy of the region struggles to regain the average 7 percent growth rates it enjoyed through most of the 1990s. 

 Chile grew 5.4 percent last year but a slowdown this year prompted the central bank to lower its 2001 growth forecast to 4.3 percent from 5.6 percent. It sees inflation this year at 3.2 percent. 

 Low prices for copper, Chile's top export, and a global slowdown could lead to further cuts in growth estimates. 

 But Eyzaguirre said the domestic and regional economic troubles do not warrant a dramatic drop in the peso, blaming the currency volatility on excessive market speculation. 

 The government fears a sharp decline in the peso could fuel inflation, which has been capped by sluggish spending in the first half of the year. 

 "We say very clearly that in the event the price of the dollar gets out of hand and this has an impact on inflation, obviously we would not rule out any measure," Eyzaguirre said. 

 On Thursday, the Chilean Central Bank will hold its monthly monetary policy meeting to assess whether to alter its benchmark lending rate or maintain it at its current annualized rate of 3.5 percent. 

 The institution has cut rates five times this year to kick-start consumer demand, seen as holding back growth.

title: Emerging Debt-Sentiment sagging depsite technical bounce.
text:
NEW YORK, July 6 (Reuters) - Emerging market bonds on Friday rose for the first time in nine trading sessions in a technical bounce, but confidence was frail amid political strife in Argentina and concern that Brazil's efforts to prop up its flagging currency were failing. 

 "There is continued political noise in Argentina and uncertainties about the effectiveness of intervention efforts announced in Brazil," said Lacey Gallagher, director of Latin American research at Credit Suisse First Boston. 

 The J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Index, which on Thursday lost 2.6 percent, widened three basis points to 809 basis points over U.S. Treasuries. 

 Technical analysts said Argentine FRBs and Brazil C bonds were "deeply oversold" on Thursday. On Friday, the FRB rose 3 percent to 77.750 points, and the C bond rose three-quarters of a point to 72.625 points. 

 "External debt markets are up purely on the back of shortcovering. Higher prices do not indicate a change in sentiment and people are squaring their books before they go home," a head emerging market trader said. 

 Meanwhile the Brazilian real ended firmer on Friday after a yo-yo session in which the Central Bank sold dollars to boost the currency after it plumbed record lows against the U.S. dollar. 

 The real, which is off 24.8 percent for the year, ended at 2.435 per dollar. 

 IMPASSE BROKEN 

 An impasse between the Argentine federal government and province leaders was broken on Thursday when the government agreed to hand over $600 million to the provinces in exchange for a series of spending cuts. 

 The Buenos Aires province will cut $500 million, the other 11 provinces will cut an additional $150 million, and the federal government itself will slash $150 million off its expenditure sheet. 

 "There's still not consensus across the political spectrum in terms of an economic policy approach so the agreement with the governors beginning with the Province of Buenos Aires - and we expect more - is positive but it's not the only political issue." 

 Michael Gavin, head of Latin American research at UBS Warburg, said the main risk in Argentina relates to whether the current market panic translates into a financial one leading to sharp declines in bank deposits. 

 "Deposits in the banking system have been relatively stable recently and ... there has been no indication of a deposit run amid (Thursday's) panic ... we think yesterday's price action was more a reflection of panic selling than a response to any specific news," Gavin said. 

 Argentina's four-day peso-denominated interbank lending rate hit 20 percent on Friday ahead of a long weekend - Argentina is closed on Monday for Independence Day - in another sign of growing discontent with the country's inability to turn around ten straight quarters of economic contraction. 

 And Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo in Rome announced changes to the $850 million Letes auction, cutting the maturity of the domestic bonds from one year to 90 days. 

 Meanwhile, emerging market star Mexico, with one foot in the full investment grade door, succumbed to the pessimism as its benchmark 2026 global bond fell 0.750 points to 124.375 - its lowest level since May 30.

title: Emerging Debt-Shortcovering bounce yet sentiment shaky.
text:
NEW YORK, July 6 (Reuters) - Benchmark emerging market bonds on Friday rose for the first time in nine trading sessions in a technical bounce, but confidence was frail in the absence of political consensus toward economic policy approach in Argentina and amid concern that Brazil's efforts to prop up its flagging currency were failing. 

 "There is continued political noise in Argentina and uncertainties about the effectiveness of intervention efforts announced in Brazil," said Lacey Gallagher, director of Latin American research at Credit Suisse First Boston. 

 The J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Index, which on Thursday lost 2.6 percent, widened three basis points to 809 basis points over U.S. Treasuries. 

 Technical analysts say Argentine FRBs and Brazil C bonds were "deeply oversold" on Thursday. On Friday, the FRB rose a full point to bid around 76.500 and the C bond inched 0.625 points higher to bid around 72.500 points. 

 "External debt markets are up purely on the back of shortcovering. Higher prices do not indicate a change in sentiment and people are squaring their books before they go home," a head emerging market trader said. 

 Moreover, the Brazilian real fell to record lows early on Friday, trading at 2.560 per dollar. The slump came despite the Central Bank's announcement on Thursday that it would spend $6 billion in the foreign exchange market by the end of the year to support the currency that has so far this year lost 31 percent of its value. 

 IMPASSE BROKEN 

 An impasse between the Argentine federal government and province leaders was broken on Thursday when the government agreed to hand over $600 million to the provinces in exchange for a series of spending cuts. 

 The Buenos Aires province will cut $500 million, the other 11 provinces will cut an additional $150 million, and the federal government itself will slash $150 million off its expenditure sheet. 

 "There's still not consensus across the political spectrum in terms of an economic policy approach so the agreement with the governors beginning with the Province of Buenos Aires - and we expect more - is positive but it's not the only political issue." 

 Michael Gavin, head of Latin American research at UBS Warburg, said the main risk in Argentina relates to whether the current market panic translates into a financial one leading to sharp declines in bank deposits. 

 "Deposits in the banking system have been relatively stable recently and ... there has been no indication of a deposit run amid (Thursday's) panic ... we think yesterday's price action was more a reflection of panic selling than a response to any specific news," Gavin said. 

 UBS holds a neutral position on Argentine bonds - meaning the bank recommends investors should hold the same ratio of Argentine bonds as allocated in the EMBI-plus at 21 percent: "But we advise investors to position for a technically driven relief rally in the days ahead," Gavin said. 

 Even emerging market star Mexico, with one foot in the full investment grade door, succumbed to wave of selling in Latin America. The 2026 bond fell 0.875 points to bid around 124.250 points.

title: Emerging Debt-Down amid Argentine economy, Brazil real woes.
text:
NEW YORK, June 28 (Reuters) - Emerging market sovereign bond prices drifted slightly lower on Thursday as investors looked for positive news to counter recent signs of weakness in the Argentine economy and nagging worry about Brazil's currency. 

 "The market is a little weaker today because there are no positive developments and we do not see real money stepping in at these levels to support prices," said Owi Ruivivar, fixed income strategist at BNP Paribas. 

 Emerging market bond spreads widened by three basis points to 746 over U.S. Treasuries, according to J.P. Morgan's Emerging Markets Bond Index Plus. Argentina's portion of the index widened seven basis points to 1,003 while Brazil spreads remained flat at 845. 

 Wider spreads reflect the perception of increased risk as measured against safe-haven U.S. Treasury bonds. 

 "The market is trading off of the negative developments that have accumulated over the last week, such as the inefficacy of the Central Bank intervention in Brazil and disappointing retail sales data from Argentina," Ruivivar said. 

 On Wednesday, Brazil's Central Bank intervened aggressively in the foreign exchange market, carrying out four emergency operations to prop up the wilting real, which ended nearly one percent stronger. 

 Argentina supermarket sales fell 2 percent in May versus the same month in 2000 and May construction activity fell 1.1 percent year-on-year, Economy Ministry data shows. 

 Argentina's new global bond due 2008 fell a half point to bid 77.8, while the country's FRB paper shed 1/8 point to bid 83-3/4. 

 "Argentine FRB bonds are very vulnerable right now due to a deterioration in Argentine fundamentals, as will be the new 2008s and 2018s," Ruivivar said. 

 Meanwhile, the U.S. Federal Reserve on Wednesday cut U.S. interest rates a modest quarter-percentage point, slowing the pace of its aggressive rate-cutting campaign while signaling it remained ready to do more if needed. 

 "There might have been some people who were hoping for 50 basis points who took a bit of profit," emerging debt trader said. "If we would have seen a 50 basis point cut, our market might have taken a little relief from that and rallied." 

 VENEZUELA DIPS WITH OIL PRICES 

 Venezuelan DCB bonds dropped 3/8 to bid 83-3/8 while the country's spread widened four basis points to 842 on Thursday amid jitters in the oil market. The solvency of Venezuela, a major oil exporter, is seen by Wall Street as dependent on petroleum prices remaining high. 

 NYMEX crude oil futures extended losses early Thursday after plummeting Wednesday, amid growing worries that the weakening economy is cutting demand. 

 NYMEX August crude fell 39 cents to an early low of $25.22 a barrel, extending an overnight loss of 24 cents. On Wednesday, the contract plunged $1.37 and hit a 14-month low. 

 "We recommend a defensive position on Venezuela, Argentina and Brazil," Ruivivar said. "We continue to like Mexico." 

 Ratings agency Standard & Poor's has said it is considering raising Mexico to investment grade status thanks to the country's improving fundamentals. 

 Ruivivar said her favorite Mexican bond is the global due 2019. "This is Mexico's cheapest dollar-priced bond and should attract good crossover investor activity," she said.

title: Peru's Toledo says secures Congress support-analyst.
text:
NEW YORK, April 26 (Reuters) - Leading Peruvian presidential candidate Alejandro Toledo told Wall Street economists on Thursday that he has negotiated majority support for his economic reforms in Congress, a development that would improve his prospects for reviving economic growth, a participant in the meeting said. 

 "He told us today that he has undergone negotiations to assure a majority in Congress with other parties if he were to be elected, " Miguel Palomino, chief economist for Latin America at Merrill Lynch, told Reuters after the meeting. 

 "This is positive in that it implies significantly improved governability," Palomino said. 

 It was not immediately clear with whom Toledo could have struck a deal. His Peru Posible will be the biggest force in the new Congress, but has no majority. The next biggest is the American Popular Revolutionary Alliance (APRA) of his rival in the upcoming runoff election, ex-president Alan Garcia. 

 Whoever wins the runoff - likely to occur on June 3 - is likely to have to strike a deal with the Unidad Nacional (National Unity) party of defeated first-round contender Lourdes Flores or the Independent Moralizing Front (FIM) of ex-legislator Fernando Olivera. Peruvian analysts see much of Flores' support going to Garcia. 

 The first round of voting for president was on April 8, the same day the new Congress was elected. The incoming legislature will hold its first session on July 27, one day before the new president is due to take office. 

 Toledo, a former World Bank economist, was in New York to sell his economic program to analysts who have been concerned that the campaign is drifting in a fiscally irresponsible direction as Toledo and Garcia compete for votes. 

 "I AM NOT A POPULIST," TOLEDO SAYS 

 His message was summed up in a brief statement he made to reporters between meetings when he said, "No soy un populista," or "I am not a populist." 

 JP Morgan sovereign debt strategist Luis Oganes said Toledo was convincing. 

 "We all know Mr. Toledo is facing a very populist candidate and that the second round campaign could become a war of populist ideas," Oganes said. 

 One concern voiced recently by Wall Street was that Toledo had proposed a series of tax cuts intended to boost consumption. 

 "But he stressed and clarified that fiscal discipline would not be sacrificed at the expense of trying to promote consumption by way of tax cuts," Oganes said. "That was an important message for us." 

 Peru's economy has declined this year amid political turmoil left in the wake of former President Alberto Fujimori, who fled to Japan late last year after being fired amid a bribery scandal centering on his former intelligence chief. 

 Interim Economy Minister Javier Silva Ruete has trimmed Peru's gross domestic product (GDP) forecast for 2001 to 1-2 percent from a target set with the International Monetary Fund of 2-3 percent, a ministry spokesman said. 

 Peru's sol currency sank through a psychological level of 3.6 to the dollar on Wednesday, a fresh historic low, before recovering on central bank intervention amid a confidence crisis in Argentina, that has affected regional markets. 

 Toledo, a centrist free-marketeer with leftist rhetoric, finished first in the April 8 elections but failed to secure the outright majority he predicted and was forced into a runoff by Garcia, whose 1985-90 government left Peru in economic chaos.

title: Brazil's Real Ends Weaker Despite Ctrl Bank  Intervention
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- The downward slope for Brazil's real steepened Thursday on mounting worries of continuing recession in Argentina, leading the central bank to intervene in the market for the first time in as many times to stop the currency from weakening. 

 Concern that newly-appointed Argentine Economy Ministry Ricardo Lopez Murphy may not be able to pull that country out of a three-year recession drove the real to a new 24-month closing low of BRR2.096 to the dollar, despite the central bank intervention. 

 The weakening was amplified by fears that Brazil's trade deficit will widen in coming months after two explosions earlier today halted production at a key oil rig off the coast of Rio de Janeiro. Brazil may have to spend an additional $50 million monthly on oil imports until the rig resumes production. 

 The monetary authority entered the market selling dollars a couple of hours after the real crossed the key psychological barrier of BRR2.10/dollar for the first time since March 1999. The real strengthened to BRR2.074 almost instantaneously before losing ground again. 

 "The outlook hinges on the situation in Argentina," said a trader. "If things don't improve there, the real won't recover." 

 The real has lost 6.5% of its value since the start of the year amid concerns over the global economic slowdown and Argentina. The continued weakening is now raising concern that inflation may rise and upset the government's 4% target this year. 

 "If the real remains too weak, inflation may rise as companies will seek to pass on to consumers their increased costs," said Simone Passini, an economist with UBS Warburg in Rio de Janeiro. 

 The central bank's decision to sell dollars on the market was welcome by traders and analysts, who said the real was weakening amid thin liquidity on speculation, rather than on concrete facts. 

 "This kind of movement, which is purely speculative, is bad for the market because it contaminates expectations," said Passini, referring to the impact of the real's weakening on other asset prices. 

 A clear example was the sharp drop in Treasury bond prices on the secondary market. The yield on Treasury bills due Feb. 2002, the most liquid federal bond, rose 27 basis points to 17.03%. The central bank's benchmark short-term rate currently stands at 15.25%. 

 The weakening currency will also have a negative impact on public accounts, widening the country's fiscal deficit. Brazil has foreign debt totaling some BRR102 billion and dollar-indexed domestic debt of BRR120 billion. 

 Marcelo Carvalho, chief economist at J.P. Morgan Chase in Sao Paulo, says that, as a rule of thumb, a 10% rise in the real's quote against the dollar will translate into a fiscal cost of roughly 2% of gross domestic product over 12 months.
