title: UPDATE 1-Brazil, Argentina to set common economic goals.
text:
(updates with Buenos Aires Declaration details paras 4, 9, 13 and 14) 

 BUENOS AIRES, April 28 (Reuters) - Brazil and Argentina agreed on Friday to set common debt, deficit and inflation targets next March with a view to integrating six regional economies into an EU-like common market, ministers said. 

 "Next March we will have convergence targets," Brazilian Finance Minister Pedro Malan told reporters. "The idea is to keep inflation under control and ensure fiscal austerity." 

 Foreign, finance and defence ministers from South America's two largest nations met Thursday and Friday to forge closer trade, diplomatic and military ties to convert the Mercosur customs union into a European Union-style common market. 

 Among the 30 points of the so-called Buenos Aires Declaration is a resolution to eliminate intra-Mercosur nontariff barriers to trade by June 30, 2000. 

 Brazil and Argentina are members of the world's third largest trade bloc, which also includes Paraguay and Uruguay. Chile and Bolivia are associate members of the bloc that links 210 million people who produce $1 trillion in goods and services. 

 "We're seeking a common market with the free circulation of goods, services and people," said Brazilian Foreign Minister Luiz Felipe Lampreia. 

 Chile and Bolivia will be invited to talks aimed at setting common macroeconomic targets which would see the region's economies march at the same pace, said Argentine Economy Minister Jose Luis Machinea. 

 Brazil's more than 30 percent devaluation in January 1999 priced many Argentine exports out of the Brazilian market. The devaluation surprised Brazil's Mercosur partners and led to many trade disputes. 

 "We've also discussed the subject of setting up permanent (trade) tribunals," Argentine Foreign Minister Adalberto Rodriguez Giavarini said. Disputes have mostly been settled by political intervention by Brazil and Argentina's presidents. 

 The declaration proposes "scaling back investment incentives to limit distortions" in the regional market. Argentine provincial governors often complain some Brazilian states offer large tax breaks to attract manufacturers. 

 Common economic goals should help keep those dangers in check and assure the region's economies move in sync. 

 Brazil and Argentina agreed to begin sharing debt, deficit and inflation statistics in September. This would serve as an early warning mechanism for potential future economic shocks. 

 Sharing data is a "fundamental step" to setting common debt, deficit and inflation targets, Brazil's Malan said, adding convergence would be achieved in years, not decades. 

 A bilateral macroeconomic monitoring group consisting of central bank and finance ministry officials will oversee the sharing of data and future adherence to the targets. Officials from the four other nations will be invited to join the body. 

 A task force will also work to detect money laundering. 

 The future deal has been dubbed "little Maastricht" due to its similarities to the EU's 1997 macroeconomic Maastricht Treaty which led to last year's creation of the euro currency. 

 Mercosur monetary union, however, may be a long way off with Argentina keener than Brazil. 

 Argentina has a matching amount of U.S. dollars in central bank reserves for every peso in circulation to ensure its currency is valued at a par with the greenback while Brazil's real currency floats freely on foreign exchange markets. 

 Joint infrastructure, transport and energy projects to improve the flow of goods were discussed, Brazil's Malan said. 

 Argentine Industry Secretary Debora Giorgi said the partners agreed to study reducing Mercosur's common external tariff capital goods imports to improve regional productivity. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 2000.

title: Argentina to enter "most uncertain year of decade".
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Dec 29 (Reuters) - Argentina's economy is entering 1999 at a slow pace after the global financial storm swamped growth last year and blew clouds of uncertainty over emerging markets, though analysts say strong fundamentals bode well for a robust recovery once the panorama clears. 

 Private forecasts of Argentine economic growth range from zero to 3 percent, a sharp drop from the 4.8 percent expected for this year and the heady 8.6 percent growth registered the previous year. 

 Analysts say 1999 could hold some unpleasant surprises since the root causes of the external shocks that hit Argentina during 1998 have not yet disappeared. 

 Economist Miguel Angel Broda said 1999 could mark "the most uncertain year of the decade. Economic performance will depend on four variables: the speed at which capital flows recover, the rhythm of growth of domestic credit, Brazil and politics." 

 The massive withdrawal of capital from emerging markets after Russia's debt default last August was a nightmare for Argentina, whose economic system is highly dependent on inflows of capital. 

 After almost 50 years of state intervention and regulation of the economy, Argentina adopted a liberal model in the early 1990s, opening up the economy, dismantling price regulation and privatising state companies. The change has boosted economic growth but put the economy at the mercy of international capital flows. 

 The country's currency board system requires the Central Bank to match money in circulation with dollar reserves, and a debt burden of nearly 30 percent of gross domestic product raises the need for nearly constant refinancing. 

 As a result of the lack of liquidity in international markets during 1998, Argentine interest rates rocketed. That contributed to a trimming of 1998 growth estimates to 4.8 percent from the 5.3 percent forecast by the government early this year. 

 The drop in economic activity meant fiscal revenues came in under expectations, leading the government to overshot a 1998 fiscal deficit target set as part of an agreement with the International Monetary Fund. 

 Neighbouring Brazil, Latin America's largest economy, has proved an unsettling source of instability, too. Strong trade ties and geographic proximity assure that Argentina and Brazil will remain closely linked in the minds of investors. In Argentina's case, that can be dangerous when capital get jumpy. 

 Indeed, the still-cautious mood of foreign investors and uncertainties about the success of Brazil's fiscal reforms will continue to weigh on Argentina next year. 

 Politically, 1999 is a key year for Argentina. It will mark the first time in 10 years that the Argentine people will not have the option of voting for Carlos Menem, who since 1989 has billed himself as the father of economic prosperity. 

 He was reelected in 1995 largely because of his economic successes but cannot run for a third straight term. 

 This time the opposition Alliance is seen by most opinion polls as the most likely winner of the October presidential election. That has heightened caution among investors, even though Alliance leaders have repeatedly vowed they will not tamper with current economic policies. 

 "Investors will take their time after the change of government. They will wait until March or April 2000 to see what happens," private consultant Orlando Ferreres said. 

 Still, Argentina's fundamentals are strong and the economy is likely to respond quickly and positively to any hint of recovery in Brazil, analysts say. 

 "A period of much-slower growth lies ahead. Both investment and consumer spending are set to weaken," according to a report by Dresdner Kleinwort Benson. "Nonetheless, given its strong fundamentals, Argentina will be an early beneficiary of an eventual change in sentiment towards Brazil." 

 ((Buenos Aires bureau, 541 318-0654, buenosaires.newsroom@reuters.com)))).

title: Venezuela/Defy Odds/Devaluation -4: International Selling
text:
Internationally, Brady bonds and American depositary receipts trading in New York took a nosedive Thursday, and markets from Mexico to Argentina plunged. 

 Analysts fear that a messy bolivar devaluation will be the final blow for much-abused investors in emerging markets, and could put undue pressure on other Latin American currencies such as the Brazilian real and the Mexican peso. 

 "If the bolivar goes the Brazilian real will go next and that will pull Argentina and the rest of Latin America with it," said Marcelo Simini, fund manager for investment bank Merchant Bankers Asociados SA in Buenos Aires. 

 Others were slightly more optimistic on damage control. "If Venezuela devalues there will be a lot of pressure to devalue in Brazil. But Brazil plays hard ball and I think it will resist the pressure," said Roger Heal, an analyst at West Merchant Bank Ltd in Buenos Aires. 

 In Mexico, the key IPC index fell 2.9% to 3498.81 while the peso closed at a record low of a midrate of 9.3450 pesos to the dollar from 9.1970 Wednesday. 

 For Mexico, there's an additional concern: the possibility that Venezuela's deteriorating economic outlook could undermine the country's commitment to reduce crude exports in a joint effort with Mexico and Saudi Arabia aimed at boosting world oil prices. 

 In Brazil, the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange's Bovespa index fell to a nine-month low, closing 6.4% lower at 7991, while the real finished flat - thanks to apparent intervention by the central bank. 

Argentina's Merval index dropped 6.1% to 441.83. In Chile, the peso ended at 472.40 pesos to the dollar from 471.90 the previous day, while the IPSA stock index shed 3.9%. 

 Venezuelan Brady bonds were pummeled in New York. The country's Pars fell 6 1/2 to 59 bid, while the DCBs plummeted 12 5/8 points to 46 7/8 bid.

 The peso was trading at 0.9999 peso to the dollar, compared to 0.9988 peso on Friday. The peso's floor on the dollar is 1.0000 peso under a 1991 law that put the currencies at a one-to-one parity. 

 The trader at one Argentine bank said that the slightly higher liquidity levels were the result of first-line banks loaning funds to each other. 'But the market in general is extremely illiquid,' he said. 'Second- and third-line banks can't get funds from anyone,' he said. 

 He said that the market remains jittery about continued fallout from the currency crisis in Mexico, although devaluation in Argentina seems more unlikely as time goes on. 'People are concerned but at the same time they have confidence in the government,' the dealer said. 

 The additional funds in first-line banks pushed interbank interest rates lower. The overnight rate on peso-denominated loans between first-line banks, or call money, dropped to 16% from 21% Friday. Call money in dollars held stable at 8.5%.

title: Argentina stocks slip on profit-taking, peso flat

BUENOS AIRES, Argentina, Sept 22 (Reuters) - Argentine stocks slipped on Thursday amid profit-taking a day after shares notched a new high, traders said.  

The MerVal index <.MERV> of 11 leading stocks dipped 0.39 percent to close at 1,652.38. The index has accumulated a gain of 20 percent so far this year.  

Trade volume was a brisk 84.1 million pesos ($28.9 million).  

"The fall was foreseeable because the MerVal seemed weary of rising, with many highs and few corrections," said Ruben Pascuali, trader at Mayoral Bursatil brokerage.  

"There could be more profit-taking given a slowdown in some economic variables and above all because of the result of yesterday's auction, which shows disinterest in placing bonds at the yields that the government wants," he added.  

Argentina offered $800 million in Boden 2015 dollar-denominated bonds on the local market to help finance debt payments later this year, but the average yield on bids was 8.8 percent, a rate the government was unwilling to pay.  

MerVal heavyweight Grupo Financiero Galicia was among Thursday's losers, shedding 1.2 percent to end at 2.46 pesos.

text:
BUENOS AIRES, Sep 09, 2005 (ODC via Comtex) --  

(Recasts to update with central bank intervention data)  

The Argentine peso retreated Friday as continued central bank intervention, aimed at weakening the local currency, got a boost from new bank rules for trade finance.  

Meanwhile, local bonds remained well bid.  

The peso closed at ARS2.9125 against the dollar, weaker than Thursday's close at ARS2.9050.  

Fernando Izzo, a currency trader with local ABC Mercado de Cambio, said central bank dollar-buying was clearly evident through parts of the trading session. The central bank reported later that it bought $22 million in the open market Friday.  

Izzo expects that the monetary authority will have an easier time maintaining a weaker peso from now on, thanks to a new rule the central bank published Thursday night that places tighter controls on exporter financing. The move is expected to close loopholes that some investors had been using to get around Argentine capital controls.  

"Now dollars won't be able to happily roll into the stock and bond markets," Izzo said. "The expectation is that there will be less dollars now with this dollar selling restriction."  

As such, "the central bank will likely buy less" dollars on a daily basis to maintain a weaker peso that favors Argentine exports, Izzo said.  

Elsewhere, the local bond market was "basically strong," although in weaker volumes from days in which stronger gains have been seen, said Javier Salvucci, an analyst at Silver Cloud Advisors in Buenos Aires.  

He said the fact that many bonds had held to their recent gains even though they may have reached the top end of their trading limits is "a good signal" for the market.  

Nor did there seem to be any disruption in the market from news that the government is planning to issue another 2015 bond in two weeks. The Boden 2014, one of the most actively traded peso bonds and one with a similar maturity as the planned new bond, rose slightly to ARS99.50 from its close of ARS99.4 on Thursday.  

The par bond in pesos, which some Wall Street analysts have been recommending as a beneficiary of declining global interest rates was unchanged at ARS47.2. The discount bond in pesos was also unchanged at ARS123.15.

title: UPDATE:  Argentina  Bonds, Peso Up As Global Mood Improves
text:
(Updates with intervention results from Argentine Central Bank)  

BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Locally traded Argentine bonds extended their recent gains Tuesday as improved international sentiment continued to favor emerging market debt.  

The gains accompanied a pickup in demand for the Argentine peso, where the central bank intervened heavily to prevent a stronger rally. The peso closed at ARS2.9075 to the dollar, slightly stronger than its close of ARS2.91 on Monday.  

Argentine bonds have been on the rebound since last week, when a decline in U.S. Treasury yields sparked investor demand for emerging market debt and fixed income assets. And, as U.S. equities rallied on return from the Labor Day long weekend that was aided by a decline in oil prices, the upbeat investor sentiment continued.  

The buying saw the most liquid issue, the peso-denominated discount bond, rise 1.14% to ARS124 by late afternoon, while the peso-denominated par bond had gained 0.84% to ARS48.2, adding to gains it saw on Monday.  

The par bonds are currently being bought ahead of its first interest payment since Argentina's restructuring, which occurs at the end of September.  

The same will be paid on the dollar-denominated par bond, which trades in the U.S. and which also gained Tuesday. It was up 2.02% at a dollar equivalent ARS37.8 by late afternoon.  

The same interest was not seen for other dollar-denominated bonds that don't face such a payment, such as the Boden 2012, up 0.03% at a dollar equivalent ARS256.1, and the dollar-denominated discount bond, unchanged at ARS98.1.  

In the currency market, volumes showed a strong recovery from the thin holiday trading levels of Monday, said Daniel Bou Kahir of the Banco de la Pampa, who noted total turnover in the electronic market of around $180 million. Most of this appeared to be dedicated toward peso buying, he said, which likely drew the central bank in as an intervening dollar buyer.

title: Argentina  Peso Weakens On More  Intervention ; Bonds Mixed

text:
BUENOS AIRES, Aug 09, 2005 (ODC via Comtex) --   

(Updates with central bank intervention data)   

The Argentine peso weakened for the fourth straight session Tuesday on steady central bank intervention, which Economy Minister Roberto Lavagna told business leaders will remain an important part of the government's economic policy.   

Meanwhile, bonds began to recover from a recent bout of profit-taking.   

The peso closed at ARS2.8750 against the dollar, slightly weaker than ARS2.8700 on Monday and weaker than ARS2.8600 on Aug. 3, when record central bank dollar-buying helped hold the local currency at a strong point.   

Lavagna told business leaders Tuesday at a conference of the Argentine Industrial Union in Cordoba that the current competitive exchange rate "is not enough, is not a sufficient condition" for sustained growth, "but at the same time without it there is no sustainable growth and social development program. In other words, it is a necessary condition."   

Although the peso has strengthened from the ARS3.00 level that the local currency maintained for some time after the end of the one-to-one "convertibility" peg to the U.S. dollar in January 2002, most economists say they believe the peso is severely undervalued relative to competing currencies, such as the Brazilian real, which has rallied tremendously over the past year.   

Daniel Bou Kahir, a currency trader at local Banco de la Pampa, said the government will end up paying a price for maintaining a weaker peso.   

"It is going to continue to emit pesos, and going to have to pay higher yields to absorb those same pesos. Nothing is free," he said.   

Bou Kahir said the central bank was busy buying dollars throughout the day, and the monetary authority reported later that it bought $75.7 million during the session.   

In the local bond market, profit-taking continued into the morning, but quickly fell off in the afternoon as bonds began to recover lost ground, said Noelia Lucini, an analyst at Capital Markets Argentina.   

Investors were especially quick to return to the restructured discount bond in pesos, which was last quoted at ARS120.20, up from ARS119.7 on Monday. The restructured par in pesos also was rebounding to ARS45.55 from ARS44.70. Among the few notes still seeing some profit-taking was the Bocon Pro 12, down to ARS168.80 from ARS169.50.   

"It looks like the profit-taking is over for now, but the rest of the month should be much more selective than July and June," Lucini said.

text:
BUENOS AIRES, Jul 21, 2005 (ODC via Comtex) --  

The Argentine peso ended Thursday unchanged as heavy central bank intervention managed to offset an early gain on news that China has allowed its currency, the yuan, to trade against a basket of foreign currencies.  

The peso closed at ARS2.8625 to the dollar, unchanged from Wednesday's close. The currency gained to ARS2.8600 during the first hour of trading, but was held there as the central bank stepped in to buy dollars. Heavy buying during the last hour managed to push the peso back to end unchanged on the day.  

Meanwhile, locally traded bonds were mostly down on some mild profit taking triggered by the revaluation news.  

China's decision to scrap the yuan's peg to the dollar will likely make it harder for the Argentine government to target a weaker peso that favors exports, analysts say.  

On one hand, if a stronger yuan "reduces the inflow of Chinese imports, importers won't have to buy as many dollars to pay for the goods," said trader Daniel Bou Kahir with local Banco de la Pampa. On the other hand, "if we sell more exports to China, more dollars will come in from exporters. That will mean that the central bank will have to emit more pesos, with the related inflationary concerns," he added.  

Prior to the entrance of foreign investors with the conclusion of Argentina's long-awaited debt restructuring this year, the local currency market had settled into a routine in which cereal exporters repatriated overseas dollar earnings and the central bank steadily bought dollars to maintain a weaker peso that favored exports. The government aimed to hold the peso near a 3-to-1 mark against the dollar.  

But meeting that goal has become increasingly difficult to achieve as foreign investors flood in seeking peso-denominated bonds and other investments. Consequently, the central bank has had to step up its dollar buying in recent months, only to see the peso reach its strongest point in more than a year.

Argentine bonds were flat or down slightly Friday on some mild profit taking after a strong month, while heavy intervention by the central bank managed to hold the peso flat on the day at ARS2.8875.  

Paulino Seoane, a fixed income analyst with local Lopez Leon Brokers, said volume was low ahead of the U.S. independence holiday on Monday. "From noon on there was nothing going on; Monday should be even slower," he said.

In the currency market, the central bank was busy buying dollars all day to offset heavy repatriations of overseas dollar earnings by cereal exporters, said Hernan Korin, a local portfolio manager with Supervielle Asset Management.  

The central bank should curb its heavy intervention by mid-July as cereal exporters "liquidate" less overseas earners in the wake of the year's heaviest harvest period, he added.  

In addition to heavy intervention by the central bank, the government has recently launched a series of measures aimed at sustaining a weaker peso that favors Argentine exports.  

Last week, the central bank began requiring importers to purchase foreign currency at the moment in which they place an order for foreign-made consumer goods. On Wednesday the Economy Ministry published a resolution that extended a recently imposed 30% lockup on foreign inflows to Argentine residents who bring in more than $2 million a month. Previously, the 30% restriction had applied just to foreigners.  

The creative measures have led some economists to believe that the monetary authority is obsessed with keeping the exchange rate from rising and is neglecting its primary goal of price stability.

title: UPDATE 2-IMF urges Argentina to tighten policies
text:
(Updates with more details)  

WASHINGTON, June 30 (Reuters) - The International Monetary Fund on Thursday urged Argentina to tighten fiscal and monetary policies to contain inflation, and repeated calls for a strategy to deal with creditors left hanging since a 2002 debt default.  

"Macroeconomic policy stance could weaken in 2005 relative to 2004, at a time when the output gap is closing and inflationary pressures are mounting," the fund said in an annual review of the Argentine economy.  

The IMF has warned that the balance of inflation risks had moved to the upside and could undermine growth.  

The fund urged Argentina's government to act on structural reforms to boost productivity and growth; to take steps to strengthen the financial system; and normalize relations with creditors to regain full access to international capital markets.  

Most IMF board directors said it was "appropriate" for Argentina to draw from its international reserves to service the country's debts, including repayments to the IMF.  

However, several directors urged caution saying such a move should not weaken the central bank.  

Argentina is one of the IMF's biggest debtors and owes the fund $14 billion of which $2.2 billion falls due this year.  

The government and the fund are preparing for talks in July on a new fund-supported economic program, possibly backed by an IMF loan, that analysts have said could help the country roll some of that debt over.  

The current program was suspended nearly a year ago as Buenos Aires hammered out a massive debt exchange with private creditors that was rejected by 24 percent of the bondholders.  

The IMF said the debt swap was an important step toward smoothing relations with creditors, but said Argentina should develop a strategy to deal with those still left holding defaulted bonds.  

It also urged Argentine to engage in talks with bilateral creditors through the Paris Club of western creditor nations.  

The global lender said the Argentine economy had bounced back, which offered the country an opportunity to leave the crisis behind.  

The IMF said the primary budget surplus of 3.8 percent of gross domestic product in 2005 meant a sizable injection of fiscal stimulus, but urged more.  

"(IMF) directors noted that further fiscal consolidation is needed to avoid budgetary financing gap from arising in the second half of 2005, and emphasized the need to maintain tight expenditure for the rest of the year," the fund said.  

The IMF welcomed the rise in interest rates but said additional tightening was needed as well as less foreign exchange intervention.  

The central bank has increased interest rates three times by a total of 125 basis points since January, but renewed foreign exchange interventions since April have accelerated base money.

title: Argentina's  forex  policy: is it stoking inflation?
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina, June 30 (Reuters) - Argentina's two-year-long weak currency policy has helped fuel economic growth through strong exports but now risks stoking inflation, analysts say.  

The International Monetary Fund has cautioned Argentina on its foreign exchange strategy. The issue is expected to be part of upcoming loan negotiations scheduled to start next month.  

The government's target exchange rate of about 3 pesos to the dollar, aimed at sustaining double-digit annual export growth, is at odds with the regional trend where the major currencies have appreciated sharply.  

The central bank has made record dollar purchases in the market this month to restrain the strengthening of the peso, boosted by a growing foreign trade surplus.  

To finance the purchases, the bank has to print more pesos, and that creates inflationary pressure, economists from Wall Street and the International Monetary Fund say.  

In the last five weeks the government has imposed new restrictions on incoming capital to curb peso strengthening.  

Yet the currency <ARSB=> has kept on gaining, nudging 13-month highs of 2.89/2.8925 on June 16 and up nearly 3 percent so far this year. This is despite other measures adopted, including new restrictions on incoming capital.  

"They're trying to block the sunlight with a finger," said Carola Sandy, analyst with Credit Suisse First Boston. "The market knows that sooner or later the peso is going to appreciate," she added.  

Exporters say the undervalued currency has allowed thousands of small and medium-sized manufacturers to gain access to foreign markets and boost economic development whereas many would have been hurt by a free-floating currency.  

But on Wall Street and at the International Monetary Fund economists say the government's excessive printing of more pesos to finance its dollar purchases is too quickly accelerating the money supply, injecting greater demand pressures in the economy.  

They suggest Argentina loosen its grip on the currency and thus ease inflationary pressure.  

In a report obtained on Wednesday, the IMF said the current policy "could be classified, under empirical rule, as a currency peg."  

"Staff stressed that continuing with such a policy risked that real appreciation pressures would materialize in the form of domestic price inflation," it said.  

Next month, the IMF and Argentina are to resume talks in broken nearly off a year ago on a new Fund loan agreement.  

The government has battled higher-than-expected inflation this year -- consumer prices have risen 5.2 percent in the first five months of this year -- through price agreements with key industries. The government sees 2005 inflation at between 8 percent and 11 percent; economists fear double-digit growth.  

Argentina "will be forced into a more active, anti-inflationary policy by early 2006." UBS said in a note.  

A NEW PEG?  

Argentina ended a decade-old currency peg to the dollar, known as convertibility, in January 2002 in the midst of an economic collapse, triggering a 75 percent depreciation in the following months.  

But by early 2003 the central bank succeeded in controlling the peso at about 3 per dollar through heavy dollar purchases in what critics call a "neo-convertibility" of 3-to-1.  

That intervention escalated this year amid a huge influx of dollars stemming from a large trade surplus -- $3.6 billion in the January-April period -- and first-quarter net portfolio inflows of $1 billion, according to the central bank.  

The bank offset those pressures by buying a record $1.58 billion in dollars so far in June. The peso has remained stable as a result and closed at 2.8875/2.89 per dollar on Wednesday.  

To mop up the excess pesos it is printing, the central bank issues more bills, or Lebacs, at higher interest rates.  

Some local economists and business leaders argue this "sterilization," or neutralization of new peso supply, is working. Inflation fears are overblown and the policy should continue, they say.  

"The key variable for sustaining the import substitution model is a weak peso and if you ask me, the model has been successful so far," said Maximiliano Ginzburg, president of MG Forex Argentina consultancy.  

Traders said central bank intervention has eased in late June as the capital controls take effect.  

"My sensation is that the nominal exchange rate is going to stay at current levels. (Exporters) are not thinking about today's exchange rate, they're thinking about eight months, 10 months or two years from now and that's their conviction," said Marcelo Elizondo of Export.ar, an exporters' association.

title: Argentina  Peso Weaker On Ctrl Bank  Intervention , Bonds Up

BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--The Argentine peso slid one centavo Monday on continued central bank intervention, while bonds were mixed as the government quoted an upcoming coupon for new restructured discount notes.  

The peso closed at ARS2.8900 against the dollar, a full centavo weaker than Friday's ARS2.8800 close.  

Carlos Lizer, a currency analyst at local Puente Hermanos attributed the drop to "heavy intervention by the central bank. And there is also the new measure from the central bank involving importers." The measure, issued Thursday, requires importers to move forward purchases of dollars to be used to buy incoming goods. As of Friday, importers must now exchange pesos for dollars on the shipping date.  

The peso had gained on the dollar over the past two months on a combination of incoming foreign investment dollars tied to the nation's recently settled debt swap and heavy seasonal dollar selling by cereal exporters repatriating overseas earnings.  

But with the government seeking to hold the peso closer to the ARS3.00 mark to benefit Argentine exports, government and central bank planners began deploying an array of measures aimed at softening the peso.  

Last week's foreign exchange requirement for importers followed an Economy Ministry measure earlier this month that imposes a one-year lockup, in an interest-free account, of 30% of all portfolio inflows.  

In the local bond market, the government quoted its third coupon on newly restructured discount bonds in pesos and dollars to be paid out Thursday.  

Although the news technically should have pushed prices down, continued heavy buying of discount peso notes meant the bond was virtually unchanged from Friday's close, said fixed-income analyst Adolfo Zuberbuhler at local Banco Finansur.  

"The price is the same as Friday's close, so the coupon was absorbed in the price," he said. "The discount in dollars was also quoted, but didn't see as much volume. The rest of the bonds were firm, but saw little volume."  

The peso-denominated discount bond was last quoted at ARS101.10, unchanged from Friday's close, while the discount in dollars slid on the coupon quote to ARS260.00 from ARS268.00.

title: DJ UPDATE: Argentina Bonds Fall After Recent Gains;Peso Flat
text:
BUENOS AIRES, May 18, 2005 (ODC via Comtex) --  

(Updates with price for the newly issued Boden 2014 bond and figures on central bank intervention.)
  

Argentina's local debt market succumbed to light profit-taking Wednesday, giving up some of its gains from a favorable U.S. court ruling that effectively cleared the government to complete its $103 billion debt restructuring.  

Meanwhile, the Argentine peso closed local trading flat at ARS2.885 to the dollar despite continued strong dollar buying by the central bank.  

Local bonds had risen strongly after a U.S. federal appeals court overturned Friday an embargo on $7 billion in defaulted Argentine bonds. With this roadblock eliminated, the government should now be able to settle its delayed debt swap. Investors took profits on recent sessions' gains on Wednesday, with most of the actively traded notes falling back.  

The Boden 2008 was quoted in late-afternoon trading at ARS115.63, down from Tuesday's close of ARS116.4. The Bocon Pro 12 was at ARS148.35, down from ARS149.8. Bucking the trend was the benchmark dollar-denominated Boden 2012, which was at ARS251, up from ARS250.25.  

Analyst Javier Salvucci of Silver Cloud Advisors said there is little consensus over when the new securities under the debt restructuring will be delivered, and the lack of clarity is lending some caution to local fixed-income trading. Salvucci said some market players were speaking of a July settlement date, while others still see the new bonds arriving much sooner - possibly within weeks.  

"I don't know if there's worry," Salvucci said. "The fairer word would be caution because the worry was placed over whether the debt swap would be freed. This issue is now closed and the market is a little more positive."  

The Bocon Pro 13, a peso-denominated note that Salvucci said is most similar to the upcoming discount bond to be issued under the restructuring, was quoted at ARS61, down slightly from ARS61.5. Salvucci said the Bocon Pro 13 rose nearly 7% in the sessions after the Friday court ruling in the U.S. and is the best barometer of how the new debt will behave when secondary trading in the new bonds begins.  

On Wednesday, the Boden 2014 was quoted at ARS81.30. It was the first session of trading for the ARS1 billion in Boden 2014 bonds that the government auctioned earlier this month. This was the reopening of an old issue but the first time that Argentina's Treasury had voluntarily placed debt since February 2001. The Boden 2014 bonds had priced at ARS78.7 when they were issued.  

Meanwhile, analysts say the anticipated arrival of the new bonds under the restructuring hasn't yet been felt in the local currency market, which this week has been focused on exporter-related inflows and peso-buying from companies that have large income tax payments due.  

"There are huge tax collections this month," said trader Daniel Bou Kahir of Banco de la Pampa. "For that reason, (dollar) selling has accelerated and this has produced a small revaluation of the Argentine peso."  

The local currency strengthened to ARS2.885 on Monday and hasn't budged from that level, despite aggressive dollar-buying from the central bank and state-owned Banco de la Nacion. The monetary authority bought a high $99.5 million during Wednesday's session.  

Bou Kahir noted that the pesos streaming in from tax payments go into the accounts of the national tax agency held at Banco Nacion. The state-owned bank in turn uses that money to buy dollars or participate in the securities repurchase, or repo, market.  

The central bank uses the repo market, as well as weekly auctions of Lebac notes, to absorb excess liquidity and offset its foreign exchange interventions. On Tuesday, the monetary authority issued a record ARS1.898 billion in Lebac and longer-dated Nobac notes. Over the last week, the central bank has also absorbed ARS2.818 billion through repo transactions. The combined effect of these absorptions has fully compensated for the monetary authority's more active dollar-buying in the foreign exchange market. Since May 10, the central bank has bought a total $547.1 million. This exceeds its dollar purchases for the entire month of April.

title: UPDATE: Argentina Bonds Fall After Recent Gains;Peso Flat
text:
(Updates with price for the newly issued Boden 2014 bond and figures on central bank intervention.) 
   

BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Argentina's local debt market succumbed to light profit-taking Wednesday, giving up some of its gains from a favorable U.S. court ruling that effectively cleared the government to complete its $103 billion debt restructuring.  

Meanwhile, the Argentine peso closed local trading flat at ARS2.885 to the dollar despite continued strong dollar buying by the central bank.  

Local bonds had risen strongly after a U.S. federal appeals court overturned Friday an embargo on $7 billion in defaulted Argentine bonds. With this roadblock eliminated, the government should now be able to settle its delayed debt swap. Investors took profits on recent sessions' gains on Wednesday, with most of the actively traded notes falling back.  

The Boden 2008 was quoted in late-afternoon trading at ARS115.63, down from Tuesday's close of ARS116.4. The Bocon Pro 12 was at ARS148.35, down from ARS149.8. Bucking the trend was the benchmark dollar-denominated Boden 2012, which was at ARS251, up from ARS250.25.  

Analyst Javier Salvucci of Silver Cloud Advisors said there is little consensus over when the new securities under the debt restructuring will be delivered, and the lack of clarity is lending some caution to local fixed-income trading. Salvucci said some market players were speaking of a July settlement date, while others still see the new bonds arriving much sooner - possibly within weeks.  

"I don't know if there's worry," Salvucci said. "The fairer word would be caution because the worry was placed over whether the debt swap would be freed. This issue is now closed and the market is a little more positive."  

The Bocon Pro 13, a peso-denominated note that Salvucci said is most similar to the upcoming discount bond to be issued under the restructuring, was quoted at ARS61, down slightly from ARS61.5. Salvucci said the Bocon Pro 13 rose nearly 7% in the sessions after the Friday court ruling in the U.S. and is the best barometer of how the new debt will behave when secondary trading in the new bonds begins.  

On Wednesday, the Boden 2014 was quoted at ARS81.30. It was the first session of trading for the ARS1 billion in Boden 2014 bonds that the government auctioned earlier this month. This was the reopening of an old issue but the first time that Argentina's Treasury had voluntarily placed debt since February 2001. The Boden 2014 bonds had priced at ARS78.7 when they were issued.  

Meanwhile, analysts say the anticipated arrival of the new bonds under the restructuring hasn't yet been felt in the local currency market, which this week has been focused on exporter-related inflows and peso-buying from companies that have large income tax payments due.  

"There are huge tax collections this month," said trader Daniel Bou Kahir of Banco de la Pampa. "For that reason, (dollar) selling has accelerated and this has produced a small revaluation of the Argentine peso."  

The local currency strengthened to ARS2.885 on Monday and hasn't budged from that level, despite aggressive dollar-buying from the central bank and state-owned Banco de la Nacion. The monetary authority bought a high $99.5 million during Wednesday's session.  

Bou Kahir noted that the pesos streaming in from tax payments go into the accounts of the national tax agency held at Banco Nacion. The state-owned bank in turn uses that money to buy dollars or participate in the securities repurchase, or repo, market.  

The central bank uses the repo market, as well as weekly auctions of Lebac notes, to absorb excess liquidity and offset its foreign exchange interventions. On Tuesday, the monetary authority issued a record ARS1.898 billion in Lebac and longer-dated Nobac notes. Over the last week, the central bank has also absorbed ARS2.818 billion through repo transactions. The combined effect of these absorptions has fully compensated for the monetary authority's more active dollar-buying in the foreign exchange market. Since May 10, the central bank has bought a total $547.1 million. This exceeds its dollar purchases for the entire month of April.

title: Argentina  Central Bk Absorption Mutes  Forex Intervention
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Argentina's central bank issued ARS1.898 billion ($1=ARS2.885) in Lebac notes Tuesday, a record placement that is helping to offset the monetary authority's historically high foreign exchange interventions over the last week.  

According to central bank data, the monetary authority offered a total of ARS1.2 billion in Lebac and longer-dated Nobac notes to roll over ARS1.397 billion coming due this week. The central bank received ARS2.099 billion in bids and ultimately accepted ARS1.898 billion, widening its original offer and absorbing a net ARS501 million. Roberto Drimer, a fixed-income analyst at local consultancy Argentine Research, said the ARS1.898 billion placement is the largest since the Lebac program began in 2002.  

The central bank uses its weekly Lebac auctions, as well as the repurchase securities market, to soak up excess liquidity and manage the money supply. These absorptions offset the monetary authority's dollar purchases in the foreign exchange market, where intervention has turned sharply upward in recent sessions.  

Over the last week, the central bank has hit its highest daily intervention levels of the year, buying $101.5 million during Monday's session alone - its largest daily purchase in nearly two years. The central bank has bought $447.6 million in the foreign exchange market since May 10. In April, total intervention was $473 million.  

However, the central bank's record absorptions have muted the effect of the historically high quantity of pesos being put into the system. In addition to the ARS501 million soaked up Tuesday in the weekly Lebac auction, the central bank has also absorbed a significant amount - some ARS2.818 billion - through repurchase securities transactions over the last week. As a result, the monetary system has seen net absorption over the last week of about ARS2.021 billion.  

"With yesterday's successful Lebac placement, the fear that the central bank won't comply with its monetary program is substantially reduced," analysts from FyE Consult wrote in a Wednesday report, noting that interest rates for the various Lebac series rose less than expected.  

The central bank, which was aggressively expanding monetary supply at the end of 2004, has a contractionary policy for 2005. Faced with a surprise resurgence in inflation, the monetary authority's dollar-buying significantly dwindled in the first quarter of the year.  

However, the central bank is still seen aligned with the administration's desire to see a "pro-competitive" exchange rate between ARS2.90 and ARS3.00 to the dollar. Because the central bank's newly aggressive foreign exchange interventions haven't led to a net injection of pesos into the system, its dollar purchases could be seen as more of an effort to manage the exchange rate than to comply with money supply goals.  

The central bank, however, says it buys dollars to balance against the exporter-related inflows that generally dominate local foreign currency trading. Drimer of Argentine Research said exporter repatriations should drop off in the second half of the year.  

-By Wailin Wong, Dow Jones Newswires; 5411-4311-3125; wailin.wong@dowjones.com [ 18-05-05 1546GMT ]

title: Argentina stocks dip after big gain on debt ruling
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina, May 17 (Reuters) - Argentine stocks retreated slightly on Tuesday after posting hefty gains in the wake of a U.S. court decision to lift a freeze on Argentine bonds and clear the way for the country's debt swap, traders said.  

The MerVal index <.MERV> finished 0.92 percent lower at 1444.73 points, trimming the gain so far this month to 7.1 percent. Volume fell to 62.5 million pesos ($21.6 million) from a high 91 million pesos on Monday.  

"The MerVal took a reasonable breather, taking into account that the decline happened with low volume. This is not worrisome profit-taking," said Francisco Marra of Bull Markets Brokers.  

A U.S. federal appeals court in New York on Friday lifted an embargo by holdout creditors on $7 billion in Argentine bonds involved in the debt swap, originally scheduled for April 1.  

The government could offer this week the new bonds to creditors who accepted the swap terms, allowing Argentina to complete the biggest sovereign restructuring in modern times.  

Grupo Financiero Galicia , which accounts for 25 percent of the index, fell 0.83 percent to 2.38 pesos, while steelmaker Acindar dropped 1.88 percent to 6.25 pesos.  

In the foreign exchange market, the peso <ARSB=> closed 0.09 percent weaker at 2.89/2.895 per dollar thanks to central bank intervention to soak up high dollar liquidity.  

Argentina is awash in dollars thanks to its current soy harvest, the biggest export earner, and good sentiment after the U.S. court decision that opened the way for the debt swap.

title: DJ  Argentina  Peso Weaker On More  Intervention ; Bonds Mixed
text:
BUENOS AIRES, May 11, 2005 (ODC via Comtex) --  

The Argentine peso weakened slightly Wednesday on continued heavy dollar buying by the central bank, leading some fixed-income analysts to predict that more intervention will indirectly push down bond prices.  

The peso closed at ARS2.8975 to the dollar, slightly weaker than ARS2.8925 on Tuesday.  

Meanwhile, bonds were mixed amid low volume as investors continue to wait for a U.S. appeals court to rule on a distressed debt holdout case involving the embargo of $7 billion in defaulted bonds tendered in Argentina's restructuring.  

In the past week, increased central bank dollar buying has pumped more than 1 billion pesos into the financial system. The increased buying has led many analysts to believe that the monetary authority will have to raise interest rates more aggressively to reabsorb the new bills and avoid an inflationary impact.  

But rising interest rates would undermine local bond prices, said Juan Ignacio Gomez Vega, a fixed income analyst with local InvertirOnline.  

Beyond the debt swap settlement, which has been held up by the U.S. lawsuit, "the rest of the year will depend on how the central bank tries to manipulate the money supply," Gomez Vega said.  

"The central bank has three objectives at once: a weak peso, low interest rates, and low inflation. That doesn't happen anywhere in the world, yet here we are trying," he said. "We'll have to see how this soap opera develops. When interest rates start going up, bonds will go down."  

Among losers Wednesday, the dollar-denominated Boden 2012 was last quoted at ARS245.5, down from ARS246.25 in moderate volume, Gomez Vega said. Among peso-denominated gainers, the Boden 2008 was at 114.9, up from 114.7, while the Bocon Pro 12 rose to ARS143.9 from ARS143.6.  

In the foreign exchange market, "the central bank was busy buying dollars all day," said Hector Blanco, a trader with ABC Mercado de Cambio. "There was a rush of heavy dollar buying in the last 10 minutes of the session that looked like it probably came from (state-run) Banco de la Nacion."  

Banco de la Nacion, the Treasury's banker, is not required to publish its daily buying data, although traders suspect it has stepped up dollar purchases this year to help the central bank.  

The central bank was to announce its dollar buying later in the day. On Tuesday it bought $79.5 million after buying at least $85 million in the previous three sessions.  

The monetary authority's dollar buying offsets dollar selling by cereal exporters seeking to repatriate overseas earnings. Cereal exporter repatriations are expected to hit their peak this month and next as the year's main harvest wraps up.  

-By Drew Benson, Dow Jones Newswires; 5411-4311-3127; andrew.benson@dowjones.com  

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

title: Argentina  Bonds Dn On Crt Delay, Peso Flat In  Intervention
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Argentine bonds fell Tuesday as the apparent delay in a U.S. court decision fed into concerns about the fate of the country's debt restructuring.  

Meanwhile, the Argentine peso was little changed, though traders said that was because of a fourth day of heavy intervention by authorities to stem the effect of massive inflows of dollars from exporters.  

Noelia Lucini, an analyst at Capital Markets Argentina, said the market had expected the U.S. Court of Appeals to have by now decided on a pending case concerning two bondholders' bid to embargo $7 billion in defaulted bonds tendered in Argentina's restructuring. A decision had been expected a few days after a final hearing was held on Wednesday, April 27.  

The delay is moderating the earlier optimistic expectation that the court's decision would come down in Argentina's favor and clear the way for the country to complete its restructuring, Lucini said.  

"Without any new developments in this case, it is natural that there would be something of a selloff," Lucini said, noting that investors are speculating that the appeals court judges are having a hard time coming to a shared opinion.  

She said most of Argentina's pre-restructuring performing bonds fell Monday. The dollar-denominated Boden 2012 was last quoted at a dollar-equivalent ARS246.50, down from ARS248.50, and the Boden 2013 was at ARS215.50, down from ARS217.00. The peso-denominated Bogar 2018 was at ARS125.30, down from ARS125.50.  

In the foreign exchange market, the central bank - possibly helped by the government-owned commercial bank, Banco de la Nacion - again showed its capacity to offset the peso-appreciating impact of exporter dollars. The peso closed Tuesday at ARS2.8925, only slightly stronger than its close of ARS2.8950 on Monday.  

With a bumper harvest coinciding with tax season, during which exporters tend to repatriate their earnings to make their annual payments, dollar sales have been heavy over the past few days. On the other side of the flow, however, the central bank has been aggressively buying up those dollars, which has had the effect of keeping the currency stable.  

Official data aren't yet available from the central bank, but traders are expecting to see similar dollar purchase numbers as those of the prior three trading days, each of which produced central bank purchases of more than $85 million. The central bank makes such purchases with freshly minted pesos, thus using its foreign intervention to inject money into the financial system.  

"Quite clearly it is the policy of the central bank to keep the peso around ARS3.00 to the dollar," said Carlos Lizer, an analyst at local brokerage Puente Hermonos.  

Lizer said if the central bank starts to take a more sidelined role - perhaps to ensure that its new peso issuance doesn't exceed its own targets for monetary growth - Banco de la Nacion has plenty of cash with which to take over the role of weakening the peso. That's because the bank receives the deposits of the government tax agency, which are rising during tax season and which would simply enter a neutral money cycle as incoming tax revenue are used to pass pesos to exporters, who in turn use them to pay their own taxes.  

-By Michael Casey, Dow Jones Newswires; michael.j.casey@dowjones; 54-11-4313 1918 [ 10-05-05 2027GMT ]

title: Argentina Ctrl Bk Buys Yr-High $85M;Peso Flat;Bonds Mixed
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--The Argentine peso ended flat on the day Thursday, but it took a year-high $85.2 million in dollar buying by the central bank to hold the local currency steady.  

Meanwhile, locally traded Argentine bonds were mixed, with more gainers than losers on continued optimism a day after the government announced lower-than-expected inflation data for April.  

The peso closed at ARS2.8975 for the third straight day.  

"There was a lot of dollar selling by exporters and the central bank and (state-run) Banco de la Nacion steadily intervened," said trader Carlos Lizer at Puente Hermanos. Exporters and the monetary authority are the two main players in Argentina's illiquid peso market.  

The central bank's intervention Thursday marked its biggest dollar buy since it purchased $100 million on Dec. 30, 2004.  

Lizer said he expects volume to stay strong because exporter repatriations of overseas dollar earnings will remain heavy in the near term with the year's main harvest season is at its peak. Thursday exporter repatriation data was to be released later in the day.  

"The monetary authority is going to continue to buy dollars to keep the peso near ARS2.90. The exchange rate may vary some, but not much," he said. The government has said it wants a competitive exchange rate that favors Argentine exports.  

In the bond market, "it was a mostly positive session," said fixed-income analyst Diego Zavaleta at Besfamille Sociedad de Bolsa.  

Among gainers, the dollar-denominated Boden 2013 was last quoted at ARS217, up a peso on the day, while the Bocon Pro 12, a peso note, was up at ARS141.4 from ARS141. Among sliding peso notes, the Boden 2008 was at ARS115.29, down from ARS115.5, while the Bogar 2018 was down at ARS123.75 from ARS124.  

Zavaleta described volume, wich was at ARS220 million, as solid. "Yesterday's inflation data helped the market today," he said.  

The government announced Wednesday that the consumer price index rose 0.5% in April from March and was up 8.8% on the year. That followed a 1.5% increase in March, when the year-on-year inflation rate of 9.1% sparked concerns that the central bank could hit its full-year target ceiling of 8.0%.  

April's month-on-month figure came in under the 0.8% median forecast from the central bank's most recent weekly survey of economists.

title: Argentina  Peso Gains Despite  Intervention ; Bonds Mixed
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--The Argentine peso gained slightly Friday, despite continued intervention by the monetary authority, while locally traded bonds were mixed.  

The peso ended at ARS2.9000 against the dollar, slightly stronger than ARS2.9025 at the previous close. The currency has remained virtually unchanged since last Friday after it crossed the ARS2.90 mark that week on decreased intervention.  

The central bank and state-run Banco de la Nacion were both actively buying dollars on Friday, said portfolio manager Hernan Korin at Supervielle Asset Management.  

Traders say the central bank buys dollars in the foreign currency market to keep the peso from strengthening on heavy demand from exporters. Argentine President Nestor Kirchner has supported that belief by saying that he wants the peso to remain weak in order to make the country's exports more attractive on world markets.  

The central bank has significantly scaled back its dollar-buying this year, however, to meet tighter monetary policy goals. Traders say that Banco de la Nacion, the Treasury's banker, has picked up the slack.  

Although Banco de la Nacion doesn't provide daily data about its dollar-buying, the Treasury reported Thursday that it bought $1.7 billion during the first quarter of this year - a significant increase from $129 million purchased in the same period of 2004.  

"They say there is independence, but it is a coordinated effort," between the central bank and Banco de la Nacion, Korin said. "The state puts pesos into Banco de la Nacion and the bank uses them to buy dollars to keep the peso weaker than 2.9," he said.  

Meanwhile, investors in the local bond market remained largely on the sidelines Friday as they wait for a U.S. appeals judge to hear a lawsuit filed by holdout creditors who have delayed a settlement of the country's $103 billion debt swap.  

"It was too quiet today," said fixed-income analyst Alejandro Barros at Banco Piano.  

"I have the impression that there will be a positive resolution for Argentina. If that is the case, we should expect to see an upward trend for about a month," he said. "But we have to see what the judges say. There is a lot of uncertainty."  

A U.S. appeals court in New York is slated to hear the case on Wednesday.  

The Bocon Pro 12 saw the most action Friday, Barros said. The peso-denominated note was last quoted at ARS135.4, down slightly from ARS135.8 a day earlier. The Bocon Pre 8, another peso bond, was up at ARS161.5 from ARS161, while the dollar-denominated Boden 2012 was down at ARS243 from ARS244.32.

title: Argentina Peso Weakens, Ending 3-day Rally; Bonds Mixed
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Steady intervention by Argentina's central bank and state-run Banco de la Nacion managed to slightly weaken the peso Friday, putting an end to a three-day rally for the local currency.  

Meanwhile, activity in the bond market remained low a week after the Buenos Aires Stock Exchange delivered a blow to market confidence by canceling operations in its gray market for restructured debt to be issued in the nation's now-delayed swap settlement.  

The peso closed at ARS2.895, slightly weaker from ARS2.8925 on Thursday.  

"The central bank was busy (buying dollars) from the very start of today's session," said trader Hector Blanco with local ABC Mercado de Cambio. "And the Banco de la Nacion was much more active than the central bank."  

Banco de la Nacion has been busy this year buying dollars to help the central bank hold the peso steady near ARS2.90 against the dollar, traders say.  

The help comes as the central bank has set tighter monetary policy goals this year and is now grappling with the rising specter of inflation. The government reported Tuesday that the consumer price index rose in March by an unexpectedly high 1.5% on the month.  

Volume in the local exchange market was down by nearly a third, Blanco said, noting that cereal exporters - the other main players in the market besides the monetary authority - appeared to repatriate less overseas dollar earnings than on Thursday. [ 08-04-05 1958GMT ]  

In the local bond market, "it was a very boring day," according to fixed income analyst Adolfo Zuberbuhler with Banco Finansur.  

The peso-denominated Boden 2008 and Bocon Pre 8 saw the most volume, with interest coming from hedge funds looking for short-term gains, he said.  

As such, both notes were up on the day. The Boden 2008 was quoted at ARS114.4, up from ARS114.3, while the Bocon Pre 8 was at ARS160.1 from ARS159.6. Among losers, the Boden 2012 was down to ARS244 from ARS245.03.  

Meanwhile, activity in the gray market remained stagnant, Zuberbuhler said.  

Gray market trading had taken place in both the Buenos Aires Stock Exchange and the Open Electronic Market. But when a lawsuit by holdout creditors led the government to delay the debt swap settlement beyond the April 1 target date, the stock market canceled all of its transactions.  

On Friday, Argentina's two leading private bank associations asked the regulatory authority that oversees the stock exchange to reverse last week's gray market decision. The cancellation came as a blow to investors, many of whom had bought in the stock market to sell in the Open Electronic Market, or vice versa.  

"There hasn't been any legal action taken yet," said Zuberbuhler. "They just filed an official statement."  

Asked if he thought the stock exchange would restore its gray market, the trader said he doubted it.  

"There are some investors and analysts out there who think it is a possibility, but I don't," he said.

title: Argentina weighs capital controls after debt deal.
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina, March 10 (Reuters) - Argentine President Nestor Kirchner said he is weighing whether to implement capital controls given that more currency will enter the country now that its sovereign debt has been restructured.   

 "We are going to take a close look at the influx of capital ... It is fundamental that we analyze this in-depth as other countries have done," Kirchner said late on Wednesday in a televised interview on Argentine channel TN.   

 The president referred to Chile's "successful" capital controls model, in place since the early 1990s, but said he was not planning to implement the same scheme.   

 Last week, Argentina announced that creditors holding 76 percent of the country's defaulted sovereign debt had accepted its world-record $102.6 billion debt swap.   

 Kirchner also said Argentina needed to maintain a competitive rate of the peso against the dollar, despite its tendency to strengthen against the U.S. currency, partly because of the greater influx of foreign capital. The peso closed on Wednesday at 2.93/935 per dollar.   

Argentina's central bank intervenes in the foreign exchange market nearly every day to buy dollars and thereby keep the peso competitive for exports.   

 In the interview, Kirchner said foreign exchange reserves were about $21 billion. Argentina had foreign exchange reserves of $19.6 billion at the end of 2004.

title: Argentina  Peso Weakens Again On  Intervention ; Bonds Down
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--The Argentine peso slid for the second straight session Tuesday as the monetary authority continued to step up dollar buying to take advantage of a lull as investors wait for official debt swap results, traders said.  

The peso lost a centavo against the dollar on the day to close at ARS2.95.  

Meanwhile, local bonds issued after Argentina's December 2001 default slipped slightly across the board on low volume.  

Many observers expect the peso to see a strong rally on an inflow of foreign investment dollars if the $103 billion debt swap is deemed a success. Initial indications suggest that the swap was well received and the government plans to release preliminary data about its acceptance rate Thursday.  

Currency trader Daniel Bou-Khair of local Banco de la Pampa said foreign investors are "still waiting for confirmation" and didn't begin buying pesos in large amounts Tuesday.  

As such, the monetary authority "is being more aggressive this week - taking advantage of an opportunity to weaken the peso," he said.  

Traders see the government trying to hold the peso near a three-to-one ratio against the dollar to give Argentine exports a competitive advantage. Additionally, the government has calculated its budget this year using that exchange rate, they add.  

Addressing the legislature Tuesday morning, President Nestor Kirchner appeared to affirm such speculation, saying that a "realistic exchange rate is fundamental," adding that the value of the peso needs to be "pro-production, pro-national employment." [ 01-03-05 1949GMT ]  

In the bond market, post-default bonds lost some ground in a quiet session. Volume in locally traded debt has fallen off sharply since Friday's close of the debt swap offering put an end to the market for defaulted notes.  

In afternoon trading, the benchmark dollar-denominated Boden 2012 was quoted at ARS257.5 compared with ARS260.5 a day earlier, while the peso-denominated Boden 2008 was off a peso at ARS113.2.  

Meanwhile, traders are waiting for the emergence of a gray, or "when and if," market for the new bonds, which are slated for issue on April 1.  

"Right now there is only limited activity," said fixed income analyst Mariana de Mendiburu of local Silver Cloud Advisors. "Many investors, especially institutional investors, are waiting for March 18," when the official final results are expected.

title: Argentina stocks climb again, debt deadline nears.
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina, Feb 22 (Reuters) - Argentine stock prices resumed their upward climb on Tuesday as optimism flourished with the country's debt swap offer four days before its close.   

The MerVal index of the 12 leading stocks rose 1.43 percent to 1,556.03, a hair off its all-time high close of 1,557.77 last Friday.   

The index has risen 13 percent so far in February as investors bet the government will get a strong acceptance rate for its swap of $102.6 billion of defaulted debt for $41.8 billion in new bonds, at a loss to the investor of up to 70 percent.   

"The market depends on the result of the debt swap," said Horacio Corneille, head of the brokerage of the same name. "If acceptance reaches 80 percent, the MerVal may decline because it already anticipated that. But if it is over 80 percent, we could have a new rise."   

Italy's regulators said Tuesday Argentina had reported that creditors holding $41 billion of debt were on board as of last Friday, equal to 50 percent of the principal or 40 percent of the principal plus past due interest.   

Analysts said many investors, especially foreign funds, will sign up in the last days.   

Volume on the MerVal continued high at 111.9 million pesos ($38.4 million) with buying concentrated in heavyweights.   

Petrobras Energia Participaciones closed 2.2 percent higher at 4.16 pesos, while Grupo Financiero Galicia, which accounts for 25 percent of the market, advanced 1.91 percent to 2.66 pesos.   

In the foreign exchange market, the peso eased as the central bank and state-run Banco de la Nacion bought dollars to arrest the Argentine currency rise, traders said.   

The currency closed at 2.91/2.915 per dollar, 0.17 percent weaker than Monday's close. The peso gained 0.26 percent on Monday as the central bank did not intervene due to the U.S. holiday.   

Argentina seeks to keep the peso weak for export purposes. But the peso has gained 2 percent so far in 2005 as dollars from grain exports and foreign investment funds flood the market.

title: Argentina  Peso Down On Ctrl Bank  Intervention , Bonds Flat
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--The Argentine peso weakened in the final hour of trading Tuesday, driven lower by late dollar purchases made by the central bank.  

Meanwhile, Argentine local debt was mostly flat as the fixed income market readied itself for the end of Argentina's $103 billion debt restructuring this Friday.  

The peso closed at ARS2.9225 to the dollar, weaker than its close of ARS2.91 on Monday. Traders said the central bank entered the market late in the day to perform one of its customary dollar-buying interventions.  

"The central bank is trying to maintain the peso ahead of the debt exchange," said Fernando Santiago Izzo of local brokerage ABC Mercado de Cambio. He noted that state-owned Banco de la Nacion also purchased the U.S. currency on Tuesday.  

Many analysts expect the peso to come under upward pressure after the debt exchange closes on Friday. If the restructuring is successful, as most expect, there could be a large influx of funds into Argentine asset markets from foreign investors looking to profit from a post-exchange rally.  

Traders reported that volume recovered to average levels after a quiet session on Monday due to the U.S. holiday. Izzo said volume is likely to grow this week as exporters increase repatriations of overseas foreign earnings in advance of the expected peso rally. That, in turn, is expected to drive the peso higher.  

Traders say this could pose a significant challenge for the central bank, which has long been the sole dominant provider of dollar demand in the local market, and seems to strive to keep the peso at about ARS2.90 against the dollar. To keep it there, the central bank may have to significantly increase its dollar purchases, which may put it at risk of surpassing money supply limits. [ 22-02-05 1939GMT ]  

The local market for post-default bonds was quiet, much as it has been for the past few days. Three-day settlement periods mean time has effectively run out for those looking to buy into the debt exchange by acquiring defaulted debt. This has effectively frozen the defaulted debt market, which in turn has sapped volumes from the performing debt market.  

But traders say that market is simply in a waiting pattern, with only days to go before the final exchange data are released.  

"Almost all the performing debt have been rising slowly, nothing great but in positive terrain, and mostly for the peso-denominated debt," said Javier Salvucci. "A positive result is almost a foregone conclusion now, all we need is the final level of acceptance, which should be above 75% and could easily be over 80%."  

He said the implied yield on the new bonds to be issued was above the current return on a lot of the performing debt, suggesting that the latter have been driven upward by fluid liquidity.  

He said longer-dated performing debt might "plateau" as investors seek out the new, long-dated restructured bonds once their secondary market opens after the exchange's settlement is completed in early April. However, shorter-dated performing Argentine bonds could continue to be driven higher if international conditions remain favorable, especially given that a successful restructuring is considered a boon to all classes of Argentine debt.  

Reports emerged earlier Tuesday that the government had told Italian regulator Consob in its weekly report on the status of its exchange that some $41 billion in bonds had been tendered as of Friday last week, the end of the fifth week of the six-week exchange. It was not possible to determine an accurate acceptance rate from that data.

title: DJ Argentina  Central Bank  Buys Dlrs To Weaken Peso; Debt Up
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Feb 10, 2005 (ODC via COMTEX) --  

Late session intervention by Argentina's central bank Thursday managed to weaken the peso, a day after it hit its strongest point against the dollar since May. Meanwhile, local bonds continued to rally in reaction to news that the yield on 10-year U.S. Treasurys ended below 4% for the first time in three months Wednesday. The peso closed the day at ARS2.91375 against the dollar, slightly weaker than Wednesday's ARS2.90875. Heavier than usual volume suggested that investors may be returning to the otherwise illiquid currency market, dominated by cereal exporters selling dollar earnings and the central bank buying the U.S. currency, trader Fernando Santiago Izzo said. "If it weren't for the central bank and Banco de la Nacion intervention, the peso would be much stronger," said Izzo, of local brokerage ABC Mercado de Cambio. Constrained by tighter monetary policy goals for the first quarter, the central bank has significantly reduced its dollar buying this year. Observers believe the monetary authority has been trying to keep the exchange rate near ARS3 to the dollar in a bid maintain Argentine export competitiveness. Since mid-January, peso traders have also noticed increased dollar buying by state-owned Banco de la Nacion, which is less restricted than the central bank. Analysts also believe that Banco de la Nacion dollar buying is picking up in preparation for bondholder payments expected in the coming months. Both the central bank and Banco de la Nacion intervened Thursday, with the latter buying the bulk of the dollars to push back the peso, Izzo said. He speculated that the bank has set ARS2.90 as the peso's new ceiling against the dollar.

title: Argentina  Peso Loses Ground On  Intervention ; Bonds Mixed
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Another late-session dollar buy by state-run Banco de la Nacion pushed the peso weaker for the third straight day Thursday as some observers said that the central bank's somewhat unpredictable intervention this month has begun to discourage trading.  

Meanwhile, bonds were mixed amid low volume, with so-called performing debt issued after Argentina's December 2001 debt default seeing some gains.  

The peso closed at ARS2.945 against the dollar Thursday, off from ARS2.9425 a day earlier, and amid continued low volume.  

Echoing an article in local newspaper Infobae, currency trader Carlos Diaz with local brokerage firm Giovinazzo noted that investor uncertainty, based on unpredictable central bank intervention, has kept many out of the market.  

The uncertainty has helped push down trading volumes during this normally slow summer vacation month. Average daily volume this month is at $81 million, down from nearly $160 million in December.  

The central bank has stayed out entirely for almost half of the trading days this month - a notable shift after it bought $1.4 billion in December - the largest month of dollar purchases for the monetary authority last year.  

The central bank reported that it didn't intervene in Thursday's session, although Diaz said Banco de la Nacion did. The exact amount wasn't immediately available, however.  

Despite Thursday's decline, the peso has gained ground in the first weeks of 2005. This week, traders expect daily volume and gains to remain constant due to investor uncertainty about monetary policy and general waiting for news about the success or failure of the Argentina's ongoing debt swap. [ 20-01-05 2101GMT ]  

In the bond market, traders expect volume to remain low until the debt swap offering period closes on Feb. 25. As participating bondholders turn in their defaulted notes, liquidity in the local bond market is expected to drop off.  

So far, however, there is no indication of decreased liquidity, said Juan Ignacio Gomez Vega, an analyst with local InvertirOnline.  

"Many individual investors are being cautious and waiting for the deadline to approach. As it does we may see some contagion as investors identify indications" of a prevailing mood to participate or reject the offer, he said.  

In the meantime, performing notes saw some gains Thursday, while defaulted bonds were mostly flat with some losses, he said.  

Among notable movers, the benchmark dollar-denominated Boden 2012 was quoted in trading at ARS248.50, up from Wednesday's close at ARS246.6, while the Boden 2008, a peso note, was up to ARS110.25 from ARS109.88 a day earlier. Both of the Boden bonds are post-default notes.

title: Argentina Peso Continues To Gain Against Dlr; Bonds Up
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Argentina's central bank continued to crank up its intervention in the local currency market Wednesday, but again failed to restrain the strengthening peso, which marked its fourth day of gains against the sliding dollar.  

Meanwhile, the debt market saw gains as investors sought out bonds amid tight supply.  

The peso closed at 2.9350 to the dollar, up more than a centavo from ARS2.9525 on Tuesday.  

Argentina's central bank purchased $40 million on the open market Wednesday, the largest single-day buy since mid-June. The purchase marks a sizable increase from daily purchases of about $30 million in recent weeks.  

Under central bank chief Martin Redrado, the monetary authority has used large dollar purchases to maintain the peso in a tight range of about ARS2.96 to ARS2.98 against the greenback.  

As a result, the peso now appears cheap in comparison to the euro, and more importantly, the real from neighboring Brazil, as the dollar continues to weaken against these currencies.  

Daniel Bou-Kahir, head of the currency desk at local Banco de la Pampa, said that Wednesday's market was filled with peso-buyers, helping fuel the peso's drive upward against the dollar.  

He also noted that Argentine cereal "exporters are getting ahead on their liquidations," motivated by concerns about the dollar's continued slide.  

"The peso strengthening is more speculative than based on concrete news," Bou-Kahir said when asked about a Tuesday announcement by Argentine officials that Chinese companies are interested in investing nearly $20 billion in local projects.  

Instead, "exporters are worried about a weakening dollar and covering their positions," Bou-Kahir added.  

Along with the central bank, Argentina's grain exporters are the largest actors in the illiquid peso market as they repatriate dollar-denominated earnings.  

On Tuesday, grain exporters liquidated $63.9 million, a considerable increase from their dollar sales over the past week that hovered around $30 million. Wednesday figures were due in later in the day. [ 17-11-04 1954GMT ]  

In the debt market, bonds generally gained as investors sought out local notes.  

"The market is very well bid today," said one local bond trader, who described volume as slightly higher than average. "It's hard to find paper. Especially for investors looking to buy in size," he added.  

The continued demand for Argentine bonds comes as investors remain generally optimistic about the nation's debt swap offer, slated to open on Nov. 29 and close on Jan. 17.  

And the good vibe got a boost late Tuesday - after the local market close - when New York District Court Judge Thomas Griesa turned down a bondholder bid for an injunction on the debt restructure offering.  

In afternoon trading, the peso-denominated benchmark Boden 2008 was up to 108.64 from 107.5, while the Pre-8, a peso note, was rising from 145.75 to 146.80.  

-By Suzelle Tempero and Drew Benson, Dow Jones Newswires; 5411-4311-3127; andrew.benson@dowjones.com [ 17-11-04 2036GMT ]
