title: Argentina  Peso Stronger Despite  Intervention ; Debt Mixed
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--The Argentine peso strengthened against the dollar for the third straight day Tuesday as the central bank failed to offset exporter repatriations, despite engaging in some of its heaviest dollar buying in recent months.  

Meanwhile, Argentine bonds were mixed as investors awaited news out of a New York courtroom, where a judge Tuesday opened two lawsuits filed by disgruntled bondholders seeking an injunction against Argentina's long-awaited debt swap.  

The peso strengthened against the dollar to ARS2.9525 from ARS2.9550, even as the central bank bought $37 million - its largest purchase since Martin Redrado took over the monetary authority in September.  

"There's been a recuperation of the peso and the market's volume has been due to a lot of action on part of the cereal exporters," said Daniel Bou-Kahir, head of the currency desk at local Banco de la Pampa.  

On Monday, cereal exporters, who are the biggest dollar sellers in the peso market, liquidated $27.3 million in foreign earnings. Over the past week, they have repatriated between $27 million and $37 million.  

The central bank, meanwhile, has been purchasing around $30 million a day in the open market in recent weeks.  

"The bank was there, but obviously not enough because the peso has strengthened," Bou-Kahir said.  

Expectations regarding possible announcements of Chinese investment during a visit by Chinese Premier Hu Jintao, who arrived in Buenos Aires on Tuesday, have had little effect on the peso market, Bou-Kahir said.  

Early rumors in the local media had predicted an incredible $20 billion investment package, but a visiting Chinese official in town last week rejected that as unreasonable.  

"Talk is different from action, and nobody is going to come in here and just fix everything," Bou-Kahir added.  

Hu and Argentine President Nestor Kirchner were expected to hold a news conference Tuesday evening to announce more modest investment accords. [ 16-11-04 2020GMT ]  

In the debt market, bonds saw a mix of minor gains and losses as investors awaited news about two lawsuits seeking to derail the restructuring of Argentina's $103 billion in defaulted sovereign debt.  

"Investors are waiting to see what happens in New York," said trader Paula Premrou of local brokerage Lopez Leon.  

Judge Thomas Griesa of the U.S. District Court in Manhattan was scheduled to open two lawsuits by disgruntled creditors on Tuesday seeking an injunction on the debt swap, which the Argentine government plans to open on Nov. 29 and close on Jan. 17.  

But Premrou said traders hadn't heard any news from New York as the bond market wrapped up for the day.  

In late-session trading, the dollar-denominated benchmark Boden 2012 was down 0.4 to 237.25, while the Pre-8, a peso note, was leading gainers, up 0.8 to 145.75.

title: Argentina  peso stable on  intervention , stocks fall.
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina, April 16 (Reuters) - Argentina's peso closed stable on Friday as the Central Bank continued to intervene to halt the appreciation of a currency that has neared eight-month highs amid strong exports.   

Shares meanwhile closed lower, dragged down in low volume with few buyers in the market after future options expired the previous session.

title: Argentina's Peso Strengthens As Exporters Return To Mkt
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--The Argentine peso strengthened modestly Tuesday, as exporters started to return to the market after having been sidelined during a more volatile trading period at the end of last month.  

The peso closed at ARS2.955 to the dollar in the interbank market, one centavo stronger than its ARS2.965 close on Friday. Monday was a holiday for financial markets in Argentina.  

Traders said it appeared the central bank intervened with its routine dollar-buying, but this was overwhelmed by dollar supply from the exporters. The monetary authority has repeatedly bought $30 million a day in the market over the past two months to help supplement otherwise thin natural demand for the dollar.  

"Although the central bank was active, what we are seeing now is what we expected to see toward the middle of the month, and that is the growth in inflows from exporters," said one trader with an international bank. He said the biggest Argentine exporters, the grain producers, remain somewhat sidelined and that when they start transferring their foreign earnings into local currency, the upward pressure on the peso will be stronger.  

However, the market can be expected to abide by the new trading range it appeared to establish after a big selloff in the peso two weeks ago, he said. Whereas formerly the peso was in a range of ARS2.80 to ARS2.90 to the dollar, it now looks to be trading between ARS2.90 and ARS3.00.  

"I would expect to see some (dollar) long positions put on" as the peso approaches ARS2.90 to the dollar, the trader said.  

Official data later showed that the central bank markedly increased its daily intervention level Tuesday. The monetary authority bought $40 million for the day. This was a big departure from the standard $30 million level of intervention for most of the past two months, and one of the biggest daily dollar purchase figures for the year.  

Separately, the central bank fixed its reference rate at ARS2.9547 to the dollar.

title: Argentina's Prat Gay Stresses Peso In Free Float Regime
text:
PILAR, Argentina (Dow Jones)--In the wake of sharp slide in the peso against the dollar last week that raised speculation the central bank is targeting a lower level for the local currency, central bank president Alfonso Prat Gay insisted Tuesday the peso will stay in a free-floating arrangement.  

The central bank's repeated interventions to buy dollars against the peso in the foreign exchange market were entirely driven by monetary policy goals - efforts to boost the monetary base as a stimulative measure - rather than a exchange rate target, Prat Gay said in a speech to a major business conference.  

"It must remain absolutely clear that we are in a regime of floating currency," Prat Gay said. He was speaking at the annual conference of Argentina's leading business organization, the Argentine Industrial Union, in Pilar, just outside Buenos Aires.  

The central bank president said, however, that the free float - adopted in January 2001 after Argentina ended the peso's one-to-one peg to the dollar - didn't preclude interventions for pursuing monetary goals. It doesn't mean, Argentina can't have an "active monetary policy," he said.  

Moreover, he sought to play down the continued attention on the peso's value to the dollar, rather than other currencies.  

The peso's slide to an eight-month low of ARS2.958 to the dollar in the interbank market on Friday had raised talk of a ARS3.00 target, but Prat Gay emphasized that the protection of Argentina's competitiveness should be considered against the multitude of currencies against which the local currency floats.  

"A multilateral competitive rate" is important, he said, adding that "we shouldn't tie ourselves to the dollar."  

Whereas the peso lost 3.3% against the dollar last week, boosting the competitiveness of Argentine products in the U.S., it has gained even more in competitiveness against the euro, against which the dollar itself has been hitting record lows.  

The peso's sharp move last week came as the central bank continued its policy of buying dollars in the open market. Although traders had expected it to hold back from such purchases once the peso dropped below ARS2.90 to the dollar, the monetary authority continued to accept dollar offers in a way that led many to conclude it was now deliberately targeting a lower rate.  

However, Prat Gay was insistent Tuesday that the central bank's goal is one of "stability" in the exchange rate and avoiding "volatility" rather than exchange rate targeting.  

This is consistent with the central bank's official position for much of this year. In the absence of any natural demand for dollars while many Argentine borrowers are still not servicing defaulted foreign currency debt, the central bank has insisted on filling that gap to prevent disorderly movements as export-driven peso demand flows in unabated.  

"This obsession with confusing exchange rate policy with monetary policy or the rate of exchange with the price of the dollar doesn't have to exist," Prat Gay said Tuesday.  

"We all know that just as we tied ourselves to the dollar in the 1990s while the dollar was rising against the rest of the world's currency, the only thing we achieved was to (import) deflation," he said. "To tie ourselves to the dollar at this moment when it is falling would be to import inflation."  

Prat Gay named no individuals in his speech, but his position stands in contrast to views widely believed to be held by certain officials within the government of President Nestor Kirchner. These people say Argentina should strive to keep the peso below ARS3.00 to the dollar, a level consistently cited by exporters and industrialists.  

Earlier this year, in comments that got him in hot water with the presidential office, Prat Gay called Kirchner's stated interest in attaining that rate "an enormous mistake."  

There may also be a difference of opinion arising with Economy Minister Roberto Lavagna. Apparently differing from Prat Gay's interpretation of currency interventions as a monetary policy tool rather than an exchange rate-targeting tool, Lavagna was quoted by local media earlier Tuesday as saying that "managing the exchange rate is central for avoiding internal and external deficits."  

Lavagna may get a chance to respond to Prat Gay when he speaks midday Wednesday at the same conference.  

Meanwhile, Prat Gay also addressed another issue that seems to have aroused differences of opinion with the Economy Minister, that of the central bank's plan to introduce an inflation-targeting system. Last week, Lavagna seemed lukewarm to this idea - which Prat Gay maintains will be a central objective next year - when he warned against "falling in love with these policy tools."  

In his speech Tuesday, Prat-Gay appeared to play down the notion that the inflation-targeting regime would be a rigid system and that there would be flexibility in the way it is managed.  

He said it is important to "move rapidly to an inflation-targeting regime," but added there "doesn't have to be an obsession with the price index, nor is it a fashion."  

"It is something that any central bank has to do when it must defend the value of the currency," Prat Gay said, in reference to the oft-cited third article of the Central Bank's charter that makes defending the peso's purchasing power its central objective.  

Separately, Prat Gay also called on the government to quickly move to scrap the "distortive" tax it imposes on financial transactions.  

"We hope it will be one of the first on the list at the moment of thinking about reducing taxes," he said, noting the huge costs that the so-called checking tax imposes on companies wanting to use the financial system.  

Meanwhile, he also claimed that the long-awaited revival of credit is starting within the embattled financial sector, noting that private sector loans have grown 9% in four months. "I believe we have reason to be optimistic about the financial system recovering" from last year's financial crisis, Prat Gay said.  

He also emphasized measures taken to create protections against volatility now that the peso has been devalued and that the economy has been "pesified." Among these, he said, were recent measures to promote a peso futures market and a plan to create more cooperation with six different regional central banks. He did not elaborate on this latter idea.  

-By Michael Casey and Laurence Norman, Dow Jones Newswires; michael.j.casey@dowjones.com; 54-11-4313 1918

title: Argentina Peso Dips Again As  Central Bank  Stays In Market
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Argentina's peso closed at its weakest level in over three weeks Thursday, as higher central bank activity once again outweighed the supply of dollars from exporters.  

The peso was one centavo weaker at ARS2.865 per dollar at 1750 GMT, shortly before the market closed. Tuesday the local currency saw its sharpest fall in some weeks, dipping two centavos against the U.S. currency. Wednesday the peso was flat.  

Traders say the key factor in this week's falls has been the central bank, which has stepped up its interventions from some $5 million a day in early October to $35 million per session this week. With the supply of export dollars not lifting in tandem with the stronger intervention, the peso has fallen back.  

That pattern continued Thursday, said one trader at a foreign bank in Buenos Aires.  

"The central bank probably weighed in with around $35 million again. It seems to be keeping up the same levels that we have seen in the past few weeks," he said.  

The central bank's heavy interventions nonetheless raise questions about the direction of the peso in the weeks ahead. Under last month's accord with the International Monetary Fund, the amount of pesos the central bank can issue to buy dollars is limited, with analysts saying Argentina's top bank has the space to buy around $15 million a day.  

That means the bank must reduce its interventions from current levels if it is to comply with the accord, even if it means letting the peso strengthen.  

"These kind of interventions will have to be sporadic and not permanent if Argentina is to keep within the limits laid down," says Rafael Ber, senior analyst at local financial consultancy Argentine Research.  

And with exports likely to increase from November as the agricultural season gets into full swing, the central bank may find it even tougher to stop the peso appreciating.  

The central bank says it is not interested in any particular value for the peso against the dollar, but President Nestor Kirchner and other top officials have said they want the peso around the ARS2.90-ARS3.00. A weak peso helps exporters and companies producing goods that were imported before last year's 70% fall in the peso. Export duties are also a key source of tax income.  

-By Laurence Norman, Dow Jones Newswires; 5411-4311-3127; laurence.norman@dowjones.com  

As traders had predicted, the central bank later announced it had purchased net $35 million.

title: Argentine Peso Strengthens To ARS2.795/Dollar
text:
BUENOS AIRES -(Dow Jones)- Argentina's peso closed one centavo higher Thursday despite continued peso selling by the central bank. 

 At 1750 GMT, shortly before the local market closed, the peso was quoted at ARS2.795 to the dollar, up one centavo from Wednesday's close of ARS2.805 per dollar. 

 Traders said that market activity varied little from preceding sessions. 

 "We keep seeing the same pattern of exporters buying pesos and the Central Bank selling them," said one trader with a Buenos Aires-based brokerage house. 

 In recent months, the central bank has adopted an interventionist policy to soak up dollars being sold-off by exporters, who have to repatriate their foreign currency in Argentina. 

 Analysts say the monetary body's intervention should ensure that there are no brusque movements in the peso in future sessions. 

 "This dollar-buying measure used as part of the central bank's interventions is going to keep the peso trading at these levels," said Vladimir Werning, chief economist for J.P. Morgan Chase in Buenos Aires. 

 And the central bank hasn't suggested such intervention would be stopped anytime soon. 

 Addressing the Argentine Senate on Thursday, Central Bank President Alfonso Prat Gay said the monetary authority has set broad money growth targets for the year and expects to emit more pesos - ranging from ARS1.7 billion to ARS6.4 billion - in the second half of the year. Most of the money issued is used by the bank to purchase dollars. 

 Traders said they noted a pickup in activity ahead of Friday's Independence Day holiday in the U.S. 

 Volume running through the electronic trading system was $112 million, up about $12 million from Wednesday. 

 With the peso seeming to have found more stability in the last couple of weeks - after rising 20% in the first half of the year - there's less pressure on the central bank to intervene as heavily as it did last month, analysts say. While the monetary authority bought up $1 billion during June, this month has begun with the bank buying only some $36 million in dollars in the past two days. 

 Nonetheless, the peso's appreciation this year has provoked complaints from local producers who say it's hurting their competitiveness in international markets. And some analysts agree that the stronger peso is hurting an export-driven economic recovery from years of recession. 

 Yet, on Thursday, Prat Gay dismissed those claims. In his presentation to the senate, he reiterated that the peso's performance against the currencies of Argentina's major trading partners - Europe and Brazil - hasn't matched its appreciation against the dollar. Indeed, over the past year the peso has been nearly flat against the euro and has weakened in recent months against Brazil's real, he said. 

 "You shouldn't look at how much the dollar is worth in pesos, but how much the peso is worth in other currencies," Prat Gay said. "One can't go about blaming the exchange rate," for the downturn. 

 -By Craig Fagan, Dow Jones Newswires; 5411-4311-3125; argentina@dowjones.com

title: Argentina Peso Closes Flat Amid Modest Dollar Inflow
text:
BUENOS AIRES -(Dow Jones)- Argentina's peso closed flat Thursday, with central bank intervention pushing the peso lower in late trading after the local currency had edged higher at the session's start. 

 At 1750 GMT, shortly before the local market closed, the peso was trading at ARS2.795 to the dollar, unchanged from Wednesday's close. 

 Traders said a modest supply of dollars from exporters Thursday meant the central bank didn't have to issue too many pesos to hold back the dollar. 

 "The only people that were selling dollars are those that had no other choice like exporters," said Adrian Rodriguez, a trader with a local exchange house in Buenos Aires. 

 Exporters have been putting upward pressure on the peso for months as they liquidate hard currency earnings back into pesos. 

 The central bank spent $42.8 million Thursday to stem the peso's rise. 

 The Argentine monetary authority has been the principal buyer of dollars through most of this year, helping boost its reserves but placing more pesos into circulation. 

 Analysts have been eyeing these central bank interventions because of concerns they could unduly accelerate the money supply and inflation. 

 On the heels of Argentina's financial crisis, inflation surged to 41% in 2002, and there were widespread forecasts that the country would relive its hyper-inflationary episodes from the late 1980s. However, inflation was brought under control from last September and the consumer price index has risen only some 2.5% in the past six months. 

 This improving panorama has given the central bank more flexibility to act to stem the peso's rise. 

 -By Craig Fagan, Dow Jones Newswires; 5411-4311-3125; argentina@dowjones.com

title: Argentina Peso Continues Recovery, As Exporters Weigh In
text:

title: Argentina  Peso Weakens On  Central Bank Intervention
text:
BUENOS AIRES -(Dow Jones)- Argentina's peso weakened two centavos Monday, as the central bank continued to intervene heavily in the local market, 

 At the close of the local market, the peso was trading at ARS2.775, two centavos weaker than the 12-month high it reached at the local market's close on Friday. 

 "Today the tendency of the last few weeks continued," said Carlos Lizer, a trader with local stockbrokers Puente Hermanos. "The central bank is still intervening and the exporters are liquidating their dollars. There's no change in the market." 

 The central bank bought $126 million Friday and $1.2 billion in the month to date. While figures for Monday weren't immediately available, Lizer said he believes the monetary authority bought a similar amount as last Friday in the latest session. 

 Exporters and the central bank have been the dominant participants in the local currency market lately. Exporters have kept a steady stream of dollars coming into the country as they repatriate their foreign earnings, while a lack of payments on dollar-denominated debts means the central bank is the only one looking to buy the U.S. currency. 

 But a strong peso threatens exporters and import-substitution industries, two sectors that have benefitted from the local currency's sharp depreciation against the dollar last year. 

 The International Monetary Fund is expected to allow the central bank to issue more pesos and expand the monetary base beyond previous targets. Analysts estimate the Washington-based agency will allow the issuance of between ARS3.0 billion and ARS4.0 billion worth of new pesos. The government and IMF officials, who have been meeting with Argentine authorities since early last week, may announce new official targets for monetary growth later Monday.

title: Lavagna: Argentina Not In  Forex  Talks With Brazil -Estado
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Argentine Economy Minister Roberto Lavagna Thursday said he isn't talking with Brazilian officials about adopting policies to control foreign exchange rates, local news agency Agencia Estado reported. 

 Lavagna apparently discarded an intervention plan presented Monday by Argentina's Vice Foreign Minister Martin Redrado that would aim to keep Brazil's real and Argentina's peso at around three per dollar to facilitate trade flows. 

 Redrado's plan perplexed Brazilian officials, who have strongly stated they won't heed exporters' calls to forcibly weaken a real that has strengthened 20% since Jan. 1. 

 Lavagna also backed the idea of so-called four-plus-one trade talks between the U.S. and members of trade bloc Mercosur to complement negotiations for the hemisphere-wide Free Trade Agreement of the Americas. Mercosur includes Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay. 

 Lavagna held meetings Thursday with Finance Minister Antonio Palocci and Central Bank Economic Policy Director Ilan Goldfajn and President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. 

 Lavagna is visiting Brasilia with Nestor Kirchner, who is expected to defeat former President Carlos Menem in May 18 presidential elections in Argentina.

title: Argentina  Peso Stronger Despite Near Record  Intervention
text:
BUENOS AIRES -(Dow Jones)- Argentina's peso strengthened to a new 12-month high against the dollar Thursday, brushing off Tuesday's further easing of currency controls and some of the heaviest intervention by the central bank on record. 

 Traders said the central bank may have equaled the record single day purchase of $124 million set in January, as it tried to stem the peso's appreciation. 

 The peso closed the day at ARS2.765 per dollar, three centavos stronger than Wednesday's close of ARS2.795. 

 Analysts said the peso is rising on investment from abroad and the closing out of long-dollar holdings. 

 It is not yet known how much the central bank purchased on Thursday. What is known is that without today's intervention and the heavy central bank activity of prior days, the peso would be considerably stronger. Many say that without intervention, it would be in the ARS2.50 to ARS2.60 range against the dollar. 

 Since the start of the year, after it had become clear that last year's flood of money out of the country had abated, the peso has strengthened around 20% against the dollar. But even then, with an economic recovery helping stabilize local confidence, analysts tended to attribute the peso's climb more to a lack of demand for the dollar - because of constraints on companies' ability to pay their foreign debts - than from a strong demand for pesos. 

 All that was happening, they would say, was that the relentless repatriation of exporters' dollars - especially during the current harvest season - was providing a one-way flow that was not matched on the other side. Without capital outflows, the central bank was the only participant buying dollars. 

 On Thursday, however, traders said the environment seemed to have changed, with several new factors encouraging Argentines and foreign investors to move into pesos. 

 One is that the dollar has been falling across the world in recent weeks. At the same time, the peso's rise - even during the uncertainty of a presidential campaign and after the easing of currency controls - has convinced Argentines who held onto the U.S. currency during the crisis of recent years, to trade them in for pesos. Traders also said that foreign investment in Argentina's rebounding financial assets is putting the dollar under pressure. 

 "We're seeing an unwinding in long dollar positions going on here and dollar inflows that are related to investment in local assets," said one trader at a foreign bank in Buenos Aires. "There is something new going on here." 

 The peso's rise Thursday follows the central bank's decision to further lift currency controls that were introduced in early 2002 to stem the sharp depreciation of the peso. The local currency lost 70% of its value against the dollar last year. 

 The central bank measures gave exporters more time to repatriate their dollar earnings, made it easier to import goods and gave companies and individuals more freedom to buy dollars and pay dollar debts. 

 However, the measures did not manage to break the peso's rise, which some argue will harm the economic recovery by hurting the export sector and other industrial sectors. 

 An analyst at one Argentine bank said with neither the state nor companies paying foreign debt since Argentina's 2001 debt default, it was hard to see what authorities could do to stem the peso. 

 "For now, they can try and liberate more (controls) and allow companies to start paying their capital and interests payments. The truth is, no-one is paying anything here," he said. 

 The analyst said, however, that Argentine firms and individuals would only start considering paying their external debts once this month's second round of presidential elections was out the way and a new government was installed. That would mean the peso strengthening further in the coming weeks. 

 -By Laurence Norman, Dow Jones Newswires; laurence.norman@dowjones.com; 54-11-4311 3127 

 Official figures released after the market close revealed that the central bank bought $144.1 million Thursday, surpassing the January record for dollar purchases by the monetary authority.

title: Brazil Lacks Interest In Argentine  FX Intervention  Idea
text:
BRASILIA -(Dow Jones)- Argentina wants to adopt a joint currency targeting system with its northern neighbor at a time when Brazilian officials indicate that intervention is a dirty word. 

 That means a plan Argentine Vice Foreign Minister Martin Redrado presented Monday in Brasilia that would aim to keep Brazil's real and Argentina's peso around three per dollar may be rejected unless it's revised. 

 Though the blueprint would mark the strongest effort yet to integrate the currencies since the Common Market of the South, or Mercosur, trade bloc adopted it as a medium-term goal in the late 1990s, it likely won't be put into practice for a long time. Mercosur includes Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay. 

 "There's no timeframe for implementation," Redrado said in Brasilia. He suggested attaining near parity between the peso and real by adopting trading bands or increasing the use of reciprocal credits. "This would be a transitional system to a common currency." 

 Brazilian Central Bank Governor Henrique Meirelles and Finance Minister Antonio Palocci, the top economic policy-makers in President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's center-left administration, have said repeatedly in the last month that they won't intervene in the foreign exchange market or adopt currency targets. 

 Monday, Meirelles and Palocci tried to distance themselves from Redrado's approach. 

 Meirelles said he was unaware of any debate on currency bands. Palocci met Redrado and said they didn't discuss foreign exchange bands but agreed to study "macroeconomic policy convergence" between the two countries. 

 There are a host of stumbling blocks to Redrado's plans. Mercosur leaders have never said how the central bank for an integrated currency would be composed, and heavyweight Brazil would prefer to create currency integration without using interventions. 

 Redrado's scheme also assumes a win of Argentina's presidential election May 18 by government-backed candidate Nestor Kirchner over former President Carlos Menem, who opposes Mercosur currency integration and strongly favors closer ties with the U.S. 

 Redrado said the creation of a band for the peso and real would give more certainty to exporters, importers and investors. On the trade front, Redrado indicated Brazil will offer increased export financing to Argentina. 

 Though currency weakness rattled their economies for much of 2002, worries of excessive currency strength have recently jumped to the forefront of economic policy debates in Argentina and Brazil. 

 Since January, the peso and real have each gained about 20% against the dollar - prompting fears that surging exports and increased import substitution may slow to the  detriment of the countries' best performing sectors. 

 The peso hit its highest levels in more than a year last week and Monday closed at ARS2.80 a dollar, while the real finished at BRL3.04 and is hovering around its strongest levels since August. 

 Top aides of Lula, who is still trying to cultivate a pro-market image after decades of advocating policies that frighten investors, say intervening in the currency markets is a tricky game that's not worthwhile. 

 But Lula's planning and trade ministers have advocated interventions to ensure exports keep growing and the current account gap continues narrowing. 

 Lula himself last week suggested too much real strength was bad. But that surprised investors and he quickly backtracked. 

 "The real will continue to fluctuate and the government won't interfere with it," he said Friday. 

 -Terry Wade and Gerald Jeffris, Dow Jones Newswires; 5511.9117.0969; brazil@dowjones.com 

 (Michael Casey in Buenos Aires contributed to this report)

title: Argentina  Peso Flat As Ctrl Bank Tones Down  Intervention
text:
BUENOS AIRES -(Dow Jones)- The Argentine peso ended local trading Friday flat on the day, with the central bank's strong intervention of Thursday seemingly succeeding in signaling a ceiling for the local currency, which has strengthened 15% this year. 

 At the close of trading on the local Buenos Aires market, the peso was quoted at ARS2.905 to the dollar, unchanged from Thursday's close. 

 The central bank was far less active in the market Friday, buying just $4 million from banks in the open market and not buying any dollars from exporters. On Thursday, by contrast, in one of its biggest interventions in recent months, the central bank bought a total of $22 million from both exporters and banks. 

 Traders said the message was clear that the government does not want to see the currency strengthen much further. A stronger peso would undermine the interests of exporters, while some of the sharp gains have been at such a pace that the central bank is believed to be concerned about monetary stability. 

 With Thursday's intervention, "the central bank sent a message that they are concerned with the large gains in the currency," said one trader with an international bank, who said he believes the monetary authorities will be content to let the peso sit at these levels for a while. 

 Indeed, analysts believe that uncertainty ahead of April 27 elections may start to do the government's job for it as investors begin to take more cautious positions. 

 For the time being, the central bank is trying to get the market to function more independently. There's been a distinct lack of natural demand for dollars since the peso dropped 70% last year after a financial crisis in which the government defaulted on $141 billion in sovereign debt and abandoned the peso's one-to-one peg to the dollar; there's no offshore debt service payments being made by either the government or by many companies and there's very little importer demand for foreign currency. But because there's a big inflow of dollars for exporters, the central bank has had to fill the gap. 

 However, traders said the flows were more two-way in Friday's market, with more genuine demand for dollars slowly surfacing. 

 -By Michael Casey, Dow Jones Newswires; 54-11-4313 1918; michael.j.casey@dowjones.com

title: Argentina Seeks New Accord To Keep Fuel Prices Steady
text:
BUENOS AIRES -(Dow Jones)- Argentina's government confirmed Tuesday it is holding talks with oil companies, aimed at extending accords that have kept the domestic fuel price steady in recent months, despite the huge volatility of the international oil price. 

 "We have spoken with producers and refineries," Cabinet Chief Alfredo Atanasof said at a daily press briefing. "You will note that during these months, the (international) price per barrel has increased considerably at some moments, yet the fuel price on the internal market has not gone up, thanks to the accords we've reached. Of course, we are working to extend these accords." 

 In late December, the government pushed an accord between oil refineries and producers, which sought to stabilize the domestic price per barrel at $28.50 for three months. Because producers fixed the price of crude, refineries were able to keep the fuel price steady. 

 The accord had several exit clauses, one of which was triggered if the international oil price went over $35 per barrel for 10 consecutive days. When that happened in late February, refineries and producers - under pressure from the government - agreed to extend the accord for another month, avoiding an increase in the fuel price, even while the international oil price soared to near $40 per barrel. 

 The international oil price per barrel closed Monday below $29 per barrel. 

 Atanasof gave no details as to whether the government was hoping refineries and producers would extend the exact same agreement as was signed last month, or whether an accord would have new elements. 

 President Eduardo Duhalde's government has insisted that oil companies shouldn't make extraordinary profits from the current international tensions surrounding Iraq. Officials have warned that rising fuel prices would spark inflation and seriously damage the many fuel dependent sectors of the economy. In addition, the government says, volatility in the domestic price makes it very hard for many businesses to make plans for the months ahead. 

 Meanwhile, for the second time in a week, Atanasof said he was unconcerned by the recent strengthening of the peso, saying it wouldn't bite into tax receipts and that there was no need for intervention to stem the currency's rise. 

 "No, we understand that it doesn't significantly affect the State's level of income." Atanasof said when asked about the effects of the peso's rise. "In any case, the value of the dollar is a value that is regulated by the market. As long as more dollars come in ... that price naturally lowers," he added. 

 Boosted by the inflow of dollars from exporters and weak demand for greenbacks, the peso has reached its strongest level in 11 months in recent days, closing at ARS3.00 per dollar on Monday. At 1650 GMT on Tuesday, the peso was trading at ARS2.94 per dollar. 

 Atanasof's comments mark a clear break with what senior officials have said in recent months. As the peso edged toward the ARS3.00 per dollar mark from the start of the year, the government warned that a stronger peso could hit Argentina's export-led economic recovery and weaken tax receipts. 

 Export duties account for some 15% of Argentina's overall tax income. 

 The Central Bank intervened strongly in the currency market at the turn of the year to stem the peso's rise. In recent weeks, however, it has done little to prevent the strengthening of the peso, other than gradually scale back year-old currency controls. 

 -By Laurence Norman, Dow Jones Newswires; 5411-4311-3127; laurence.norman@dowjones.com

title: Argentina Ctrl Bk Says It's Beating IMF Targets - Reports
text:
BUENOS AIRES -(Dow Jones)- The Argentine central bank president said the country isn't just matching but beating monetary targets laid down by the International Monetary Fund, according to media reports Thursday. 

 In a briefing to local reporters late Wednesday, Alfonso Prat Gay said he was slashing the organization's targets for monetary absorption in the first half of the year, as high tax collections meant the central bank was printing far fewer pesos than they had predicted would be necessary. 

 Last month, days after Argentina signed a short-term debt rollover accord with the IMF, Prat Gay announced that because of Treasury financing needs, which would require the printing of 3 million pesos ($1=ARS3.205), the central bank would have to absorb some ARS4 billion in the first half of 2003 to meet the June IMF money-in-circulation target. 

 The money-in-circulation target was the key monetary goal the IMF set Argentine authorities as part of the IMF accord. 

 On Wednesday, however, Prat Gay said that after January's record tax collection, which left the federal government with a primary surplus of ARS829 million - the IMF primary surplus target was ARS420 million - he was revising his estimates. 

 The central bank now reportedly estimates Treasury financing needs of ARS1.2 billion for the first half of this year, which means that the amount of pesos the central bank will have to absorb will be just ARS2.2 billion by June. 

 With the new money absorption target in place, there will be less pressure for the central bank to raise interest rates on its short-term government notes, or LEBACs. Demand for the notes has been relatively weak over the past two weeks, with potential investors staying out the market in the expectation that authorities will hike the rate as time runs out for them to absorb pesos. 

 "There is a perception that the central bank is desperate to sell LEBAC in March and it is going to pay whatever rate. We don't feel that is the case," local daily Infobae quoted Prat Gay as saying. 

 The papers also reported that Prat Gay said Argentina's monetary reserves - $9.44 billion as of Monday - are around $1 billion higher than the IMF's minimum target for March, giving the central bank the chance to sell dollars to absorb up to ARS3 billion, if necessary. 

 In a bid to build confidence in the central bank, Prat Gay said his organization would post on its Web site the new targets and the daily progress toward them. 

 With Argentina coming out ahead of its monetary IMF targets, Prat Gay repeated his prediction that inflation this year will be within the government's 22% target, rather than the IMF forecast of 35%. 

 The revised monetary targets were confirmed by the central bank later Thursday in a report sent to Dow Jones Newswires. 

 The revisions come days ahead of the arrival of the first IMF mission charged with reviewing the progress of President Eduardo Duhalde's government toward meeting the legislative, fiscal and monetary goals laid down in the IMF accord. 

 A team, headed by the IMF's Deputy Director of the Western Hemisphere Department, John Dodsworth, will arrive in Buenos Aires over the weekend, IMF Latin American spokesman Francisco Baker confirmed Thursday. 

 Meanwhile, Prat Gay signaled the bank will seek to end its interventions in the market and move toward a system of "free float." 

 "The price of the dollar must be fixed by the market," business daily Ambito Financiero quoted him as saying. 

 By the end of 2002, the central bank was buying up to $120 million a day, in a bid to prevent the appreciation of the peso, which is considered to pose a risk to the country's export sector. 

 Since then, the central bank has lifted a range of currency controls in a bid to stimulate the market's demand for dollars. The authority's intervention in the market has since dropped to around $15 million daily in the last few weeks. 

 Analysts have said they expect the remaining currency controls to be lifted in coming months. If that sparks stronger demand for the greenback, the central bank could further reduce their interventions without worrying that the dollar would weaken. 

Argentina's peso lost 75% of its value in the first half of last year, after the government ended an 11-year period when the peso was pegged to the dollar. In a bid to support the local currency, authorities introduced a range of currency controls, including demanding that exporters sell all their greenbacks to the central bank. 

 However, since last June, the peso has gradually climbed some 20%, with much of that gain in the last three months. 

 That has led to fears among industrialists that the country's exporters may lose their competitive edge and Argentines might start buying imports again, instead of locally-made goods. 

 -By Laurence Norman, Dow Jones Newswires; 5411-4311-3127; laurence.norman@dowjones.com

title: Argentine GDP 4Q Grew 2% On 3Q - Lavagna
text:
BUENOS AIRES -(Dow Jones)- Argentine Economy Minister Roberto Lavagna insisted Wednesday his government would only meet upcoming debt payments when a debt rollover accord had been struck with the International Monetary Fund. 

 In a press conference at the Economy Ministry, Lavagna said press reports suggesting Argentina would use its reserves to pay some $2 billion to the Inter-American Development Bank, the World Bank and the IMF this week, even if a debt accord was not sealed first, were false. 

 "The Argentine government has explained its position various times ... It is impossible to make the payments outside the framework of a refinancing program" from the IMF, Lavagna said. 

 Argentina is seeking to persuade the IMF to roll over around $5 billion in debt payments to the Washington-based agency over the next six months. 

 Lavagna's comments come hours after the IDB confirmed that Argentina had not made a payment of some $681 million due Wednesday. 

 The IDB press release quoted Lavagna saying he expected only a "brief" delay before making the payment. 

 Argentina argues that to use currency reserves to make payments to multilateral without first having a debt rollover accord in place would leave the government unable to control monetary policy. 

 In the press conference, Lavagna said he did not feel hurried to seal an IMF accord by Friday, when Argentina must make a payment of around $1 billion to the IMF and a further $700 million to the World Bank. 

 "We'll keep working. There's no great urgency, neither for Argentina, nor for the IMF, as far as I understand," he said without explicitly ruling out whether Argentina would make either of Friday's payments. 

 The Economy Minister even said Argentina could make its payments before a deal is formally approved by the IMF board, as long as the IMF had already promised an accord. 

 Lavagna admitted policy differences remained between Argentina and the IMF, with the main disagreement focusing on monetary policy. 

 "There's a question about monetary expansion...whether to maintain more or less pesos in circulation," he said, detailing that the Washington-based agency was especially concerned about what Argentine authorities would do in the coming months. 

 The numbers of pesos in circulation has increased sharply in the past couple of months, as Argentina's Central Bank purchases dollars from exporters and consumers demand pesos to spend on their Southern Hemisphere summer vacation. 

 There are some concerns that the increased money supply could feed inflation, if demand for pesos drops off. 

 Lavagna gave no details of what the IMF had demanded in a draft of a final accord approved by Argentina Monday. 

 He said the IMF's permanent staff now has the draft final accord, drawn up by Argentine officials and an IMF team in Buenos Aires in recent days. The government is awaiting the staff's reply, he said. 

 Argentina has been seeking to wrap up an IMF accord for much of the past year, but a deal has run into repeated dead-ends. 

 Last week, however the IMF's executive board said they "looked forward to the early realization" of an accord with Argentina, reviving hopes of a deal. 

 Argentina is seeking to avoid defaulting on its debts to international lenders and being completely cut off from the international financial community. 

 In December 2001, Argentina defaulted on most of its $141 billion public debt. 

 A relaxed Lavagna also tackled a range of other policy issues during an hour-long news conference, in which the official broke off several times to joke with reporters. 

 Lavagna said the Central Bank may order a further easing of year-old currency controls, after two batches of measures in the past three weeks, aimed at making imports easier and facilitating Argentines' access to dollars. 

 "It's clear there is an over offer (of pesos). So there is no point in maintaining restrictions which limit the demand" for dollars, he said. 

 A further relaxing of controls could stem a recent appreciation of the peso, which the government says threatens Argentina's growing levels of exports and hits at tax income, which is heavily dependent on export duties. 

 The peso has strengthened nine centavos against the dollar in the past two sessions to reach ARS3.245 per dollar. 

 Lavagna also confirmed that Argentina plans to choose next week which bank it would ask to act as an adviser on renegotiating its foreign debt. 

 Lavagna said six banks had presented offers Thursday, each of them of "high quality." This weekend, officials will decide which of the offers met the government's requirements and next week, he said, officials will pick one of the remaining banks for the job. 

 Lavagna reiterated the role of adviser would be to prepare strategy and options for the government and wouldn't include conducting the negotiations. 

 He also promised that the government would make fresh announcements in the days ahead aimed at reordering Argentina's internal debt. 

 Lavagna also spoke about the economy, announcing that Argentina's economy expanded for the third consecutive quarter in the past three months. 

 Fourth quarter gross domestic product was up 2% on the previous quarter, while between April and December the economy grew 3%, he said. 

 "I believe this leaves no doubt about what direction things are going in," he said. 

 Argentina has been in recession since mid-1998. In 2002, the economy is estimated to have contracted 11%-12%. 

 Lavagna also said that between April and November 2002, 861,000 jobs were created, of which 530,000 were created "via public intervention." 

Argentina's official unemployment rate dropped from 21.5% in May to 17.8% in October. 

 However some say the jobless rate should be higher, if government-created "jobs" on public works projects are not all taken into account. Critics say in many cases, only the wages, not the jobs actually exist. 

 Finally, Lavagna referred to Tuesday's talks between Duhalde and his officials and Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. 

 Calling the talks very significant, he stressed the commitment of the two sides to move toward a common currency and confirmed the neighbors would create a "Monetary Institute" to help them achieve that. 

 He also said Argentina's recent entry into the Andean Development Corporation, or CAF, would give the country access to around $200 million in public or private sector credits from the regional lender. 

 -By Laurence Norman, Dow Jones Newswires; 5411-4311-3127; laurence.norman@dowjones.com

title: Chile's Massad Warns Of Downside Risk To GDP Forecasts
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- Chilean Central Bank Governor Carlos Massad said Tuesday there is a downside risk to the country's economic growth forecasts, given the shaky environment globally and in its own backyard. 

 "We judge the bias to be downward," said Massad in a speech at the Council of Americas in New York. 

 The central bank has already revised downward its 2002 economic growth forecast to the 2.0% to 2.5% range, as much of the global economy sputters and financial shock waves emanate from Argentina and Brazil, its two larger South American neighbors. 

 Chile's economy is one of the most outward looking in the world, with exports of goods and services comprising an estimated 36% of gross domestic product. During the 1990s, it routinely booked 5%-plus GDP growth. 

 The central bank is forecasting tentatively that GDP will grow between 3.5% and 4.5% in 2003 and 5% in 2004, but Massad acknowledged he wasn't heartened by the mood at the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund in Washington this past weekend. 

 "As the meetings went on, the question marks were bigger and bigger," he said in reference to the global economic outlook. 

 The IMF is projecting Latin American GDP will contract 0.6% this year, despite pockets of growth in a handful of countries, including Chile. 

 The slowdown in the world and regional economy has pushed prices for copper, Chile's single-largest export, down to around $0.67 a pound, "the lowest we've had since 1934" in real terms, according to the central banker. 

 Regional turmoil isn't helping matters. Massad estimated that the travails of Argentina, where the economy is expected to contract around 15% in the wake of last December's debt default, have probably had a negative impact of half a percentage point on Chile's GDP. 

 Market upheaval in Brazil this year ahead of presidential elections has probably had a negative impact of only around 0.2 or 0.3 percentage point of GDP, according to the central banker, who pointed out that Chilean corporate investments in Brazil are only about half as big as in Argentina. 

 But he admitted that his country is vulnerable to a continued market sell-off in Brazil, which has seen its currency weaken around 40% and bond spreads widen more than 1500 basis points this year amid growing fears that it too may be headed to default. 

 "The main risk," Massad warned, is that a Brazilian crisis might "weaken the capacity of the markets to discriminate the situations of different countries." 

 Chile is South America's last remaining investment-grade credit, after ratings agencies demoted Uruguay to junk status as contagion from Argentina and Brazil overwhelmed the tiny country. 

Forex Intervention Only In `Extraordinary' Case



Chile's markets have been feeling some heat in recent weeks, with the
peso weakening to CLP748.80 to the dollar Monday, a new record closing
low and down 8.3% from the end of June.



"We are looking closely at what's going on with the peso rate," said
Massad, adding that the bank's international reserves, at around $15
billion, are available to intervene in the foreign exchange market if
necessary.



But he also suggested that he wasn't overly concerned with the current
exchange rate, and that intervention would require more than the peso
weakening only against the greenback, given the country's diversified
export markets.



"For intervention to be justified, we have to consider that the
situation is extraordinary, that is, that the peso is not moving with
the rest of the currencies, but that it has taken a loss by itself,"
said Massad, adding that this hasn't been the case until now.



He also noted that a weaker peso helps the export sector, which, along
with construction, is the main driver of the Chilean economy.



And unlike Argentina and Brazil, which are saddled with heavy
dollar-linked debt obligations, a weakening local currency actually
eases fiscal pressures in Chile, given that the government only has $7
billion in foreign debt, Massad added.



Chile last intervened in the foreign exchange market last year, in the
wake of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks on the U.S. that sent financial
markets reeling.



Massad said he felt comfortable that Chile will be able to meet its 3%
inflation target this year. He pointed out that yields on domestic debt
indicate that the market also believes annual inflation will be around
3%, not just this year, but over the next five years.



-By Mike Esterl, Dow Jones Newswires; 201-938-4026;
mike.esterl@dowjones.com

title: Argentine peso firmer, shares dip on regional woes.
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina, Aug 1 (Reuters) - Argentina's peso firmed on Thursday on Central Bank intervention while shares fell amid investor fears over debt-laden Brazil and crisis-hit Uruguay. 

 Argentina's peso traded at 3.65/3.67 per dollar in large-scale transactions in afternoon dealings on the foreign exchange market, up from Wednesday's close at 3.71/3.73. 

 The peso is still down about 70 percent this year, though it gained 4.5 percent in July amid signs of economic stability after Argentina's chaotic four-year recession. 

 "Regional uncertainty is entrenched and all the bourses are paying the consequences," said one local trader. 

 Uruguay's economy has been hammered by a run on banks, a dive in reserves and consumer spending, and the ripple effects of Argentina's own prolonged economic crisis. 

 Brazil, meanwhile, is being buffeted by fears that the regional giant could be pushed toward default on its $250 billion public debt if a leftist wins the October presidential election. 

 Argentina's leading MerVal share index was down 1.87 percent at 352.60 on moderate volume of 15 million pesos. The index is now up nearly 10 percent since the beginning of the year, having clawed back from sharp losses in recent months. 

 The International Monetary Fund said on Thursday that talks about a potential new loan for Argentina were going well, but it said more work remained before a new loan could be agreed on. 

 Argentina has been in talks for months to restart aid from the IMF, and in recent weeks the pace of negotiations has quickened. The IMF cut off access to a $22 billion credit line in December after the government failed to control public spending. 

 The IMF also said it was in talks with Brazil to extend its current aid package through the end of 2003 but declined to comment on whether additional cash would be sent to the Latin American giant. 

 The IMF said it was approaching talks with Uruguay on how to deal with a banking crisis there with a sense of urgency but hinted that no deal was imminent. 

 Shares in Argentine energy group Perez Companc, the target of a $1.13 billion takeover bid by Brazil's Petrobras, continued their decline, trading at 1.74 pesos. 

 Perez shares are down more than 18 percent since the deal, dependent on Perez restructuring its debt, was announced on July 22. Investors are worried about the buyout's effect on minority shareholders.

title: Advisers: Scrip Makes Stable Argentine Peso Impossible
text:
WASHINGTON -(Dow Jones)- A panel of independent advisors charged with helping Argentina develop a strategy for rebuilding its economy said Monday the government may eventually use inflation-targeting to guide monetary policy, but not until it can credibly control liquidity in the economy. 

 Further, the panel said a degree of autonomy for the central bank is necessary for an inflation-targeting regime to work, according to their report released Monday. 

 "A monetary anchor is a necessary (though not sufficient) condition for the restoration over time of price stability," the panel said. 

 "In the short-term, the stability of the monetary anchor depends largely on how the Corralito and the Corralon are managed," the panel said, referring to the government's freeze on deposits in the banking system. "In the longer-term, as is discussed below, it depends also on a fiscal position that strictly limits the need for monetary financing of the government." 

 The International Monetary Fund and the government of Argentina called on the advisory group of four widely-respected monetary policy experts to provide an outside perspective on the slow-going work by the two sides to develop an economic program. The recommendations dispensed by the panel, more general policy guidelines than a specific plan, don't differ much from the advice offered in public by IMF officials. For example, the IMF has frequently said that Argentina needs some sort of monetary anchor, or economic target, to help policy-makers control inflation. 

 The IMF has also said that Argentina would need to find a way to slowly release banking deposits into the economy as it recovers to avoid the excess liquidity that would fuel inflation. The government has had few takers of its voluntary program to exchange deposits for long-term government bonds. Meanwhile, money leaks steadily out of the banking system as deposit-holders win court injunctions, known as amparos, for the immediate release of the funds. 

 "The continuation of amparos is simply not compatible with adequate monetary control," the panel said. "Addressing this problem requires not just a temporary stay on amparos, but a clear strategy for preventing their reemergence." 

 Without forwarding a specific approach, the experts said it would be possible for the government to begin releasing frozen assets, especially those of small holders, increase the ability of deposit holders to transfer the deposits that remain frozen, and ensure that release of the deposits is controlled. Because it is impossible to say how quickly Argentines would voluntarily return freed-up deposits to the banking system, the government must have a plan for adjusting the amount of deposits released and a way to reabsorb excess pesos in the economy, the panel said. 

 But sales of foreign exchange to absorb pesos, a method used heavily in the past, isn't a good option for the government, because restoring confidence in the economy requires rising foreign exchange reserves, the panel said. The country's large trade surplus should make building reserves possible, the experts said. 

 In addition, Argentina should refrain from using foreign exchange reserves to intervene in financial markets to support the peso, the experts said. The government should instead view the peso's value on foreign exchange markets as a sort of progress report on its economic policies and adjust them should the peso weaken too much. Also, the group stressed the need for the government to control issuance of currency substitutes commonly used by some state governments to pay bills. 

 "The Panel wishes to underline that the development of a financial system based on a stable peso is not compatible with the continued existence of alternative currency issues," according to the report. "The faster these alternative currencies are retired, the sooner the basis will be laid for a credible national currency." 

 Although the group said it is opposed to dollarization  for Argentina, saying that adopting the U.S. currency wouldn't solve the deep-seated problems in the economy and would limit policy options, it also noted that the dollar will continue to be used as a parallel currency for the foreseeable future. Also, the group warned that inflation stemming from peso depreciation has yet to run its course. 

 Argentina's government will have to control spending to make a inflation-targeting regime successful, the panel said. While the government has no current need to borrow from the banking system to finance a fiscal deficit, that is true only because it has suspended debt service. Meanwhile, Argentina's public debt, both nominally and relative to the size of its economy, is growing as a result of indexation. 

 "All this means a sustained effort to improve the fiscal position on a durable basis is a priority, if the instruments of monetary policy are not to be overburdened," the panel said. "Argentina will of course need to aim in the years ahead for a fiscal outcome that is substantially better than simply covering expenditures before debt service." 

 Finally, the group said that for inflation-targeting to work, the central bank must have enough autonomy to make decisions free of political pressure and fear of personal consequences. 

 "Obviously such a situation cannot be mandated by fiat or achieved overnight," the panel said. "But it should be the government's objective to develop structures that allow the (Argentine central bank) to become an institution that has earned a level of respect now enjoyed by its peers in a number of other countries." 

 Respected former Central Bank Governor Mario Blejer has complained over the deterioration in central bank independence amid the deepening economic crisis. In particular, Blejer wanted central bank officials to have legal immunity for monetary policy decisions. He stepped down from his post last month. 

 Commenting on the report in a statement, IMF Managing Director Horst Koehler said the Fund and Argentina would continue to discuss these issues and "move toward a Fund-supported program as soon as the authorities are in a position to ensure their implementation." 

 Andrew Crockett, general manager of the Bank for International Settlements; John Crow, former governor of the Bank of Canada; Luis Angel Rojo, former governor of the Bank of Spain; and Hans Tietmeyer, former President of the German Bundesbank, formed the advisory group. 

 -By Elizabeth Price, Dow Jones Newswires; 202-862-9295; Elizabeth.Price@dowjones.com

title: Argentine stocks soar on bank rumors, peso firms.
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina, July 8 (Reuters) - Argentine stocks soared on Monday on continued talk of a new government plan to save the financial system from collapse, while heavy Central Bank intervention sent the peso slightly higher. 

Argentina's leading MerVal share index closed 5.06 percent higher at 402.12 points in heavy turnover of 37.4 million pesos. Overall, 25 shares advanced, 15 declined and 11 shares traded unchanged. 

 Continuing a trend from last week, banking shares led the charge as investors continued to bet the government would force a switch of bank deposits into public bonds. Analysts say the unpopular move analysts say is necessary with banks short on cash amid a chaotic four-year recession. 

Central Bank president Aldo Pignanelli on Monday ruled out an obligatory deposits conversion, echoing comments over the weekend from President Eduardo Duhalde, but traders said they believed the government would eventually be forced to face reality and make the switch. 

 "The deposit switch is a reality the government can not avoid," a stocks trader said. 

 Bank Bansud gained 10 percent to 0.924 pesos, while Banco Frances jumped 6.2 percent to 2.23 pesos.

title: Argentine stocks dip, peso off despite  intervention .

 stocks fell on Monday afternoon, while the peso weakened 

 despite heavy buying by the Central Bank, traders said, citing 

 mounting fears over the stubborn recession afflicting Latin 

 America's third largest economy,

 percent to 307 points in below-average volume of 10.8 million 

 pesos. The MerVal is down 5 percent since Jan. 2 and off 3 

 percent in June as investors fear the long recession could 

 leave Argentine companies unable to pay their debts.

 traded unchanged.

 unchanged at 0.19 pesos after last week's gain of 45 percent on 

 rumors it might sell its main unit, Argentina's largest private 

 bank Banco Galicia.

 after a local bank said it had rejected a $101 million debt 

 payment originally due in U.S. dollars made instead with 104.57 

 million pesos ($28 million).

 large-scale transactions in the foreign exchange market ARSB=) 

 compared with Friday's close of 3.73/3.75. 

 Traders said the peso's fall came despite the Central 

 Bank's efforts to prop up the currency by selling by midday an 

 unusually heavy $40 million out of U.S. dollar reserves that 

 have dwindled by nearly 50 percent this year. 

 "We're looking at a complicated week because Argentina is 

 trying to reach a deal with the IMF, but also there are some 

 complications around the region that are putting a worrying 

 pressure on business," said a banking analyst. 

 Economy Minister Roberto Lavagna is slated to travel to 

 Washington this week to try to end months of stalemate and 

 reach an aid deal with the International Monetary Fund. 

 Many analysts fear, however, that Argentina will not be 

 able to make spending cuts or keep monetary policy as tight as 

 the IMF demands in return for aid.

 Argentina. Brazil's real currency has hit all-time lows on debt 

 and pre-election jitters.

 per dollar by the end of 2002 and that the monetary authority
