title: Argentine IMF deal seen way off as mission ends.
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina, June 21 (Reuters) - The IMF wrapped up a visit to Argentina on Friday under a cloud, with the Central Bank chief poised to quit and no sign of fully-fledged aid talks on the horizon. 

 The impending exit of Central Bank head Mario Blejer - an ex-IMF official who is at daggers drawn with the government over monetary policy - is another body blow to the floundering government, as fears of Argentine contagion and debt woes in neighboring Brazil rippled through Latin American currencies. 

 The government played up the visit by the International Monetary Fund, which arrived last week to crunch numbers and lay the groundwork for possible talks to restart frozen aid. 

 But there were no statements from the IMF that typically follow progress in talks to announce a move to a next stage - which Argentina hopes will be a fully-fledged negotiating mission. It remained unclear whether the Washington-based lender was satisfied with Argentina's promises and policies. 

 "I think it (the IMF) is still going to find that Argentina is far away from being ready," said Freddy Thomsen, economist at ING Barings in Buenos Aires. 

 Caretaker President Eduardo Duhalde, drafted in after an elected government was toppled amid bloody riots in December, is forging ahead with a plan to offer bank depositors bonds in lieu of their savings. 

 Argentines are furious at the confiscation of their savings, which have been decimated in dollar terms since January's botched devaluation followed a default on part of the $140 billion debt pile. 

 "The subject of the bonds for savings plan is closed," a senior economy ministry source said on condition of anonymity. 

 But the IMF wanted the bonds forced on savers for fear they would withdraw their cash at the earliest opportunity, turn it into dollars and stuff it under the mattress. That would weaken the peso, which is already down 70 percent against the dollar since a decade-old currency peg was scrapped in January. 

 The fund also wants clear signs that a government pressured by growing poverty and unemployment will stick to vows to end the runaway spending that landed Latin America's No. 3 economy in its worst ever financial crisis in the first place. 

 Duhalde desperately needs IMF aid to stabilize the economy and fend off social unrest and the hyperinflation that gripped Argentina in the late 1980s - which could force his exit. 

 Neighboring Uruguay has already been forced to float its own currency because of Argentina's spiraling crisis. 

 Any IMF deal - which analysts say would likely be little more than a roll-over of the debt Argentina owes it in coming months - is vital because other potential lenders like the World Bank are citing it as their cue to offer cash. 

 Markets are forecasting that Argentina's peso has much further to fall. The IMF has publicly said it wants the peso anchored by strict monetary policy. 

 Sources close to talks with the IMF have said the fund was almost certain to insist that Argentina stick to a flexible exchange rate, vow only minimal intervention in the currency markets, limit how many pesos the Central Bank can print, and stop provinces from printing bonds as scrip currency. 

 The Central Bank head's resignation - which a government source told Reuters would be tendered next week, after weeks of speculation - is yet another complication. 

 "Blejer's departure definitely would mean the government would be losing one of its most credible figures to negotiate with the IMF," said Fernando Losada, senior Latin America economist ay ABN Amro in New York. 

 "On the other hand the person who was leading the negotiations with the IMF was Economy Minister Roberto Lavagna in the past few days. My impression is the talks between Buenos Aires and Washington are not easy, but I wouldn't say that there's no hope." 

 Argentine officials say Lavagna should travel to Washington next week to follow up the fund's advance mission. (With reporting by Jorge Otaola and Guido Nejamkis).

title: FEATURE-Argentina frustrated by failure to stop peso fall.
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina, June 17 (Reuters) - Paper IOUs in lieu of savings, central bank intervention, scrambling for export dollars - Argentina is frantically scouring for ways to stem the peso's free-fall since it devalued the national currency in January. 

 Experts say the government's tactics to support the sliding peso, which has lost nearly three quarters of its value against the dollar since being unhitched from a decade of parity with the greenback, could easily fail as they are just generating more uncertainty in a chaotic and recession-hit economy. 

 "Every peso I get I convert into dollars - whatever the rate," said exasperated depositor and lawyer Analia, who, like thousands of Argentines, saw her bank savings frozen by the government in December to ward off financial collapse. 

 The peso is now worth just 28 U.S. cents after Argentina's worst-ever economic crisis culminated in a default on part of the $140 billion public debt pile and a ruinous devaluation. 

 Caretaker President Eduardo Duhalde, Argentina's fifth leader since mid-December, desperately needs to stabilize the currency to fend off dangers of a return to the nightmare hyperinflation that gripped Argentina in the late 1980s, a scenario that could force his exit. 

 Analysts say a scheme to end the freeze but at the same time avoid a stampede to the dollar by letting depositors opt either for bonds and certificates or wait for the money to be returned at some point in the future is a non-starter. 

 "Accept bonds from this government? No way. That's madness. What are the chances of ever seeing that money again?" said Analia. 

 Their savings ravaged by the peso's demise, and with dollars second nature after a decade of using them interchangeably with pesos at one-to-one, few Argentines will ever trust their own currency again, polls show. 

 Like thousands of Argentines, Analia plans to turn her money into safe-haven dollars if banks return savings as the government plans to allow. 

 IMF ADVICE SHUNNED 

 The IMF wanted Argentina to make the savings bond plan mandatory, fearing the public will take their cash at the earliest opportunity, turn it into dollars and stuff it under the mattress, further weakening the peso. 

 The dollar obsession had led some economists, and former President Carlos Menem, to argue that Argentines are voting with their feet by lining up to buy dollars. Why not make the dollar the official currency rather than the peso, they ask? 

 Duhalde is against dollarization, but while he has no plans to re-peg the peso, he has left the door open to a new fixed rate as statistics show that half of the 36 million population has been forced into poverty, unable to buy food or clothing as the weak peso has sparked an inflationary spiral. 

 With markets predicting the peso will trade at up to 9.0 to the dollar a year from now in the speculative forward currency markets from around 3.6 currently, the stock exchange has suggested trading peso futures contracts to help stabilize the currency by giving markets a heads-up as to where its value is trending. 

 As Argentines rush to buy dollars in the absence of an International Monetary Fund aid deal, analysts see the peso sliding further as a four-year recession grinds on in Latin America's crippled No.3 economy. 

 Near-daily central bank intervention has gnawed Argentine reserves to danger levels that experts say are near the bare minimum needed to underpin the economy. Reserves have fallen over 30 percent since the end of 2001 to around $10 billion. 

 "The government is sticking to its idea of a floating exchange rate, and all it is doing is losing reserves on the one hand and watching the peso lose ground on the other," said Carlos Arbia, chief economist with Exante consultancy. 

 Arbia favors pegging the peso at 3.0 or 4.0 to the dollar to end the endless intervention. "We're calculating by July the peso could be between 5.80 and 6.00 to the dollar," he added. 

 MONETARY EXPANSION 

 Argentina's leaders have made matters worse by printing money - either in the form of pesos or paper bonds used by the provinces to make ends meet and pay the workers of a bloated state - pressuring inflation and hitting the exchange rate. 

 Analysts estimate the Central Bank has printed 7.0 billion pesos ($2 billion) since mid-February amid a cash crunch - about double its original target - on top of some 5 billion pesos of scrip printed by poor provincial governments. 

 The government is also pressuring grain exporters to cash in dollar revenues to help prop up the local currency. 

 But farmers are holding off selling much of their output for fears earnings, which are in pesos, will be depleted by inflation or get stuck in the bank. 

 As a result exporters are bringing fewer dollars into the economy to buy the grain in the first place, which leaves fewer to be cashed in to help boost the peso. 

 "Farmers are holding back (their grain) ... due to the uncertainty, which means grain shipments are being delayed, which means exporters are not bringing in more dollars," said agricultural analyst Daniel Miro of Novitas consultancy. 

 The IMF wants the peso anchored by strict monetary policy. 

 Sources close to talks between Argentina and the IMF say the fund is almost certain to insist that Argentina stick to a flexible exchange rate, vow only minimal intervention in the currency markets, limit how many pesos the central bank can print and stop provinces from printing bonds as currency. 

 An IMF rescue package is vital for Argentina, because other lenders like the World Bank that could potentially front aid are taking their cue from the fund. 

 "The fundamental problem is (that) the quantity of pesos constantly being dumped on the market is pressuring the exchange rate," said economist Camilo Tiscornia of thinktank Orlando Ferreres in Buenos Aires. 

 "A deal with the fund will not calm things in itself.... I think (the peso) is going to rise," he added. (With reporting by Walter Bianchi and Athena Jones).

title: Argentina Departs IMF Meetings With No Cash In Pockets
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 WASHINGTON -(Dow Jones)- Argentine officials left the spring meetings of the International Monetary Fund empty-handed Sunday as the Fund balked at a new round of emergency financing and South America's second-largest economy sank deeper into crisis. 

 Managing Director Horst Koehler said he had "a very good  meeting" with Argentine Economy Minister Jorge Remes Lenicov  Saturday, but that Remes now had to return to Buenos Aires and "work further" before multilateral aid starts flowing south again. 

 Koehler added that an IMF mission would probably only return to Argentina in mid-May, making the government's goal  of securing more than $9 billion in stopgap loans within the next month increasingly unlikely. 

 "We are in a very profound crisis," Remes acknowledged to a group of reporters Sunday. 

 Better guarantees that Argentina's provinces will adhere  to tight fiscal goals remains a major sticking point - as does the absence of some fundamental numbers. 

 "The IMF needs to have a consolidated account about the fiscal situation in Argentina. This is possible, this is needed," Koehler said in a press conference Saturday. 

 The IMF halted a $22 billion bailout package in December  after Argentina overshot its fiscal targets. The country subsequently defaulted on $141 billion in public sector debt, before devaluing its currency in January. 

 The situation has deteriorated since then. The IMF is now forecasting that the Argentine economy, in recession since mid-1998, will contract another 10% to 15% this year. 

 Argentina's central bank announced late Friday it was shuttering banks and the foreign exchange market indefinitely, and President Eduardo Duhalde warned Saturday "that the financial system could collapse." 

 Remes told reporters on Sunday he didn't know when the banks, which are widely regarded as insolvent, would reopen again. 

 Government officials were working overtime over the weekend in Buenos Aires to draft legislation that would force depositors who win lawsuits against bank withdrawal restrictions to accept their savings in bonds instead of cash. 

 Anywhere from $50 million to $200 million a day left the  banking system in recent days, even though the government froze most bank accounts in early December to halt a run on deposits. About a third of the seepage was due to court rulings overturning the restrictions, according to estimates. 

 Remes told an IMF committee Saturday that it would take 45 days for Argentina to craft a plan to rehabilitate the financial sector. 

 In addition to restoring confidence in the banks, the IMF is pushing Argentina to revise bankruptcy legislation, adopt a less-interventionistforeign exchange policy and put  guarantees in place to ensure that foreign and local creditors get treated equally. 

 Its main demand, though, is that the federal government secure ironclad agreements with each of the 23 provinces on spending cuts. 

 The provinces recently agreed in principle to slash last  year's deficits by 60% and scrap a revenue-sharing pact that had guaranteed them a fixed amount of monthly transfers, regardless of how much tax revenue the federal government collected. 

 Remes said the federal government couldn't impose its will on the governors, some of whom have sharply criticized the IMF's austerity demands in recent days, but that it was planning a new round of accelerated negotiations. 

 "I believe there's a clear recognition that times are urgent," he said Sunday, adding that an accord with the governors was possible "in a couple weeks." 

 Ann Krueger, the IMF's first deputy managing director, promised the Fund would move rapidly to negotiate a letter of intent after the preconditions are met. 

 "The mission getting back there in May can be achieved quite quickly once there is action on the agreement with the  governors," she said in a press conference Sunday. 

 But Argentina's political landscape remains uncertain at  best. Last week, Alfredo Avelin, the governor of San Juan, roundly rejected the austerity demands of the IMF, exclaiming in a local radio interview that the "Fund can go  to hell." 

 Argentines are also increasingly frustrated with government decrees that have prevented them from accessing their savings. Already in December, four of Duhalde's successors resigned in quick succession because of violent street protests against bank withdrawal limits. 

 Brazilian Finance Minister Pedro Malan Sunday urged the international financial community to step up its efforts in helping his neighbor - but didn't sugarcoat the problems Argentina faces. 

 "The situation in Argentina is extremely difficult," he acknowledged in a press conference.  "Its complexity suggests that there is no easy and rapid solution." 

 Argentina also recently asked the IMF to spearhead an effort that would allow for a standstill in corporate debt obligations, as scores of local companies fall behind in payments in the wake of January's peso devaluation. 

 That plan appears to be grounded, though. Remes said on Sunday there were no discussions on the subject during this weekend's meetings. 

 Since the government junked the peso's decade-old parity  against the dollar, the local currency has shed more than two-thirds of its value despite a web of capital controls designed to stanch outflows. 

 "We will continue working," said Remes on Sunday, as he prepared to head back to Buenos Aires. 

 -By Mike Esterl, Dow Jones Newswires; 202-289-4187; mike.esterl@dowjones.com

title: Argentina's Peso Flat; IMF-Govt Talks For Aid Continue
text:
BUENOS AIRES -(Dow Jones)- Argentina's peso remained in a holding pattern Thursday as Argentine economic and monetary managers and an International Monetary Fund mission hold talks on how to strengthen the currency. 

 Commercial banks quoted the peso at a mid rate of ARS2.77 per dollar, virtually unchanged from Wednesday's close. 

 Since devaluation in January, the Argentine central bank has been hard pressed to subdue dollar demand and yank rival, provincial currencies out of circulation. 

 The IMF's chief negotiator for Argentina, Anoop Singh, is in Buenos Aires this week. The official said Wednesday that the IMF is providing the central bank here advice on future monetary policy. 

 Meanwhile, some traders said that the currency market was "little moved" by IMF statements late Wednesday that the Fund is committed to aiding the crisis-wracked country. 

 At the same time, the IMF has hinted Argentina should refrain from interventions and let the market set rates for the peso. Other traders said the peso was stable against the dollar with the central bank forcing larger companies, such as exporters and banks, to sell off a large portion of their dollars. 

 -By Tom Darin Liskey, Dow Jones Newswires; (5411) 4314-2757; tom.liskey@dowjones.com

title: Argentina  Ctrl Bank Tuesday  Intervention  Totaled $36 Mln
text:
BUENOS AIRES -(Dow Jones)- Argentina's central bank on Tuesday sold $26 million worth of greenbacks and bought $10 million, for a net intervention of $16 million, the bank said in a statement. 

 The bank said the session's currency trading totaled between $400 million and $450 million, in-line with traders'  and analysts' daily estimates since the peso began to float  against the dollar on Feb. 11. 

 The bank said its dollar sales and more from the nation's exporters caused the peso to strengthen. The peso rose to about US$ 0.37 on Tuesday from a post-devaluation low of US$ 0.32 on Monday and Friday. 

 On Monday and again Tuesday, the central bank sold dollars at below-market rates through more than a dozen government-run and private commercial banks. 

 Fearing stiff penalties under Argentine criminal law, exporters and banks are abiding by central bank orders demanding that they convert almost all their dollars into pesos much more quickly than they had before the currency began to float against the dollar. 

 The central bank, anxious to keep a lid on consumer prices, is using a combination of dollar sales and regulations to bolster the peso. 

 -By Tim Loughran, Dow Jones Newswires; 5411-4313-1918; argentina@dowjones.com

title: Argentine peso hits new low, cenbank  intervenes .
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina, March 22 (Reuters) - Argentina's Central Bank on Friday intervened in the foreign exchange market to offer dollars at 2.45 pesos to prop up the peso as it slid to record lows, traders said. 

 The intervention came as Argentina's peso traded at 2.75/2.77 (buy/sell rate) on Friday for large-scale transactions in the foreign exchange market - a slide of nearly 64 percent since January's devaluation. 

 The peso was pegged at par to the dollar for more than a decade until January when the cash-strapped government of Latin America's No. 3 economy devalued the currency before fully floating it in February.

title: Argentina Throws Weight In  Forex  Mkt, But Economy Stuck
text:
NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- Argentine authorities showed Friday they can brake the peso's slide. Now they've got to figure out a way to get the economy moving again. 

 The central bank threw a bunch of wrenches in the nascent currency market during the last 36 hours, intervening directly on Thursday by selling more than $100 million in dollars and then ordering banks to limit their holdings of U.S. dollars to 5% of what they had at the end of November. 

 The moves worked, with the peso strengthening Friday to end at ARS2.323 to the dollar after sinking below ARS2.40 earlier in the week as crisis-weary Argentines sought the safety of the greenback. 

 With more than $13 billion in international reserves, a web of capital controls that has tied the flow of capital into knots, and a seemingly infinite capacity to come up with new decrees like the one on Thursday, Argentine officials appear to have sufficient tools on hand to keep the peso's decline in check for some time. 

 "They're nowhere near the threshold," says Greg Anderson, foreign exchange strategist with FleetBoston, estimating that the central bank likely has burned through less than $1 billion in reserves in recent weeks. 

 Trading volume in the peso, which was released from its dollar parity in January, remains relatively thin and is almost non-existent offshore. Foreign investors aren't in much of a position to speculate against the currency because  they'd have to borrow pesos, and there aren't any pesos to be borrowed. 

 Few think the peso would be trading under ARS240/dollar if the government didn't have so many checks and balances in  place. In a sign of how far the Argentine currency could fall, nine-month, non-deliverable peso forwards in New York were being quoted at a spread of ARS4.30-ARS4.60 Friday. 

 "One needs to understand this is political," says Alberto Bernal, Argentina economist at IDEAglobal, citing the growing anger on the streets as Argentines watch their savings evaporate. 

 Popular unrest has already prompted four presidents to resign since late December. Interim President Eduardo Duhalde, whose popularity also isn't high, vowed Friday the government will "make the dollar fall." 

 Economists say preventing the peso from overshooting also keeps a lid on runaway inflation. 

 But while they can gum up the exchange rate, Argentine officials haven't had much luck pulling the country out of crisis conditions after placing stiff curbs on bank withdrawals and defaulting on its foreign debt in December. 

 In Argentina, it's been a case of "plug one leak and another one springs open," says Larry Krohn, Latin America economist with ING Barings. 

 He says he's got no idea where the peso will end 2002, but he is forecasting a 9% economic contraction in South America's second-largest economy, which has been stuck in recession since mid-1998. 

 Argentine authorities briefly stopped intervening in the  market when a mission from the International Monetary Fund arrived last week, leading to speculation that the IMF was advising against using up reserves to prop up the currency. 

 But that theory has been jettisoned in recent days, as Argentina's central bank heightened its interventions even as meetings were being carried out with the IMF on a new emergency credit line. 

 FleetBoston's Anderson points out that the IMF isn't against temporary interventions in the foreign exchange market in order to ensure a modicum of stability. Both Brazil and Chile adopted interventionist strategies in their  local currency markets in recent years with full IMF backing. 

 But new funding from the IMF appears a long way off, as the Fund continues to insist on the government crafting a comprehensive economic plan first. 

 That means the Argentine government might have to focus on a raft of structural reforms, which is sure to include another round of unpopular austerity measures as the country  tries to return to solvency. 

 Few economists believe authorities have a plan in place that would allow them to reach 2002 budget targets. Worse, they don't see the government making any progress on 2003, either. 

 "Nobody thinks we're going to be close to any of the targets this year," says Bernal, referring to the government goals of keeping inflation at 15%, the fiscal deficit at 1% of gross domestic product and the economic contraction at 5%. 

 "The point is getting the guidelines in place for next year," he adds. 

 -By Mike Esterl, Dow Jones Newswires; 201-938-4026; mike.esterl@dowjones.com

title: Argentina 's Peso Ends Stronger On Various  Interventions
text:
BUENOS AIRES -(Dow Jones)- Argentina's peso (ARS) closed stronger Friday on central bank rules requiring banks to dump dollars, as well as a small amount of dollar sales by the monetary authority Friday, traders said. 

 Commercial banks quoted the peso closing at a midrate of  around ARS2.323/dollar for interbank transactions. On Thursday the peso closed at around ARS2.39/dollar for such transactions. 

 A resolution issued late Thursday by the central bank ordered banks to limit their holdings in dollars to just 5% of what they held on Nov. 30. The resolution ordered banks to sell off their excess dollars by the close of business Friday. 

 Yet in what many say has become the central bank's characteristic mode of operation, the monetary authority Friday sent banks a communique altering the earlier order. The central bank now says commercial banks can keep at least  $1 million or 5% of what they held on Nov. 30, whichever sum amounts to less. The central bank also expanded the measure to include all accounts the bank holds overseas and all liquid investments abroad. 

 Traders said the central bank's resolution is just one of many desperate measures to prop up the peso, which has plunged by as much as 60% since it was devalued and began to  float in early January. 

 "These are strong measures coming at a difficult time for Argentina," said Rafael Ber, an analyst at Argentine Research Consultancy. Ber characterized the measures forcing  banks to sell off large parts of their dollar positions as "a way to control the market, without using (central bank) reserves." 

Central bank reserves have been dwindling steadily since  the government scrapped the country's 11-year currency board, which pegged the peso 1:1 to the U.S. dollar. On Friday the central bank reported that net foreign reserves had dropped $60 million in a day to $13.54 billion, as of March 13. 

 For the most part the central bank's intervention has been carried out through almost-daily dollar sales, traders say. In the days after the peso began to float freely on January 11, the central bank would sell around $25 million to $50 million per session, traders said. 

 On Thursday traders said the central bank intervened at its highest levels since the January devaluation, selling anywhere from $135 million to $150 million Thursday. 

 Though traders couldn't provide a figure for Friday's intervention they said it appeared to be more along the lines of the less severe earlier interventions, and was nowhere near as high as Thursday's action. 

 As a matter of policy the central bank doesn't comment on its market intervention. 

 -By Dawn Weiner, Dow Jones Newswires; 5411-4311-3127; argentina@dowjones.com

title: Argentina Ctrl Bank -2: `We'll Make Dollar Fall': Duhalde
text:
Executives at local banks and officers of the Argentine Banking Association were still evaluating the new central bank order and weren't immediately available for comment. 

 In a Friday interview with Radio America and without mentioning specific actions, President Eduardo Duhalde said "We'll make the dollar fall." 

 On Thursday, the central bank spent between $100 million and $150 million buying pesos in an effort to bolster the currency. Earlier in the week, after Duhalde made similar comments, the central bank spent an estimated $80 million to buy pesos. 

 Duhalde and central bank president Mario Blejer both said the government will use all resources available to it to keep the dollar at about ARS1.65. 

 Critics on Wall Street and in Argentina oppose the government's spending of scarce hard currency reserves to protect an overvalued peso while local companies can't get credit to remain operating, and bondholders can't get repaid for the sovereign debt they own. 

 On Jan. 6, Argentina devalued the peso from its 11-year, 1-to-1 peg with the dollar by an initial 29%. The Duhalde administration began to float the peso against the greenback on Feb. 11, several months ahead of schedule. 

 About $400 million a day trades in Argentina's infant currency market, according to the latest estimates of the Forex Club of Argentina. 

 "We're taking our first steps. Now all volume is related to (the needs of importers and exporters). "We haven't begun the speculative market," said Jose Alfredo Nogueira, of the ABC Mercado de Cambios, a former banker. 

 By some calculations, the central bank has spent between $700 million and $900 million to slow the slide in the peso. The central bank refuses to comment on what it spends each day in the currency markets. 

 To some analysts, the central bank's intervention policy is confused and misguided. 

 "In Argentina, many politicians and even some economists don't understand the first thing about (currency) markets," Nogueira said. 

 The government's main goal is to prevent the four-digit annual hyperinflation of the late 1980s that forced Argentina in 1991 to peg its currency to the U.S. dollar at a rate of 1-to-1. 

 Argentina is struggling to escape a four-year recession that has forced urban unemployment past 20% and pushed tens of thousands of middle-class families into poverty. 

 The Duhalde administration hopes that if it can keep a lid on consumer prices, it can prevent the street protests and supermarket looting that forced the Dec. 20 resignation of former President Fernando de la Rua. 

 -By Tim Loughran, Dow Jones Newswires; 5411-4313-1918; tim.loughran@dowjones.com. 

 Late Friday, the central bank issued an update of Rule 3511 that tightened some, and loosened other, restrictions on dollar holdings. 

 On the one hand, the central bank said that banks' new General Exchange Position as defined by Rule 3511 would include the sum of all types of cash and liquid investments held in any form overseas. 

 Also, any Argentine bank that fails to report its dollar holdings to the central bank at the end of each day, by 2300 GMT, will not be able to participate in the currency market, the central bank said. 

 On the other hand, the central bank amended Rule 3511 to say that all local banks are entitled to have at least $1 million in dollar holdings each day, easing the original terms set Thursday. 

 The central bank said that some smaller banks, if forced to abide by Rule 3511's original 5% threshold, might not be able to serve their customers properly. 

 -By Tim Loughran, Dow Jones Newswires; 5411-4313-1918; tim.loughran@dowjones.com.

title: Argentina Peso Opens Up;Ctrl Bk Orders Dumping Of Dollars
text:
BUENOS AIRES -(Dow Jones)- Argentina's peso opened stronger Friday on new central bank regulations that are forcing many banks to sell off most of their dollar positions. 

 Commercial banks quoted the peso opening at a midrate of around ARS2.325 a dollar for interbank transactions. On Thursday, the peso closed at ARS2.39/dollar for such transactions. 

 A resolution issued late Thursday by the central bank ordered banks to limit their holdings in dollars to just 5% of what they held Nov. 30. The resolution also ordered banks to sell off their excess dollars by the close of business Friday. 

 Traders said the central bank's resolution is just one of many desperate measures to prop up the peso, which has plunged by as much as 60% since it was devalued and began floating in early January. 

 For the most part, the central bank's intervention has been carried out through dollar sales almost daily, traders said. In the days after Jan. 11, when the peso began to float freely, the central bank would sell around $25 million to $50 million a session, they said. 

 On Thursday, traders said the central bank intervened at its highest level since the January devaluation. Traders estimated that the monetary authority sold $135 million to $150 million to keep the peso from a further free-fall. But the currency still closed weaker Thursday, at ARS2.39/dollar against the previous day's close of ARS2.36/dollar. 

 Analysts and traders have criticized the central bank interventions as wasting Argentina's precious reserves. 

 Jose Nogueira, head of brokerage ABC Mercado de Cambios, speaking in a conference Thursday, criticized the central bank's intervention policy. "You can't regulate a market by going out and tossing around $1 million or $2 million...Selling dollars at ARS2.30 when the market price was ARS2.40 - who does that benefit?" Nogueira said. 

 -By Dawn Weiner, Dow Jones Newswires; 5411-4311-3127; argentina@dowjones.com

title: Argentina to make exporters exchange  forex  faster.
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina, March 15 (Reuters) - Argentina plans to change the rules requiring exporters to exchange foreign currencies with the Central Bank for the local peso so those funds are turned in more quickly than currently, President Eduardo Duhalde said on Friday. 

 "We are changing the rules so they (exporters) are obliged to liquidate fast. The old rules allowed them to liquidate every 180 days, which is excessive," Duhalde told local radio. 

Argentina's Central Bank has intervened in the past three sessions, selling dollars in increasingly large amounts to try to prop up the peso after it fell to a historic low of 2.48/2.50 on Tuesday. This is 60 percent down from its level in January when it was devalued after 10 years of parity to the dollar. 

 "We will bring the dollar down," Duhalde said. "When will we do it? Well, that is up to the central bank." 

Central bank foreign reserves stand at about $13.7 billion which could continue to be used to defend the peso. The reduction in the time exporters have to exchange foreign currencies for pesos could also push the peso higher by injecting more dollars in the local market.

title: Argentina 's Peso Ends Weaker Despite Heavy  Intervention
text:
BUENOS AIRES -(Dow Jones)- Argentina's peso (ARS) closed slightly weaker Thursday, despite the central bank's most significant intervention since the currency began to float in early January. 

 Traders estimated the central bank sold around $120 million to prop up the ever-weakening currency. 

 Commercial banks quoted the peso closing at a midrate of  around ARS2.39/dollar for interbank transactions. On Wednesday the peso closed at ARS2.36/dollar for such transactions. 

 Other traders estimated the central bank sold as much as $150 million Thursday. 

 Traders said the bank intervened Thursday around ARS2.32 to ARS2.38. The central bank's intervention Thursday was the highest level of dollar sales since the peso began floating at the beginning of the year. 

 Still, the monetary authority couldn't keep the price of the peso from falling, traders noted. "It's the forces of the market versus the central bank," and the central bank is losing for now, one trader said. 

 The trader said the central bank blew through $18 million in about one minute in early trading, when it intervened around ARS2.32 and ARS2.34. 

 The central bank as a matter of policy doesn't comment on interventions. 

 The peso, which for 11 years was pegged 1:1 to the U.S. dollar, began to float freely in early January after the government devalued the currency. 

 Government and monetary officials, from President Eduardo Duhalde to Central Bank President Mario Blejer, have vowed to use the country's hard-currency reserves to prop up the peso. Officials have said the government would like to see the peso trading at ARS1.60/dollar. 

Foreign exchange houses in downtown Buenos Aires were selling dollars to the public around ARS2.42 and buying greenbacks for around ARS2.28. 

 -By Dawn Weiner, Dow Jones Newswires; 5411-4311-3127; argentina@dowjones.com

title: Argentine Peso Forwards Market Paints Gloomy Outlook
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- Argentina's beleaguered currency staged a rally in the local spot market Wednesday as the central bank intervened directly and prepared to issue short-term debt securities to sop up liquidity. 

 But Argentine peso forward contracts traded in the U.S. suggest any recovery will be short-lived, as market participants continue to bet on steep declines against the greenback. 

 "Some people find the spreads too rich, but generally people would like to sell the peso," said Clyde Wardle, a New York-based emerging markets foreign exchange strategist at HSBC Holdings. 

 Argentina's spot currency strengthened to ARS2.28 to the dollar in Buenos Aires trading early Wednesday, after closing at ARS2.41 Tuesday. Local traders said the central bank again sold dollars to prop up the peso in the local market, after selling as much as $80 million Tuesday. 

 By comparison, U.S.-based market participants say one-month non-deliverable peso forwards are trading at around ARS2.65 in the offshore market, which is free of the capital controls imposed by the Argentine government in December to stem money flight. 

 Things are seen only getting worse for the peso, with three-month, six-month, nine-month and 12-month NDF rates being quoted, respectively, at around ARS3, ARS3.75, ARS4 and ARS4.6. 

 Offshore volume is extremely thin, with daily volume in the NDF market estimated at around $20 million, and a futures market featuring physical delivery of the Argentine currency has yet to take shape. 

 "There is so much news and rumors coming out of the local spot market that people don't really know what to do," said Anshu Goyal, a New Jersey-based foreign exchange trader with Lehman Brothers. 

 That has created some wide spreads between bid and ask rates on NDFs, further crimping volume. 

 Traders said the bulk of activity is focused on one-month NDF contracts, and is mostly comprised of dealers adjusting positions. 

 But the trend is definitely stacked towards dumping the peso, which the government began to float in January after scrapping a currency board that had pegged it at parity with the U.S. dollar for more than a decade. 

 The country defaulted on its foreign debt in late December and saw four presidents resign in quick succession as Argentines took to the streets to protest a four-year recession and a freezing of bank deposits. 

 To right itself, the government is lobbying the International Monetary Fund to lend it $20 billion to $25 billion in emergency funding. But foreign investors aren't holding their breath, even as the Fund continues to huddle with officials in Buenos Aires. 

 "We continue to believe that a deal with the IMF is still far away from materializing," Goldman Sachs wrote in its daily emerging markets report Wednesday, adding that IMF mission head Anoop Singh has maintained a "severe tone" since arriving in Argentina last week. 

 IMF spokesman Thomas Dawson suggested as much in London, cautioning that the consultations are "not likely to be an extremely rapid process." 

 U.S. analysts believe the IMF will also urge Argentina to limit its direct interventions in the foreign exchange market in order to conserve scarce funds. 

 In what could also bring new pressure on the peso, President Eduardo Duhalde said this week that Argentina hopes to eliminate limits on bank account withdrawals within three months. The curbs were put in place in December in order to prevent a run on banks, and have dried up liquidity in the local economy. 

 "As liquidity comes back in the onshore market, that'll also weaken the peso," predicted HSBC's Wardle. 

 If the controls are kept in place, the Argentine economy will continue to contract sharply, which would be another reason to sell, analysts add. The government has been forecasting a 5% contraction in gross domestic product this year, but many in the private sector predict the contraction will be twice that. 

 In a bid to blunt peso-selling pressures in Buenos Aires and create an interest rate benchmark, the central bank on Wednesday planned to offer investors ARS50 million in seven-day bills and $25 million in dollar-denominated securities. 

 Lehman's Goyal said there "definitely" was no interest among U.S. investors to take on the central bank notes, given the continued uncertainty in Argentina. 

 Even in Argentina, participation will likely be limited to state-owned banks and other entities with no choice in the matter, Wardle added. 

 Wardle said HSBC expects the peso to end the year at between ARS3.50 and ARS4 to the dollar. 

 -By Mike Esterl, Dow Jones Newswires; 201-938-4026; mike.esterl@dowjones.com

title: The rate differential between bonds with Argentine and foreign law is the highest since debt exchange
text:
Despite the recent improvement, the spread by legislation recently reached its highest level since debt exchange, amid indefinitions over an agreement with the Paris Club and the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

Recent news of negotiations with agencies positively affected bonds, although the impact was greater on foreign law.

At times of increased uncertainty regarding the ability to pay Argentina's debt commitments, investors tend to favor foreign-underned securities, to the detriment of local law.

In recent weeks we have seen a steady expansion in spreads of local law bonds over those of foreign legislation. That is, those governed by Argentine law show higher yields than those that respond to international laws, which is justified on the basis that the latter show greater relative demand.

In this way, the spread by legislation averages 165 basis points, and in some tranches, the spread reaches the highest level since debt exchange.

The spread between laws in the short tranche (bonds at 2029 and 2030) operates with a rate differential of approximately 165 points. This implies a record since restructuring for bonds by 2030 while by 2029 it means trading in the highs zone since debt redemption.

Meanwhile, those who expire in 2035 trade a spread of 50 basic points, which is also at a higher rank since debt exchange.

Finally, in the longer sections, at 2038 and 2041, high differential levels are also observed and in areas of maximums since redemption.

Pedro Siaba Serrate, a strata of Portfolio Personal Inversiones (PPI), added that from late March until now, the weighted average price of securities bounced from the post-restructuring lows to levels he did not see since mid-February, with greater focus in recent days thanks to the good climate of global emerging debt and positive signs regarding renegotiation with the Paris Club.

On the other hand, he added that there was particularity that NY Law instruments received this rebound more directly while local titles lagged behind.

"Looking at the historical evolution, the weighted spread legislation peaked at 169 base points during the holiday Tuesday, although on Wednesday with activity in the local square, this spread was rearranged in the area of 151 basic points," said PPI's strata.

With a similar view, Julio Calcagnino, market analyst at TSA Stock Market Group of the Transatlantic Group, stressed that until last week, all Argentine dollar bonds traded with a above-average legislation gap observed throughout 2021 for each case.

"At the cross-sectional level, the largest spread was observed in 2029 and 2038, both above the average of all papers. In May, foreign law bonds were revalued more than their local counterparts. Without a clear impact of Fernandez and Guzman's tour in Europe on debt negotiation processes with the IMF and the Paris Club, all of this would point to opportunity purchases due to widespread devaluation of local roles," Calcagnino said.

The TSA Stock Market specialist also recalled that some foreign investment banks, such as Citi, recommended the construction of long positions on Argentine bonds, mainly GD29 and GD30, in view of a possible pro-opposition election scenario.

"The spread movement could be due to some timely appetite from outside investors, who would opt for international law bonds to the detriment of local ones," he said.

Causes of spread expansion

Spread expansion is generally associated with increased uncertainty regarding Argentina's ability to re-pay its debt, so investors seek protection on assets with legal jurisdiction abroad to the detriment of bonds governed by local courts.

However, market analysts add other issues related to flows and dollarization of portfolios to explain this behavior.

Rodrigo Benítez, chief economist of Quinquela Fondos, explained that the spread of legislation has been expanding to the extent that the value of bonds falls and they are operated with parities in mind, i.e. their recovery value in the event of non-payment.

In other words, when bonds fall, the risks associated with a credit event tend to grow and investors are often looking for greater protection in foreign-underned bonds at that time.

In addition, the chief economist of Quinquela Fondos argued that the spread between legislation currently shows heterogeneous situations depending on the term of the bonds and is explained by issues of dollarization of portfolios.

"In the short sections (2029-2030) the spread is higher and is in line with the maximum levels since its issuance (7.7% in 2029 and 9.3% in 2030). This situation may be explained in the volume of portfolio dollarization operations. These bonds, for their higher liquidity, are the most commonly used for The Settlement Count (CCL) and MEP transactions. In addition, they are the ones used by the Central Bank of Argentina (BCRA) to intervene in these markets containing spreads. That is to say that they are the bonds that have the highest demand both in their operation in pesos and in foreign currency," the economist said.

Finally, Benitez noted that investors betting on long-term holdings choose foreign law, on the other hand those who only use them as instruments to dollarize operate preferably under local law.

In this line, he said that two particularities have been combined over the past week that have impacted the spread by legislation: "First, the political uncertainty that has been generated around the official position in view of the outstanding negotiations with the Paris Club and the IMF," he explained

"On the other hand, while there were maturities of peso bonds of more than $60 billion held by foreign investors, the bulk of portfolio dollarization operations remain local traders, who use bonds under Argentine law to dollarize, but immediately sell those positions," he said.

Overview of IAS 29

Pursuant to IAS 29, the financial statements of an entity whose functional currency is that of a highly inflationary economy, as mentioned above, should be reported measured in terms of the measuring unit current as of the date of the financial statements. All the amounts included in the statement of financial position which are not stated in terms of the measuring unit current as of the date of the financial statements should be restated adjusted applying the general price index. All items in the statement of income should be stated in terms of the measuring unit current as of the date of the financial statements, applying the changes in the general price index occurred from the date on which the revenues and expenses were originally recognized in the financial statements.

Adjustment for inflation in the initial balances has been calculated considering the indexes based on the price indexes published by the National Institute of Statistics and Census (Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censos or 'INDEC,' per its initials in Spanish).

The principal inflation adjustment procedures are the following:

• Monetary assets and liabilities that are recorded in the current currency as of the financial position's closing date are not restated because they are already stated in terms of the currency unit current as of the date of the financial statements. • Non-monetary assets and liabilities are recorded at cost as of the financial position date, and equity components are restated applying the relevant adjustment ratios. • All items in the consolidated income statement are restated applying the relevant conversion factors, as described in Note 1.1.2 to our consolidated financial statements contained in this annual report. • The effect of inflation in the Group's net monetary position is included in the consolidated income statement, in the item 'Results from exposure to changes in the purchasing power of money.' • Comparative figures have been adjusted for inflation following the procedure explained in the previous bullets. • Upon initially applying inflation adjustment, the equity accounts were restated as follows: ○ Capital stock was restated as from the date of subscription or the date of the most recent inflation adjustment for accounting purposes, whichever is later. ○ The resulting amount was included in the 'Results from exposure to changes in the purchasing power of money' account.

Item 3.D Risk Factors

You should carefully consider the risks described below, as well as the other information in this annual report. Our business, results of operations, financial condition or prospects could be materially and adversely affected if any of these risks occurs. In general, investors take more risk when they invest in the securities of issuers in emerging markets such as Argentina than when they invest in the securities of issuers in the United States and other more developed markets. The risks described below are those known to us and that as of the date of this annual report believe may materially affect us.

Risks Relating to Argentina

Substantially all of our operations, property and customers are located in Argentina. As a result, the quality of our assets, our financial condition and the results of our operations are dependent upon the macroeconomic, regulatory, social and political conditions prevailing in Argentina from time to time. These conditions include growth rates, inflation rates, exchange rates, taxes, foreign exchange controls, changes to interest rates, changes to government policies, social instability, and other political, economic or international developments either taking place in, or otherwise affecting, Argentina.

The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic and government measures to contain the virus adversely affected, and could continue to affect, our business and results of operations, and, as conditions continue to evolve in 2021, we cannot accurately predict the ultimate impact on us.

In December 2019, COVID-19, a novel strain of coronavirus (SARS-COV-2) causing a severe acute respiratory syndrome, was reported to have surfaced in Wuhan, China. COVID-19 has since spread across the world, including Argentina, and on March 11, 2020, the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic. As of April 27, 2020, around 2.9 million cases had been confirmed in Argentina, along with a death toll of approximately 62,000. In response, countries have adopted extraordinary measures to contain the spread of the virus, including imposing travel restrictions and closing borders, requiring closures of non-essential businesses, instructing residents to practice social distancing, issuing stay at home orders, implementing quarantines and similar actions. The ongoing pandemic and these extraordinary government measures have disrupted global economic activity and resulted in significant volatility in global financial markets. According to the IMF estimates, the global economy declined 3% in 2020. In turn, Latin America's economy is estimated to have decreased 5.2%, while Argentina's GDP declined 9.9% according to INDEC. The outbreak of COVID-19 has caused significant social, business, economic and market disruption globally. While the long-term impact on the global economy and financial markets is still uncertain, it is expected to be significant, although the accelerated vaccination programs, could lead to a fast global recovery in 2021.

The Argentine government adopted and continues to adopt multiple measures in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, including a nationwide mandatory lockdown that began on March 19, 2020 and was extended until November 6, 2020, and the mandatory shutdown of businesses not considered essential, including bank offices, which extended until mid-April 2020. As of the date of this annual report, banks are considered essential businesses and are permitted to open to provide most services to clients, in each case with prior appointment, provided that certain health and safety requirements are complied with. At the same time, in order to mitigate the economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and mandatory lockdown and shutdown of non-essential businesses, the Argentine government has adopted social aid, monetary and fiscal measures. On December 29, 2020, the Argentine government started a national vaccination program initially targetted to health professionals. Several vaccines against COVID-19 have been approved for their administration in Argentina, including Sinopharm, Sputnik V and AstraZeneca. After a period of relaxation of the aforementioned restrictive measures and following a large rise in the number of infections in the previous weeks, on April 8, 2021 the government announced a national night-time curfew and additional restrictions.

We cannot assure you whether these measures will be sufficient to contain a severe second wave spread of the virus and prevent a more severe health crisis in Argentina, and if the government will be able to prevent a new economic downturn in 2021, following the economic recovery experienced in the second half of 2020 and first months of 2021.

Some of the measures adopted by the Argentine government adversely affected, and could continue to affect, financial institutions, such as our Group. These temporary measures have included: (i) postponement of loan payments without punitive interests, (ii) deferral of unpaid loan installments from April 2020 to March 2021, (iii) prohibiting banks to charge fees for ATM transactions, (iv) freezing mortgage payments and suspending foreclosures, (v) the automatic refinancing of credit card payments and reduction of the maximum interest rates that can be charged on credit cards, (vi) imposing a minimum interest rate to be paid on time deposits, (vii) imposing the grant of loans to SMEs at subsidized rates, and (viii) forbidding bank account closures. Additionally, some of the government measures were aimed at encouraging bank lending, such as (i) limitations on banks' holdings of notes from the Central Bank (LELIQ), in order to make liquidity available and encourage the provision of credit lines to SMEs, (ii) lowering of reserve requirements on loans to households and SMEs, and (iii) the easing of bank loan classification rules (providing an additional 60 days of non-payment before a loan is required to be classified as non-performing). Some of these measures have been lifted and other softened in the first months of 2021, although the majority of them continue in effect. Moreover, banks dividend distributions are currently suspended until June 30, 2021, and employees' layoffs are prohibited until at least May 31, 2021. For more information on regulations in connection with the COVID-19 pandemic and their impact on our Group, see 'Item 4.B.-Business Overview-Argentine Banking Regulations - Government Measures in Response to the Ongoing COVID-19 Pandemic' and 'Item 5.A Operating Results - The Ongoing COVID-19 Pandemic.' Although these measures may help attenuate the economic impact on the Argentine economy overall, they had and may continue to have a negative impact on our business and results of operations.

The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic and government measures taken to contain the spread of the virus have adversely affected, and could continue to affect, our business and results of operations. Since early stages of the pandemic outbreak, we have transitioned a significant part of our workforce to work remotely, which continues as of the date of this annual report, and which may exacerbate certain risks to our business, including an increased reliance on information technology resources, increased risk of phishing and other cybersecurity attacks, and increased risk of unauthorized dissemination of sensitive personal information. Moreover, we faced and could continue to face various risks arising from the economic impact of the pandemic and government measures, such as (i) a higher risk of impairment of our assets, (ii) lower as a consequence of the temporary restrictions on charging certain fees to customers, and as a result of lower interest rates on loans promoted by the Central Bank and minimum interest rates imposed on deposits, (iii) a possible significant increase in loan defaults and credit losses, with a consequent increase in loan loss provisions, and (iv) a decrease in credit demand and in our business activity in general, particularly new retail lending. During 2020 we have updated and enhanced our expected loss models and have created provisions related to COVID-19, thereby increasing our coverage ratio; however, it is still uncertain how a further spread of the virus could impact in the economy and the ability of our customers to pay their obligations.

We are continuing to monitor the impact of the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic across our businesses. The ultimate impact of the pandemic on our business, results of operations and financial condition remains highly uncertain and will depend on future developments outside of our control, including the intensity and duration of the pandemic, whether new variants of the COVID-19 arise, and the government measures in response of the COVID-19 pandemic, including the vaccination program. To the extent the COVID-19 pandemic adversely affects our business, it may also have the effect of heightening many of the other risks described in this 'Risk Factors' section.

Our business is largely dependent upon macroeconomic, political, regulatory and social conditions in Argentina.

Substantially all of our operations, properties and customers are located in Argentina and, as a result, our business is to a large extent dependent upon macroeconomic, political, regulatory and social conditions prevailing in Argentina. Developments in economic, political, regulatory and social conditions in Argentina, and measures taken by the Argentine government, have had and are expected to continue to have a significant impact on our business, results of operations and financial condition. Argentina is an emerging market and investing in such markets generally carries additional risks.

The Argentine economy has experienced significant volatility in past decades, including multiple periods of low or negative growth and high levels of inflation and currency depreciation. According to restated information released by Argentina's National Statistics Institute (Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censos or 'INDEC' per its acronym in Spanish), Argentina's real GDP grew by 2.7% in 2015, decreased by 2.1% in 2016, grew by 2.7% in 2017, decreased by 2.5% in 2018, decreased by 2.2% in 2019. In 2020, Argentina's GDP decreased by 9.9%, due in large part to the effects of the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic.

Argentine economic conditions are dependent on a variety of factors, including the following: (i) domestic production, international demand and prices for Argentina's principal commodity exports; (ii) the competitiveness and efficiency of domestic industries and services; (iii) the stability and competitiveness of the Argentine peso against foreign currencies; (iv) the rate of inflation; (v) the government's fiscal deficits; (vi) the government's public debt levels; (vii) foreign and domestic investment and financing; and (viii) governmental policies and the legal and regulatory environment. Government policies and regulation -which at times have been implemented through informal or de facto measures and have been subject to radical shifts- that have had a significant impact on the Argentine economy in the past, have included, among others: (i) monetary policy, including exchange controls, capital controls, high interest rates and a variety of measures to curb inflation; (ii) restrictions on exports and imports; (iii) price controls; (iv) mandatory wage increases or prohibition of dismissals; (v) taxation; and (vi) government intervention in the private sector.

Legislative mid-term elections in Argentina will take place in October 2021, by virtue of which one third of the seats in the senate, and half of the seats in the house of representatives, will be up for election. Political uncertainty in Argentina regarding the policies that may be adopted in the future by the government could lead to further volatility and adversely affect Argentina's economy.

We cannot assure you that developments in Argentina will not affect macroeconomic, political, regulatory or social conditions in the country and, consequently, affect our business, result of operations and financial condition.

If the current levels of inflation continue or increase, the Argentine economy and our financial position and business could be adversely affected.

In the past, inflation has materially undermined the Argentine economy and Argentina's ability to create conditions that would permit growth. High inflation may also undermine Argentina's competitiveness abroad and lead to a decline in private consumption which, in turn, could also affect employment levels, salaries and interest rates. Moreover, a high inflation rate could undermine confidence in the Argentine financial system, reducing the Peso deposit base and negatively affecting long-term credit markets.

The INDEC reported a cumulative variation of the CPI of 47.6% for 2018, 53.8% for 2019 and 36.1% for 2020. According to the market expectations survey published by the Central Bank, this tendency is expected to persist, as expectations for 2021 CPI are around 46%.

There can be no assurances that inflation rates will not continue to escalate in the future or that the measures adopted or that may be adopted by the administration to control inflation will be effective or successful. Inflation remains a challenge for Argentina. Significant inflation could have a material adverse effect on Argentina's economy and in turn could increase our costs of operation, in particular labor costs, and may negatively affect our business, financial condition and results of operations.

Fluctuations in the value of the Argentine Peso could adversely affect the Argentine economy.

Fluctuations in the value of the Peso continue to affect the Argentine economy. Since January 2002, the Peso has fluctuated significantly in value. Persistent high inflation, together with formal and de facto exchange controls, have resulted in the past in an overvalued official exchange rate. Compounded by the effects of exchange controls and restrictions on foreign trade, highly distorted relative prices have resulted in the loss of competitiveness of Argentine production, impeded investment and caused economic stagnation. In 2015, the Peso lost approximately 52% of its value with respect to the U.S. Dollar, including a 37.3% depreciation during the last quarter of 2015, mainly concentrated in the month of December when the former administration eased exchange restrictions. In 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2020, the Peso depreciated 8%, 15.6%, 50.7%, 36.6% and 29%, respectively, with respect to the U.S. Dollar. As of April 27, 2021, the exchange rate was Ps.93.34 per U.S. Dollar.

The depreciation of the Peso may have a negative impact on the ability of certain Argentine businesses to service their foreign currency denominated debt, lead to inflation, significantly reduce real wages and jeopardize the stability of businesses whose success depends on domestic market demand, and also adversely affect the Argentine government's ability to honor its foreign debt obligations. In turn, a significant appreciation of the Peso against the U.S. Dollar also presents risks for the Argentine economy, including the possibility of a reduction in exports as a consequence of the loss of external competitiveness. Any such appreciation could also have a negative effect on economic growth and employment and reduce tax revenues in real terms.

The Argentine government's ability to obtain financing from the international loan and capital markets may be limited or costly, which may impair its ability to implement reforms and foster economic growth.

The Argentine government has defaulted on its sovereign debt instruments several times in the past. The most recent financial difficulty to meet its foreign financial obligations occurred in 2019/2020, in the midst of restructuring negotiations with private creditors. As a result, the Argentine government may not have access to international financing, or its access may be costly, may would limit its ability to make investments and foster economic growth. Additionally, companies in the country's private sector may also have difficulty accessing international financing at reasonable costs or at all, as has occurred on prior occasions.

During March 2020, the Argentine government initiated discussions with various groups of creditors to discuss a path for Argentina's debt sustainability. With respect to Argentina's international bonds, in April 2020, the Argentine executive branch approved the restructuring of certain eligible global bonds issued under foreign laws for up to U.S.$65 billion. On August 31, 2020, the Argentine government announced that it had obtained the consents required to exchange 99% of the aggregate principal amount outstanding of all series of eligible bonds, following which the exchange was consummated.

On August 18, 2020, the Argentine government offered holders of its foreign currency bonds governed by Argentine law to exchange such bonds for new bonds, in terms that were equitable to the terms of the invitation made to holders of foreign law-governed bonds. On September 18, 2020, Argentina announced that holders representing 99.4% of the aggregate principal amount outstanding of all series of eligible bonds invited to participate in the local exchange offer had participated. As a result of the exchange offer, the average interest rate paid by Argentina's foreign currency bonds governed by Argentine law was lowered to 2.4%, compared to an average interest rate of 7.6% prior to the exchange.

Notwithstanding the foregoing, despite the renegotiation efforts carried out by the Argentine government during 2020, since September 2020, bond prices have dropped, and the probability of default derived from prices of credit default swaps on Argentine sovereign bonds is around 95% over a ten-year term as of the date of this annual report.

In addition, in June 2018, the Argentine government and the IMF signed a three-year, U.S.$50 billion loan agreement, as further amended to U.S.$57.1 billion through 2021 (the 'IMF 2018 Agreement'). Following an IMF report in February 2020 stating that Argentina's debt may not be sustainable, the Argentine government requested to begin discussions with the IMF to renegotiate the IMF 2018 Agreement. As of the date of this annual report, negotiations with the IMF are ongoing.

We cannot assure you that Argentina will be able to favorably complete the restructuring of its sovereign indebtedness with respect to the IMF 2018 Agreement. In addition, due to past or future defaults on its indebtedness, we cannot assure you that Argentina will have access to international financing in the future, on favorable terms or at all. If Argentina is not able to access financing, it may not be able to foster economic growth and invest in the country. As a result, we cannot assure you that private companies in Argentina will have access to financing on favorable terms or at all, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition and results of operations.

The maintenance or implementation of additional exchange controls regulations, restrictions on transfers abroad and capital inflow restrictions could limit the availability of international credit and could threaten the financial system, which may adversely affect the Argentine economy.

In the past, the Argentine government has increased controls on the sale of foreign currency, limiting transfers of funds abroad. Measures taken by the Argentine government significantly curtailed access to the official foreign exchange market and, as a result, an unofficial U.S. Dollar trading market developed in which the Peso-U.S. Dollar exchange rate differed substantially from the official Peso-U.S. Dollar exchange rate. While the former administration had initially eliminated foreign exchange restrictions in 2016, in September 2019, in response to significant capital flight from the country, the Argentine Central Bank imposed restrictions on foreign exchange transactions, which were effective until December 31, 2019. Following the change in government in December 2019, the Fernández administration has extended the measures, and established further restrictions, including a new tax (impuesto PAIS) on certain transactions involving the purchase of foreign currency by Argentine residents.

The current exchange controls apply with respect to access to the foreign exchange market by residents for savings and investment purposes abroad, the payment of external financial debts abroad, the payment of dividends in foreign currency abroad, payments of imports and exports of goods and services, and the obligation to repatriate and settle the proceeds from exports of goods and services for Pesos, among others. For further information, see 'Item 10.D - Exchange Controls'.

It is not possible to anticipate for how long these measures will be in force or if additional restrictions will be imposed. The Argentine government could maintain or impose new exchange controls, restrictions and take other measures in response to capital flight or a significant depreciation of the Peso, which could in turn limit access to the international capital markets and affect the Argentine economy. In addition, such evolving exchange control restrictions and measures may result in Argentine Central Banks's information requests, enforcement actions and penalties due to diverging interpretations of foreign exchange regulatoins.

As a related matter, the international reserves deposited with the Argentine Central Bank have fluctuated significantly. The international reserves of the Argentine government amounted to U.S.$39.4 billion as of December 30, 2020. Future measures taken by the Argentine government could further reduce the level of international reserves deposited with the Argentine Central Bank in the future.

In addition, since the imposition of exchange controls, the difference between the official exchange rate, which is currently used for both commercial and financial operations, and other informal exchange rates that arise implicitly as a result of certain operations commonly carried out in the capital market (dollar 'MEP' or 'contado con liquidación'), have broadened deeply during 2020 creating a gap of approximately 60% with the official exchange rate as of April 27, 2021.

The Argentine government could maintain a single official exchange rate or create multiple exchange rates for different types of transactions, substantially modifying the applicable exchange rate at which we acquire currency for different purposes. Furthermore, existing or future measures could undermine the Argentine government's public finances, which could adversely affect Argentina's economy, which, in turn, could adversely affect our business, results of operations and financial condition.

The Argentine economy could be adversely affected by economic events in other markets.

Argentina's economy remains vulnerable to external shocks that could be caused by adverse regional or global developments. A significant decline in the economic growth of any of Argentina's major trading partners (including Brazil, the European Union, China and the United States) could have a material adverse impact on Argentina's balance of trade and adversely affect Argentina's economy. In addition, Argentina may be affected by economic and market conditions in markets worldwide, as was the case in 2008, when the global economic crisis led to a sudden economic decline in Argentina in 2009. In 2018, emerging market economies were affected by the change in the U.S. monetary policy, resulting in the unwinding of investments and increased volatility in the value of their currencies, including the Argentine Peso.

In the past, emerging market economies have been affected by changes in U.S. monetary policy, at times resulting in the unwinding of investments and increased volatility in the value of their currencies. If interest rates rise significantly in developed economies, including the United States, emerging market economies, including Argentina, could find it more difficult and expensive to borrow capital and refinance existing debt, which would negatively affect their economic growth.

The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has had, and continues to have, a significant impact on the global economy and the economies of countries across Latin America, the full impact of which cannot be accurately predicted at this time.

Argentina could be adversely affected by negative economic or financial developments in other countries. We cannot assure you that developments in other markets will not affect macroeconomic, political or social conditions in Argentina and, consequently, our business, results of operations and financial condition.

Government or labor pressure to grant salary increases and/or additional benefits may affect business conditions in the country.

In the past, the Argentine government has passed laws and regulations forcing privately owned companies to maintain certain wage levels and provide added benefits to their employees. Additionally, both public and private sector employers have been subject to significant pressure from the workforce and trade unions to grant salary increases and other benefits. The Argentine government has increased the minimum monthly salaries on numerous opportunities. In addition, the Argentine government has arranged other measures to mitigate the impact of inflation and exchange rate fluctuation in wages, or the consequences of the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic.

Labor relations in Argentina are governed by specific legislation, such as Labor Law No. 20,744 and Collective Bargaining Law No. 14,250, which, among other things, dictate how salary and other labor negotiations are to be conducted. Most industrial or commercial activities are regulated by a specific collective bargaining agreement that groups together companies by industry and trade unions. While the process of negotiation is standardized, each chamber of industrial or commercial activity negotiates the increases of salaries and labor benefits with the relevant trade union of such commercial or industrial activity. Parties are bound by the final decision once it is approved by the labor authority and must observe the established salary increases for all employees that are represented by the respective union and to whom the collective bargaining agreement applies.

We cannot assure you that the Argentine government will not adopt future measures requiring that employers increase salaries and/or employee benefits, prohibition of dismissals, duplication of severance payments or that our employees and/or labor unions will not pressure for such measures themselves. Any such increase could result in an increase in our operating expenses and, therefore, adversely affect our results of operations.

Government intervention in the Argentine economy could undermine business and investor confidence.

The Argentine government exercises substantial control over the economy and may increase its level of intervention in certain areas of the economy, including through the regulation of market conditions and prices.

In the past, the Argentine government has increased state intervention in the economy, including through expropriation and nationalization measures, price controls and exchange controls and restrictions on capital flows. For example, in 2008, the administration absorbed and replaced the former private pension system for a public 'pay-as-you-go' pension system. As a result, all resources administered by the private pension funds, including significant equity interests in a wide range of listed companies, have since been administered by ANSES. In 2014, the Argentine government enacted law No. 26,991, which enables the Argentine government to intervene in certain markets when it considers that any party to the market is trying to impose prices or supply restrictions in the market. This law applies to all economic processes linked to goods, facilities and services which, either directly or indirectly, satisfy basic needs of the population (so-called 'basic needs goods'), and grants broad powers to the relevant enforcing agency (Secretariat of Commerce) to become involved in such processes. In addition, in August 2020, the executive branch issued Decree No. 690/2020 which, among other measures, amends the current legal framework to (i) declare information and communications technology services and access to telecommunications networks as essential and strategic public services, (ii) establish new rules regarding the pricing of such services, and (iii) declare mobile telephone services a public service.

In addition, as a result of the public health emergency declared by the Argentine government due to the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, several measures have been adopted to limit the impact on the Argentine economy, including freezing rent prices and public services tariffs, and the prohibition of work dismissals, among others.

In the future, the level of intervention in the economy by the Argentine government may continue or increase, which may adversely affect Argentina's economy and, in turn, our business, results of operations and financial condition.

High public expenditure could result in long lasting adverse consequences for the Argentine economy, which in turn could adversely affect our business, financial condition and results of operations.

During the last years, the Argentine government has substantially increased public expenditures, and has resorted regularly to the Central Bank and to the ANSES to source part of its funding requirements.

In 2018, 2019, and 2020, public sector expenditure increased approximately 22.4%, 37.2% and 52.7%, respectively, and the government achieved a primary fiscal deficit of 2.4%, 0.4% and 6.5% of GDP, respectively, according to the Ministry of Treasury. Primary fiscal deficit for 2020 was partly explained by a decrease in Argentine government income (equivalent to 0.7% of GDP) and an increase in public expenditure (equivalent to 3.5% of GDP). Additionally, the economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic has also required and may continue to require the Argentine government to increase public spending.

We cannot assure you that the Argentine government will not seek to finance its deficit by gaining access to the liquidity available in the local financial institutions. In that case, government initiatives that increase the exposure of local financial institutions to the public sector could affect our liquidity and assets quality and have a negative effect on clients' confidence in the financial system.

A decrease in international prices for the main commodities exported by Argentina could negatively affect Argentina's economic condition.

Argentina's reliance on the export of certain commodities, particularly soybeans and its by products, corn and wheat, has made the country more vulnerable to fluctuations in their prices. A decrease in commodity prices may adversely affect the Argentine government's fiscal revenues and the Argentine economy as a whole.
