title: Fitch Downgrades YPF's IDRs to 'RD' on Exchange Completion; Subsequently Upgraded to 'CCC'
text:
Release date - 18022021

Fitch Ratings has downgraded YPF S.A.'s Long-Term Foreign and Local Currency Issuer Default Ratings (IDRs) to 'RD' from 'C', due to the conclusion of its announced exchange offer.

Fitch has simultaneously upgraded YPF's Long-Term Local and Foreign Currency IDRs to 'CCC' from 'RD', and upgraded the company's senior unsecured notes to 'CCC'/'RR4' from 'C'/'RR4'. The stand-alone credit profile was revised to 'b' from 'c'.

The downgrade and simultaneous upgrade reflect the completion of the announced exchange for its seven outstanding international bonds totaling $6.2 billion notes. Per Fitch's 'Distressed Debt Exchange Criteria,' the IDRs are downgraded to 'RD' upon completion and re-rated as the exchange resulted in a material reduction in the original terms of the bonds, evidenced by the extension of maturities and discounted coupon payment for two-years from issuance of the new notes.

On Feb. 11, 2021, YPF announced the results of the exchange offer. YPF received 59.79% acceptance to exchange the outstanding March 2021 notes for the new senior secured 2026 notes, which are secured by a reserve and payment account, and with 50% of YPF's stake in YPF Luz pledged as collateral. Hold-out bond holders received the cash payment for the outstanding 40.21%, which was approved by the Central Bank of Argentina and has been settled. YPF also announced that it received 43.12% exchange for its April 2024 notes, 37.15% for its March 2025, 24.55% for its July 2025, 19.07% for its July 2027, 20.21% for its June 2029, and 28.45% for its 2047.

Collectively when including the 2021 exchange offer, YPF successfully exchanged $2.0 billion of its $6.2 billion outstanding bonds. The $2.0 billion exchange was allocated among three bonds. First, $775 million for the senior secured 2026 notes, which will have a coupon of 4.0% for the first two years through December 2022, and 9% thereafter, with a quarterly amortization payment made equally beginning in 2023. Second, $748 million for the senior unsecured bond due 2029 was issued with a coupon of 2.5% for the first two years through December 2022, and 9% thereafter with equal semi-annual amortization payments beginning in 2026. Third, $576 million for the senior unsecured bond due 2033 with a coupon of 1.5% through 2022 and 7% thereafter with annual amortization beginning 2029.

Fitch estimates the exchange offer will save YPF approximately $105 million in interest expense annually through the end of 2022, which Fitch expects the company will allocate to upstream capex to ramp up production, increasing production by up to 40,000boed, when assuming that unconventional wells average cost is $5.5 million in Vaca Muerta and each new well produces on average 1,000boed. After 2022, Fitch estimates the company's annual interest from its international bonds from 2023 through 2025 will be approximately $50 million higher before the exchange offer. On a consolidated basis, Fitch's estimates YPF's annual interest expense will average $700 million through 2023.

YPF ratings are in line with Fitch's 'Government Related Entities (GRE) Criteria.' YPF is majority owned by the government and strategically important to the country. YPF's dominant market share in the supply of liquid fuels in Argentina, coupled with its large hydrocarbon production footprint in the country, could expose the company to government intervention through pricing policies or investment strategies. Argentina exerts strong control over YPF through energy regulations and/or its 51% economic interest in the company. Furthermore, Fitch believes Argentina would have strong incentives to support the company under a distress situation as a result of the strong socio-political and financial implications of a default.

KEY RATING DRIVERS

Links to Sovereign: YPF is closely linked to the Republic of Argentina due to its ownership structure, as well as recent government interventions. Argentina controls the company through its 51% stake, and provincial government officials serve on the company's board of directors. In addition, the republic sometimes governs the company's strategy and business decisions. The Argentine government has a history of significant interference in the oil and gas sector. For example, via Decree No. 1277, the government set regulations related to investment levels in the oil and gas sector and domestic price reference points.

In 2019, the government issued Decree 566/19, which negatively affected YPF's cash flows. Although YPF is a leading energy company in Argentina, government policies continue to present challenges, inhibiting its business strategy.

Moderate Leverage: Fitch believes YPF has a moderate leverage profile mostly due to a high total debt/1P and weak EBITDA/interest expense ratio in 2020, which is expected to improve over the rated horizon. Fitch estimates YPF's total debt/EBITDA will be 3.6x in 2020 and improve to an average of 2.3x over the rated horizon; however, YPF's total debt/1P is high, estimated to be USD8.00 per boe, and consistent with the 'b' category. Furthermore, Fitch estimates YPF's EBITDA to interest expense will be 2.6x in 2020 and improve to an average 4.0x thereafter.

High Production Cost Profile: Fitch's rating case assumes production will remain flat averaging 515,000boed over the rated horizon. YPF's cost of production is slightly lower than the guaranteed price under Barril Criollo between May and mid-August 2020 and Fitch's assumed Brent price for 2021 of USD48.00boe. Fitch estimates YPF's half-cycle costs of USD26.5boe and full-cycle cost of USD41.5boe, which are both high and above average for players in the region.

The company's high cost is mostly attributed to higher than average lifting cost of USD13.5boe and high interest cost per barrel of USD5.0boe in 2019, estimated by Fitch. The company's full-cycle break-even implied prices were above weighted average realization prices for oil and gas, primarily as a result of decreasing domestic gas prices and high level of gas production, which accounts for approximately 49% of total production during 2019 (Crude oil production comprised 44% and natural gas liquids 7%).

Volatile Operating Environment: The volatile economic environment in Argentina has inhibited YPF from implementing its business strategy, i.e. unconventional development in Vaca Muerta. Pandemic-related quarantine measures have further stressed the company, as demand for fuels has decreased, gasoline volumes dropped by 70% and diesel by 34%, jet fuel 95%, with a total demand decrease of 50% in April 2020, compared with the previous year. Volumes appear to have recovered but remain below historical averages.

Fitch estimates Argentina's real GDP will contract by 11.2% in 2020, after negative average growth rate over the last three years. Inflation is expected to average 47% between 2020 and 2022, and government debt/GDP ratio is estimated to be 102% in 2020 and 105% in 2021, with a majority of government debt being external 75%-80% over the same time frame.

DERIVATION SUMMARY

YPF's linkage to the sovereign is similar in nature to its Latin American national oil companies (NOCs) peers, namely PEMEX (BB-/Stable), Petrobras (BB-/Negative) and Ecopetrol (BBB-/Negative), and government-owned entities ENAP (A-/Stable), and Petroperu (BBB+/Negative). These companies all have strong linkage to their respective sovereigns given their strategic importance to each country and the potentially significant negative social and financial implication a default could have at a national level.

YPF's upstream business closest peers are Pemex, Petrobras and Ecopetrol. YPF's total production averaged 514,000boed, and the reserve life was 5.7 years, most comparable with Ecopetrol with a 2019 production of 725,000boed and a reserve life of 7.8 years, but less than Petrobras' production of 2.6 million boed and a reserve life of 10 years and Pemex's production at 2.8 million boed and a reserve life of 9.5 years.

YPF has a strong capital structure reporting a gross leverage ratio defined as total debt/EBITDA of 2.4x in 2019 and total debt/1P of USD7.67 per boe compared with Ecopetrol at 1.1x in 2019 and USD5.80 total debt/1P, Petrobras at 2.3x and USD6.60 per boe and Pemex at 6.2x and USD14.70 per boe.

Unlike its peers ENAP, Petrobras, Pemex and Petroperu, YPF is not the sole provider of refined fuels in Argentina. In 2019, the company had nearly a 60% market share. YPF is an integrated energy company, similar to Petrobras and Pemex, offering the company more financial flexibility, while ENAP is predominately a refining company that sells to marketers.

Historically, YPF has operated autonomously with periodic controls of fuel prices and crude, which are currently in effect. Similar to Pemex and Petrobras, YPF has administered an import-parity pricing policy, but is evidence of government intervention with Decree 466/19 and other price controls in 2018 to tame inflation, which is projected to be 50% in 2020. Until recently, YPF has had success in tightening the spread between import parity and local prices.

When compared with downstream-focused entities ENAP and Petroperu, YPF has a lower total debt/EBITDA ratio of 2.4x in 2019 compared with ENAP at 6.7x and Petroperu at 18.0x. Petroperu's elevated leverage is explained by its investment plan to increase capacity by 2021, while ENAP has maintained a higher leverage profile for an extended period of time, but the company is highly strategic for the Chilean governments, and thus it rating is aligned as a result.

KEY ASSUMPTIONS

Fitch's Key Assumptions Within its Rating Case for the Issuer

Average gross production of 515,000boe from 2020-2023;

YPF will be able to increase domestic prices in pesos somewhat but not enough to fully reflect the impact from the recent peso depreciation and international hydrocarbon price increase;

Criollo barrel of USD45/bbl in place from May through Mid-August2020 and applied Fitch's price deck thereafter;

Natural gas prices decrease to USD2.70/MMBTU in 2020, USD3.00/MMBTU in 2021, USD3.25/MMBTU in 2022 and USD3.57/MMBTU in 2023;

Capex cut to be FCF positive over the rated horizon due to refinancing risk;

Downstream sales volume follow Real GDP forecasts;

USD111 million of net proceeds associated with the sale of 11% stake in Bandurria Sur to Equinor and Shell; and a 50% stake in offshore area CAN_100 to Equinor in 2Q20;

Fitch ARS/USD forecasts for year average and end of period during 2020-2022;

Reflects exchange offer with coupon adjustment period per bond;

Annual average capex of $2.5 billion from 2021-2024.

RATING SENSITIVITIES

Factors that could, individually or collectively, lead to positive rating action/upgrade:

The Foreign Currency IDR is linked to the sovereign rating of Argentina and thus an upgrade can only occur if there is an upgrade of the country ceiling of Argentina.

Factors that could, individually or collectively, lead to negative rating action/downgrade:

Argentina's sovereign rating is currently at the lowest level (CCC) allowed under Fitch's sovereign criteria; therefore, a downgrade of Foreign and Local Currency IDR would reflect Fitch's belief that a default of some kind appears probable, or a default or default-like process has begun for the corporate, which will be represented by a 'CC' or 'C' rating.

BEST/WORST CASE RATING SCENARIO

International scale credit ratings of Non-Financial Corporate issuers have a best-case rating upgrade scenario (defined as the 99th percentile of rating transitions, measured in a positive direction) of three notches over a three-year rating horizon; and a worst-case rating downgrade scenario (defined as the 99th percentile of rating transitions, measured in a negative direction) of four notches over three years. The complete span of best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings for all rating categories ranges from 'AAA' to 'D'. Best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings are based on historical performance. For more information about the methodology used to determine sector-specific best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings, visit https://www.fitchratings.com/site/re/10111579.

LIQUIDITY AND DEBT STRUCTURE

Adequate Liquidity: YPF reported USD1.3 billion in cash and cash equivalents in 3Q20. Per Fitch's estimates, this covers roughly two years of interest expense. The company's debt maturity profile did improve after the completion of its exchange particularly the exchange of its 2021 notes to 2026. Fitch expects YPF will continue to roll-over short term bank and trade financing debt over the rated horizon, and its first international bond maturity is in April 2024.

REFERENCES FOR SUBSTANTIALLY MATERIAL SOURCE CITED AS KEY DRIVER OF RATING

The principal sources of information used in the analysis are described in the Applicable Criteria.

ESG CONSIDERATIONS

YPF has an ESG Relevance Score of '4' for Governance Structure due to Argentina federal government's majority ownership in YPF, which has a negative impact on the credit profile, and is relevant to the rating in conjunction with other factors.

Unless otherwise disclosed in this section, the highest level of ESG credit relevance is a score of '3'. This means ESG issues are credit-neutral or have only a minimal credit impact on the entity, either due to their nature or the way in which they are being managed by the entity. For more information on Fitch's ESG Relevance Scores, visit www.fitchratings.com/esg.

title: Five reasons why Argentine country risk rose to its highest level in more than two months
text:
Foreign dollar bonds resumed the bearish path on the last wheels and yesterday country risk reached 1,461 points, the highest figure since November 2 last year. Even Argentine country risk is now about 300 points higher than it did in early September, when the brand new government securities issued by debt restructuring with private creditors came to market.

This securities redemption, for more than $100 billion, was the most successful achievement in the management of Minister Martín Guzmán, in a 2020 plagued by bad news, with GDP falling to about 10 percent.

JP Morgan's country risk index measures the spread of the rate of return on US Treasury bonds (a very secure asset) with its emerging similar ones.

1) Uncertainty over economic policy:

Behind the increase in country risk is the perception of investors from abroad, who see with distrust the economic future of Argentina, with a high fiscal deficit and the possible continuity of restrictions in the face of the advancement of the Covid-19 cases. If after three years of recession the economy does not return to a persistent path of growth, fiscal solvency to deal with debt payment from 2023 will also be weakened.

"The lack of a credible economic plan, uncertainty about negotiations with the IMF, a regrowth of Covid-19 cases, and new restrictions are the main reasons for this correction, while emerging markets and Brazil take advantage of the tailwind and the value of their assets grew considerably," Said Portfolio Personal Investments.

2) Need according to the IMF:

The Argentine Government negotiates with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) an Extended Facilities Agreement, a package usually given to countries experiencing a balance-of-payments crisis. Argentina seeks to postpone the return of disbursements made during 2018 and 2019 for about USD 44 billion, which expire between 2022 and 2023. The agency, in return, calls for an economic programme that includes reforms that balance public accounts.

A GMA Capital report stressed that "Argentina could find a trend change with an agreement with the IMF," while "advances linked to an understanding with the Fund could be more effective in lowering country risk from the current 1,400-point zone and giving renewed momentum to fixed income and stocks."

Country risk had fallen to the 1,100-point zone in September, following debt redemption, now the October highs are approaching, when it touched 1,500

Research for Traders experts also warned of weakness in Argentine fixed income "mainly because of growing mistrust of the future of the domestic economy, and in a context where the Government negotiates with the IMF a credit of extended facilities."

"We hope that the pace of meetings, all virtual, will accelerate in the coming weeks," IMF spokesman Gerry Rice said on Thursday. He added that it shared the view of the Argentine authorities that the country needed a carefully balanced set of policies to promote stability, restore confidence, protect the most vulnerable and lay the foundations for sustainable and inclusive growth.

3) External volatility:

With the announcement of a multibillion-dollar fiscal stimulus plan by US President-elect Joe Biden, U.S. Treasury bonds were re-operated and return rates returned to their highest level in ten months.

The 10-year Treasury bond now yields about 1.1% per annum and this increase in US debt spreads to a rise in U.S. premiumsemerging countries, with amplified impact on Argentina's sovereign titles.

4) Official interventions:

Intervention and regulations of public bodies in the stock exchange dollars (MEP and liquidation) market also affect dollar bond valuations: if they fall, the rate of return rises and country risk increases.

The ban on privateers from buying more than $100,000 nominal per week of sovereign bonds, in particular the Bonar 2030 with Argentine law (AL30) - which is used by public bodies to intervene the market through mass sales - forces investors to come to other securities. The chosen one is the Bonar 30 with New York Law (GD30), which when liquidated by investors to make dollars, falls into its hard currency quote.

5) Doubts about corporate debt:

This week YPF creditors rejected a $6.2 billion oil bond restructuring plan. As a state-owned company, this lack of dollars to honor commitments abroad was assessed by market operators as a negative factor in the weighting of sovereign securities.

On 15 September, the Central Bank established that it will provide companies with only 40% of the currencies they require to write off debts abroad and the rest will have to deal with their own holdings or restructure their liabilities.

In mid-October, partial relief was provided for firms with debt incurred abroad. The BCRA announced that it will allow firms with debts over $1 million to use export currencies to cancel them, although companies must report each spin greater than $50,000.

title: Argentine peso maintains controlled fall with  central bank intervention
text:
BUENOS AIRES, 1 Dec (Reuters) - Argentina's wholesale weight and exchange rate in alternative markets began December with a central bank-controlled devaluation (BCRA) and interventions by official entities to prevent further loss of value, operators said Tuesday.

They added that the monetary entity keeps its sights on the level of liquidity in a month that, out of seasonality, companies require more pesos for the payment of the aguinaldo medium, which would help it to further curb the bleeding of its hit international reserves.

"The exchange rate gap is around 78/83% - below the 120/130% highs reached in October. However, the gap remains at still very high levels by forcing the central bank to maintain foreign exchange sales to contain the pace of devaluation of the wholesale exchange rate," said portfolio personal investment brokerage.

Argentina is in negotiations with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to postpone maturities of a $44 billion loan in an economy hit by the coronavirus pandemic.

The Nation's Senate, with 65 votes in favor and none against, averaged Monday night's penalty on the "Law for the Sustainability of Public Debt" bill. The draft states that the budget law must establish the maximum percentage to be issued in foreign currency and under foreign law with respect to the total authorized issues.

* Wholesale weight lost a slight 0.11%, at 81.39/81.40 per dollar at 12.50 local time (1550 GMT), after BCRA sold $325 million from its reserves in November to bring the currency down by 3.66%. Thus, it supplied private demand, payment of imports and financial debt of companies.

* "Sales are significantly lower than those recorded in recent months (...) The combination of measures that stimulated foreign exchange settlement with mechanisms introduced to order the payment of imports and corporate debts led to the exchange market and improved the outlook," said a BCRA source.

* The Chamber of The Oil Industry of Argentina (CIARA) and the Center for Cereal Exporters (CEC), entities representing 40% of Argentine exports, announced that during the last month companies in the sector liquidated $1,734.3 million, higher by 1.1% compared to October. title: Guzman's nod to Pesce on dollar control
text:
Economy Minister Martín Guzmándetailed on Wednesday that the stock of reserves held by the Central Bank, free of bank lace, reaches $28.365million to date and flatly derailed the use of currencies deposited by financial institutions. The official made this clarification before a senator's consultation during his presentation by the Upper House Budget Committee on the bill to prohibit the Executive from taking up debt and agreeing to fund the Monetary Fund without congressional authorization.

He also referred to the hedge funds that entered the country during the macrism to speculate on carry trade and now push on the exchange rate. The official considered "central to the ordering of the Argentine economy and part of the roadmap for more permanent sustainability". He spinning the course of indebtedness, which generated "$37.7 billion relief in the coming years," as it progresses in a program with the IMF to refinance lending to the country.

"Theissue of debt in the form of government securities is over and we are now with the IMF; and we always maintained is that sustainability must be a state policy. That's why the Nation's Congress needs to play a more important role in strengthening debt sustainability," he said.

The initiative sent to the Senate determines in its first article that "the General Budget Act of the National Administration for each financial year shall provide for a maximum percentage for the issuance of government securities in foreign currency and under foreign law and jurisdiction with respect to the total amount of public securities issues authorized for that financial year".

In its second article, it provides that "any financing program or public credit operation carried out with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), as well as any extension of the amounts of those programs or operations, will require a law" of Congress "that expressly approves it". "Thestatus of programmes with the IMF is also placed because it has consequences thattranscend governments," Guzman added.

Debt versus weights

Consultations by opposition senators focused on the bimonthly situation of the Argentine economy. As for the level of BC reserves available to sustain the exchange rate, the minister noted that the figure is "$28.365 billion". "Those are lace-free. There is also the Chinese swap, the Fund's SDs and the gold. They are liquid even though they all have different degrees of liquidity that deserve different levels of analysis," Guzman said. In lace there are $11.158 million,which ensured "not used" to intervene in the market.

The minister further stated that "today Argentina has a robust commercial surplus with seasonality month and month and with swings day by day". "There are no substantial debt payments for restructuring and capital control with relative effectiveness to contain the pressures that can be seen on the foreign exchange front for financial reasons," said the owner of the Palace of Finance accompanied by Finance Secretary Diego Bastourre and Argentine representative to the IMF, Sergio Chodos.

With regard to negotiations with the Fund, he assured that the project proposing Congress' endorsement for debt-taking "facilitates an agreement with the agency" and assured that, "in dialogue with ministers from the G20 countries, the initiative has been very well received because it gives legitimacy to the process". Guzman reiterated that he will submit "tocongressional consideration the agreement with the Fund and the economic team will be on hand to explain whether we consider that what is agreed is aligned with the health of the country."

With reference to the issuance of debt in indexed pesos, the Minister of Economy said it seeks to "strengthen borrowing in pesos with peso returns." "There is a positive net voluntary pessification. title: Argentina's assets close with hedge improvements over peso depreciation
text:
BUENOS AIRES, 8 Oct (Reuters) - Argentina's bonds closed with slight improvements on Thursday, following a bearish start, while stocks strengthened their upward trajectory in the face of speculative portfolio recompositions given the persistent depreciation of the peso in the absence of a clear economic plan, operators said.

They added that market interest now focuses on the activity of an International Monetary Funds (IMF) mission visiting the country to begin laying the groundwork for the renegotiation of a $44 billion credit in 2018.

"There are currently no positive signs that can bring about a change in pessimistic market expectations, which is reflected in lower turnovers," said Portfolio Personal Investments (PPI).

The Government launched a package of measures a week ago to revive the economy, mainly with the transitional reduction in soybean and derivatives withholdings that may encourage exports, although expected results are not met according to analyst consensus.

"In Argentina, with a run of regulations and interventions, the government threw overboard the mood improvement it had achieved with the delayed but successful debt redemption" for about $100 billion with private holders, said Christian Reos, analyst at the brokerage Allaria Ledesma and Compañía.

* Bonuses in the over-the-counter market ended with a faint average improvement of 0.1%, where the reference 'Bonar 30' rose by 0.8%, in a place that accumulated a decrease of 4.2% in the last five business days.

* Traders note that the high dollar yields offered by local bonds, in a 14% and 15% tone, do not attract investors for risk aversion.

* Country risk developed by JP bank. Morgan was down 15 units, to 1,358 basic points, to 17,00 local time (2000 GMT), away from the 1,297 units with which he closed the previous month.

* In the stock market segment, the leading S&P; Merval index improved by 1.66%, at an average close of 45,482.18 points, accumulating a 10.23% improvement in the last six business sessions with financial stocks leading the trend.

* "Local assets continue to reflect investor caution, while continuing to monitor exchange rate dynamics on a daily basis, as it is the most urgent imbalance to resolve in the short term, as well as fiscal and monetary policy signals that may come from the IMF's mission," one economist said.

* Wholesale peso fell a faint 0.03% to 77.11/77.13 per dollar, with the central bank (BCRA) regulating the liquidity of the square since opening.

"Private market sources estimated that the central bank sold between $15 million and $20 million to supply wholesale demand," said Gustavo Quintana, operator of PR Corredores de Cambio.

* The monetary entity last week abandoned a daily uniform devaluation scheme to adapt the value of the peso to the rate of depreciation required by the situation.

* "In Argentina dollars are missing (...) Net reserves (from the BCRA) drilled $7 billion and liquid reserves dangerously broke $1 billion. The dynamics then became unsustainable and monetary authority reinforced the trap in the middle of last month, even at the cost of increasing the gap and uncertainty," said consultancy Ecolatina.

* In other foreign exchange alternatives, the 'Liquidation Count' (CCL) of the stock market square operated at 153.1 pesos per dollar, in the Electronic Open Market (MAE), the so-called 'MEP dollar' was traded at 140.6 units, and in the marginal strip, the currency marked a new historical minimum level of 158 per dollar and a gap of 104.85%.

title: More trap is no solution
text:
Argentina needs no more interventionism, but regains confidence through a coherent plan that turns its vicious circles into virtuousThe functioning of an economy has an inexorable rule: when you try to solve a problem by attacking its consequences and not its causes, not only does it not solve it, but add new problems. A second rule: if difficulties are expected to resolve themselves, the damage caused to society will be more destructive than if their solution is properly designed. And in an unscheduled process in which the facts are not foreesed, the most harmed will be those with the least capacity to defend themselves against harm.Recent exchange and financial measures are unaware of these rules. Persistent drainage of Central Bank reserves causes loss of confidence. The government's ability to correct the structural problems of our economy is not believed.

 Moreover, every step he has taken since his assumption, on 10 December 2019, has been counterceding to the direction indicated by common sense.This fundamental failure should not be attributed to the pandemic, but to a vision of the problems overshadowed by retrograde ideologisms and to a management that favors obtaining judicial impunity for corruption during the previous management of those who now govern. For the latter there is a carefully crafted plan, while there is no plan for economic management.The presentation of the 2021 budget confirms this shortcoming gradually that the poor coherence and unrealism of its assumptions will be analysed. There is no confidence in the Government's ability to resolve the serious economic situation. A currency issuance is observed in unreleased magnitudes, which even the most layman foreshadows higher inflation. The data show that the highest weight retention during quarantine for a few weeks is being reversed to apply to consumption, but in a significant share, to dollar savings.The philosophy of these exchange-change measures has been to try to correct the problems of the trap with more trap and also to transfer the costs to the private sector. This is clear for companies that need foreign exchange to comply with credit services taken in foreign currency. They will no longer be able to do so with the official exchange relationship with which they export or the one governing the imports with which they must compete. They now warn that a step has been taken towards the unfolding of the foreign exchange market, as the facts will have to use a strong dollar for the cancellation of its debts abroad. The Government requires restructuring maturities and, if not, will not sell dollars for that purpose. It will not be easy for companies to renegotiate with their creditors, which will be inevitable for those who do not want or cannot meet their payments at a substantially higher exchange rate. The detrimental impact this measure will have on trust can be understood. It's the opposite of what it takes to correct the causes of the problem.The purchase of $200 per month for savings has not been abolished, but purchases in foreign currency by credit card will be deducted from the quota from now on and a 35% advance in income tax has been incorporated. Thus, along with the tourist tax, it takes the cost of a dollar to 131 pesos. Even if the tax could be recovered, this seemed to the government enough to discourage purchases from the Central Bank. However, any increase in the quote on the informal market will make it interesting to buy dollars from the reserves again. This increase has already begun.When the same good has two different prices in the same place, naturally people and companies try to buy it at the lowest price andsell it to the major. The same goes for the dollar, and this applies not only to personal purchases to save - it would be leaking - but also to business operations. Underbilled exports or overbilled imports, as well as export smuggling and other mischief, cannot be avoided. The trade balance vanishes at the same time as a breeding ground for corruption is generated, and we know the propensity for these vices of those who now rule.For companies that adhere to ethical rules, this scenario is extremely daunting. They may desist from investing and, more seriously, from operating in the country that imposes these practices. It is no coincidence that so many major companies are deciding to withdraw from Argentina.Prevention and combat against covid-19 has led to costs. It has also happened in other countries. But the economic and social consequences have been substantially more serious in Argentina. Macroeconomic imbalances. particularly fiscal spending multiplied between 2002 and 2015, when public spending increased from 39% to 46% of GDP. Neither this overflow, nor a deforming labor legislation, nor the tangle of regulations, nor the suffocating tax pressure could be properly corrected in Macri's management.Overcoming it through structural reforms is now a necessary but not sufficient condition for regaining confidence. Added to this should be an improvement in legal certainty characterized by a genuine division of powers, effective combat of drug trafficking and greater guarantees for personal security. From the highest levels of government, unrestricted respect for property law should be demonstrated and not reversed, as has been the case. If all this had an execution principle within an orderly plan, confidence would resurface and the current vicious circles would become virtuous. Then the president of the Central Bank would not have to appeal to one or be distressed by his reserves. When so many measures undermine the building of the trust needed to bring the stage back, citizens wonder whether it is gross impericiate or whether other unconfessable targets move our rulers.

title: ANALYSIS-Argentina  currency  crackdown dims investor hopes of economic rebound
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Sept 17 (Reuters) - Argentina's standing in global markets is at risk once again after it moved this week to further restrict access to dollars as foreign reserves dry, a move analysts say will hit its much-needed economic revival and investor sentiment.

The central bank on Tuesday tightened the noose for dollar purchases, adding a 35% tax on people who tap a $200 monthly quota, and said card payments abroad would be included in the allowance. It also limited corporate access to foreign currency.

The move sparked a selloff of Argentine bonds and stocks, while the price of dollars in unofficial markets spiked, widening a large gap with the official rate. It also put Argentina's inclusion in the MSCI Emerging Markets Index at risk.

"It shows total desperation," said Agustín Monteverde, an economist at consultancy Massot Monteverde & Asociados in Buenos Aires. "They have just hung a sign around their necks that says 'meltdown'."

The tightened controls underscore how Argentina's left-leaning Peronist government is struggling to unwind interventionist policies that have long dogged the resource-rich country, despite sealing a major recent debt restructuring deal.

The central bank now finds itself in a precarious position, with net reserves having fallen to as low as $6.8 billion including holdings of gold, according to a J.P. Morgan estimate, despite capital controls put in place last year.

Barclays said in a note that the controls would "buy some time," but the measures, together with the country's forecast for a deep 4.5% fiscal deficit in 2021, raised worrying signals.

"This is more evidence that authorities are not willing to address the fiscal and monetary imbalances driving the capital flight and reserves drain. And they weaken growth prospects."

The South American nation is headed for a 12% economic contraction this year, which would mark the third straight year of recession, and is just emerging from its ninth sovereign default after restructuring nearly $110 billion in foreign currency debt.

It faces negotiations with the International Monetary Fund to delay more than $40 billion in payments due in the next few years. Investors said tighter controls could muddy those talks.

Capital controls have created a nearly 90% divergence between official and unofficial peso rates, while the central bank has been printing money to help support emergency government measures to battle the fallout from the coronavirus pandemic.

Meanwhile, dollar demand has remained high, with Argentines long wary about the stability of their currency and high inflation, and fearful of a repeat of the draconian measures of previous governments, including forced conversions of dollar deposits to pesos.

Central bank reserves are officially at $42.5 billion, though on net terms could be as low as $2.9 billion, excluding gold, J.P. Morgan calculates. That would be down from a comparable $10.1 billion at the end of last year.

'KICKING THE CAN'

Gustavo Ber, chief economist at consultancy Estudio Ber, said the tightened controls had a negative impact on traders.

"Within a climate of mistrust, these would-be measures do not resolve underlying imbalances, but can only stretch out the process of draining reserves over time," he said.

J.P. Morgan said in a note that it was matter of Argentina "kicking the can down the road".

"In all, we see in these measures a temporary policy arrangement that does not tackle the factors behind the monetary disequilibrium, while jeopardizing the pace of an already timid activity recovery pace post-COVID-19."

The measures will hurt companies' access to dollars in the official market for settling debt services, with the government looking to encourage firms to lower their debt loads in foreign currency.

President Alberto Fernández defended the measures, saying dollars should be for investment, not savings.

"We are building the logic of an economy that no longer promotes speculation and wants dollars to stop being a speculation tool," he said.

Some 3.9 million Argentines bought dollars in August in the official market, according to estimates from market operators. Many sold them immediately in informal markets, where they can turn a quick profit due a much high dollar valuation there.

Economists said the move dimmed hopes for a solid macroeconomic plan that would generate confidence in the country, lower pressure on the peso and lead to dollars coming back via investment.

"The government had two paths: to finally propose an economic program that would allow it to get out of capital controls and allow public accounts to be put in order, or a new very restrictive tourniquet," said Fausto Spotorno, an economist at the Orlando Ferreres & Asociados consultancy.

"The latter is what it has just done." (Reporting by Eliana Raszewski and Jorge Otaola; Additional reporting by Rodrigo Campos; Editing by Adam Jourdan and Paul Simao)

title: *Fitch Rtgs: Argentine Banks Increased Public-Sector Exposure a Credit Negative
text:
9 Sep 2020 16:00 ET  Press Release: Fitch Rtgs: Argentine Banks Increased Public-Sector Exposure a Credit Negative


 
 
The following is a press release from Fitch Ratings : 
      Fitch Ratings-New York/Santiago-09 September 2020: Interventionist regulations by Argentina's central bank (BCRA), such as capping interest rates offered on loans, placing floors for deposit rates amid very low credit growth and forbearance programs that exclude bank holdings of newly issued sovereign debt from regulatory limits for public-sector debt exposures, have increased Argentine banks' exposure to the public sector, Fitch Ratings  says. These developments are viewed negatively from a credit perspective, given the government's weak financial profile and the banks' increasing concentration risk as a result of these measures. Amid a backdrop of inflation adjustments enacted this year that eroded bank profitability, interest rate caps and floors further reduced Argentine banks' profitability. Banks have been forced to invest their excess liquidity in public sector assets, mainly central bank securities and other sovereign bonds, given the lack of alternative profitable options. At current low levels, public sector assets do not affect the banks' ratings (IDRs of 'CC'); however, this exposure could become more of a constraint over the medium term as the sovereign is lifted out of default. Fitch expects banks' public-sector holdings to decline gradually when private sector lending resumes, although this will be heavily dependent on the path of the economic recovery. However, some banks only invest in BCRA assets as they have significantly less risk than sovereign bonds, although some asset classes are less profitable. Fitch believes this strategy is much more conservative and supportive of credit. To compensate for interest rate controls, the Central Bank has been reducing the legal reserve requirement (encaje) and expanding the limit for Leliq (central bank short-term securities), which pay a 38% interest rate. When banks take deposits at 33%, part of the funds held to meet the legal reserve requirement are placed in Leliqs at 38%. The rest are either lent to the private sector, invested in REPOS with the BCRA that pay 19%, or are invested in more risky options (like sovereign bonds linked to inflation). Nearly the only type of private-sector credit currently growing in Argentina is under the credit facility for small and medium-sized enterprises established by the central bank, which carries an interest rate of 24% 

The recent agreement for the sovereign debt restructuring is good news for the financial system but is only the first step of many that the government has to take to reduce the huge macroeconomic imbalances and revive the economy. The agreement is positive, as it will likely help to normalize relations with the international financial community. It should also boost investor, business and hopefully consumer confidence, which will contribute to economic recovery and benefit the banking system. The agreement also opens the door for international debt issuances for the private sector. This will also provide more flexibility for those banks that need to refinance maturing debt or access longer term funding at lower interest rates, although most banks do not need external financing due to current liquidity levels. Nevertheless, risks to Argentina's operating environment amid the pandemic fallout are clearly skewed to the downside, which led to Fitch's revision of its outlook on the operating environment and asset quality scores to negative from stable for these banks. Market volatility, a sustained contraction in real terms of loans, rising nonperforming loans, higher credit costs and rising administrative expenses due to high inflation will further exacerbate financial profile risks.

title: Fitch Rtgs: Argentine Banks Increased Public-Sector Exposure a Credit Negative
text:
Fitch Ratings-New York/Santiago-09 September 2020: Interventionist regulations by Argentina’s central bank (BCRA), such as capping interest rates offered on loans, placing floors for deposit rates amid very low credit growth and forbearance programs that exclude bank holdings of newly issued sovereign debt from regulatory limits for public-sector debt exposures, have increased Argentine banks’ exposure to the public sector, Fitch Ratings says. These developments are viewed negatively from a credit perspective, given the government’s weak financial profile and the banks’ increasing concentration risk as a result of these measures.

Amid a backdrop of inflation adjustments enacted this year that eroded bank profitability, interest rate caps and floors further reduced Argentine banks’ profitability. Banks have been forced to invest their excess liquidity in public sector assets, mainly central bank securities and other sovereign bonds, given the lack of alternative profitable options. At current low levels, public sector assets do not affect the banks' ratings (IDRs of ‘CC’); however, this exposure could become more of a constraint over the medium term as the sovereign is lifted out of default. Fitch expects banks’ public-sector holdings to decline gradually when private sector lending resumes, although this will be heavily dependent on the path of the economic recovery. However, some banks only invest in BCRA assets as they have significantly less risk than sovereign bonds, although some asset classes are less profitable. Fitch believes this strategy is much more conservative and supportive of credit.

To compensate for interest rate controls, the Central Bank has been reducing the legal reserve requirement (encaje) and expanding the limit for Leliq (central bank short-term securities), which pay a 38% interest rate. When banks take deposits at 33%, part of the funds held to meet the legal reserve requirement are placed in Leliqs at 38%. The rest are either lent to the private sector, invested in REPOS with the BCRA that pay 19%, or are invested in more risky options (like sovereign bonds linked to inflation). Nearly the only type of private-sector credit currently growing in Argentina is under the credit facility for small and medium-sized enterprises established by the central bank, which carries an interest rate of 24%

ArgentinaSovereignExposure

The recent agreement for the sovereign debt restructuring is good news for the financial system but is only the first step of many that the government has to take to reduce the huge macroeconomic imbalances and revive the economy. The agreement is positive, as it will likely help to normalize relations with the international financial community. It should also boost investor, business and hopefully consumer confidence, which will contribute to economic recovery and benefit the banking system. The agreement also opens the door for international debt issuances for the private sector. This will also provide more flexibility for those banks that need to refinance maturing debt or access longer term funding at lower interest rates, although most banks do not need external financing due to current liquidity levels.

Nevertheless, risks to Argentina's operating environment amid the pandemic fallout are clearly skewed to the downside, which led to Fitch’s revision of its outlook on the operating environment and asset quality scores to negative from stable for these banks. Market volatility, a sustained contraction in real terms of loans, rising nonperforming loans, higher credit costs and rising administrative expenses due to high inflation will further exacerbate financial profile risks.

title: Argentine reserves drip out even as government tightens controls
text:
BUENOS AIRES, June 4 (Reuters) - Argentina's foreign currency reserves are falling fast despite the government's tightening of access to dollars, hitting the lowest level since early 2017 in May as the country struggles to control the coronavirus and a long-simmering debt crisis.

Central bank reserves fell almost $1 billion last month as the entity looked to prop up Argentina's peso, and have tumbled around $3 billion since early January. They now stand at $42.6 billion, down from a peak near $80 billion early last year.

The low levels have raised a red flag as Argentina looks to hike emergency spending to fight the COVID-19 pandemic, dig out of a biting recession and appease foreign creditors pushing for a bigger payout in a $65 billion debt restructuring.

The central bank has sought to restrict companies' access to dollars in recent weeks. Private citizens can only buy $200 in foreign currency on the official exchange market per month, and must pay a steep tax.

"Despite the restrictions on buying foreign currency ... growing uncertainty has unleashed a new round of falling reserves," local consultancy Ecolatina said, adding the "alarming levels" could prompt more tightening.

The South American country imposed tough capital controls last year after a market crash led to a dramatic pick-up in foreign currency demand, as the central bank looked to prop up a weakened peso and savers shifted to safe-haven dollars.

Argentine officials say they want to relax controls once the economy has been stabilized and a debt deal reached. But fears remain about a damaging run on the peso in a country that has struggled to build confidence in its currency for years.

The central bank's current international reserves amount to less than the total value of Argentina's imports last year.

Central bank interventions have helped keep the peso mostly stable recently, but its value on unofficial markets has plummeted, creating a worrying gap with the official rate.

The government is inching closer to a vital debt restructuring, but still faces tough hurdles to reach a comprehensive deal with creditors.

"While the negotiations last, we expect strong control over foreign exchange operations will remain in place given the backdrop of falling reserves and high demand for dollars," said Argentine financial advisory Portfolio Personal Inversiones.

pressure as the number of coronavirus deaths and infections
surged in China.

title: Argentine peso edges down as  central bank intervention  sets price floor

BUENOS AIRES, Oct 31 (Reuters) - Argentina's peso currency edged down on Thursday morning, held largely in check as the central bank offered $50 million in the foreign exchange market, in effect setting a price floor at 59.99 pesos per greenback.

The embattled currency, which has steadied since Argentine authorities imposed capital controls last month, dipped 0.4% to 59.95 pesos per dollar, traders said.

Argentina's markets have been held in limbo following a general election on Sunday, as traders and investors await signals from President-elect Alberto Fernandez about the future direction of Latin America's no. 3 economy. (Reporting by Jorge Otaola; Writing by Adam Jourdan)

title: JP Morgan regroups: abandons license to trade on the Porteña Stock Exchange
text:
By Carlos Burgueñocburgueno@ambito.com.arThe very low level of operations in the Argentine capital market that has declined since the 2018 crisis; the little certainty that this can be recovered in the medium term and some distrust of what an eventual next opposition-toned government (especially to financial business in Argentina in general) could cause one of the most waged houses by the government of Mauricio Macri a few days ago he made a final decision. JP Morgan returned on 2 October (the news became known in recent days) its license to operate on the local market, through a letter sent to the National Securities Commission (CNV) where the international bank deregistered as a stockbroker. While it was a house of operations that was hardly in use, the resignation of operation and the delivery of the license somehow mark an end of time.

 The license had been opened in early 2016 to operate in what was expected to be an expansive capital market and growing in both volume and widespread profits. A spiralization of local and global interest in betting on offers that would theoretically multiply before a country that, hand in hand with the new government, would return to capitalism after the populist experience, especially after the last four years of management of Cristina Fernández de Kirchner.

JP Morgan not only opened a representation on the Buenos Aires Stock Exchange (it had withdrawn in 2002, after the crisis of convertibility), but also bet big on the success of Christianity. The Us entity had been the workplace of several of the most important officials of the Macrism. Among others they had passed through their Offices of Wall Street and the rest of the world Alfonso Prat Gay, Luis "Toto" Caputo and Vladimir Werning,all men of maximum responsibility in different stages of the first three years of government of Mauricio Macri,who also maintained management relationships with the bank during his task in the civil service. It had also been a key strategic ally in the first two years of Change management. It had opened an office in Argentina in mid-2015 and intervened in the most important operation of the Government of Mauricio Macri: the placement of the Bonds of the Argentine Republic at the beginning of the management Let's change to pay the holdouts. In total, JP Morgan had participated in voluntary debt placements of about US$2.3 billion in Macri's first year in power, outperforming other houses such as Citigroup, Santander, BBVA and Deustche Bank and HSBC, all entities that, with more or more or more less presence, they had always operated in the country and had never left the local square, even in the times of default and Kirchnerism. The good relationship continued (and intensified) throughout 2017 and until March 2018 JP Morgan recommended to its customers in its reports to bet on Argentina. Even in a job given to the bank's management slums around the world in the first week of April 2018 (already with the novelty of the consolidated Fed's interest rate hike), it recommended the long-term peso positions issued by the Argentine government and the Bank centrico. Including the Lebac.

However, on April 25, 2018 the romance ended. On that day they began to reach the capital market, and violently (at any exit price) orders to buy positions in Lebac from "big hands", which by definition, can decide, for better or worse, the fate of an entire period of Operations. The rumor thatcirculated that day in the international banks that operated Lebac the most (both American and European) was that the sellers were few. No more than three. And that the intention was to part with all the holding in that central bank title and buy dollars quickly, closing the "carry trade"circuit. The price offered at the beginning of the day was $20.50, almost a peso higher than the quote just a day earlier, thus the conviction of the orders created even more slobs in Argentine traders. The biggest surprise came when it became known, almost by an oversight of one of the bond sellers to one of the Central Bank authorities, which at the center of sales was the US bank JP Morgan. On that day, it began to detach from the most symbolic titles of Macrism: the Lebac of the BCRA,the instrument by which Argentina's exchange rate stability was also maintained.The April 25 financial chronicle described a "perfect storm." All the ghosts numbed on some side of the screens of the country's major operators in the country and the world coincided in a single day: the March rate rise in the United States, the start of the trade crisis with China, the local ghost of the indomitable inflation and its battle against interest rates in pesos, end-of-month payments to importers, delay in the settlement of the sogera, the beginning of the application of the financial income tax and its influence on the profits of the Lebac , the eternal debate within the Macrism over the rise of tariffs, the threat of further spikes in fuels and the eventual lack of dollars from drought. Analysts were already publicly questioning the effects of that failed 28-D press conference (2017) at which Marcos Peña live and live took away the BCRA in view of the whole country's responsibility to control the monetary base and set the goals for to address the most important problem in the Argentine economy: inflation. Since that post-election day, Peña took personal control of the official management of the Argentine economy, a decision that had not yet been digested by the markets, and which raised doubts about the true official conviction of placing the fight against the inflation in the maximum ranking of official priorities.

JP Morgan's call to part with the Lebac, buy dollars and leave the Argentine market generated widespread fear in the government. To such an extent that the decision to accept the transaction was consulted with Mauricio Macri himself, who authorized the departure of the BCRA dollars to supply the demand of the American bank. Immediately after the sale of dollars to JP Morgan was endorsed, two other major trades completed the need for foreign exchange sales outflows out of BCRA's reserves for $1.472 million. A record number, which with weeks would be surpassed. A few weeks after that April 25, JP Morgan himself was distributing a lapidary report to his VIP clients. In it he considered whether the tool that the BCRA had implemented to deal with the run (the interest rate rise) could be insufficient antidote to the obvious capital flight that had been initiated and revised to the worse all its forecasts for the economy Argentina in 2018: 2.4% growth and 22% inflation. It also advanced a dollar to 24 pesos as of December. Given what happened at the end of 2018, the advances were even children.

title: The dollar's multiple prices returned to Argentina and analysts see potential risk
text:
GUSTAVO STOCKThe multiple dollar quotes are back in Argentina. Like what happened during the iron exchange rate strain imposed by the government of Cristina de Fernández de Kirchner between 2011 and 2015, in the last three weeks the mechanisms to circumvent the restrictions launched on 1 September last were reactivated.In addition to the increase in demand for the parallel dollar or "blue" that is achieved through caves or "trees", legal operations have been growing strongly with which you can buy foreign exchange in the capital market, either to leave them in the country or to send them to an account on the outside."In this new change control, the restrictions are basically aimed at companies.

 That's why companies that want to dollar their portfolios and turn dividends or resources abroad have no choice but to turn to the MEP dollar or the Settlement Spot," says Eric Ritondale, chief economist at the consulting firm Econviews in Buenos Aires.The MEP is the dollar that is obtained through the purchase in pesos of bonds that are then sold in dollars in the local market. The Count with Settlement arises from a similar mechanism, but the difference is that the sale of the bonds or shares is credited abroad, allowing to take away currencies from the country.Unlike the trap implemented by Kirchnerism, the current controls impact people less. At that time, all individuals who wanted to buy dollars had to go through the Federal Revenue Administration (AFIP) filter first. That discretionary lock limited the purchase of dollars on the official market to the extreme for various purposes, from treasure to trips abroad. This time, however, the new controls allow the purchase of up to $10,000 per month per person without the need to ask for any authorization. In addition, there are no restrictions on accessing dollars for travel or any extra taxes for purchases abroad.Control is much stricter for companies. Companies and institutional investors are prevented from buying foreign exchange on the official market for treasure and can only access dollars on the official market to pay for imports or debt.It is the cost that companies are paying for the value of the dollar to be able to take currency out of the country, as is apparent from the Settlement Counted transactions."Companies are prohibited from transferring profits or dividends abroad, which leads them to become more than through alternative mechanisms taking into account the fear of what will come," says Fernando Baer, associate economist at Quantum Finance in Buenos Aires. "Disarming the current exchange rate scheme of restrictions will necessarily push up the price of the dollar, and those expectations make those who want to have dollars pay a higher price through the available roads," he added.Last Friday, the value of the dollar that resulted from the Operations of Counted with Settlement reached 68.29 Argentine pesos. In practice, that means companies prefer to pay 20.5% overcost over the wholesale official exchange rate to$yupuitize their portfolios and place currencies outside the country. The MEP dollar, meanwhile, closed at 65.86 Argentine pesos, 16.2% more than the official exchange rate.With the limitations on the purchase of dollars, the government of Mauricio Macri managed to stabilize the price of the US currency in the official market around 57 Argentine pesos and, as important as that, stop the massive withdrawal of deposits from banks. However, analysts focus on the evolution of the gap between the official exchange rate and the rest of the quotes resulting from legal transactions forbuy currency. "For now, access to the exchange market is not as restricted as in the kirchnerism years, and so there isn't as big a gap as that at the time," Ritondale says. "But if the controls were to intensify, the gap will surely tend to grow to 50%," he added.The likelihood of the bolt being reinforced is tied to the dollar shortage.Although the gross reserves of the Central Bank of the Argentine Republic (BCRA) add up to about US$ 50 billion, if they discount, among other items, a currency swap with the Bank of the People's Republic of China, loans with the International Bank of Basel and a portion of the disbursements of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) which is intended only to strengthen stock, net reserves amount to about US$ 13 billion."If the $5.4 billion IMF disbursement that was scheduled for this month is not finally realized, the government is going to have to turn to the BCRA to honor the debt by December," Ritondale says. Treasury maturities add up to $6.5 billion by the end of the year.With ever-increasingly limited firepower to intervene in the exchange market, no one in Argentina rules out that change control is spinning. "Most likely in the coming weeks we will see hardening of exchange rate restrictions in areas where the BCRA detects that there are more leaks," Baer says.Copyright Grupo de Diarios América - GDA/El Pais/Uruguay

title: Christine Lagarde: "Without the IMF, the situation in Argentina would be much worse"
text:
Christine LagardeOutside the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the agency's former managing director, Christine Lagarde, gave an interview to the AFP agency in which she referred to the decision to approve the two stand-by agreements with Argentina and assured that, without the intervention economic crisis in the country "would be much worse."

"What would have happened if we hadn't been there? if we hadn't done anything? I think it would have been a lot worse. For me there is no doubt about this,"said Lagarde, who formally left her post on 13 September and is quick to become the next president of the European Central Bank (ECB). The leading candidate to succeed her in her previous role is Bulgarian economist Kristalina Georgieva.

In addition, Lagarde indicated that in June 2018, when the IMF approved the first salvage - of US$50 billion - Argentina was in a situation of financial isolation where the agency had become the only source of financing international lybere that the country could count on. "I went that way, I touched the doors of many countries. I received many kind words and gentle supports, but no funding," he said.

"When Argentina knocked on our door it was in a particularly difficult situation. We tend to forget about that because everyone is focused on Argentina today,"he added.

While Lagarde also stated that even in the early stages of programme implementation, she considered that "there was little chance" of it's stabilizing the economy. But he emphasized that the work of the entity is to provide support.

Three months after the first loan, and after the first loan failed to bring calm to economic players at both the national and international levels, the IMF expanded the credit to $57 billion: at least as of June 2019, this figure accounted for 61% of total loans provided by the entity around the world.

title: UPDATE 1-Argentine peso steady after further controls, dips in black market
text:
(Adds black market peso rate, central bank intervention)

BUENOS AIRES, Sept 12 (Reuters) - Argentina's peso was steady on Thursday morning at around 56.2 per U.S. dollar after the country announced further control measures to protect the embattled currency, though it dipped in the unofficial black market.

Argentina's central bank late on Wednesday announced measures requiring anyone buying foreign currency to present a sworn oath promising to wait at least five days before using it to purchase bonds, closing a loophole that had allowed people to turn a quick profit.

The gap between the official spot rate and the black market rate widened, however, on Thursday morning with traders quoting the unofficial price down 1.26% to 59.75 per dollar. The gap is a sign people think the spot price is artificially high.

Traders said on Thursday the central bank was offering dollars in the market from its reserves to shore up the peso, which lost a quarter of its value in August after a shock landslide primary election defeat for President Mauricio Macri.

Argentina authorized currency controls earlier this month after the peso plunge, an about-face by President Mauricio Macri, who had previously lifted many protectionist practices of his predecessor, Cristina Fernandez de Kirchner. title: UPDATE 7-Wall Street traders pump up Argentine peso as  currency  controls hit home
text:
(Adds Fitch upgrade, updates other prices)

By Cassandra Garrison and Jorge Otaola

BUENOS AIRES, Sept 3 (Reuters) - Argentina's peso surged on Tuesday, pumped up by Wall Street traders cheering President Mauricio Macri's capital controls that are aimed at protecting the beleaguered currency.

The peso closed 5.39% higher at 55.98 per U.S. dollar, traders said, its strongest level in a week after a near record low close on Friday. Country risk, which soared to its highest level in more than a decade last month, also fell.

Traders said the central bank intervened to support the peso in the afternoon by selling dollars from its reserves. The bank, which declined to comment, has intervened in the past, selling nearly a billion dollars in the second half of last week alone.

The currency rebound gives some relief to Macri, after a shock primary election battering last month sparked a sharp crash in the country's bonds, equities and the peso, which lost around 26% of its value against the greenback in August alone.

Argentina's S&P Merval stock index, however, took a hit in afternoon trading, closing down 11.9% at a two-year low in a slide that local analysts attributed to global trade jitters.

"All the markets are in the red and a weakened country like Argentina, with a complicated political situation, gets hits even more," said Hector Scasserra, director of local brokerage firm Arpenta Sociedad de Bolsa.

In Europe, the pounding of Argentina's bonds also eased after they had fallen to record lows on Monday, while there were tentative gains in some foreign-traded bank shares.

Ratings agency Fitch upgraded Argentina's long-term issuer debt rating to "CC" or just barely above default from "restricted default" saying the new rating reflects their view that "a further default or debt restructuring of some kind is probable."

Frankfurt-listed American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) of Grupo Financiero Galicia were up 0.6% after having tumbled 7.7.% on Monday while Banco Macro SA's ADRs fell over 6% in New York, where markets were closed on Monday for a holiday.

MarketAxess data showed Argentina's century bond traded marginally higher while the January 2028 bond dipped under 37 cents on the dollar.

The black market peso, available via unofficial traders, also rose on Tuesday, although not as sharply as the official spot rate. Following a fall on Monday, it has now diverged from the official rate by the largest margin since 2015, a sign of tension over pricing of the currency.

STILL AN EMERGING MARKET

Index provider MSCI said it was closely monitoring developments in Argentina but that the country's "emerging market" status for the purpose of MSCI indexes remained valid for now as MSCI Argentina only held foreign-listed shares.

Argentina was included in the emerging markets index in May, potentially boosting inflows to the eight stocks that were added.

Any reclassification of Argentina in the widely followed indexes would first require a public consultation from MSCI.

On Sunday, the government authorized the central bank to restrict purchases of dollars as it burns through its reserves to prop up the peso. The currency controls were a 180-degree turn for Macri, a free-markets advocate who abolished capital controls after he came to power in 2015.

It was the government's latest attempt to stabilize the peso, which has lost around 20% of its value since opposition presidential candidate Alberto Fernandez emerged as the clear front-runner in the Aug. 11 primary election.

On Tuesday, the government also said in a decree published in the country's official gazette that it would unilaterally hike the minimum wage by 35% over the next few months. Argentina's 12-month inflation is running at close to 55%.

Fernandez and his running mate, former President Cristina Fernandez de Kirchner, are considered a riskier prospect by investors, who fear Argentina could return to the interventionist policies of her former government.

On Monday, central bank president Guido Sandleris called Argentina's financial system "strong" and said the bank would adhere to its strict monetary policy, despite the currency restrictions.

Sandleris, speaking at a news conference, said the bank was in talks with the International Monetary Fund to "redefine" the monetary goals for September under its $57 billion financing agreement. (Reporting by Marc Jones in London; Cassandra Garrison, Eliana Raszewski and Jorge Otaola in Buenos Aires and Rodrigo Campos in New York; Writing by Adam Jourdan; Editing by Rosalba O'Brien, Steve Orlofsky and Sandra Maler)

title: The five points to understand argentina's new change control
text:
Instead of distinguishing itself from rival Cristina de Kirchner as an alternative to avoid ingenuity, Macri takes similar measures. (PanAm Post Photomontage)Starting Monday, September 2, Argentines will have to ask permission to buy dollars. Two months to go until the elections and President Mauricio Macri signed a decree imposing limits on the purchase of foreign exchange, and outrage was unleashed over the return of a measure imposed by his predecessor, who now ran for the vice presidency, Cristina Fernández de Kirchner.

After the STEPS, the primary presidential election, the threat of the return of Kirchnerism caused a collapse in markets and the loss of the value of the peso against the dollar. With which, the Argentines went to the banks to withdraw their savings or, to kill them.

To curb this phenomenon, through the DNU (Decree of Need and Urgency) 609/2019, now the limit to buy dollars per month is 10,000. This compares to the exchange rate trap imposed by its predecessor who is now seeking to return to power.

Macri rose to power and the first thing he did was revoke the change control that CFK imposed just days after assuming the presidency, in October 2011 and progressively increased until 2015. It imposed 15 restrictions on the purchase of dollars and consumption, even outside the country, requiring citizens to have authorization from the tax collection authority: AFIP. While the current limit is on the maximum purchase and not on the extraction or consumption.

With the dollar hovering around 60 pesos, the purchase limit amount would be 600,000 pesos. So the measure would not affect the bulk of the population, more considering that the minimum wage is 12,500 pesos per month; that is, the maximum amount exceeds 48 times.

What to understand:

Until now, the absence of "banking trap" was the only hallmark that the Macri government held with Kirchnerism. They're back in the way of agricultural withholdings last year. There is no strong economic differentiation to show, compared to elections where they were marked as an alternative to the above.The news was announced on the same day that the most anticipated football match of the year, Boca – River, was played. It had been said that on Monday there was going to be news and that the senators would know beforehand, but the news appeared in the media before the Argentine superclassic to de-hide it.Although the UND has a deadline of December this year, it is possible that if the situation is not in place, the deadline will be extended. This is often the case in Argentina with all the strong interventions of the state in the economy. VAT at 21% in the 90s was to be temporary, the check tax also, the same with social plans, etc., which means that the temporary deadline will not be met.It is worth noting the institutional breakup involved in the measure, since the decree restores to the Central Bank of the Argentine Republic the power to approve or to fail the purchase/sale of dollars. Faculty that had been taken away from him by lifting the previous government's trap. So it's much easier to restrict amounts and transactions now. And although the amount they determined now, $10,000 per month doesn't affect the bulk of the population, a pandora's box opens, because the number could change from 10,000 to 100.It's news again.the parallel dollar, known as the blue dollar; name that arises during Kirchnerism, is now back on everyone's lips. The informal dollar was already almost even lyfore d'olading with the banks, now one official price will emerge and another will emerge on the black market.Exporters must also settle currencies for their exports to the local market within five business days (maximum) after collection or 180 days after the boarding permit and 15 days for commodities.

Summary of measures

Posted by Agustín Etchebarne on Sunday, September 1, 2019

PanAm Post consulted with economist Roberto Cachanosky on this subject and explains that:

"When quantitative restrictions are made to the purchase of a good at a maximum price, it is because it is being rationed by quantity. This happens when you put a maximum price on any merchandise. Every maximum price is always put below the market price. No one puts a maximum price at the same price as the market or above the price at which the market operates.

Since the offer of the good in question does not reach that artificially low price, in this case the dollars, the decision of governments is to ration by quantity. It is the same as when you put a maximum price on toilet paper and then it is established that each person cannot carry more than four rolls per purchase. Here a maximum amount of dollars is set to be purchased per month for each individual and the shift official will decide how much you authorize to buy from the companies. The obligation to enter grain export currencies in a short time will cause the producer to retain more grains to save on grains that are dollars. So exports can decrease and foreign exchange income from exports to be lower than expected by adding more exchange rate tensions to existing ones."

Now is growing expectations of how this UND will affect the local economy and this, in turn, the presidential elections that are coming, where the current representative participates as an alternative to the return of the allies of Raul Castro and Nicolás Maduro, but instead to highlight the differences he has with them to excel, he adopts similarities.
