title: Argentina's dollar fever
text:
The problems generated by the dollar in Argentina became part of the permanent agenda of the whole society. The current management took the issue seriously and tried incessantly to reduce the fiscal deficit, contract the monetary issue and increase international reserves.

Each of these issues was addressed consistently, achieving considerable changes that, by the way, are quantitatively measurable. Since August 2018, the Government has reduced the money issue to virtually zero, narrowed the primary deficit by 2.5%, and doubled international reserves via IMF borrowing.

However, and despite this, the dollar in Argentina went from $20 in April 2018 to $60 per dollar in August 2019. A 200% change. How is this possible? How do you explain such a slump after so much effort?

The dollar went from $20 in April 2018 to $60 in August 2019.

To measure the effectiveness of an action, it is always advisable to measure it comparatively with a similar one. One case is the exit from convertibility, where the dollar went from being worth $1 in December 2001, to $2.8 per dollar in 2003, (180%). In 2002 the worst crisis in Argentine economic history was experienced, however the devaluation (considering the context) was even more benign than the current one.

Another valid comparison is that which occurred in Argentina during the second largest global crisis in history: "Lehman Brothers", in 2009. The devaluation at the time was 30%. In both cases, the shift government increased its fiscal deficit and expanded and relaxed the amount of currency in the hands of the public.

But then, if the current government was more tax and monetary success, is there anything clearly identifiable that previous governments have done and the current one never did to prevent a cash run?

It is highly likely that this is happening in the field of exchange rate intervention. Central banks in emerging countries have several ways of intervening in the exchange market:there are ineffective, medium-effective and highly effective ways. The difference between the ineffective and the highly effective is that the former accompany a devaluation by softening it (what we see today), while the latter reverse the devaluation generating appreciation of the local currency.

Intervening in a market requires intelligence and a specific strategy to make intervention as effective as possible. The key is how the Central Bank sells the reserves. Passive intervention strategies prevent the price from rising from a certain level, or ensure that the value in question does not rise so quickly, simply by accompanying it.

The other way of trading implies that when the central bank decides to intervene, it sells dollars at sequentially lower prices. This way of intervening is called active intervention strategies.

Our central bank, in the last four years never used the active intervention mechanism,always used the liability, supplying foreign exchange to the market, but increasingly, at ever higher prices, generating a scope of negotiation between the rest of buyers and sellers at ever-higher values. However, the most effective mechanism would have been to sell at lower prices.

But if the Central Bank actually sold the dollar at lower prices, is it possible that there is more demand at those levels, and therefore would it lose its reserves more quickly?

Conversely than the rest of the products, in the case of the dollar, a higher price, rather than meaning lower demand(if the price of the tomato is higher, less tomato), implies an increase in appetite for ticket purchase. This happens because an x-price risather generates massive advertising via average, leading to increased demand for coverage from the public.In the case of the dollar, a higher price generates an automatic retraction of the offer.

According to the law of supply and demand, if the price of the tomato goes up, on the supply side (sell side) there will be more tomato producers eager to offer their merchandise. However in the case of the dollar, a higher price generates an automatic retraction of the offer,that is, who planned to sell dollars, in the face of the accelerated price rise, retracts and sells less or sells nothing. The combination of these two factors creates a pressure effect on trading, which spirals the value of the currency to completely unexpected levels, which in many cases are inconsistent with the fundamentals of the economy.

So are we saying that, in certain situations, the dollar rise could be a possible bubble? In certain situations, most likely. It is still difficult for this bubble to burst on its own, because product prices inflation, causing the dollar's ridiculously high price to cease to be so, and for other domestic prices to settle to the new level of the US currency and not Vice versa.

Therefore, with an active intervention by the BCRA what is generated is a drop in the price that prevents the mass spread of the product and thus prevents greater demand. On the other hand, eventually by generating a considerable drop in the price (clicking the bubble), exporters/dollar sellers know that waiting for a higher price is pointless and thus avoiding the speculation that the drip sale produces. The conclusion, even when it seems crazy, is that at many times in time, lower dollar prices mean lower demand and higher exchange supply of foreign exchange.

To synthesize, we will say that a considerable price increase, at a certain moment, awakens what we call "dollar-fever or dollar fever" in society. So avoiding abrupt climbs, it is possible to keep the virus asleep.

A change in currency behavior, leading to recurring, unexpired hikes, recreates widespread behavior that spirals demand for dollars and reduces the supply/sale of dollars to a minimum. An active dollar-fever virus.

In my 17 years participating in the exchange market I have seen the different efforts of the Argentine Central Bankintervene, I have also monitored the interventions of the Turkish lira and the Brazilian real. And in all cases, except in these last 4 years in our country, central banks when they intervene do so with active policies,lowering the price of the dollar, or what is the same, appreciating the domestic currency, punishing with this those who bought expensive on the one hand, and hurting those who speculated waiting too long to sell at a higher price, on the other.

Passive intervention policies are apparently primarily responsible for the spiralization of the dollar price in Argentina.

Passive intervention policies, it appear to be primarily responsible for the spiralization of the dollar price in Argentina, and each exchange rate increase of this kind, was responsible for a subsequent spiral in inflation that caused it to that high price of the dollar, become the new floor, and the conditions are prepared for a next round of feedback between dollar and domestic prices.

It is not rational that in a 12-month period, where international variableshad remained stable, local variables (deficit, issue and reserves) improved ostensibly, the currency performed bullishly in the range of permanent historical crisis. After the result of the STEPS and debuting the default of the debt, you reach a fire scenario, with the house already incinerated and with very little water available. Let's hope it's not too late.

title: UPDATE 16-Argentina says to extend maturities of international bonds, IMF debt
text:
(Adds bond market and political context)               

By Eliana Raszewski and Hugh Bronstein               

BUENOS AIRES, Aug 28 (Reuters) - Argentina will negotiate with holders of its sovereign bonds and the International Monetary Fund to extend the maturities of its debt obligations as a way of ensuring the country's ability to pay, Treasury Minister Hernan Lacunza said on Wednesday.               

At a news conference after meetings with an IMF team visiting Argentina, Lacunza said the government would "re-profile" the maturities of debt owed to the IMF under a $57 billion standby agreement.               

Interest and principal payments on bonds issued under international and local law will not be altered in the re-profiling. The changes in maturities would be aimed at obligations held by institutional, rather than individual investors, he said.               

"The priority today is to guarantee stability, because it is useless to launch reactivating measures if there is no stability. The first thing is to recover that stability," Lacunza said at the news conference in Buenos Aires.               

The peso took a beating during the day, even though the central bank heavily intervened in the foreign exchange market for a second consecutive day.               

Argentine asset prices have gotten slammed since the Aug. 11 primary election showed business-friendly President Mauricio Macri has surprisingly little public support in his campaign to win a second term in the October general election. He was trounced in the primary by center-left Peronist challenger Alberto Fernandez, who is now the clear front-runner.               

"President Macri instructed me to solve the short-term problem to guarantee electoral stability, but also in the medium- and long-term so as not to leave a problem for the person who follows, be it he or another candidate," Lacunza said.               

He said the measures were taken "so that the president can deploy his policies without the restriction of imminent, or too high, debt maturities."               

Argentina's peso closed 3.1% weaker at 58.1 per dollar on Wednesday, even as the central bank sold $367 million of its reserves in a second consecutive day of heavy intervention aimed at controlling the peso's fall.               

Worries over Argentina's ability to meet its dollar-denominated debt obligations have increased since the Aug. 11 primary. The peso has lost almost 22% of its value against the U.S. dollar since then. The weakness of the currency has inflamed market concerns about Argentina's ability to pay its dollar-denominated obligations.               

Changes in the maturities of short-term debt, known as Letes and Lecap, will be between three and six months, Lacunza said.               

He said changes in maturities of bonds issued under Argentine law would require approval from Congress.               

"The markets will see this as a default," Hernan Esteves, economist with Buenos Aires consultancy FyEConsult, told Reuters.               

"The problem is that you have a debt restructuring proposal launched by one government, but that will have to be executed by the next government," Esteves said. "That makes it very difficult to manage an orderly restructuring."               

During trading hours on Wednesday, both Argentina's century bond and the January 2028 traded near 42.5 cents on the dollar, their lowest on record according to MarketAxess data.                              

"RECOGNIZING REALITY"               

"I don't like to use the word default. I prefer to think of it as recognizing reality," said Roger Horn, executive director and senior emerging market strategist at SMBC Nikko Securities America in New York. "With bonds trading in the 40s (cents on the dollar) the market was already expecting a worst-case scenario. It's better to deal with it now than six months from now."               

The IMF said in a statement that it was analyzing the government's new debt plan. Argentina has taken "important steps" to address liquidity needs and safeguard reserves, said the statement from IMF spokesman Gerry Rice.               

The central bank issued a statement saying it would continue to implement a "restrictive monetary policy" and continue intervening in the foreign exchange market to bolster the peso.               

The pushing out of debt maturities was aimed in part at preserving the central bank's dollar reserves, which stood at $57.9 billion as of Aug. 26.               

"The decisions that have been taken prioritize the use of international reserves to preserve monetary and financial stability, even if this implies delaying payments to large public debt investors," central bank chief Guido Sandleris said in a separate statement.               

"These decisions should lessen the pressure on the foreign exchange market, reduce the eventual demand for foreign currency and guarantee the availability of resources to limit volatility," it said.               

Macri took office in late 2015, promising to use orthodox economics to end the cyclical crises that have afflicted Argentina for decades.               

But he overestimated his ability to attract the foreign direct investment needed for sustainable growth, while under-estimating the effect that cutting public utility subsidies would have on inflation. His popularity fell as consumer prices, especially home heating gas and electricity bills, shot higher.               

The economy is currently in recession with 55% inflation.

title: Reserves already down $9.5 billion in August: the 7 causes behind the collapse
text:
Guido Sandleris (Maximiliano Luna)In the midst of the crisis that untied among investors following the RESULT of the PASO, the Central Bank's reserves suffered a drastic decline, which threatened at least to remain or even accelerate in the coming weeks. Stock closed on Friday at $58.259million, but with a risk of a sharp decline in the coming months.

The phenomenon, which is one of the main reflections of the level of market mistrust in Argentina, is monitored daily by the bCRA owner, Guido Sandleris. Obey not one but multiple causes. At some point you can see the fall in reserves as the counter-face of the government's need to avoid another spike in the dollar's price in the pre-election and perhaps after the election as well.

In August alone, the fall in reserves already exceeds USD 9.5 billion, with a level ending Friday at $58.2 billion. Presidential candidate Alberto Fernandez suggested the need to "take care" of reservations, but this desire is in the way of a major obstacle. It would be difficult not to use them if at the same time it is intended to control a new exchange rate jump following the devaluation that led to the dollar from $46 to $55 in the wholesale market after the August 11 primary election. Much more considering that anxiety will increase as the election approaches.

Central BankSpecifically, what is behind this accelerated loss of reserve level? The seven main reasons are as follows:

Debt maturities: This is the main target of IMF disbursements, which originally led Argentina to ask For financial assistance from Washington. All capital and interest maturities are paid on the Fund's loan, with the consequent impact on reserves. It is within the terms of the agreement and has been fulfilling the various obligations month by month. However, the debt repayment failed to restore investor confidence and markets remain closed to voluntary financing for Argentina.

Currency interventions of theCentral: after the STEPS, the institution that chairs Guido Sandleris began selling dollars directly to supply more supply to the market and stop the escalation of the currency. It had not done so until now, as it had been softening exchange rate movements with futures sales and raising the interest rate. These sales are directly reflected in the reserve stock.

Treasury Dollar Sale: As part of the negotiation reached with the agency earlier this year, an agreement was reached for the Treasury to sell $60 million daily through tenders, until the end of the year. In this way, efforts were made to supply the market with a constant supply of dollars to avoid abrupt fluctuations in the exchange rate. This objective had been achieved in a reasonable way, until the result of the STEPS caused a big jump in the exchange rate.

Not Letes renewal: it is also linked to the need to pay the debt. But in this case, as these were short-term maturities, dollar debt renewal had been adequately met. It is possible that in the nextTuesday's tender will only get a partial renewal of the $900 million in Letes that are held by the private sector. If so, the Treasury will have to pay with dollars that are deposited in the BCRA. Until the end of the year, the maturity of these very short dollar securities amounted to up to USD 6.5 billion.Return of a loan to banks: it happened in the last week. The fall in bonds prompted a clause that allowed a consortium of six international entities to apply for the repayment of a loan granted for the purpose of strengthening reserves. The cancellation of the "repo" (loan against bond guarantee) caused in the middle of last week a decrease of USD 2.6 billion in the stock of reserves of the Central.

Fall of dollar deposits: There are few economists discussing the desirability of accounting as reserves of the fittings that banks make in the Central of fixed terms in foreign currency made by individuals and companies. Clearly these are currencies that belong to savers and cannot be used by the BCRA. Since the result of the STEPS, some US$2 billion has come out of the banks, approximately 6% of the total hard currency deposits. Banks have plenty of liquidity to cope with that exit, but it is reflected in reserve reduction.

Foreign exchange oscillation: as part of the reserves is found in other currencies, any quote change has an impact on stock. This was noted mostly in July, when the yuan's devaluation in the face of China's trade war with the United States marked a drop of nearly $300 million. This was a one-off fact, but it reflected the effect of a weakening of currencies such as the yuan or eventually the euro on reserves.

title: Economist close to Alberto F. calls for review of IMF deal by December
text:
Emmanuel Alvarez Agis, former deputy minister of Axel Kicillof and close to Alberto Fernandez, called for accelerating the renegotiation of the deal with the Monetary Fund. The economist, who this week shared a talk with former Central Bank President (BCRA) Luis "Toto" Caputo, noted that the next step by the economy minister should be to travel to the United States to bring a new agreement with the IMF and whether it can be reviewed before December, they must do it. He also praised Guido Sandleris's work this week during the exchange rate run.

Agis called for an urgent review. "If the agreement has any point where the IMF says it needs to be reviewed, it needs to be reviewednow. Because the economy cannot transit without an agreement with the IMF untilDecember, it is very important that the IMF confirms that it will disburse the money it has to disburse and at the same time it says, we have effectively wrong again with the economy Argentina and we're going to review our model."

"Thenext economy minister's first step is to take a plane toWashington. And the second will not return in 10 minutes with a non-serving agreement, as has been going on here with the agreement with the IMF," Alvarez Agis said in dialogue with Mitre's "Early Saturday" program.

"Anything done in the economy needs the IMF's endorsement because the only strong financial challenge the Argentine economy has is to return the stand by," the economist said. What has happened with the agreement with the IMF is that we have complied with it to the letter and here we are: with the exchange rate at $60, with inflation above 50% and with the economy falling for the third time in two years in a new recessionary cycle. It has to be restructured, reformulated."

In turn, Agis plotted his diagnosis of the errors of the current agreement. "On monetary policy, the IMF only in April this year understood what the real conflict of the Argentine economywas: a monetary policy that was very inadequate in the first version of the IMF, which was worse when it put us in that area of no intervention and that only in April he understood that Argentina needed the discretion to be able to intervene in the exchange market. And fiscally, it seems to me that the IMF has to understand that it is drowning the Argentineeconomy, which is in recession and which cannot continue to be asked for these levels of adjustment because all we are going to do is deepen the recession."

"The only goal we have with the IMF, which is the fiscal goal, with this level of recession, we will break in in December. In September, the IMF has to endorse the last quota for this year, and monetary targets, with this currency slump, are sure to go into crisis. The IMF is going to come and overhaul the economy and the first thing you have to understand is that the agreement is not down because the government violated it, the agreement is down because it was misconfigured and there the responsibility is shared: half the government and half the IMF".

On the other hand, Alvarez Agis was critical of the latest government measures and praised Guido Sandleris's work at the Central Bank, with whom Alberto F.'s economic team already has dialogue. "In this context I would have to take three measures: control thedollar, control the dollar and control the dollar. Taking steps to alleviate a situation you still don't know how serious it is is is a mistake. And it can feed back the phenomenon of financial instability," the economist said close to the Front of All presidential candidate.

"The President with the statements of Sunday and Monday put all Argentines at risk andgenerated a very complex financial situation. The action that the Central Bank had on Monday and all week was impeccable. title: Fearful Argentinians withdraw their dollars after election impact
text:
Argentines are withdrawing dollars from banks and prefer to keep them at home since President Mauricio Macri's defeat in the primaries caused the fall in weight.

Savers withdrew more than $700 million from their dollar accounts on Monday and Tuesday, according to the most recent official data. This equates to 2.3% of the total dollar deposits in the financial system.

Although already accustomed to currency crises, many Argentines were still traumatized by the so-called pen, an economic measure that was arranged in 2001 to freeze bank accounts and avoid dollar withdrawals.

Those dollars are considered part of the central bank's gross external reserves, and withdrawals explain why this agency's reserve fell by $2.6 billion this week to $63.7 billion.

Foreign reserves also fall because the institution sells dollars to shore up the weight; So far this week, US$503 million was used in interventions in the foreign exchange market.

title: WRAPUP 5-Argentine markets gripped for second day by election-related fears
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Aug 13 (Reuters) - Argentina's peso closed weaker again on Tuesday following a second day of market turmoil triggered by opposition candidate Alberto Fernandez's landslide victory in a primary election that dealt a severe blow to President Mauricio Macri's re-election chances.               

The peso closed 4.29% lower at 55.9 per U.S. dollar after touching 59 to the dollar earlier. The currency had hit an all-time low on Monday of 65 to the dollar, a drop of 30%, on fears that a Fernandez government could take Argentina back to interventionist economic policies.               

The central bank has sold $255 million of its own reserves since Monday to help steady the currency.               

"The market thinks Fernandez will likely default and impose capital controls and renegotiate with the IMF. In a nutshell, the market thinks Fernandez is the return of populism," said Claudio Irigoyen of Bank of America Merrill Lynch (BAML).               

Fernandez, who has former President Cristina Fernandez as his running mate, pulled off a stunning upset in the primary with a wider-than-expected 15-point lead over Macri, a free-market proponent.               

Monday's crash in the peso unnerved global equities investors, with markets already jittery over the Sino-U.S. trade war and protests in Hong Kong.               

"Yes, Argentina is a small economy. However, the last thing global markets want to see is another market-friendly government fall to populism and/or geopolitics," said Rabobank strategist Michael Every.               

A Brazilian hedge fund was among the casualties of Monday's market rout on Argentine assets, with at least 75% of its equity exposure, suffering losses between 25% and 59%.               

Newfoundland Capital Management of Sao Paulo was hit with a loss on paper of around $55 million, as its bets on four Argentine companies in agribusiness, natural gas, energy distribution and telecommunications imploded.               

The weaker peso quickly translated into higher prices on Argentine store shelves. Some shops selling household appliances in the capital Buenos Aires, at a loss for how to price their products amid the fluctuating exchange rate, stopped printing price tags and instead asked customers to inquire.               

There was also doubt over the future of an "essential goods" program introduced by Macri in April to fix low prices through October for 64 basic food products. The secretariate of trade did not respond to a request for comment on whether the government would renegotiate the prices with companies.               

Buenos Aires resident Florencia Nagy, 31, said, "The atmosphere has been tense" in the city.               

"A lot of anger, a lot of confusion, many people thinking that leaving the country could be an option," said Nagy, who said she voted for candidates from more than one party in the primary.               

BLAME GAME               

In an interview Monday, Fernandez said he was willing to cooperate with the current government after his primary triumph on Sunday sent the peso, stocks and bonds reeling.               

The primary results showed Fernandez, a former cabinet chief, was well placed to win October's general election in the first round. He blamed Macri for the market turmoil.               

"The dialogue is open, but I don't want to lie to Argentines. What can I do? I'm just a candidate. My pen doesn't sign decrees," Fernandez said in an interview with Argentine TV channel Net TV broadcast on Monday.               

Fernandez, regarded as a moderate within the Peronist movement, has said he would seek to rework Argentina's $57 billion standby agreement with the International Monetary Fund if he won the general election. He has proposed an economic and social pact to combat inflation, which is running at 55%.               

Macri, too, deflected responsibility for the financial volatility, saying at a news conference on Monday that the opposition should "self-criticize" its own policies in the wake of the market reaction.               

Macri, a scion of one of Argentina's wealthiest families, came to power in 2015 on promises to kick-start Latin America's third-largest economy via a liberalization wave.               

But the promised recovery has not materialized and Argentina is in recession.                              

'JUST AN EXAMPLE'               

Though Argentines are accustomed to a decades-long cycle of peso weakness and inflation, the severity of this week's market reaction resonated on the streets of Buenos Aires, with some bracing for a long period of economic hardship.               

"If we get the same result (as the primary) in the October election, the country will be worse off," said Jazmin Lia, a 25-year-old student who said she voted for Macri in the primary.               

"What's happening with the exchange rate and the collapse of the market is just an example of what will happen," Lia added.               

Carolina Fiuza, 31, blamed Macri for the market volatility and said it seemed more like a "strategy than a reality." She said she was not worried about the market meltdown.               

"I see people desperate for the peso value to increase. I see everyone thinking that it will devalue even worse in October. In the end, I think everything will be work out, as always," said Fiuza, who voted for Peronist candidate Roberto Lavagna in the primaries.               

Argentine assets had not recorded the kind of simultaneous fall seen on Monday since the South American country's 2001 economic crisis and debt default, Refinitiv data showed.               

Investors were still assessing the damage caused by Monday's crash. Argentina's country risk rose 164 basis points to 1,631, the highest since 2009.               

Index provider MSCI said it has not yet considered reclassifying the recently upgraded Argentina stock index out of emerging markets despite the massive spike in volatility and decline in prices.               

Argentina's century bond fell over six points on Tuesday to trade at 51 cents on the dollar, compared with around 75 cents on Friday, according to MarketAxess data.               

As concerns rise about Argentina's ability to meet its debt obligations, investors are looking closely at the government's ability to roll over its peso maturities, including short-term notes known as 'Letes.'               

"Markets will be sweating bullets each time one of these maturities come due," Jeffries Fixed Income said in a note to investors.               

Argentina on Tuesday sold $409 million in 105-day Letes, according to a statement issued by the Treasury, adding that it had canceled a planned sale of 210-day paper. The government sometimes shortens the maturities of new debt sales in times of market upheaval.

(Refiles to fix typo in headline)

By Cassandra Garrison and Hugh Bronstein

BUENOS AIRES, Aug 12 (Reuters) - Argentine President Mauricio Macri vowed on Monday to win a second term despite a surprisingly strong performance by the opposition in the primary election that set off a shockwave through markets, crashing the peso currency and sending stocks and bonds tumbling.

Macri said he would "reverse" the result of Sunday's primary, but acknowledged that a weaker peso triggered by the surge in support for Peronist opposition candidate Alberto Fernandez and his running mate former President Cristina Fernandez would fuel inflation.

The peso closed 15% weaker at 53.5 per U.S. dollar after plunging some 30% to a record low earlier in the day after the primary election prompted market fears over Argentina's potential return to the interventionist economics of the previous government.

Refinitiv data showed Argentine stocks, bonds and the peso had not recorded this kind of simultaneous fall since the South American country's 2001 economic crisis and debt default.

"I trust we will have a more even election in October that will allow us to go to a second round. Those who don't want to go back to the past will join us," Macri said at a news conference, adding that he was not considering a cabinet reshuffle.

Fernandez, a former cabinet chief, dominated the primary vote by a much wider-than-expected 15.5 percentage point margin over the president.

Fernandez has said he would seek to "rework" Argentina's $57-billion standby agreement with the International Monetary Fund if he won October's general election. An IMF spokeswoman declined to comment on the Argentine primary result, citing a policy of not commenting on political developments.

Despite Macri's struggles to turn the economy round, investors see the Fernandez ticket as a riskier prospect.

Argentine stocks were among the top losers on the Nasdaq index, and the local Merval stock index closed 31% weaker. Falls of between 18-20 cents in Argentina's benchmark 10-year bonds and century bond left them trading at around 60 cents on the dollar or even lower.

Morgan Stanley downgraded its recommendation for Argentina's sovereign credit and equities from "neutral" to "underweight" and said calculations suggest the peso could fall another 20%.

"Given the narrow path ahead, our view is that a high degree of policy continuity is a must in order to maintain macro stability," Morgan Stanley said in a research note. It predicted "further downside pressure and volatility" in bond prices.

Argentina's central bank intervened, selling $105 million in the foreign exchange market to defend the peso in the face of the massive sell-off. The auction used the bank's own reserves for the first time since September of last year, traders said.

MACRI STRUGGLES

Macri, a scion of one of Argentina's wealthiest families, came to power in 2015 on promises to kick-start Latin America's third-largest economy via a liberalization wave.

But the promised recovery has not materialized and Argentina is in recession with inflation at over 55%.

An acute financial crisis last year hit the peso and forced Macri to take the IMF loan in return for pledging to balance Argentina's deficit.

Sunday's result indicated that Fernandez had enough support to clinch the presidency in October's first round, without having to go to a November run-off election.

A candidate needs at least 45% of the vote, or 40% and a difference of 10 percentage points over the second-place runner, in order to win the presidency outright.

Argentina's main political parties had already chosen their presidential nominees, allowing the primary to serve as a first concrete measure of voter sentiment.

The peso weakening was dramatic but Win Thin, global head of currency strategy at Brown Brothers Harriman in New York, said he does not expect an emerging markets-wide contagion beyond perhaps Brazil and Uruguay given that the peso is not heavily traded.

Edward Glossop, Latin America economist for Capital Economics, predicted even higher inflation in a country that has fought against chronic rising prices for decades.

It is "completely feasible" for the peso to drop to as low as 70 per U.S. dollar, Glossop said.

Fernandez said the market reactions were in response to Macri's failures on the economy.

"Markets react badly when they realize they were scammed. We are living a fictitious economy and the government is not giving answers," he said in a radio interview Monday morning.

Voters were given a stark choice to stay the course of painful austerity measures under Macri or return to economic policies that are heavy on state involvement.

Kirchner imposed strict currency controls that slammed investment during her 2007-2015 administration. She fought with the farm sector over export taxes and presided over a multi-year standoff with bondholders that kept Argentina locked out of the international capital markets.

"I would say they (bonds) are pricing in a much higher probability of a default," said Aberdeen Standard EM portfolio manager Viktor Szabo.

Szabo did add however that they were still above the 40 cents level that would truly reflect a fully fledged default.

Fernandez prevailed on Sunday in the majority of the country's provinces, but one of the starker differences was seen in the poor suburbs of Buenos Aires.

What particularly dented Macri's support were newly impoverished Argentines who were more energized to vote to punish him at the polls, political analysts said.

Analysts predicted Sunday's results could be the final nail in the coffin for Macri.

"Macri has already implemented a number of short term measures to try and shore up support ahead of the October vote. Additional promises can be made, but the gap he needs to make up is a very wide one," said Ilya Gofshteyn, senior emerging markets strategist at Standard Chartered Bank.

Right-wing Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro warned that his country could see a wave of migrants fleeing Argentina if Fernandez wins the presidential election.

Bolsonaro has cast himself as foe to the left-wing leaders around Latin America and celebrated his friendship with Macri.

(Reporting by Cassandra Garrison and Hugh Bronstein; additional reporting by Jorge Otaola, Walter Bianchi and Marina Lammertyn; Marc Jones in London, Rodrigo Campos in New York, David Lawder in Washington; Editing by Mark Heinrich and Alistair Bell)

title: Argentine  central bank  cuts interest rate and extends  foreign exchange intervention
text:
Argentina's central bank (BCRA) said on Monday that it set up a 58% interest rate flat for July and ratified until the end of the year the limits to intervene in the foreign exchange market at 39,755 and 51,448 pesos perdollar, in an attempt to slowly reactivate the economy without softening high inflation.

For June, the reference rate for the letters 'Leliq' was 62.5%. "The exchange rate intervention policy announced in April for the April-June period extends to the month of July. That is, the BCRA will not make exchange market purchases and will be able to make sales to counter episodes of excessive volatility, inside and outside the reference area," the monetary entity said in a statement.

Private analysts project annualized inflation at around 57% over the past 12 months. Through the Monetary Policy Committee (Copom), the central bank decided to reduce the minimum cash requirement on fixed-term deposits by 3 percentage points.

This decision, according to the entity, represents a reduction of approximately 45 billion pesos (about 1.071 million dollars). "The Copom believes that the strict control of monetary aggregates carried out by the BCRA will continue to guide the disinflation process in the coming months," the monetary entity added in a statement.

title: This Week on the Frontiers, May 4th 2019
text:
Africa

Leading sub-Saharan African economies struggle to maintain growth. Economic prospects for sub-Saharan Africa's key economies are dimming, with Angola, Zambia and Nigeria all struggling to make headway. According to a report by London-based Capital Economics, Angola's economy is likely to shrink this year as a recent rise in oil production eases. Nigeria has also seen an increase in oil output recently but the non-oil economy continues to struggle, the firm said.

Among the few bright spots is Kenya, where growth remained strong late last year, according to CapEc, but a continuing drought could prove a drag on the economy this year. Ghana also seems to be stabilizing, the report said, although growth in the country's economy, which is one of the region's recent outperformers, appears to be slowing, having dropped from 7.4% in the third quarter of 2018 to 6.8% in the fourth quarter.

One longtime financial investor in sub-Saharan Africa told the Journal that opportunities in the region seem to be diminishing. "The lead of our Africa team is definitely risk-off at present -- he told me he just can't find opportunities that offer meaningful returns," the investor said.

African Development Bank to support Nigeria's cocoa sector. The African Development Bank is to invest in Nigeria's cocoa and other agricultural sectors to boost production and create special agroprocessing zones in the country, Obafemi Oredein reports. Sayina Riman, president of the Cocoa Association of Nigeria, said the move is being spearheaded by the AfDB, which has agreed to intervene in Nigeria's cocoa sector as it did in the cocoa sectors in Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire, the world's two largest producers of the commodity.

Nigeria is the world's fourth-largest cocoa producer but its production has fallen due to neglect of the sector, old and unproductive farms and farmers and poor funding by government, among other problems. Nigeria produces around 300,000 tons of cocoa, according to CAN, and moves to raise the output to 500,000 tons by government in the past eight years have failed.

Asia

Sri Lanka warns future attacks may be planned. Police say arrests and searches of dozens of locations linked to the perpetrators of the Easter bombings have turned up significant evidence that new attacks could be in the works, Saeed Shah and Uditha Jayasinghe report. Despite a state-of-emergency dragnet that has yielded over 100 arrests in 10 days, Sri Lankan authorities say they are deeply concerned that a second series of attacks could target places of worship and schools of the majority Sinhalese Buddhist community, which wasn't targeted in the initial attacks on Christian churches and major international tourist hotels.

Islamic State, the militant group originally based in Syria and Iraq, claimed responsibility for the synchronized attacks on Easter Sunday in this island nation of 21 million. The majority of Sri Lanka's population are Sinhalese Buddhists and there is a history of animosity between extremist members of the Buddhist and Muslim faiths here.

Security officials say the group formed by the attackers could have members who didn't take part in the Easter assault and are waiting to carry out further bombings.

Europe

Jaguar Land Rover moves vehicle production to Slovakia. Carmaker Jaguar Land Rover, owned by India's Tata Motors, said it would be assembling the new Land Rover Defender at its plant in Slovakia, Anthony O. Goriainoff reports. The U.K.'s largest car manufacturer built the previous Defender model at its site in Solihull, England.

Vehicle production in Slovakia has been growing steadily with output this year expected to reach 1.15 million vehicles. Four major brands -- Peugeot, Jaguar Land Rover, Kia and Volkswagen -- have established plants there, turning the small landlocked country into the world's biggest per-capita carmaker, according to Reuters.

Latin America

Argentina's central bank loosens rules for currency interventions. Argentina's central bank said it would step in to the foreign-exchange market more readily to support the peso after several days of volatility last week sent the currency plunging against the dollar, Jeffrey T. Lewis reports. The central bank said that under its new policy it would sell dollars into the market even if the exchange rate is stronger than 51.45 pesos to the dollar, which was the level the bank had previously set for interventions.

The bank said it would sell as much as $250 million if the peso weakens past the 51.45 level, and is ready to sell even more dollars if necessary to calm situations of excessive volatility. The peso strengthened more than 3% on Monday, to 44.89 to the dollar.

The IMF was tight-lipped, but first deputy managing director David Lipton issued a brief and somewhat cryptic statement on Monday acknowledging the "recalibration of intervention policies," but stopping short of explicitly approving of the move. The multilateral has a lot at stake: in October last year it entered into a $56 billion standby arrangement with the struggling South American nation.

Violence erupts in Venezuela as Guaidó calls for uprising. Thousands of Venezuelans clashed in the streets with pro-government forces on Tuesday following an audacious call by opposition leader Juan Guaidó to join him and a small group of military officers in overthrowing President Nicolás Maduro's government, Kejal Vyas reports. The violence ensued after Mr. Guaidó, flanked by a small group of rebellious National Guard troops outside a Caracas military base, called on the public to help end a punishing economic and political crisis under Mr. Maduro.

Mr. Guaidó is viewed by the U.S. and more than 50 other nations as Venezuela's legitimate leader following a 2018 election that was marred by fraud allegations. Protests continued on Wednesday but failed to gain enough traction and by Thursday, the country's government began going after opposition leaders.

U.S. President Trump, whose administration has said the Maduro regime is being protected by tens of thousands of Cuban troops, threatened Cuba with a "full and complete embargo" and "highest-level sanctions," if it continued its support.

Global

Frontier-market borrowing prompts concern. Debt levels in frontier markets continue to mount, raising concerns that countries might be overburdening themselves with loans. An analysis by the Institute of International Finance found frontier-market debt increased by more than $250 billion last year, pushing the total debt load to more than $3.2 trillion. The majority of the borrowing has been by the public sector, with government debt across the asset class reaching around 50% of GDP. Pakistan, Tunisia and Zambia's government debt grew particularly strongly in 2018.

According to the IIF, the rate of hard-currency bond issuance by frontier markets fell in the first quarter of this year, but the high level of borrowing that matures over the coming months is cause for concern. "Upcoming debt maturities will be onerous for some," the IIF's Khadija Mahmood and Juncheng Zhou said. "More than $125 billion of FX-denominated frontier bonds and loans will mature through end-2020."

Citi economist David Lubin said a recent skew toward foreign-denominated borrowing and a dependence on commodities were creating potentially difficult conditions for frontier-market borrowers. "Frontier will keep looking risky without a very substantial boost to commodity prices, a very sharp decline in the dollar, or both," he said in a report last week.

Investors retreat as frontiers lag developed and emerging markets. Investors appear to be cooling on frontier markets as they continue to lose ground to more advanced markets, according to Citi frontier market analyst Andrew Howell. While developed markets rose by 3.4% in April and emerging markets tacked on more than 2%, the FM index fell by more than 1%, undercut by an 8.3% plunge in Argentina's market as well as a fall of 6.8% in Bangladesh and 5.7% in Nigeria, Mr. Howell noted.

Egypt, Romania and Morocco gained ground, but their rise was not enough to offset the other markets' declines. Investors appear to be wary of frontier markets, pulling some $219 million out of frontier-focused funds in March. "The $219m outflow, driven by active frontier funds, was the biggest this year and indicates that fundraising is off to a challenging start in 2019," Mr. Howell said.

In her book, Cristina Fernández already showed signs that her preferred external ally is Vladimir Putin more than the global order that emerges from the big financial centers, under the influence of the United States.

title: Argentina will increase sale of dollars
text:
The Monetary Policy Committee (Copom) of the Central Bank of the Argentine Republic (BCRA) announced that the entity may make sales of dollars even if the exchange rate is below 51.44 Argentine pesos -the current ceiling of the non-intervention zone (ZNI) -, whose amount and frequency will depend on market dynamics.

In addition, if the exchange rate is above 51.44, the BCRA will increase from 150 to 250 million dollars the amount of the daily sale stipulated so far. Likewise, it may determine the performance of additional interventions to counteract episodes of excessive volatility if deemed necessary.

"We have many intervention mechanisms, the auction is going to be one of them," they said from the BCRA to El Cronista.

They also clarified that "within the zone, the amounts and frequency of the intervention are decided by the BCRA and outside the zone the amount becomes $ 250 million, with the possibility of determining additional interventions if considered."

To this, we must add the 60 million Treasury that are auctioned daily for account and order of the Treasury in two daily tranches of 30 million. In mid-April, the monetary authority announced its decision to freeze the ZNI with a floor of 39.75 and a ceiling of 51.45 pesos, so it stopped updating daily to remain fixed until the end of the year.

The decision was adopted "due to the increase in exchange rate volatility observed in recent days," which caused the dollar to advance 9% last week and to surpass 47 pesos, while the country risk jumped above 1,000 points.

The chief economist of Eco Go, Federico Furiase, said in a dialogue with El Cronista that the measure "reinforces discretion in the face of high volatility."

"It can help in the very short term, but if the pressure continues it can be a double-edged sword, given the limit of freely available reserves in a context of market closures.

"The loss of credibility is a key issue, the demand for money is very weak and inflation expectations are increasing. Increasing nominal adjustment of the exchange rate is required to maintain the real exchange rate, "he said.

The Copom considered that the BCRA "should reinforce the contractionary bias of monetary policy, intervening in the exchange market to reduce more aggressively the amount of pesos and in this way contribute to the proper functioning of said market".

The BCRA will increase from 150 to 250 million dollars the amount of the daily sale stipulated so far. "These interventions will take place both within what had been defined so far as ZNI, and outside it," the bank said in a statement.

"In all cases, the amount of pesos resulting from these sales will be discounted from the monetary base goal. "In this way, the measures allow the absorption of liquidity of pesos when the exchange rate is below 51.44 pesos and intensify this absorption when the price of the dollar is located above," he added.

Fund backs BCRA announcement Measures are adequate for Argentina's challenges: IMF Minutes after known the decision of the Central Bank of Argentina (BCRA) to intervene in the foreign exchange market still within the zone of nonintervention, that is, below 51.44 pesos, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) came out to support the measure .

"The Central Bank of Argentina today introduced important measures to address the recent volatility of the financial market and the type ofchange.

"We support these measures, which are adequately calibrated for the challenges facing Argentina," said Gerry Rice, the agency's chief spokesperson.

In a statement, the IMF, which advocated at all times a flexible exchange rate for Argentina within the standby program agreed to three years with the country, marks an important shift in its vision.

"With the IMF, we talk all the time. In fact, the decision to leave the roof of the band fixed went through 1 million iterations before, "said a government source. "It's a program of high volatility, you know. Now, what is the one that can be admitted and what is the balance between discretion and action, is evaluated on a daily basis, "he added.

Beyond the ideological position of the IMF on the free exchange rate, using the dollars that the agency lends to stop a run and that vanish and end up in the mattresses of the country is what they did not want to happen. Therefore, until today it was the refusal to intervene in the exchange market.

text:
BUENOS AIRES, April 16 (Reuters) - Argentina will freeze a non-intervention trading band for its peso currency until the end of the year, central bank head Guido Sandleris said during a news conference on Tuesday.

title: Why did the dollar jump in Argentina and what will Uruguay do?
text:
The dollar jumped yesterday in Argentina after the rise in global level that had and approached the record level in that country. Uruguay was no stranger to these events and the US currency also rose yesterday. "Beyond that this time the world dusted off more cautiously, domestic assets continue to be immersed in an adverse dynamic, which is still dominated by the growing electoral uncertainty and the economic vulnerabilities that the country has been going through," said Gustavo Ber, economist at Estudio Ber. "The international nervousness contacted the development of operations in the local market, stimulating a dollarization of portfolios," said Fernando Izzo, operator of ABC Mercado de Cambios. In Argentina, the dollar rose 1.83% to close at 41.80 Argentine pesos. So far this year accumulates a growth of 10.88%. In Uruguay, the US currency also rose yesterday (for the third consecutive day), 0.76% and quoted at a new historic high: $ 33,616.

 The new maximum is given since the Uruguayan peso began circulating on March 1, 1993, as a national currency, beyond which it is an anecdotal fact (since economically it does not imply anything for the long period that has elapsed). "The dollar today (for yesterday) rose around the world in an important way: The Federal Reserve's announcement (to keep rates throughout the year), which in theory should be an element that weakens the dollar, has had the effect to rekindle the demand for dollars due to economic agents' fears of a recession or abrupt slowdown Today (yesterday) there was a strong fall in the manufacturing production index of Germany, which is the engine of Europe, and this has caused the dollar as a safe haven currency has been strengthened, "the president of the Central Bank (BCU), Alberto Graña, told El Pais as part of an interview. Furthermore, "in the case of Argentina and Brazil (the rise) is exacerbated by the idiosyncratic problems that these countries have" that "in the case of Brazil, the news from the political front -which question the viability of the pension reform- they do not generate stability, "he said. Yesterday in Uruguay, the US currency moved to the interbank level between $ 33.50 and $ 33.67 to close at $ 33.59. To the public in the slates of Banco República (BROU), the dollar rose 22 cents to purchase and sale, reaching $ 32.90 and $ 34.30, respectively. Through the screens of the Electronic Securities Exchange (Bevsa) 55 transactions were made to negotiate US $ 17.33 million. The BCU remained without intervening in the market, as in the previous sessions, with 12 sessions without the participation of the Central of the 14 that had so far this month. Regarding what happened yesterday in Argentina and if the BCU will intervene, Graña was blunt: "We will not react based on events that occur in Argentina, unless they had a direct impact, which we do not see that is the case, in Uruguay some specific channel, we do not see that this is the case at this juncture. " "But, having said that, we have to keep a close eye on what happens in Argentina, Brazil and, ultimately, around the world," he added. The president of the BCU remarked that "this one-day or short-term episode does not merit, in a situation like Argentina's, a (political) response from us." In the week, that is to say with respect to last Friday, the dollar rose 0.5% in Uruguay. So far this month has accumulated an increase of 2.96% and so far this year of 3.79%. In Brazil, the main reference market in foreign exchange, the US dollar ended at 3.8815 reais with an increase of 2.23%. With respect to the end of last year, the variation is 0.15%. Globally, the dollar fell yesterday against the yen, but rose against the euro, as weak manufacturing data in the United States generatedworries about the global economy, while Treasury yields pointed to growing fears of a recession.> This "helps reinforce the idea that we are seeing a slowdown more significant and more widespread than the markets had anticipated a few months ago, "said Karl Schamotta, director of exchange rate strategy at Cambridge Global Payments. "What we are seeing is a kind of recognition that the Fed is reacting to deeper risks in the global economy," he added.

title: UPDATE 1-Argentina seeks market makers to help stabilize the peso - sources
text:
(Adds picture)

By Eliana Raszewski

BUENOS AIRES, March 15 (Reuters) - Argentina's central bank wants to license market makers to help stabilize its embattled peso currency when the Treasury starts newly announced dollar sales in April, two people with direct knowledge of the plans told Reuters on Friday.

The bank hopes the market makers, dealers who agree to buy and sell at set prices, would bolster liquidity in the exchange market to help avoid the sharp gyrations the peso has suffered in recent weeks when it hit a record low of 42.5 pesos per dollar in thin trading.

"We are going to take advantage of the existence of this market auction to promote the creation of market makers in the FX market, something that does not exist now," said one of the people. "It is something that we are talking with banks and it will most likely start together with the Treasury bids."

Both sources asked not to be named because the plan has not been made public. Argentina's central bank declined to comment.

Argentina's treasury minister Nicolás Dujovne revealed on Thursday that the treasury would sell $9.6 billion in dollars from April until the end of the year via daily auctions of $60 million, aiming to acquire pesos to pay for ongoing expenses.

The announcement came after a sharp fall in the peso , dragged down by emerging doubts about the progress of the economy and rising political uncertainty generated by the upcoming general elections in October.

The second person said the dollar auctions "would provide liquidity at a time when it is possible that, given the uncertainty of the electoral process, the market will have this kind of dynamic," referring to market volatility.

Argentina's peso has remained recently within a non-intervention trading band that came into effect last year, but the central bank is concerned about volatility in a market where there can be low liquidity.

"One thing is the value (of the peso), and another thing is when the variations are very abrupt and with little liquidity," the second person said. "That type of dynamic is disruptive." (Reporting by Eliana Raszewski; Editing by Adam Jourdan and Phil Berlowitz)

title: Argentina  adjusts  forex intervention  guidelines to combat inflation
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Feb 28 (Reuters) - Argentina's central bank said on Thursday it had changed its foreign exchange intervention guidelines to allow it more flexibility in combating the high inflation blighting the country.

The bank raised to $150 million from $75 million the limit of daily sales that can be made after the dollar exceeds the upper limit of its stipulated price band.

When the dollar falls below the lower limit of the band, which is modified regularly, the bids may not exceed $50 million per day, from the previous maximum of $75 million.

The dollar closed at 39.18 pesos on Thursday, when the bank's non-intervention band was between 38.617 and 49.975 pesos per dollar.

An abrupt depreciation of the peso last year has sparked a financial crisis in Argentina, exacerbated by a prolonged recession and high inflation. (Reporting by Nicolas Misculin; writing by Aislinn Laing; Editing by Rosalba O'Brien)

title: After four months of peace, the dollar is again shot in  Argentina
text:
The Central Bank had to go out to intervene so that the North American currency does not pierce the flotation band. (Twitter) The price of the North American currency was no longer the main concern in Argentina. After the last shocks and the change of authorities of the Central Bank a flotation band was stipulated and the dollar was circling within the margins expected by the Government of Mauricio Macri. The authorities had confirmed that there would be no interventions as long as the currency was quoted between 34 pesos minimum and 44 maximum.

But inflation in January, which was well above official expectations, once again increased the uncertainty about the Argentine economy and the US currency, which had been going around between 36 and 38 pesos, jumped to 41.30, which turning on the alarms.

It should be noted that the last time went from 30 to 40 in a very short time and the rates of poverty and inflation suffered serious setbacks. As soon as the dollar had crossed the barrier of 40, the newspaper headlines were already wondering if there was a possibility of a new bullfight that would pulverize the peso again and bring it to trade for 50 US dollars.

On the eve of the presidential elections, a new currency crisis can drastically change the outlook. Macri knows that if he could control only one variable to keep his chances, this would be the price of the dollar: the historic Argentine monster, which is nothing more than the representation of fiscal problems and public spending that the country historically suffers.

As the rise did not perforate the roof of the 44, technically the BCRA could not intervene in the direct market, but this does not mean that it has not operated in a different way to calm the waters. The tools that the entity has, commanded by Guido Sandleris, are the game of the interest rate and the operations in the futures market. After the first movements there were slight setbacks in the demand that once again left the dollar below 41 pesos, but the worry continues.

Now he has no room for intervention, because with such a high ceiling in the non-intervention area he has no possibility of action. "

The authorities know that they have reduced the amount of pesos available for them to take refuge in the North American currency, but they are aware that uncertainty can increase demand at any time.

The Macri Government is betting that the harvest increase the income of dollars from the month of April and thus buy some peace to get fairly calm to the primary of August. Foreign exchange earnings for export of agricultural products are fundamental, since resorting to the rate and the carry trade for investors to come to the peso in the short term is, as the saying goes, "bread for today and hunger for tomorrow". With the rates through the clouds to control the exchange rate, credit is an impediment for SMEs and the economic teamsuffers the dilemma of the "short sheet".

"The reading is that Argentina is fragile. Your GDP per capita has fallen sharply with the megadevaluation and we will be in almost permanent review. We are emerging, but we continue pondering on the border given the institutional, economic and financial fragility, "warned Fernando Camusso of Rafaela Capital.

title: Argentina  central bank  has dollar firepower to battle election uncertainty -sources
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Feb 1 (Reuters) - Argentina's central bank has sufficient dollar firepower to deal with a spike in demand for the greenback if uncertainty over the country's upcoming presidential election prompts another run on the peso, two sources at the bank said on Friday.

Investors have returned this year to pesos as the currency has stabilized after losing half its value against the dollar last year. However, there are fears this could reverse rapidly if business-friendly President Mauricio Macri fails to win a second term in October's general election.

Economic volatility is common during election years in Argentina, which has one of the highest inflation rates in the world at nearly 50 percent last year.

The stakes for the country are high. Macri's leadership, which has managed to calm markets after a tumultuous 2018, is pinning hopes on an economic revival this year to propel election hopes against the leftwing opposition.

Investors fears that if the country swings back to a Peronist president, this could lead to Macri's moves to open up the market being reversed and businesses once again looking to shift their money out of the country.

The bank source said Argentina has about $14 billion at the ready to respond to potential dollar demand, including around $10 billion that the finance ministry could sell during the year to pay expenses in pesos, and more than $3 billion the central bank has to operate in futures.

The central bank sources emphasized that the monetary authority did not anticipate coming up short if high dollar demand were to return.

"What we have to look at are the stocks in pesos that could be converted to dollars. When one looks at those stocks, it's a quite small amount," said one of the sources.

The higher demand for pesos since the end of 2018 strengthened the currency by almost 1 percent in January. The central bank has been making daily purchases of up to $50 million when the peso slips beyond the limits of a non-intervention band set as part of Argentina's $56.3 billion deal with the International Monetary Fund.

The central bank has intervened by purchasing about $560 million so far this year. (Reporting by Eliana Raszewski; writing by Cassandra Garrison; Editing by Dan Grebler)

title: Argentina and its new monetary dilemma: the peso is stronger
text:
Guido Sandleris, president of the Argentine central bank, faces an unusual problem. The peso has recovered so much in recent months that it is conducting tests with a currency exchange designed to help the bank rebuild its credibility.

The band was created in September with the endorsement of the International Monetary Fund, when the peso was losing half of its value in the midst of a massive sale. It was supposed to allow a slow and controlled weakening of the currency, which now floats within a certain range that adjusts daily. If it deviates above or below this range, the central bank can - but is not obligated to - sell or buy dollars to intervene in the exchange rate.

Few economists expected the peso to become one of the best-performing emerging market currencies. It has rebounded 10% against the dollar since the implementation of the plan - which also meant freezing the amount of pesos in circulation and keeping interest rates close to 60 percent - a high global figure. While a stronger currency helps Argentina fight inflation and adjust its external accounts, it could hurt the credibility of the bank again depending on the management of Sandleris.

"We believe that the central bank must communicate its strategy clearly, otherwise its credibility could be compromised," said Priscila Robledo, economist at Continuum Economics.

"Buying dollars to increase the liquidity of the peso and at the same time pay extremely high rates to reduce the monetary base does not seem to be the best strategy."

Reduction of fees? So far, Sandleris' efforts to defend the band have not worked. The central bank has bought US $ 190 million since January 10, but the peso has remained mainly below the defined range. The currency closed at 37.5 per US dollar on Wednesday, within the range of the band.

The faster reduction in interest rates could boost debt and economic growth, and at the same time reduce the demand for pesos in the market. But that strategy carries its own risks. The ex-president of the central bank, Federico Sturzenegger, lowered the interest rates in January 2018, only to have to raise them sharply in April. He resigned in June, admitting that he had lost credibility.

"What they do not want is to lower rates at a time when confidence has been restored only to raise them again if the dollar rises again," said Sebastián Martínez, a macroeconomic analyst at Argentine consultancy ABECEB.

Much of the recent gains in the peso are simply a correction to last year's losses, combined with an increase in global investors' appetite for risk this year. At a national level, inflation is slowing down and the president, Mauricio Macri, a favorite of the market, has seen an increase in approval rates.

However, there are good reasons to expect that the weight will weaken. Argentina is in the middle of a recession, inflation is expected to close this year around 30% and the uncertainty of the October presidential elections could trigger another currency crisis.

"They are going with care but I think they are going to continue buying," said Soledad Tortarolo, head of fixed income research at the Allaria Ledesma & CIA brokerage in Buenos Aires. She predicts that the bank will increase the daily amount it can buy to US $ 150 million. "It is important that they defend the zone of non-intervention."

The Argentina entry and its new monetary dilemma: the peso is stronger was first published in La Tercera.

title: IMF Executive Board Completes First Review Under Argentina's Stand-By Arrangement, Approves US$5.7 Billion Disbursement
text:
Release date - 26102018

The Executive Board of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) completed today the first review of Argentina's economic performance under the 36-month Stand-By Arrangement (SBA) that was approved on June 20, 2018.

The completion of the review allows the authorities to draw the equivalent of about US$5.7 billion (SDR 4.10 billion), bringing total disbursements since June to about US$20.4 billion (SDR 14.71 billion). The Board also approved an augmentation of the Stand-By Arrangement to increase access to about US$56.3 billion (equivalent to SDR 40.71 billion or 1,277 percent of quota)[1]. The authorities have requested the use of this IMF financing as budget support.

Argentina's strengthened economic plan aims to bolster confidence and stabilize the economy through a reduction in the budget deficit, the adoption of a simpler monetary policy framework, and freely floating the exchange rate (with foreign currency intervention limited to cases of an extreme overshooting of the currency). Protecting the most vulnerable in Argentina continues to be a central component of the authorities' efforts including by prioritizing social assistance spending and planning for an increase in spending on social assistance programs in the event that social conditions deteriorate.

Following the Executive Board discussion of Argentina's economic plan, Ms. Christine Lagarde, the IMF's Managing Director, stated:

'Argentina has faced difficult market conditions but the authorities have remained steadfastly committed to the Stand-By Arrangement's main policy objectives to address longstanding vulnerabilities, protect the vulnerable, ensure that the public debt remains sustainable, reduce inflation, and foster growth and job creation.

'To achieve these goals, the authorities have redoubled their reform efforts by accelerating the reduction in the fiscal deficit to reach primary balance in 2019 and achieve a primary surplus starting in 2020. The 2019 budget, which is anchored by this target, has been approved by the Lower House. Its passage into law will be key to restoring confidence and ensuring policy continuity.

'The authorities have redesigned their monetary policy framework with strict limits on the growth in the monetary base. This framework is expected to provide a simpler and more effective anchor that will decisively lower inflation and inflation expectations.

'The authorities are allowing the currency to freely float. However, in the event that there is a significant overshooting of the exchange rate, the Central Bank is prepared to intervene in a limited, simple, and rules-based way.

'The program continues to emphasize improving gender equality, protecting society's most vulnerable, and laying the foundation for growth and job creation. The authorities have already taken measures to increase social assistance programs and have prioritized social assistance and childcare spending in the 2019 Budget.

'Despite the challenging environment the government has proactively strengthened its policy plans. Important challenges remain. However, full implementation of the policies that underpin the Stand-By Arrangement, together with strong support from the international community, should allow the country to return to macroeconomic stability and fulfill its full economic potential, for the benefit of all Argentines.'

Annex

The main elements of Argentina's revised economic plan are summarized below:

Fiscal Policy: The authorities are fully committed to reducing the federal government's financing needs and placing public debt on a firm downward path. They aim to strengthen the country's fiscal position by achieving a primary balance in 2019 and primary surpluses starting in 2020. To this end, the government is seeking support in the Argentine Congress for revenue-enhancing and cost-cutting measures that include: introducing taxes on exports, increasing the wealth tax, scaling back inefficient energy subsidies, reprioritizing capital spending, and improving the structure of federal transfers to provinces.

Monetary Policy: To decisively reduce inflation, the Central Bank will shift toward a stronger, simpler, and more verifiable monetary policy regime, temporarily replacing the inflation targeting regime with a monetary base target. At the center of the new framework is a commitment to cap the growth of money to zero percent per month (calculated as the change in the monthly average) until June 2019, with the aim of decisively bringing down inflation and inflation expectations. This framework is supplemented by a commitment not to allow short-term rates to fall below 60 percent until 12-month inflation expectations decisively fall for at least two consecutive months.

Exchange Rate Policy: The Central Bank of Argentina (BCRA) has adopted a floating exchange rate regime without intervention. However, in the event of extreme overshooting of the exchange rate, the BCRA may conduct limited intervention in foreign exchange markets to prevent disorderly market conditions. Such intervention would be unsterilized.

Social Protection and Gender Equality. The draft federal budget strengthens the social safety net. The floor on social assistance spending and the framework for adjusting social spending will be maintained. The draft budget increases social spending and preserves health spending (while better targeting health outlays to the most vulnerable). It also includes a 12 percent expansion of public childcare in an effort to raise female labor force participation (particularly for lower income households). With the support of the World Bank, the National Social Security Administration (ANSES) will continue to improve targeting and expand coverage of the universal child allowance (AUH). Finally, the government has also developed a system to improve the monitoring of social conditions to better respond to emerging needs of low income households.

Augmentation and Re-phasing of Fund Resources. Under the revised arrangement, Fund resources for Argentina in 2018-19 have increased by US$19 billion. A total of about US$ 56.3 billion would be made available to Argentina for the duration of the program through 2021.Fund disbursements for the remainder of 2018 would more than double compared to the original Fund-supported program, to a total of US$13.4 billion (on top of the US$15 billion already disbursed). Planned disbursements in 2019 are also nearly doubled, to US$22.8 billion, with US$5.9 billion planned for 2020-21. The resources available in the program are no longer expected to be treated as precautionary and the authorities have requested the use of the IMF financing for budget support.

title: UPDATE 1-Argentina peso's slide may test band under IMF deal- economists
text:
(Recasts with comments from analysts, peso close)

By Gabriel Burin and Scott Squires

BUENOS AIRES, Sept 28 (Reuters) - Argentina's peso in the coming days could test the limits of a currency band aimed at stemming central bank intervention under a revised $57 billion agreement with the International Monetary Fund, economists said on Friday.

As part of the revised deal, Argentina's central bank announced it would establish a trading band for the peso between 34 and 44 per dollar. The band would depreciate daily at a rate that would come to 3 percent per month. As long as the peso stays in the band, the central bank will not intervene in currency markets.

Argentina's currency has been at the center of emerging market turmoil this year. It lost a further 3.87 percent on Friday to close at 41.3 per dollar, bringing losses for September to 10 percent, traders said.

The peso is down nearly 55 percent against the dollar this year as foreign investors fled amid fears President Mauricio Macri's center-right government might be unable to service its debt next year.

Analysts said the market looked ready to test the limits of the currency band next week. The central bank has spent $16 billion so far this year propping up the peso.

"We are concerned that a wide band could lead markets to test the currency and push it to the upper limit of the no intervention zone, even if the peso has already undergone a significant devaluation," Morgan Stanley said in a report.

The central bank also has hiked interest rates to a punishing 60 percent in a failed bid to control inflation, which is expected to top 40 percent by year end.

Argentina's new Central Bank President Guido Sandleris - an economist and academic appointed on Tuesday after his predecessor unexpectedly resigned, said attacking inflation rather than controlling the exchange rate would be the central bank's priority.

"Foreign exchange futures exerted pressure on the peso and the outlook still looks uncertain next week," said Gustavo Quintana, a trader at local brokerage PR Corredores de Cambio.

Sandleris met with banking executives on Thursday to discuss raising reserve requirements but there is no date set for any announcement, newspapers Cronista and BAE reported, citing sources present in the meetings. His predecessor Luis Caputo, a former Wall Street trader, raised reserve requirements several times since July to reduce liquidity.

Under the IMF deal, the central bank has dropped an inflation target in favor of limiting money supply. Sandleris said it will target zero growth in the monetary base until June 2019, down from the current growth rate of 2 percent a month.

The central bank is also discussing a reduction in the amount of short-term debt, known as Lebac, allowed to replace hard cash in bank reserves, the reports said.

IMF Managing Director Christine Lagarde said the financing agreement, the largest in the Fund's history, would boost loan disbursements by $19 billion through the end of 2019 to calm investor fears. (Reporting by Gabriel Burin, Walter Bianchi and Scott Squires Writing by Scott Squires Editing by Daniel Flynn, Steve Orlofsky and David Gregorio)

title: New Zealand to Hit Tourists With New Levy -- Market Talk
text:
2106 ET - New Zealand expects to raise an extra NZ$80 million ($53.3 million) annually with a new NZ$35 levy on foreign tourists. The government has been mulling such a tax as tourist numbers overwhelm infrastructure and the environment. The country has in recent years been a vacation hotspot for wealthy Americans. While critics say the levy may harm tourism, which last year bypassed dairy as New Zealand's biggest export, Conservation Minister Eugenie Sage says the money will help "improve the protection and enhancement of New Zealand's distinctive natural environment and improve tourism planning." Almost 4 million tourists visited New Zealand the past year; the country's population is 4.7 million. (rob.taylor@wsj.com; @WSJRobTaylor)

1932 ET - JPMorgan sees a 30% chance of the next rate move for New Zealand's central bank being a cut. But for that to happen, the investment bank acknowledges the job market needs to deteriorate more than appears likely. Meanwhile, fiscal policy is likely to become gradually more supportive over time. (james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)

1855 ET [Dow Jones }--Argentina's central bank says it will stop intervening in the foreign-exchange market when the exchange rate is between 34 pesos to 44 pesos to the US dollar. But if it breaches the upper limit of the so-called "non-intervention zone," central bank president Guido Sandleris says the monetary authority will sell up to $150M to shore up the peso, which has depreciated sharply this year. The change in policy comes as the IMF agreed to increase its bailout program for Argentina, after objecting to the central bank's FX interventions while calling for a free-floating currency. (ryan.dube@wsj.com; @duberyan)
