"We are attacking the root cause of inflation," Sandleris says. "The objective is that it will decline as fast as possible." The change in policy comes as the IMF boosted its bailout package for Argentina to $57.1B from $50B. The central bank also committed to not intervene in the exchange market when the exchange rate is between 34 pesos to 44 pesos to the USD, Sandleris says. Argentina's interventions were a cause of conflict with the IMF , which supports a free-floating currency. (ryan.dube@wsj.com; @duberyan)

1753 ET - Australian house prices are expected to remain in retreat until 2020, says ANZ. That's an extension of the big Aussie bank's earlier assumption that a slide, already in place for a more than a year, would bottom out in 2019. Further tightening of mortgage credit availability is likely, while the banks are expected to continue raising interest rates on home loans, it says. At some point, the RBA will chime in with its own increases. (james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)

1748 ET - Governor Adrian Orr continues to have doubts about the economic outlook in New Zealand, despite recent robust GDP data and clear signs that business confidence is in recovery. The RBNZ left its cash rate at 1.75% as expected and said it is unlikely to change through 2019 and into 2020. Crucially, the next move could be up or down. Still, there are signs core inflation is starting to rise, but the RBNZ will look through it as it likely reflects a temporary rise in fuel prices. Global trade tensions are a threat to growth, he says. (james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)

1505 ET - Fed Chairman Jerome Powell takes on the Trump Administration's aggressive trade actions gingerly. "We are not responsible for trade policy and we don't comment on particular trade actions," Powell says at the press conference. But he notes "we have been hearing a rising chorus of concern" even as their hasn't been as much impact in actual economic data so far. Powell says an outcome with lower tariffs would be good for the economy. But if a lot of barriers go up and stay there, then "that's going to be bad" for the American economy. He also says on the prospects tariffs boosting inflation: "You could see prices moving up. You don't see it yet" but the tariffs could give firms cover to boost prices. (michael.derby@wsj.com)

1445 ET - In his press conference after the FOMC meeting, Fed Chairman Jerome Powell was asked about whether President Donald Trump 's criticism of rate rises are a problem. Powell doesn't say the president's name and falls back on central bank boilerplate, noting "we don't consider political factors or things like that" when making policy. Instead, he says the Fed focuses on its mission. (michael.derby@wsj.com)

1415 ET - US government bond yields tick lower, then pare their declines, after the Federal Reserve raises short-term interest rates and removes the word "accommodative" from its policy statement. Investors had been widely expecting the central bank to raise rates in September, but had been less sure of whether the Fed would signal a more aggressive approach to future rate increases. That had driven yields higher heading into Wednesday's meeting, although traders said on first glance, the Fed's latest policy statement didn't strike them as being hawkish. The yield on the benchmark 10-year US Treasury note fell to around 3.065% before recently trading at 3.078%, compared with 3.102% Tuesday. (akane.otani@wsj.com; @akaneotani)

1411 ET - The Fed's interest rate forecasts may not hold any great surprises relative to what was seen in June, but it's notable that central bankers see an extended period of time of running monetary policy above its long run level. The Fed may be dispensing with descriptions of policy as "accommodative" and Fed Chairman Jerome Powell may be pushed the concept of neutral rates off to the margin. Still, against the Fed's estimate of a long-term fed funds target rate of 3%, they see monetary policy delivering rates above that in 2019, 2020 and 2021. Given the duration of the business cycle, trade war rumblings and the worries about the yield curve, it will be very interesting to see if the Fed can deliver on such a hawkish policy outlook. (michael.derby@wsj.com)

1410 ET - The September Federal Reserve policy statement showed no change in officials' characterization of the economy and its strength compared with the previous policy statement. Officials said the labor market has continued to strengthen, while the economy has been rising at a strong pace. Meanwhile, inflation remains near the central bank's 2% target. The main change in September's statement, other than the rate increase decision, was the drop of "accommodative" in the description of interest rates. (sarah.chaney@wsj.com)

1407 ET - Twelve of 16 Fed officials now expect four interest rate increases this year, more than in previous months, according to new economic projections. In June, eight Fed officials expected at least four rate rises in 2018. The higher number of officials projecting four rate bumps signals a stronger belief among officials that the economy is running strong, necessitating gradual rate increases to keep it from overheating. (sarah.chaney@wsj.com)

title: Argentina and the IMF agreed to raise the financial agreement to US $ 57,100 million
text:
Argentina reached on Wednesday a new credit agreement with the International Monetary Fund ( IMF ), which raises the stand-by loan of US $ 50,000 million agreed last June to US $ 57,100 million. The multilateral body foresees an acceleration of disbursements, in order to reduce the fiscal deficit to zero next year. Economy Minister Nicolás Dujovne said the agreement would lead Argentina's GDP to expand 5.2% in 2019.

As part of the agreement will proceed with the acceleration of disbursements. The Economy Minister explained that this year the country will receive US $ 13,400 million of the US $ 6,000 originally planned, while in 2019 the amount will rise from US $ 11,400 million to US $ 22,800 million. "These funds are no longer precautionary, but may be used as a budget support," he said.

Although the money will not necessarily be used to repay the debt, according to The Guardian as part of the agreement, it was agreed that the Central Bank of Argentina will intervene to stabilize its currency only if the peso depreciates below 44 pesos per dollar. It is currently at 39 pesos per dollar after losing 50% of its value since the beginning of the year.

The announcement of the US $ 57.1 billion loan - the largest in the history of the IMF, according to the agency's director, Christine Lagarde - comes a day after Luis Caputo's resignation as president of the Argentine Central Bank. Caputo, according to Reuters, was an investment banker who had had differences with Dujovne and the IMF for his handling of the exchange policy. In his place was appointed Guido Sandleris, an academic close to the Minister of Economy.

It should be recalled that the IMF and Argentina signed four financial assistance agreements between 1991 and 2001 and, during that period, the external debt of the southern country went from about US $ 70,000 million at the end of 1990 to more than US $ 140,000 million registered in 2001, according to the newspaper El País. A 2004 report by the IMF's internal audit unit concluded that the multilateral body did not provide sufficient oversight and overestimated the growth and success of the economic reforms in 2001.

title: Now bet that the dollar does not exceed 47 pesos at the end of the year
text:
The government and the IMF modified the exchange regime. There will be no intervention as long as it fluctuates between $ 34 and $ 44. The amounts will rise 3% per month. If the dollar goes up, they will only sell $ 150 million a day.

Buenos Aires. The Government and the International Monetary Fund agreed to modify the exchange regime of Argentina and from today the Central Bank will intervene only when the price of the dollar pierces a minimum of 34 pesos or exceeds a maximum of 44 pesos, with a monthly adjustment of three hundred.

With this new scheme, the administration of Mauricio Macri is betting that the value of the ticket in the market does not exceed 47 pesos at the end of the year. A level very far from the average price of 40.10 pesos that the Government itself reflected in the 2019 Budget.

IMF: US $ 7,100 million more and change in monetary policy The market will give its verdict today after the announcement Caution about politics, with warnings from economists The new regime was explained yesterday by the new president of the Central Bank, Guido Sandleris, who replaced the resignation Luis Caputo and personally negotiated this new scheme with the IMF.

The official clarified that the Central Bank will no longer attempt to fix the price of the ticket, as long as it does not leave the established bands.

"Argentina is vulnerable to disruptive volatility, since the exchange rate plays a key role in inflation expectations," he said.

He added: "These bands should be interpreted as guides on what can be expected from the behavior of the Central Bank in each zone".

From now on, when the Central Bank observes that there is excessive volatility, that is to say, rises or falls very strong in short periods of time, it will start to intervene buying or selling dollars.

The entity will act then when the dollar is below 34 pesos (which is unlikely to happen) or above 44 pesos. If the dollar is located between those points, there will be no intervention: it is what is called flotation.

Maximum expected values

Those tips are not fixed. This "band" of intervention will be adjusted daily at a rate of three percent per month until the end of the year. That means that, at the end of October, the ceiling of the dollar will be 44 pesos; in November, of 45.32 pesos, and at the end of December, of 46.68 pesos.

If the value of the currency exceeds the predicted ceilings, the Central Bank will go out to the market to sell up to 150 million dollars. With this, it will provide liquidity and will lower -according to Sandleris- the value up to the level intended.

The sum that it can offer is not significant in light of what the Central's interventions were during the run against the peso that began last April.

When you sell dollars, the Central will withdraw the pesos and not reinject them in any other way, so that in that way you will reduce more the peso currency to lower the demand for dollars.

"We are aware of the risks that an excessive appreciation of the exchange rate represents for the real economy," said Sandleris.

This ensures that the Central will not drop the price of the ticket below what the Government intended, ie 34 pesos.

The Cambiemos coalition does not want the economy to lose competitiveness after paying the political cost of the 50 percent devaluation so far this year.

Comfortable in 40

Sandleris said it yesterday very clearly: "As a Central Bank, we are very comfortable with the level of the exchange rate that is currently registered."

The authorities consider that a rapid nominal appreciation of the national currency is "a sign of greater confidence", and thatthe demand for pesos will increase. If that happens, the Central Bank will buy dollars to swell its reserves.

Sandleris believes that the dollar's price bands provide "a very clear and transparent framework" for exchange intervention to limit the excessive volatility of the exchange rate.

That is, it gives predictability to economic agents: investors, savers and consumers.

Neither goals nor rates

For the head of the BCRA, this "financial storm" showed two vulnerabilities in Argentina: the fiscal deficit and inflation. "As a government, we have made mistakes, underestimated the difficulty of correcting the imbalance received and the speed at which international conditions would change."

In this context, Sandleris argued that the "inflation targeting regime did not give the expected results", which is why it will be "left aside", while the agency will now address "the control of the amount of money in the economy". " "We will take the necessary measures so that the monetary base grows zero percent in nominal terms from here to June 2019," he said.

The other major change announced yesterday points to interest rates. The Central Bank will no longer fix the reference rate, which is why the 60 percent rate left by Luis Caputo disappears.

As announced yesterday, the reference interest rate of the Leliq will fluctuate daily according to market demand.

The core of the agreement point by point

The new program with the IMF that will mark the economy.

Insured commitments. The agreement with the IMF guarantees not to fall into default at least until 2020.

More money The credit increased by 7,100 million dollars, so it will be 57,000 million.

Disbursements There will be an advance payment of disbursements for this year and 2019. In the remainder of the year will reach 13,400 million and the next will arrive 22,800 million.

Back. Macri will have 36,200 million dollars from the IMF until the end of his term, that is, some 18,800 million more than originally agreed (in June).

Available Program funds will no longer be treated as "precautionary" and will be available for use as budget support. That is, the Government may spend the tickets.

Intervention. For the dollar, there will be free float between 34 and 44 pesos initially. If the dollar pierces or exceeds these limits, the Central Bank will buy or sell currencies.

Without inflation goals. The inflation targeting regime was eliminated.

Issue. There will be a very strict control over the amount of money in the economy. The monetary base will grow 0% until June 2019.

title: IMF Expands Aid Package for Argentina
text:
The International Monetary Fund agreed to boost its bailout package signed with Argentina in June, providing additional financial support and accelerating the disbursement of funds as the administration of embattled President Mauricio Macri

confronts market turbulence and social unrest.

Argentina Finance Minister Nicolas Dujovne and IMF Managing Director Christine Lagarde said Wednesday that the new agreement will increase the bailout size by almost 15% to $57.1 billion, providing an extra $19 billion in financing through the end of 2019, when Mr. Macri’s term ends. It commits Argentina to maintaining a floating exchange-rate regime without intervention.

“The Fund remains fully committed to helping Argentina tackle the problems that it faces,” Ms. Lagarde said during a joint news conference with Mr. Dujovne in New York.

The deal seeks to address concerns about the country’s ability to service its rising debt load and secure funds to cover government spending.

“This will permit our country to leave behind the path of turbulence we’ve been exposed to recently and return the Argentine economy to the structural conditions we need for stable growth,” Mr. Dujovne said.

The deal still needs to be approved by the IMF’s board to take effect.

The expanded program will aim to reduce the country’s double-digit inflation by replacing inflation targets with monetary base goals to contain the money supply, the IMF said. It also will require the central bank to maintain its high interest rate, which was increased to 60% in August.

The IMF added that the central bank will be able to conduct limited intervention in the foreign-exchange market only if there is “extreme overshooting of the exchange rate.”

The central bank won’t intervene in the exchange market when the exchange rate is between 34 pesos and 44 pesos to the U.S. dollar, Argentina’s new central bank president Guido Sandleris said later on Wednesday. The peso closed weaker Wednesday at 38.52 to the dollar.

Mr. Macri was forced to ask the IMF for help earlier this year, after rising interest rates in the U.S. pummeled the peso and investors sold assets in emerging markets. But the aid package failed to contain the peso’s steady weakening, forcing the government in August to ask for more IMF funds and faster disbursements. The Argentine currency has lost half of its value against the dollar so far this year.

“I don’t imagine Argentina will be able to tap external markets again very soon, after all they’re going to have a very deep recession, high inflation, uncertainty about the election next year, so there are still a lot of fundamental questions about how stable the macro situation is going to be,” said Gustavo Rangel, Latin America’s chief economist for ING. “It will take some time for them to really be able to access the market again.”

Mr. Dujovne then announced austerity measures in early September, including deep cuts to subsidies and public works as part of an effort to balance a wide budget shortfall and meet IMF conditions.

The IMF deal comes a day after Argentina’s central bank president, Luis Caputo, unexpectedly resigned less than four months into the job amid reports of disputes with the fund over the bank’s exchange rate policy. Under Mr. Caputo, the central bank intervened in the foreign-exchange market, burning billions of dollars in reserves to contain the peso selloff. The IMF objected to that, backing a free-floating currency.

He was replaced by Mr. Sandleris, a top Finance Ministry official who was educated at Columbia University. On Tuesday, Mr. Sandleris said the central bank’s main objective is to reduce inflation, currently at 34%.

Mr. Sandleris said at a press conference that the central institution will ensure zero nominal growth in the monetary base—bills and coins in circulation and banks’ deposits at the central bank—between now and next June in its effort to bring inflation down, which he added implies a significant monetary contraction.

Argentina’s economy contracted 2.7% in July from the year-earlier month as the country’s financial crisis hit consumer demand. In the second quarter, the economy fell 4.2% from a year earlier.

The economic crisis has rattled Mr. Macri’s administration as it faces growing anger among Argentines upset with the sharp contraction and high inflation. On Tuesday, Argentina’s powerful unions held a national strike, warning that it would increase protests if the government doesn’t reverse austerity measures.

“If there isn’t a plan B, there won’t be a truce with Argentina’s union movement,” said union leader Juan Carlos Schmid.

After taking office in late 2015, Mr. Macri had hoped to avoid social upheaval by gradually unraveling his predecessor’s free-spending policies rather than implementing the kind of economic shock therapies that sparked unrest and led to the downfall of previous presidents. His government relied heavily on foreign credit to plug the deficit, raising concerns among economists as the cost of servicing the debt now increases due to the weaker peso.

Argentina’s debt ratio will reach 84% of gross domestic product by the end of the year, compared with 57% a year earlier, consultancy Oxford Economics said this week. “Argentina’s debt-to-GDP ratio is rising at an unsustainable pace,” the firm said.

1753 ET - Australian house prices are expected to remain in retreat until 2020, says ANZ. That's an extension of the big Aussie bank's earlier assumption that a slide, already in place for a more than a year, would bottom out in 2019. Further tightening of mortgage credit availability is likely, while the banks are expected to continue raising interest rates on home loans, it says. At some point, the RBA will chime in with its own increases. (james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)

1748 ET - Governor Adrian Orr continues to have doubts about the economic outlook in New Zealand, despite recent robust GDP data and clear signs that business confidence is in recovery. The RBNZ left its cash rate at 1.75% as expected and said it is unlikely to change through 2019 and into 2020. Crucially, the next move could be up or down. Still, there are signs core inflation is starting to rise, but the RBNZ will look through it as it likely reflects a temporary rise in fuel prices. Global trade tensions are a threat to growth, he says. (james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)

1505 ET - Fed Chairman Jerome Powell takes on the Trump Administration's aggressive trade actions gingerly. "We are not responsible for trade policy and we don't comment on particular trade actions," Powell says at the press conference. But he notes "we have been hearing a rising chorus of concern" even as their hasn't been as much impact in actual economic data so far. Powell says an outcome with lower tariffs would be good for the economy. But if a lot of barriers go up and stay there, then "that's going to be bad" for the American economy. He also says on the prospects tariffs boosting inflation: "You could see prices moving up. You don't see it yet" but the tariffs could give firms cover to boost prices. (michael.derby@wsj.com)

1445 ET - In his press conference after the FOMC meeting, Fed Chairman Jerome Powell was asked about whether President Donald Trump 's criticism of rate rises are a problem. Powell doesn't say the president's name and falls back on central bank boilerplate, noting "we don't consider political factors or things like that" when making policy. Instead, he says the Fed focuses on its mission. (michael.derby@wsj.com)

1415 ET - US government bond yields tick lower, then pare their declines, after the Federal Reserve raises short-term interest rates and removes the word "accommodative" from its policy statement. Investors had been widely expecting the central bank to raise rates in September, but had been less sure of whether the Fed would signal a more aggressive approach to future rate increases. That had driven yields higher heading into Wednesday's meeting, although traders said on first glance, the Fed's latest policy statement didn't strike them as being hawkish. The yield on the benchmark 10-year US Treasury note fell to around 3.065% before recently trading at 3.078%, compared with 3.102% Tuesday. (akane.otani@wsj.com; @akaneotani)

1411 ET - The Fed's interest rate forecasts may not hold any great surprises relative to what was seen in June, but it's notable that central bankers see an extended period of time of running monetary policy above its long run level. The Fed may be dispensing with descriptions of policy as "accommodative" and Fed Chairman Jerome Powell may be pushed the concept of neutral rates off to the margin. Still, against the Fed's estimate of a long-term fed funds target rate of 3%, they see monetary policy delivering rates above that in 2019, 2020 and 2021. Given the duration of the business cycle, trade war rumblings and the worries about the yield curve, it will be very interesting to see if the Fed can deliver on such a hawkish policy outlook. (michael.derby@wsj.com)

1410 ET - The September Federal Reserve policy statement showed no change in officials' characterization of the economy and its strength compared with the previous policy statement. Officials said the labor market has continued to strengthen, while the economy has been rising at a strong pace. Meanwhile, inflation remains near the central bank's 2% target. The main change in September's statement, other than the rate increase decision, was the drop of "accommodative" in the description of interest rates. (sarah.chaney@wsj.com)

1407 ET - Twelve of 16 Fed officials now expect four interest rate increases this year, more than in previous months, according to new economic projections. In June, eight Fed officials expected at least four rate rises in 2018. The higher number of officials projecting four rate bumps signals a stronger belief among officials that the economy is running strong, necessitating gradual rate increases to keep it from overheating. (sarah.chaney@wsj.com)

1404 ET - Federal Reserve officials removed language in their policy statement that had described short-term interest rates as "accommodative," meaning they are still low enough to stimulate economic growth. Most officials think rates are still accommodative but are becoming less so with each rate increase, and are on track to reach a neutral level that neither spurs nor slows growth in coming months. The problem is officials' aren't sure where neutral lies or when they'll get there. Waiting until later this year or next year to drop the phrase would have risked sending an unintended message then that they agreed they were at neutral, which they are unlikely to do, given the uncertainties involved. (sarah.chaney@wsj.com)

1402 ET - Central bank officials voted to raise their benchmark federal-funds rate by a quarter-percentage point to a range between 2% and 2.25%, according to Wednesday's policy statement. The decision to raise interest rates for the third time this year is in line with expectations for the Fed to gradually raise rates as the economy remains on a path of strength. The bigger question is how Fed Chairman Jerome Powell might characterize the balance of risks at the press conference. (sarah.chaney@wsj.com)

1341 ET - One key thing to watch after the Fed meeting, assuming a rate rise happens, is what happens with the yield curve. The difference between two and 10-year Treasury securities continues to stand within spitting distance of going negative, with the spread currently right around 25 basis points. It's possible a rate rise or two more, which the Fed could easily deliver this year, could kick that spread into negative territory, with ominous portents for the economic outlook. Some key Fed officials like New York Fed leader John Williams have downplayed this relationship, but others, like St Louis' James Bullard , have cautioned against doing the "this time it's different" argument. (michael.derby@wsj.com)

(michael.derby@wsj.com)

The main change in September's statement, other than the rate increase decision, was the drop of "accommodative" in the description of interest rates. (sarah.chaney@wsj.com)

(sarah.chaney@wsj.com)

The problem is officials' aren't sure where neutral lies or when they'll get there. Waiting until later this year or next year to drop the phrase would have risked sending an unintended message then that they agreed they were at neutral, which they are unlikely to do, given the uncertainties involved. (sarah.chaney@wsj.com)

Among the companies that bucked the downturn: French energy firm Engie SA with a 1.3% rise making it the benchmark's best performer. (emre.peker@wsj.com)

1208 ET - Instinet sees the higher costs for feedstocks like ethane, used to make plastics, cutting into DowDuPont 's margins and keeping pressure on near-term earnings. The investment bank drops the chemical giant to neutral and lowers price target to $76 from $81, expecting shares to remain rangebound over the next few months. Instinet says it still views DowDuPont as an "attractive core holding in large cap chemicals," but more "patience" will be required on the part of investors. DowDuPont shares off 1.3% to $67.06. (patrick.sheridan@wsj.com)

1146 ET - Oil investors wondering if the typically low-demand fall season was ever going to arrive got their answer Wednesday, as the EIA's weekly report revealed a huge drop in refinery activity, rising oil inventories and a large drop in demand. The EIA said oil stockpiles climbed 1.9M bbls vs consensus for a 1.3M-bbl decline, while refinery activity plunged 5 percentage points to 90.4% vs expectations for just a 0.9 percentage point decline. And motor gasoline supplied to the market, a proxy for demand, plunged to 9M bpd vs 9.5M a week earlier. "Demand is weak, and it's getting weaker," Stephen Schork of The Schork Report tells WSJ. The Nymex oil contract for November moves 0.7% lower to $71.80/bbl. (dan.molinski@wsj.com)

1134 ET - Europe's steel market isn't likely to cool down in 2019, though the "huge growth" of the past year should begin to subside, Tata Steel Europe 's Chief Commercial Officer Henrik Adam says. Demand for steel remains undented in Europe--despite uncertainty surrounding trade disputes--but steelmakers will have to contend with higher prices for inputs, particularly energy, zinc and tin, Mr. Adam says. Uncertainty over raw material prices will be a key factor in negotiating steel prices in 2019, he says. "Anyone hoping for price reductions against this background is hoping in vain." (nathan.allen@dowjones.com)

0808 ET - Oil prices decline after three straight sessions of increases following a weekly report that points to rising US inventories of crude oil. Industry group API said Tuesday US crude oil stockpiles rose 2.9M bbls last week, and that gasoline inventories rose nearly 1M bbls. That suggests today's official EIA report, due at 10:30am ET, may also show bearish increases, despite a WSJ survey of analysts forecasting a 1.3M-bbl crude decline, and just a 200k-bbl rise in gasoline supplies. Brent, the global benchmark, falls 0.5% to $80.85/bbl after hitting a four-year high Tuesday, while the US benchmark WTI declines 0.6% to $71.86 after closing at an 11-week high Tuesday. (dan.molinski@wsj.com)

0747 ET - Glencore is likely to keep its credit edge over rival Anglo American into next year, says Moody's . The credit-rating agency notes that the credit quality of both companies has recovered since the commodity downturn ended in 2016. "But Glencore 's credit quality will remain stronger into 2019 thanks to its more robust business profile and better resilience to a future downturn - provided that the the U.S. Department of Justice 's recent demand for information doesn't lead to any large fines for the company or a reassessment of its business risk," says Sven Reinke, Senior Vice President at Moody's. (philip.waller@wsj.com)

"London Metal Exchange copper falls for the third day, extending the drop from a two-month high at the close of last week, as Chinese traders release supply ahead of the week-long Golden Week national holiday despite signs of rising demand from Chile," analysts at mining specialist brokerage S.P. Angel say. They note that copper closed 4.6% higher at $6,363 a ton on Friday, the highest since July 9. At 1209 BST the price was down 0.7% at $6,272 a ton. (philip.waller@wsj.com)
